chunks.heading: Abnormal Psychology, Cheatsheet
chunks.text: Abnormal Psychology, Cheatsheet MET 2026 + NIMHANS · Built 2026-05-05 · The abnormal patch. How to use. Goes deeper than the high-yield revision sheet. Read once for coverage, then revise off tables + red TRAP boxes. Anything you blank on, mark it and re-read the matching section on the next pass.

chunks.heading: 1. Defining Abnormality (4 Ds)
chunks.text: 1. Defining Abnormality (4 Ds) Deviance — statistical or social norm violation. Distress — subjective suffering. Dysfunction — impairs daily life / role functioning. Danger — risk to self or others. TRAP: Deviance alone ≠ abnormal. A genius IQ is statistically deviant but not pathological. Always need at least distress or dysfunction with it. Some textbooks list a 5th D: Duration , especially for chronicity criteria (≥ 6 months, ≥ 2 years, etc.).

chunks.heading: 2. Historical Models
chunks.text: 2. Historical Models Era Model Key name(s) Prehistoric Supernatural (demons, possession) Trephination Greek / Roman Biological, four humors Hippocrates, Galen Middle Ages Demonological return, witch trials Malleus Maleficarum (1487) Renaissance Asylum reform begins Pinel (Bicêtre, "moral treatment"), Tuke (York Retreat) 19th c. Biological, classification Kraepelin ( dementia praecox ), Bleuler (renamed schizophrenia , 4 As) Early 20th c. Psychological Freud (psychoanalysis), Watson (behaviorism) Mid 20th c. Cognitive-behavioral Beck (depression), Ellis (REBT) 1980s+ Biopsychosocial integration Engel (1977) TRAP: Kraepelin coined dementia praecox . Bleuler renamed it schizophrenia ("split mind", referring to fragmented thought, not split personality). Don't confuse with DID.

chunks.heading: 3. Approaches to Psychopathology
chunks.text: 3. Approaches to Psychopathology Approach Cause Treatment Biological Genes, neurotransmitters, brain Meds, ECT, psychosurgery Psychodynamic Unconscious conflict, early experience Psychoanalysis, free association, transference Behavioral Maladaptive learning Conditioning, exposure, reinforcement Cognitive Distorted thoughts, schemas CBT, cognitive restructuring (Beck), REBT (Ellis) Humanistic Blocked self-actualization Person-centered (Rogers), Gestalt (Perls) Sociocultural Family, culture, stigma, oppression Family therapy, community psychology Biopsychosocial All three interact ( Engel, 1977 ) Integrative Diathesis-stress Predisposition × stressor Reduce both load

chunks.heading: 4. DSM-5 vs ICD-11
chunks.text: 4. DSM-5 vs ICD-11 DSM-5 (2013) / DSM-5-TR (2022) ICD-11 (2019) Publisher APA , US-centric WHO , global Use Clinical + research Clinical + epidemiology + billing Sections 3 sections, 22 chapters; no axes (dropped from DSM-IV) Chapter 6 = mental, behavioral, neurodevelopmental OCD Own chapter (separated from anxiety) Own chapter PTSD Own chapter (Trauma- and stressor-related) Own chapter, also adds Complex PTSD Schizophrenia subtypes Removed (no more paranoid/catatonic/etc.) Removed "Mental Retardation" Renamed Intellectual Developmental Disorder Disorders of Intellectual Development Asperger's Folded into ASD Folded into ASD Bereavement exclusion (MDD) Removed (you can dx MDD within 2 mo of loss) More cautious approach Hoarding, Excoriation New in DSM-5 Also recognized Gender dysphoria Renamed from "Gender Identity Disorder" Moved out of mental disorders chapter to "Conditions related to sexual health" TRAP: Multi-axial system was DSM-IV . DSM-5 dropped axes. If a question references "Axis I disorder" it's testing pre-DSM-5 vocabulary.

chunks.heading: 5. Mental Status Exam (MSE), order matters
chunks.text: 5. Mental Status Exam (MSE), order matters ABS-MTPCIJ : A ppearance, B ehavior, S peech, M ood/affect, T hought (form + content), P erception, C ognition, I nsight, J udgment. Mood = subjective ("how do you feel?"). Affect = observed (range, congruence, intensity). Thought form = how thoughts flow (loose, tangential, flight of ideas, circumstantial, blocking, perseveration). Thought content = what (delusions, suicidal/homicidal ideation, obsessions, phobias). Perception = hallucinations (auditory, visual, etc.), illusions, depersonalization. Cognition = orientation, attention, memory, abstract thinking. Insight = awareness of being ill. Judgment = decision-making in real situations.

chunks.heading: 6. Anxiety Disorders
chunks.text: 6. Anxiety Disorders Disorder Core feature Duration Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) Excessive worry, multiple domains, hard to control ≥ 6 months Panic Disorder Recurrent unexpected panic attacks + worry about more / behavior change Attack peaks ≤ 10 min Specific Phobia Marked fear of single object/situation ≥ 6 months Social Anxiety Disorder Fear of scrutiny, judgment in social situations ≥ 6 months Agoraphobia Fear of places where escape/help is hard (≥ 2 of 5 situations) ≥ 6 months Separation Anxiety Disorder Excessive fear of separation from attachment figure ≥ 4 wk (kids), ≥ 6 mo (adults) Selective Mutism Failure to speak in specific social situations despite ability ≥ 1 month (not first month of school) TRAP: OCD is NOT in the anxiety chapter in DSM-5 (its own chapter, see §7). Same for PTSD (Trauma- and stressor-related chapter, see §8).

chunks.heading: 7. OCD & Related Disorders
chunks.text: 7. OCD & Related Disorders OCD — obsessions (intrusive thoughts) + compulsions (repetitive acts to neutralize). Ego-dystonic. Time-consuming (≥ 1 hr/day) or distressing. Body Dysmorphic Disorder (BDD) — preoccupation with perceived flaw in appearance. Hoarding Disorder — persistent difficulty discarding possessions. New in DSM-5 . Trichotillomania — recurrent hair-pulling. Excoriation — recurrent skin-picking. New in DSM-5 . TRAP: OCPD ≠ OCD . OCPD = perfectionist, rigid personality style , ego-syntonic, in the personality disorders chapter. OCD = ego-dystonic obsessions/compulsions, in OCD-related chapter.

chunks.heading: 8. Trauma- & Stressor-Related
chunks.text: 8. Trauma- & Stressor-Related PTSD — exposure to actual/threatened death/serious injury/sexual violence + intrusion symptoms (flashbacks, nightmares) + avoidance + negative alterations in cognition/mood + arousal/reactivity. Duration > 1 month . Acute Stress Disorder — same symptom clusters but duration 3 days to 1 month . Adjustment Disorders — emotional/behavioral symptoms within 3 months of stressor; doesn't meet criteria for another disorder. Reactive Attachment Disorder — withdrawn, emotionally inhibited toward caregivers; from severe early neglect. Disinhibited Social Engagement Disorder — overly familiar with strangers; from severe early neglect. ICD-11 adds Complex PTSD — PTSD core + disturbances in self-organization (DSO): emotion dysregulation, negative self-concept, relational disturbance.

chunks.heading: 9. Mood (Depressive + Bipolar) Disorders
chunks.text: 9. Mood (Depressive + Bipolar) Disorders

chunks.heading: Depressive disorders
chunks.text: Depressive disorders Disorder Episode Duration Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) ≥ 5 of 9 SIG-E-CAPS, must include depressed mood OR anhedonia ≥ 2 weeks Persistent Depressive Disorder (Dysthymia) Chronic low-grade depression ≥ 2 yrs (≥ 1 yr in kids) PMDD Severe mood symptoms premenstrually Most cycles in last year Disruptive Mood Dysregulation Disorder (DMDD) Severe temper outbursts in kids Onset before 10, dx between 6-18 SIG-E-CAPS for MDD: S leep, I nterest (anhedonia), G uilt, E nergy, C oncentration, A ppetite, P sychomotor (agitation/retardation), S uicidal ideation. + depressed mood = 9 total.

chunks.heading: Bipolar & related
chunks.text: Bipolar & related Disorder Required Duration Bipolar I ≥ 1 manic episode (depression not required for dx) Mania ≥ 1 week (or any duration if hospitalised) Bipolar II Hypomania + at least one MDE; never full mania Hypomania ≥ 4 days Cyclothymia Hypomanic + depressive symptoms, never full episode of either ≥ 2 yrs DIG-FAST for mania: D istractibility, I ndiscretion (risky behavior), G randiosity, F light of ideas, A ctivity increase, S leep decrease, T alkativeness. TRAP: Bipolar I needs mania ≥ 1 week . Bipolar II = hypomania + MDE, never full mania. If they had even one full manic episode in their life, it's Bipolar I.

chunks.heading: Suicide risk, SAD PERSONS
chunks.text: Suicide risk, SAD PERSONS S ex (male), A ge (< 19 or > 45), D epression, P revious attempt, E thanol/drugs, R ational thinking loss, S ocial supports lacking, O rganized plan, N o spouse, S ickness. TRAP: Strongest single predictor of completed suicide = previous attempt . Highest-risk diagnosis = MDD with comorbid substance use.

chunks.heading: 10. Schizophrenia & Other Psychotic Disorders
chunks.text: 10. Schizophrenia & Other Psychotic Disorders

chunks.heading: Conceptual history
chunks.text: Conceptual history Kraepelin — coined dementia praecox , emphasised early onset + deteriorating course. Bleuler — renamed it schizophrenia , emphasised cognitive fragmentation. 4 As : Associations (loose), Affect (flat), Ambivalence, Autism (withdrawal). Schneider — First-Rank Symptoms (FRS): thought insertion/withdrawal/broadcasting, audible thoughts, voices commenting/arguing, made impulses/actions, somatic passivity, delusional perception. Suggestive but not diagnostic alone in DSM-5.

chunks.heading: Symptom domains
chunks.text: Symptom domains Positive (added) — hallucinations, delusions, disorganized speech, grossly disorganized/catatonic behavior. Negative (taken away) — flat affect, alogia (poverty of speech), avolition (low motivation), anhedonia, asociality. Cognitive — attention, working memory, executive function deficits.

chunks.heading: DSM-5 criteria
chunks.text: DSM-5 criteria ≥ 2 of (delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, disorganized/catatonic behavior, negative symptoms), at least one from the first three. Active phase ≥ 1 month, total disturbance ≥ 6 months (incl. prodrome / residual). Significant social or occupational dysfunction. Not better explained by mood disorder, substance, or medical condition.

chunks.heading: Duration distinguishes the chapter
chunks.text: Duration distinguishes the chapter Disorder Duration Brief Psychotic Disorder 1 day to < 1 month Schizophreniform 1 month to < 6 months Schizophrenia ≥ 6 months Schizoaffective Mood episode + psychosis, but ≥ 2 wks of psychosis without mood symptoms Delusional Disorder ≥ 1 month delusions only, no other psychotic symptoms Shared Psychotic Disorder (folie à deux) Removed as standalone in DSM-5; now under "Other Specified" TRAP: Schizophrenia ≠ DID . Schizophrenia = "split mind" (fragmented thought). DID = multiple identities. Different chapters, different mechanisms. TRAP: DSM-5 removed schizophrenia subtypes (paranoid, catatonic, etc.). They're in DSM-IV, not DSM-5.

chunks.heading: 11. Dissociative Disorders
chunks.text: 11. Dissociative Disorders Dissociative Amnesia — gaps in autobiographical memory, often after trauma. Specifier: with dissociative fugue (sudden travel + identity confusion). Dissociative Identity Disorder (DID) — ≥ 2 distinct personality states, recurrent gaps in recall. Strongly linked to severe early trauma. Renamed from Multiple Personality Disorder. Depersonalization / Derealization Disorder — feeling unreal/detached from self or surroundings, reality testing intact (key differentiator from psychosis).

chunks.heading: 12. Somatic Symptom & Related
chunks.text: 12. Somatic Symptom & Related DSM-5 renamed this chapter from "somatoform disorders." Key entries: Somatic Symptom Disorder — distressing somatic symptoms + excessive thoughts/behaviors about them. Symptoms may have a medical basis (focus is on the response). Illness Anxiety Disorder — preoccupation with having illness, few/no somatic symptoms. Replaces hypochondriasis. Conversion Disorder (Functional Neurological Symptom) — neurological symptoms (paralysis, blindness, seizures) without medical explanation. La belle indifférence (oddly calm despite symptom) is a soft sign. Factitious Disorder — intentional faking for sick role gain (no external incentive). Munchausen = on self; Munchausen by proxy = on another (often child). Malingering — conscious faking for external gain (money, avoiding work, drugs). NOT a mental disorder; coded as a V-code / Z-code. TRAP: Easy to mix up: Conversion = unconscious, no gain. Symptoms are real to the person. Factitious = conscious symptom production, sick role gain (internal psychological). Malingering = conscious, external gain (money, court).

chunks.heading: 13. Eating Disorders
chunks.text: 13. Eating Disorders Disorder Hallmark BMI / weight Anorexia Nervosa Restriction, intense fear of weight gain, body image disturbance Significantly low weight required Bulimia Nervosa Binge + compensatory behaviors (vomiting, laxatives, exercise) Typically normal or above weight Binge Eating Disorder (BED) Binges without regular compensation Often overweight ARFID Avoidant/restrictive food intake, no body image disturbance Various Pica Eating non-food substances (any age, dx ≥ 2 yrs) Rumination Disorder Repeated regurgitation (any) TRAP: Anorexia requires low weight . Bulimia does not . The defining difference between bulimia and BED is the compensatory behavior .

chunks.heading: 14. Personality Disorders
chunks.text: 14. Personality Disorders Cluster Theme Disorders A Odd / eccentric Paranoid, Schizoid, Schizotypal B Dramatic / emotional / erratic Antisocial, Borderline, Histrionic, Narcissistic C Anxious / fearful Avoidant, Dependent, Obsessive-Compulsive PD

chunks.heading: 1-line distinguishers (Cluster B is the most exam-tested)
chunks.text: 1-line distinguishers (Cluster B is the most exam-tested) Antisocial — disregard for others' rights, age ≥ 18 + Conduct Disorder before 15. Higher in males. Borderline — instability of relationships, self-image, affect; impulsivity; fear of abandonment; chronic emptiness. Self-harm common. Higher in females. Histrionic — attention-seeking, theatrical, sexually provocative. Narcissistic — grandiosity, need for admiration, lack of empathy. TRAP: Schizoid vs Schizotypal . Schizoid = detached, indifferent to relationships, no eccentric beliefs. Schizotypal = detached + odd beliefs, magical thinking, perceptual oddities. Schizotypal lies on the schizophrenia spectrum, schizoid does not (in DSM-5). TRAP: OCPD ≠ OCD . OCPD = ego-syntonic perfectionism. OCD = ego-dystonic obsessions/compulsions.

chunks.heading: 15. Substance Use Disorder
chunks.text: 15. Substance Use Disorder DSM-5 collapsed "abuse" + "dependence" into a single Substance Use Disorder spectrum. Criteria: ≥ 2 of 11 in a 12-month period. Severity: 2-3 mild; 4-5 moderate; ≥ 6 severe. 11 criteria cluster into 4: impaired control, social impairment, risky use, pharmacological (tolerance, withdrawal). Tolerance + withdrawal are pharmacological criteria but not required for diagnosis. TRAP: Tolerance/withdrawal due to prescribed meds taken as directed do NOT count toward SUD criteria.

chunks.heading: 16. Sleep-Wake Disorders (compact)
chunks.text: 16. Sleep-Wake Disorders (compact) Insomnia Disorder — difficulty falling/staying asleep, ≥ 3 nights/wk, ≥ 3 months. Hypersomnolence — excessive sleepiness despite ≥ 7 hr sleep. Narcolepsy — recurrent sleep attacks; cataplexy (sudden muscle tone loss) often present; low CSF hypocretin/orexin. Sleep apnea — obstructive (most common) vs central. Parasomnias — sleepwalking, sleep terrors (NREM); nightmare disorder, REM Sleep Behavior Disorder (REM, often pre-Parkinson's). Circadian rhythm disorders — delayed/advanced sleep phase, shift work type.

chunks.heading: 17. Childhood / Neurodevelopmental Disorders
chunks.text: 17. Childhood / Neurodevelopmental Disorders IDD (Intellectual Developmental Disorder) — onset in dev period; deficits in intellectual + adaptive functioning. Severity by adaptive function , not just IQ. Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) — social communication deficits + restricted/repetitive behaviors. DSM-5 merged Asperger's, PDD-NOS, autistic disorder into one spectrum. ADHD — inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity ≥ 6 months; onset before 12 ; ≥ 2 settings. Specific Learning Disorder — dyslexia (reading), dysgraphia (writing), dyscalculia (math). Tic Disorders — Tourette's = motor + vocal tics ≥ 1 yr, onset before 18. Communication Disorders — language disorder, speech sound disorder, childhood-onset fluency disorder (stuttering), social (pragmatic) communication disorder. TRAP: ADHD onset cutoff is before 12 (DSM-5), changed from "before 7" (DSM-IV).

chunks.heading: 18. Treatments & Therapy Quick-Map
chunks.text: 18. Treatments & Therapy Quick-Map Disorder First-line psychotherapy Common pharmacology MDD CBT, IPT, behavioral activation SSRIs (fluoxetine, sertraline) GAD CBT, applied relaxation SSRIs / SNRIs; buspirone Panic Disorder CBT (interoceptive exposure) SSRIs; benzo for acute OCD ERP (Exposure + Response Prevention) SSRIs (high dose), clomipramine PTSD Trauma-focused CBT, EMDR, Prolonged Exposure SSRIs (sertraline, paroxetine FDA-approved) Specific Phobia Exposure (in vivo, gradual) (rarely) Schizophrenia CBTp, family psychoeducation, social skills Atypical antipsychotics (risperidone, olanzapine, etc.) Bipolar Psychoeducation, IPSRT, CBT Lithium, valproate, lamotrigine, atypicals BPD DBT (Linehan), MBT, schema therapy (symptom-targeted, no specific drug) Anorexia Family-Based Therapy (Maudsley) for adolescents; CBT-E (meds limited, weight restoration first) Bulimia / BED CBT-E, IPT Fluoxetine (only SSRI FDA-approved for bulimia) ADHD Behavioral parent training, CBT Stimulants (methylphenidate, amphetamine), atomoxetine

chunks.heading: 19. Top 25 MCQ Traps (Abnormal)
chunks.text: 19. Top 25 MCQ Traps (Abnormal) OCD is NOT in the anxiety chapter (DSM-5). OCPD ≠ OCD. Schizophrenia (Bleuler) ≠ Dementia praecox (Kraepelin). Schizophrenia ≠ DID (split mind ≠ split personality). DSM-5 dropped axes; multi-axial = DSM-IV. DSM-5 removed schizophrenia subtypes. Schizophreniform = 1-6 mo; Brief Psychotic = < 1 mo; Schizophrenia = ≥ 6 mo. Bipolar I needs mania ≥ 1 wk; Bipolar II = hypomania + MDE, never full mania. MDD needs ≥ 5 of 9 SIG-E-CAPS, must include depressed mood OR anhedonia. Strongest predictor of completed suicide = previous attempt. Conversion (unconscious) ≠ Factitious (conscious, sick role) ≠ Malingering (conscious, external gain). La belle indifférence is a conversion soft sign. Munchausen = factitious on self. Munchausen by proxy = factitious on another. Hoarding and Excoriation are NEW disorders in DSM-5. Bereavement exclusion was REMOVED in DSM-5. Asperger's no longer separate dx (folded into ASD). Schizoid (detached, no odd beliefs) ≠ Schizotypal (detached + odd beliefs). OCD first-line therapy = ERP (Exposure + Response Prevention), not CBT alone. BPD first-line = DBT (Linehan). Schneider's First-Rank Symptoms are suggestive , not diagnostic alone in DSM-5. Bleuler's 4 As: Associations, Affect, Ambivalence, Autism (withdrawal). ADHD onset cutoff is "before 12" (DSM-5), not "before 7" (DSM-IV). ICD-11 adds Complex PTSD; DSM-5 does not. Anorexia

chunks.heading: 20. 30-Second Recall Script
chunks.text: 20. 30-Second Recall Script Abnormal core: 4 Ds (deviance, distress, dysfunction, danger). DSM-5 (2013, axes dropped, US, APA) vs ICD-11 (2019, WHO, global, adds Complex PTSD). MSE = ABS-MTPCIJ. Anxiety chapter has GAD/Panic/Phobia/Social/Agoraphobia (≥ 6 mo). OCD + PTSD = own chapters. Mood: MDD (SIG-E-CAPS), Bipolar I (mania ≥ 1 wk), Bipolar II (hypomania + MDE, never mania). Schizophrenia: Bleuler's 4 As, ≥ 2 of 5 symptoms, ≥ 6 mo total; subtypes removed. Personality clusters: A odd, B dramatic (Antisocial, Borderline, Histrionic, Narcissistic), C anxious. SUD = ≥ 2 of 11 criteria. Conversion vs factitious vs malingering by consciousness + gain. ERP for OCD, DBT for BPD. Built 2026-05-05 to patch the abnormal section. Pair with the high-yield abn+dev sheet and the one-day sprint plan. Sihan MET 2026 + NIMHANS Prep

chunks.heading: Today's Sprint, Abnormal Psych
chunks.text: Today's Sprint, Abnormal Psych DSM categories + key disorders · Built 2026-05-07 · 16 days to MET Why this sheet exists. You're context-switching off biopsych for a day. This is your one-day plan, not a reference doc. Three blocks, ~2.5 hrs total, with a self-test gate after each. Hit all three checkpoints and you've banked the abnormal section for revision week. Full cheatsheet High-yield one-pager

chunks.heading: Block 1, the DSM scaffold 45 min
chunks.text: Block 1, the DSM scaffold 45 min Goal: lock the structure of DSM-5 so any disorder you see has a chapter to live in. Don't try to memorize disorders here. Memorize the chapters .

chunks.heading: Read
chunks.text: Read Cheatsheet §1, the 4 Ds. Cheatsheet §2, historical models. Just the table. Cheatsheet §4, DSM-5 vs ICD-11. This table is exam gold. Cheatsheet §5, MSE order (ABS-MTPCIJ).

chunks.heading: The 22 DSM-5 chapters, the order MET likes to test
chunks.text: The 22 DSM-5 chapters, the order MET likes to test # Chapter One-line anchor 1 Neurodevelopmental IDD, ASD, ADHD, SLD, tics. Onset before 12 for ADHD. 2 Schizophrenia spectrum ≥ 2 of 5 sx, ≥ 6 mo total. Subtypes removed. 3 Bipolar & related Bipolar I = mania. Bipolar II = hypomania + MDE, never mania. 4 Depressive MDD = SIG-E-CAPS, ≥ 5 of 9, ≥ 2 wks. Bereavement exclusion REMOVED. 5 Anxiety GAD/panic/phobia/social/agoraphobia. Mostly ≥ 6 mo. 6 OCD & related OCD, BDD, Hoarding (NEW), Trichotillomania, Excoriation (NEW). 7 Trauma- & stressor-related PTSD > 1 mo. ASD 3 days–1 mo. RAD, DSED. 8 Dissociative DID, dissociative amnesia, depersonalization/derealization. 9 Somatic symptom & related SSD, IAD, Conversion, Factitious. Malingering NOT a disorder. 10 Feeding & eating AN, BN, BED, ARFID, Pica, Rumination. 11 Elimination Enuresis, encopresis. 12 Sleep-wake Insomnia, narcolepsy (cataplexy), parasomnias, OSA. 13 Sexual dysfunctions Lifelong vs acquired, generalized vs situational. 14 Gender dysphoria Renamed from Gender Identity Disorder. ICD-11 moved out of mental ch. 15 Disruptive, impulse-control, conduct ODD, Conduct Disorder, IED, Pyromania, Kleptomania. 16 Substance-related & addictive SUD = ≥ 2 of 11. Gambling = the one behavioral addiction in DSM-5. 17 Neurocognitive Delirium, Major NCD (dementia), Mild NCD. 18 Personality disorders Cluster A odd, B dramatic, C anxious. 1

chunks.heading: Block 2, key disorders deep-dive 75 min
chunks.text: Block 2, key disorders deep-dive 75 min Six disorder clusters that show up on every paper. Read each, drill the trap, write the duration / criteria threshold from memory before moving on.

chunks.heading: 2.1 Mood (cheatsheet §9), 12 min
chunks.text: 2.1 Mood (cheatsheet §9), 12 min MDD : SIG-E-CAPS, ≥ 5 of 9, must include depressed mood OR anhedonia, ≥ 2 wks. Persistent Depressive (Dysthymia) : ≥ 2 yrs (≥ 1 yr in kids). Bipolar I : ≥ 1 manic episode (≥ 1 wk, or any duration if hospitalised). MDE not required. Bipolar II : hypomania (≥ 4 days) + MDE. Never full mania. Cyclothymia : hypomanic + depressive symptoms, never full episode, ≥ 2 yrs. DIG-FAST for mania: Distractibility, Indiscretion, Grandiosity, Flight of ideas, Activity, Sleep ↓, Talkativeness. TRAP: One full manic episode in their entire history → Bipolar I, even if all current episodes are hypomanic.

chunks.heading: 2.2 Psychosis (cheatsheet §10), 15 min
chunks.text: 2.2 Psychosis (cheatsheet §10), 15 min Schizophrenia : ≥ 2 of (delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, grossly disorganized/catatonic behavior, negative sx). At least one must be from the first three. Active ≥ 1 mo, total ≥ 6 mo. Schizophreniform : 1 mo to < 6 mo. Brief Psychotic : 1 day to < 1 mo. Schizoaffective : mood + psychosis, but ≥ 2 wks of psychosis WITHOUT mood symptoms (key differentiator from mood disorder with psychotic features). Delusional Disorder : ≥ 1 mo, delusions only, no other psychotic sx. Bleuler's 4 As : Associations (loose), Affect (flat), Ambivalence, Autism (withdrawal). Note: "autism" here = social withdrawal, NOT autism spectrum. Schneider FRS : thought insertion/withdrawal/broadcasting, audible thoughts, voices commenting/arguing, made impulses, somatic passivity, delusional perception. Suggestive, NOT diagnostic alone in DSM-5. TRAP: Schizophrenia ≠ DID. Split mind ≠ split personality. Different chapters. TRAP: Subtypes (paranoid, catatonic, etc.) were dropped in DSM-5. If subtypes appear in answer choices, the question is testing DSM-IV vocab.

chunks.heading: 2.3 Anxiety / OCD / Trauma (cheatsheet §6, §7, §8), 12 min
chunks.text: 2.3 Anxiety / OCD / Trauma (cheatsheet §6, §7, §8), 12 min Anxiety chapter: GAD, Panic, Specific Phobia, Social Anxiety, Agoraphobia, Separation Anxiety, Selective Mutism. Most need ≥ 6 mo. OCD chapter (separated from anxiety in DSM-5): OCD, BDD, Hoarding (NEW), Trichotillomania, Excoriation (NEW). Trauma chapter (separated from anxiety in DSM-5): PTSD, ASD, Adjustment, RAD, DSED. ICD-11 also adds Complex PTSD (DSO: emotion dysregulation, negative self-concept, relational disturbance). TRAP: OCPD ≠ OCD. OCPD is in the personality disorders chapter, ego-syntonic, perfectionistic. OCD is ego-dystonic obsessions/compulsions.

chunks.heading: 2.4 Personality Disorders (cheatsheet §14), 12 min
chunks.text: 2.4 Personality Disorders (cheatsheet §14), 12 min Cluster Theme Disorders A Odd / eccentric Paranoid, Schizoid, Schizotypal B Dramatic / emotional / erratic Antisocial, Borderline, Histrionic, Narcissistic C Anxious / fearful Avoidant, Dependent, OCPD Antisocial : disregard for others' rights. Age ≥ 18 + Conduct Disorder before 15. Higher in males. Borderline : instability of relationships, self-image, affect. Impulsivity, fear of abandonment, chronic emptiness, self-harm. Higher in females. First-line: DBT (Linehan) . Histrionic : attention-seeking, theatrical, sexually provocative. Narcissistic : grandiosity, need for admiration, lack of empathy. TRAP: Schizoid (detached, no odd beliefs) vs Schizotypal (detached + odd beliefs / magical thinking). Schizotypal is on the schizophrenia spectrum. Schizoid is not.

chunks.heading: 2.5 SUD (cheatsheet §15), 8 min
chunks.text: 2.5 SUD (cheatsheet §15), 8 min DSM-5 collapsed "abuse" + "dependence" into one Substance Use Disorder spectrum. ≥ 2 of 11 criteria in 12 mo. Severity: 2-3 mild, 4-5 moderate, ≥ 6 severe. 4 criterion clusters: impaired control, social impairment, risky use, pharmacological (tolerance, withdrawal). Tolerance/withdrawal from prescribed meds taken as directed do NOT count.

chunks.heading: 2.6 Eating + Somatic + Dissociative (cheatsheet §11, §12, §13), 8 min
chunks.text: 2.6 Eating + Somatic + Dissociative (cheatsheet §11, §12, §13), 8 min Anorexia : low weight required. Bulimia : normal/above weight. BED : binges WITHOUT compensation. Conversion (unconscious, no gain) vs Factitious (conscious, sick role) vs Malingering (conscious, external gain). Malingering is NOT a mental disorder. DID : ≥ 2 distinct identities, recurrent recall gaps, linked to severe early trauma. Renamed from Multiple Personality Disorder. Depersonalization/Derealization : feels unreal, but reality testing INTACT (key differentiator from psychosis).

chunks.heading: 2.7 First-line treatment quick map (cheatsheet §18), 8 min
chunks.text: 2.7 First-line treatment quick map (cheatsheet §18), 8 min Disorder First-line therapy First-line meds MDD CBT, IPT, behavioral activation SSRIs OCD ERP (Exposure + Response Prevention) SSRIs (high dose), clomipramine PTSD Trauma-focused CBT, EMDR, Prolonged Exposure Sertraline, paroxetine (FDA-approved) Panic CBT (interoceptive exposure) SSRIs; benzo for acute Specific phobia In vivo exposure Rarely Schizophrenia CBTp + family psychoed Atypical antipsychotics Bipolar Psychoeducation, IPSRT Lithium, valproate, lamotrigine BPD DBT (Linehan) Symptom-targeted only Anorexia FBT (Maudsley) for adolescents, CBT-E Weight restoration first Bulimia / BED CBT-E, IPT Fluoxetine (only SSRI FDA-approved for bulimia) Checkpoint 2, no peeking. Bipolar I vs Bipolar II, what's the single differentiator? Schizophrenia duration. Schizophreniform duration. Brief Psychotic duration. OCD first-line therapy is not just CBT. What is it? Cluster B has four disorders. Name them. Conversion vs Factitious vs Malingering: what distinguishes them? How many criteria for SUD diagnosis? Which eating disorder requires low weight? Show answers Bipolar I needs ≥ 1 full manic episode (≥ 1 wk). Bipolar II = hypomania (≥ 4 days) + MDE, never full mania. Schizophrenia ≥ 6 mo. Schizophreniform 1–6 mo. Brief Psychotic 1 day to < 1 mo. ERP, Exposure and Response Prevention. Antisocial, Borderline, Histrionic, Narcissist

chunks.heading: Block 3, drill the traps 30 min
chunks.text: Block 3, drill the traps 30 min Active recall, not re-reading. This is where the day pays off.

chunks.heading: Step 1, the Top 25 traps (cheatsheet §19)
chunks.text: Step 1, the Top 25 traps (cheatsheet §19) Read each line. Cover the answer side. Say it out loud. Mark the ones you blanked on.

chunks.heading: Step 2, abnormal cheatsheet active recall
chunks.text: Step 2, abnormal cheatsheet active recall Open the abnormal cheatsheet . Cover the right column of each table, recall it from the left, then check. Spend 20-30 minutes. Mark anything you blanked on for tomorrow.

chunks.heading: Step 3, mock-style mini-drill

chunks.heading: Action Potential — Complete MET Reference
chunks.text: Action Potential — Complete MET Reference The single most testable neurophysiology topic across MET, NIMHANS, AIIMS. Built around ion movement (Na+, K+, Ca2+, Cl-), the four phases, and the rules that make MCQs predictable.

chunks.heading: 0. What an Action Potential Actually Is (start here)
chunks.text: 0. What an Action Potential Actually Is (start here) An action potential is the basic signal a neuron uses to talk. It is a short (~1 millisecond) electrical pulse that travels down the axon from the cell body to the axon terminal. When it reaches the terminal, it causes neurotransmitter release, which then signals the next neuron. Every thought, sensation, movement, and emotion you have is built out of millions of these pulses firing in patterns. So the question “how does a neuron fire?” = “how does an action potential happen?”

chunks.heading: The one-sentence story
chunks.text: The one-sentence story When a neuron is at rest, the inside of its membrane is negative relative to the outside (about -70 millivolts). When the neuron is stimulated enough, ion channels open in a precise sequence — first sodium (Na+) rushes IN making the inside briefly positive , then potassium (K+) rushes OUT bringing it back to negative — and that pulse of voltage change propagates down the axon at up to 120 m/s. That’s it. Everything else in this primer is the mechanics of how that pulse is generated, shaped, and propagated.

chunks.heading: Five things you must know before the mechanics make sense
chunks.text: Five things you must know before the mechanics make sense Neurons have a charged membrane at rest. Inside is at -70 mV, outside is the reference (0 mV). This charge difference is called the resting membrane potential (RMP) . It exists because the membrane lets some ions cross more easily than others (mostly K+ leaks out a little, leaving the inside negative). The membrane is studded with ion channels. Some are always open (“leak channels”), some open only when voltage changes (“voltage-gated”), some open only when a chemical binds (“ligand-gated”). The action potential is driven by voltage-gated channels for Na+ and K+. Ions flow because of two forces: concentration and charge. Na+ wants to enter (lots outside, little inside, attracted to negative interior). K+ wants to leave (lots inside, little outside, but pulled back by negative interior). When a channel opens, the relevant ion moves whichever way its forces dictate. Knowing which ion goes which way at each phase is the whole game. An action potential is “all or none.” If the stimulus is strong enough to push the membrane to about -55 mV (the threshold ), a full action potential fires. If the stimulus is weaker, nothing happens. Bigger stimuli do not produce bigger APs — they produce more APs per second (frequency coding). One AP looks identical to every other AP in that neuron. The signal travels because each segment of ax

chunks.heading: What an action potential looks like on a graph
chunks.text: What an action potential looks like on a graph Voltage on Y-axis (in mV), time on X-axis (in milliseconds). The whole thing takes about 2 ms. +30 ─────────────●─── PEAK (Na+ channels inactivate) ╱│╲ ╱ │ ╲ ╱ │ ╲ ← REPOLARIZATION (K+ flowing OUT) ╱ │ ╲ ╱ │ ╲ -55 ────●─╱─────│─────●──── THRESHOLD (-55 mV) ╱ │ ╲ ╱ ↑ │ ╲___ -70 ─● DEPOL │ \____ ← AFTERHYPERPOLARIZATION | (Na+ IN)│ (K+ channels still open RMP briefly, overshoots RMP)

chunks.heading: Why exams hammer this topic
chunks.text: Why exams hammer this topic Action potential MCQs test precise, factual recall of: - Which ion moves at which phase (Na+ in for depolarization, K+ out for repolarization, Ca2+ in at the terminal for NT release, Cl- in for IPSP) - Which channels open and when (voltage-gated Na+ at threshold, voltage-gated K+ slightly later, voltage-gated Ca2+ at the axon terminal) - Refractory periods (absolute = Na+ inactivated, relative = K+ still open) - Conduction speed and myelin (saltatory in myelinated fibers, fastest in A-alpha) - Synaptic transmission cascade (AP arrives → Ca2+ in → vesicles fuse → NT released → binds postsynaptic receptors → EPSP or IPSP) If you know the story below cold, you will get every single one right. If you confuse Na+ and K+, mix up depolarization and repolarization, or don’t know that Ca2+ triggers NT release, you will bleed marks. The 6 questions you got wrong on the diagnostic were all in this cluster. Now that the big picture is set, here is the mechanics in detail.

chunks.heading: 1. Resting Membrane Potential (RMP)
chunks.text: 1. Resting Membrane Potential (RMP) The neuron at rest sits at about -70 mV (range -60 to -90 depending on neuron type). Inside is negative relative to outside.

chunks.heading: Why -70 mV? Three forces.
chunks.text: Why -70 mV? Three forces. Force What it does Effect Concentration gradient K+ wants to leave (high inside), Na+ wants to enter (high outside) Sets up the chemistry Electrical gradient Inside is negative, attracts cations Opposes K+ leaving Selective permeability at rest Membrane is ~50x more permeable to K+ than Na+ (leak channels) K+ dominates The membrane settles where K+ efflux balances the electrical pull keeping K+ in. That equilibrium = ~-70 mV (close to K+’s equilibrium potential of -90 mV, dragged up by small Na+ leak).

chunks.heading: Ion concentrations (mEq/L), memorize this table
chunks.text: Ion concentrations (mEq/L), memorize this table Ion Inside Outside Equilibrium potential (Eion) K+ 140 (high) 5 (low) -90 mV Na+ 15 (low) 145 (high) +60 mV Cl- 10 (low) 110 (high) -65 mV Ca2+ 0.0001 (very low) 2 (high) +120 mV Memory hook: “K is in, Na is out, Cl is out, Ca is way out.”

chunks.heading: Na+/K+ pump (Na+/K+ ATPase)
chunks.text: Na+/K+ pump (Na+/K+ ATPase) Pumps 3 Na+ out for every 2 K+ in , using 1 ATP. Electrogenic : net export of +1 charge per cycle, contributes ~-4 mV to RMP. Maintains the gradients but does NOT directly cause RMP. RMP is caused by K+ leak channels following the K+ gradient. The pump just keeps the gradient charged up. Common MCQ trap: “What sets resting potential?” Answer: K+ permeability via leak channels. NOT the Na+/K+ pump (it’s the gradient-maintainer, not the voltage-setter).

chunks.heading: 2. The Four Phases of an Action Potential
chunks.text: 2. The Four Phases of an Action Potential +30 mV ─┐ ┌─ Peak (Na+ inactivation) │ │ │ /│ │ / │ ← REPOLARIZATION (K+ out) │ / │ │/ │ Threshold ─┼────┼──────────── -55 mV ----------/│ │\ / │ │ \ RMP ────/──┘ │ \____ ← AFTERHYPERPOLARIZATION (K+ still open) -70 mV │ \ │ \____ back to RMP └─ DEPOLARIZATION (Na+ in) Phase 1: Depolarization → Na+ channels open, Na+ rushes IN Phase 2: Repolarization → Na+ inactivates, K+ channels open, K+ rushes OUT Phase 3: Hyperpolarization → K+ channels still open, briefly overshoots RMP Phase 4: Return to RMP → K+ channels close, Na+/K+ pump restores ions

chunks.heading: Phase-by-phase ion movement
chunks.text: Phase-by-phase ion movement Phase What opens Ion movement Voltage change Threshold reached (-55 mV) Voltage-gated Na+ channels Na+ starts in Trigger 1. Depolarization Na+ channels fully open Massive Na+ in -55 → +30 mV Peak (+30 mV) Na+ channels inactivate Na+ stops Plateau briefly 2. Repolarization Voltage-gated K+ channels open (slower) Massive K+ out +30 → -70 mV 3. Hyperpolarization (afterhyperpolarization) K+ channels still open More K+ out -70 → -80 mV 4. Return to RMP K+ channels close, pump works Pump restores Na+/K+ -80 → -70 mV Memory hook: “ Na+ in, K+ out ” — that’s the whole story. Na+ rises = depolarization. K+ exits = repolarization.

chunks.heading: 3. The All-or-None Principle
chunks.text: 3. The All-or-None Principle If stimulus reaches threshold (-55 mV typical), an AP fires at full amplitude. If stimulus is below threshold, nothing happens . No partial AP. Stronger stimulus = more frequent APs (rate coding), NOT bigger APs. MCQ trap: “How does the brain encode stimulus intensity?” Answer: frequency of action potentials , not amplitude. Amplitude is fixed.

chunks.heading: 4. Refractory Periods
chunks.text: 4. Refractory Periods Two types, both critical MCQ topics.

chunks.heading: Absolute refractory period
chunks.text: Absolute refractory period Duration: about 1-2 ms . Cause: Na+ channels are inactivated (not just closed; they have an inactivation gate). Effect: No new AP can fire , no matter how strong the stimulus. Function: ensures one-way propagation of AP down axon.

chunks.heading: Relative refractory period
chunks.text: Relative refractory period Duration: about 2-4 ms after absolute. Cause: K+ channels still open (membrane is hyperpolarized). Effect: A new AP CAN fire, but requires a stronger-than-normal stimulus . Function: limits maximum firing rate (~1000 Hz max). MCQ trap: Inactivated ≠ closed. Na+ channel has 3 states: closed (resting), open (during AP), inactivated (after AP, “ball and chain” blocking pore). Resets only after repolarization.

chunks.heading: 5. Propagation Down the Axon
chunks.text: 5. Propagation Down the Axon

chunks.heading: Continuous (unmyelinated)
chunks.text: Continuous (unmyelinated) AP regenerates point-by-point along the membrane. Slow: 0.5 - 2 m/s . Found in: C fibers (slow pain, temperature, postganglionic autonomic).

chunks.heading: Saltatory (myelinated)
chunks.text: Saltatory (myelinated) AP “jumps” between Nodes of Ranvier (gaps in myelin). Voltage-gated Na+ channels concentrated only at nodes. Fast: up to 120 m/s in large myelinated A-alpha fibers. Found in: A fibers (motor, proprioception, fast pain, touch). Memory hook: “Saltatory” = Latin saltare , “to leap.”

chunks.heading: Factors that increase conduction velocity
chunks.text: Factors that increase conduction velocity Myelination (biggest factor). Axon diameter (bigger = faster, less resistance). Temperature (warmer = faster, up to a limit). Demyelinating diseases (multiple sclerosis, Guillain-Barre): slow or block conduction → numbness, weakness, vision loss.

chunks.heading: 6. Synaptic Transmission (the post-AP step)
chunks.text: 6. Synaptic Transmission (the post-AP step) When the AP reaches the axon terminal: Ca2+ channels open (voltage-gated). Ca2+ rushes IN. Ca2+ triggers vesicle fusion with presynaptic membrane (SNARE proteins, synaptotagmin = Ca2+ sensor). Neurotransmitter released into synaptic cleft. Binds postsynaptic receptors → ion flow → EPSP or IPSP. Cleared by reuptake, enzymatic breakdown, or diffusion. Why Ca2+? It’s the trigger ion at the axon terminal. Without Ca2+ entry, no transmitter release.

chunks.heading: EPSP vs IPSP
chunks.text: EPSP vs IPSP Type Ion movement Effect on postsynaptic neuron EPSP (excitatory postsynaptic potential) Na+ in (or Ca2+ in) Depolarizes, brings closer to threshold IPSP (inhibitory postsynaptic potential) Cl- in (or K+ out) Hyperpolarizes, moves away from threshold Summation rules: - Spatial: multiple synapses fire at the same time, signals add. - Temporal: one synapse fires repeatedly, signals add over time. - AP fires only if summed depolarization reaches threshold at the axon hillock (the AP initiation site).

chunks.heading: 7. The Top 10 MCQ Traps on Action Potentials
chunks.text: 7. The Top 10 MCQ Traps on Action Potentials What sets RMP? K+ permeability (leak channels), not the Na+/K+ pump. What ion triggers neurotransmitter release? Ca2+ at the axon terminal. All-or-none refers to what? Amplitude is fixed. Intensity is coded by frequency. Why can’t you fire during absolute refractory? Na+ channels are inactivated, not just closed. What causes hyperpolarization? K+ channels stay open after Na+ has stopped. Saltatory conduction needs what? Myelin + Nodes of Ranvier with Na+ channels. Fastest fiber type? A-alpha (large, myelinated, motor + proprioception). Slowest fiber type? C (small, unmyelinated, slow pain, postganglionic autonomic). Where does the AP start? Axon hillock (lowest threshold, most Na+ channels). Na+/K+ pump ratio? 3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in, per 1 ATP. Electrogenic.

chunks.heading: 8. Quick-recall summary
chunks.text: 8. Quick-recall summary Question Answer RMP value -70 mV Threshold -55 mV Peak voltage +30 mV Hyperpolarized to -80 mV Set by K+ leak channels Depolarization caused by Na+ in (voltage-gated) Repolarization caused by K+ out (voltage-gated) Hyperpolarization caused by K+ still open Returns to RMP via Na+/K+ pump (3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in) AP triggered at Axon hillock Transmitter release triggered by Ca2+ entry at terminal Absolute refractory caused by Na+ channel inactivation Relative refractory caused by K+ still open (hyperpolarized) Fastest conduction Saltatory in myelinated A-alpha (up to 120 m/s)

chunks.heading: 9. 10 MET-style MCQs
chunks.text: 9. 10 MET-style MCQs Q1. The resting membrane potential of a typical neuron is closest to: A. -30 mV B. -55 mV C. -70 mV D. -90 mV Answer C. -70 mV. A is too depolarized, B is threshold, D is K+ equilibrium potential. Q2. Resting membrane potential is primarily determined by: A. Na+/K+ ATPase B. K+ leak channels C. Voltage-gated Na+ channels D. Cl- channels Answer B. K+ leak channels. The pump maintains gradients but is not the direct voltage-setter. Common trap. Q3. During depolarization phase of an AP, the dominant ion movement is: A. K+ out B. Na+ in C. Ca2+ in D. Cl- in Answer B. Na+ in. Voltage-gated Na+ channels open at threshold. Q4. Repolarization of a neuron is caused mainly by: A. Closing of K+ channels B. Opening of voltage-gated K+ channels C. Na+/K+ pump activity D. Ca2+ entry Answer B. K+ rushes out down its gradient. Q5. The Na+/K+ ATPase moves: A. 2 Na+ out, 3 K+ in B. 3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in C. 3 Na+ in, 2 K+ out D. 1 Na+ out, 1 K+ in Answer B. 3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in. Electrogenic (net +1 export). Q6. During the absolute refractory period: A. A stronger stimulus can elicit AP B. Only Cl- channels are open C. Na+ channels are inactivated D. K+ channels are closed Answer C. Inactivated, not just closed. No AP possible. Q7. Saltatory conduction requires: A. Unmyelinated axons B. Continuous Na+ channels along the axon C. Nodes of Ranvier D. C fibers Answer C. Nodes of Ranvi

chunks.heading: 10. Memorization aids
chunks.text: 10. Memorization aids “Na+ in, K+ out” — the AP in 4 words. “3 out, 2 in, 1 ATP” — the pump. “Ca for Communication” — Ca2+ at the terminal triggers transmitter release. “Inactivated, not closed” — why absolute refractory exists. “Salt jumps Nodes” — saltatory = jumps between Nodes of Ranvier. “K sets the rest” — RMP is a K+ phenomenon. chunks.heading: Psychological Assessment, Read-First Primer
chunks.text: Psychological Assessment, Read-First Primer

chunks.heading: Psychological Assessment, Read-First Primer
chunks.text: Psychological Assessment, Read-First Primer This is written in explanation mode. Read it like a chapter, not a cheatsheet. Every fact has a “why” attached. Once this clicks, the 60-question Bio + Testing drill stops being a confusion machine and starts being a self-test. If you walk away with one mental model, it is this: a psychological test is a measuring instrument, and like any instrument, it has to be (a) consistent and (b) accurate. Consistent = reliability. Accurate = validity. Everything else in this section is either a way to estimate reliability, a way to estimate validity, a way to interpret scores against norms, or an example of a real-world test. That is the whole map.

chunks.heading: 1. Why test construction is even a thing
chunks.text: 1. Why test construction is even a thing Psychology is uncomfortably stuck between two facts. First, the things we want to measure (anxiety, intelligence, personality) are not directly observable. There is no anxiety-meter you can clip to a fingertip. Second, we still need to make decisions: should this child be in special education? Is this candidate fit for the army? Does this patient have OCD? So we build instruments out of items, like a thermometer made of questions. That is why item analysis exists. Each item is a single sensor reading. If the sensor is too easy (everyone gets it right) it tells us nothing. If the sensor is too hard (no one gets it) it tells us nothing. If the sensor agrees with the rest of the test, it is doing its job. If it disagrees, something is wrong with that item.

chunks.heading: Difficulty index, p
chunks.text: Difficulty index, p The difficulty index is just the proportion who got an item right. p = (number who got the item right) / (total who attempted) Range zero to one. p = 0.50 means half the test-takers got it right. That is the sweet spot for a free-response item, because it discriminates the most. For a 4-option MCQ, the sweet spot is closer to 0.625 because guessers will pick the right answer 25% of the time by chance, and you want item difficulty to land halfway between guessing (0.25) and ceiling (1.00). Items with p above 0.80 are too easy and items below 0.20 are too hard. Both are candidates for revision because they cannot tell strong students from weak ones.

chunks.heading: Discrimination index, D
chunks.text: Discrimination index, D This one asks: do the test-takers who scored well on the whole test do better on this item than the test-takers who scored badly? Specifically: D = p_upper - p_lower Where p_upper is the proportion correct in the top 27% of scorers and p_lower is the proportion in the bottom 27%. Range is minus one to plus one. If D is high (above 0.40), the item agrees with the overall test. Top scorers got it right, bottom scorers got it wrong. The item is a good signal. If D is near zero, the item is random noise. Both groups perform similarly. If D is negative , something is wrong. The bottom group out-performed the top group. That happens when an item is mis-keyed, ambiguously worded, or has a trick that strong test-takers over-think. Negative D means discard immediately. Always read negative D as a red flag, not as a hard item.

chunks.heading: 2. Reliability, the consistency story
chunks.text: 2. Reliability, the consistency story Reliability is not about whether the test is correct. It is about whether the test is consistent . A bathroom scale that reads 75 kg every time you step on it is reliable, even if it is calibrated wrong and the true weight is 70. A scale that bounces between 60, 90, and 80 is unreliable, full stop. Why does this matter? Because if a test is unreliable, you cannot trust any single score from it. The next time you give the same test to the same person, you will get a different answer for reasons that have nothing to do with the trait you are trying to measure. You are measuring noise. The classical test theory equation summarizes this: Observed Score = True Score + Error Reliability is the proportion of observed score variance that is true variance, not error. A reliability of 0.80 says 80% of what you are seeing is signal, 20% is noise. There are several reliability methods because there are several ways to think about “consistency”: Across time: test the same person twice on different days (test-retest). Across forms: give two different versions of the test (parallel forms). Within one administration, across items: check that the items hang together (split-half, Cronbach alpha, KR-20). Across raters: check that two judges agree (Cohen kappa for categorical, ICC for continuous).

chunks.heading: Test-retest, the time-stability check
chunks.text: Test-retest, the time-stability check Give the test on Monday, give it again three weeks later, correlate the two scores. If the correlation is high, the test is stable across time. The trap: if you wait too long, the trait itself can change, and the correlation drops not because the test is bad but because the person actually changed. If you wait too short, memory carryover inflates the correlation. The standard window is two to four weeks.

chunks.heading: Split-half plus Spearman-Brown
chunks.text: Split-half plus Spearman-Brown Give the test once, split the items into two halves (often odd-numbered vs even-numbered), and correlate the two halves. The result tells you how internally consistent the test is. Catch: by splitting, you have effectively halved the test length, and shorter tests are less reliable. So the raw split-half correlation underestimates the full-test reliability. Spearman-Brown corrects for that: r_full = 2 * r_half / (1 + r_half) If r_half is 0.60, the full-test estimated reliability is 1.20 / 1.60 = 0.75. Spearman-Brown is the standard fix you apply after any split.

chunks.heading: Cronbach alpha
chunks.text: Cronbach alpha Imagine doing every possible split-half (odd-even, first-half last-half, items 1-3-5 vs 2-4-6, etc.) and averaging the result. That mean is Cronbach alpha. It is the most common internal-consistency measure for tests with multi-point items (like Likert). Important: alpha is not a measure of unidimensionality. A test can have high alpha and still be measuring two distinct constructs. Alpha rises with item count, item homogeneity, and variance in the trait. The MET love this trap.

chunks.heading: KR-20
chunks.text: KR-20 When items are right-or-wrong (dichotomous, 1 or 0), Cronbach alpha simplifies to a special formula called KR-20 (Kuder-Richardson 20). It is the same idea, just adapted for 0/1 items. So if you see “30-item right-wrong vocabulary test, one administration, which reliability?”, the answer is KR-20.

chunks.heading: Inter-rater, kappa and ICC
chunks.text: Inter-rater, kappa and ICC What if humans do the scoring (Rorschach protocols, clinical interviews, essay grades)? Then reliability is about whether two raters agree. For categorical decisions (does the patient have OCD, yes or no?), Cohen kappa corrects for chance agreement. Kappa = 0.81 or above is almost-perfect; 0.61 to 0.80 is substantial. For continuous ratings (a 0-100 severity score), use the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC). Different forms of ICC exist depending on whether raters are random or fixed. Critical: kappa is not an internal-consistency measure. If a question describes a one-administration internal-structure test, kappa is wrong.

chunks.heading: Standard Error of Measurement (SEM)
chunks.text: Standard Error of Measurement (SEM) SEM is the practical takeaway of reliability. It tells you the band of error around any one observed score. SEM = SD * sqrt(1 - r_xx) where SD is the test’s standard deviation and r_xx is its reliability. Example: a test with SD = 20 and reliability 0.81 has SEM = 20 * sqrt(0.19) = 20 * 0.436 = 8.72. So if a person scores 100, the 68% confidence band is roughly 91 to 109 (one SEM either side). Higher reliability shrinks SEM. SEM is what lets you say “this score is meaningfully different from that one” or “this is within the noise band.”

chunks.heading: 3. Validity, the accuracy story
chunks.text: 3. Validity, the accuracy story A test can be perfectly reliable and still measure the wrong thing. Validity asks whether the test measures the construct it claims to measure. There are three broad evidence types in the classical model. (Modern theorists, especially Messick, fold them all into “construct validity,” but MET still uses the classical breakdown so know both.)

chunks.heading: Content validity
chunks.text: Content validity Does the test cover the domain it claims to cover? An anxiety scale that only asks about racing heart but ignores worry, restlessness, and sleep is content-deficient. Content validity is established by expert panels who rate whether items adequately sample the content domain. Lawshe’s CVR is the technical formula but expert judgment is the core. Do not confuse with face validity. Face validity is whether the test looks valid to a layperson taking it. That is the weakest form because laypeople are not domain experts. A test can have high face validity and bad content validity (looks plausible but misses key content) or low face validity and high content validity (rigorous content but feels weird to take).

chunks.heading: Criterion validity
chunks.text: Criterion validity Does the test correlate with a real-world outcome (the criterion)? Two flavors: Concurrent : criterion measured at the same time. Example: a new depression scale today vs an established gold standard like HAM-D today. Used when a gold standard already exists. Predictive : criterion measured later. Example: GRE today predicts graduate GPA two years later. Used when you want to forecast future behavior. Memory hook: Predictive = Postponed. Concurrent = Current.

chunks.heading: Construct validity
chunks.text: Construct validity The most abstract form. It asks: if my test really measures Construct X, then it should correlate strongly with other measures of X (convergent), correlate weakly with measures of unrelated constructs (discriminant), and behave the way theory predicts in study after study (nomological network). The classic technique here is Campbell and Fiske’s 1959 multitrait-multimethod matrix (MTMM) , which tests convergent and discriminant validity simultaneously by measuring multiple traits with multiple methods.

chunks.heading: Validity ceiling
chunks.text: Validity ceiling Validity cannot exceed the square root of reliability: Maximum validity coefficient between Test A and Test B = sqrt(r_xx_A * r_xx_B) If A is 0.64 reliable and B is 0.81 reliable, the maximum correlation between them is sqrt(0.64 * 0.81) = 0.72. Unreliable tests cannot be strongly valid. Reliability is necessary for validity, not sufficient.

chunks.heading: 4. Norms and standard scores, the comparison story
chunks.text: 4. Norms and standard scores, the comparison story A raw score by itself means nothing. “Sahil scored 47 on a vocabulary test” tells you nothing until you know what other people score. Norms convert raw scores into a frame of reference. The two most useful conversions are percentile ranks and standard scores.

chunks.heading: Percentile ranks
chunks.text: Percentile ranks The percentage of the norm group scoring at or below the person’s score. A 75th percentile means 75% of people scored at or below this person. Easy to interpret, but ordinal (the gap between the 50th and 60th percentile is much smaller than the gap between the 90th and 99th).

chunks.heading: Standard scores
chunks.text: Standard scores These convert raw scores onto an interval scale where the mean and SD are fixed. The conversion is always: Standard Score = M + (SD * z) where z is the person’s z-score from the norm group. You need to memorize a handful of standard score systems cold. They get tested every cycle: Score Mean SD Use z 0 1 Universal T 50 10 MMPI, Big Five inventories Wechsler IQ 100 15 WAIS, WISC, WPPSI Old Stanford-Binet IQ 100 16 Older SB versions Stanine 5 2 Achievement tests, range 1 to 9 Sten 5.5 2 16PF Wechsler subtest scaled 10 3 Subtests inside WAIS/WISC, range 1 to 19 The most-tested traps: - Wechsler IQ uses SD = 15. Old Binet used SD = 16. Read the question carefully. - Stanine has SD = 2, not 1. Common distractor. - T is 50/10, not 100/10. Normal-curve landmarks worth memorizing: 68% within 1 SD, 95% within 2 SD, 99.7% within 3 SD. A z of plus 1 lands at the 84th percentile. A z of plus 2 lands at the 98th percentile.

chunks.heading: 5. The major intelligence tests
chunks.text: 5. The major intelligence tests

chunks.heading: The Wechsler family
chunks.text: The Wechsler family Wechsler is the workhorse. Three versions for three age bands: WPPSI (Preschool and Primary), ages 2:6 to 7:7, currently version IV. WISC (Children), ages 6:0 to 16:11, currently version V. WAIS (Adult), ages 16:0 to 90:11, currently version IV (with WAIS-5 in rollout). WAIS-IV produces a Full-Scale IQ (FSIQ) plus four index scores: Verbal Comprehension, Perceptual Reasoning, Working Memory, Processing Speed. WISC-V expanded to five indices (Verbal Comprehension, Visual Spatial, Fluid Reasoning, Working Memory, Processing Speed) by separating fluid reasoning from visual-spatial.

chunks.heading: Stanford-Binet
chunks.text: Stanford-Binet The granddaddy. Started as Binet-Simon in France in 1905, brought to Stanford by Lewis Terman in 1916 with the famous IQ ratio formula (IQ = MA / CA times 100). Modern SB-5 abandoned the ratio in favor of deviation IQ (M = 100, SD = 15 since 2003).

chunks.heading: Raven’s Progressive Matrices
chunks.text: Raven’s Progressive Matrices Nonverbal, pattern-completion, culture-reduced. Used widely in cross-cultural research and India. Three forms: Standard (SPM), Coloured (CPM, for children and elderly), Advanced (APM, for above-average ability).

chunks.heading: Indian adaptations (high yield for both MET and NIMHANS)
chunks.text: Indian adaptations (high yield for both MET and NIMHANS) Bhatia Battery of Performance Tests of Intelligence : C.M. Bhatia, 1955. Five subtests : Koh’s Block Design, Alexander’s Pass-Along, Pattern Drawing, Immediate Memory, Picture Construction. For ages 11 to 16 with Indian norms. Malin’s Intelligence Scale for Indian Children (MISIC) : WISC adaptation, ages 6 to 15. Binet-Kamat Test (BKT) : Kamat’s Marathi/Kannada adaptation of the Binet. Seguin Form Board : Nonverbal, ages 3 to 7, measures speed of visual-motor coordination. Bhatia having five subtests is a chronic MCQ trap. Memorize the count.

chunks.heading: 6. Personality assessment, two big families
chunks.text: 6. Personality assessment, two big families

chunks.heading: Objective (self-report)
chunks.text: Objective (self-report) The big four to know: MMPI-2 / MMPI-2-RF / MMPI-3 : 10 clinical scales (Hs, D, Hy, Pd, Mf, Pa, Pt, Sc, Ma, Si) plus validity scales (L, F, K). Authored by Hathaway and McKinley. 567 true-false items in MMPI-2. The number is 10 clinical, not 8. NEO-PI-3 : Big Five (OCEAN: Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism). 240 items. By Costa and McCrae. 16PF : Cattell’s 16 primary factors plus 5 globals. 185 items. 16PF is not Big Five ; they are different theories. EPQ-R : Eysenck’s three big traits (Extraversion, Neuroticism, Psychoticism) plus Lie scale.

chunks.heading: Projective (ambiguous stimulus)
chunks.text: Projective (ambiguous stimulus) Theory: ambiguous stimuli pull unconscious material to the surface (projection). Rorschach : 10 inkblots , 5 chromatic and 5 achromatic. Hermann Rorschach, 1921. Modern scoring via Exner Comprehensive System or R-PAS. TAT (Thematic Apperception Test) : 31 cards total , 20 administered per session selected by age and sex of subject. Henry Murray and Christiana Morgan, 1935. Theory: needs-press. CAT (Children’s Apperception Test) : Bellak, 1949. Animal cards for children. Sentence Completion (RISB) : Rotter. Draw-a-Person, House-Tree-Person, Bender-Gestalt : drawing-based; HTP and DAP are Buck/Machover. The card-count traps the MET asks every cycle: - Rorschach = 10 cards (not 12, not 15, not 20). - TAT = 31 total (not 10, not 20).

chunks.heading: 7. Aptitude, attitude, interest, briefly
chunks.text: 7. Aptitude, attitude, interest, briefly DAT (Differential Aptitude Test) : 8 subtests (Verbal, Numerical, Abstract, Mechanical, Space, Spelling, Language, Perceptual). Bennett, Seashore, Wesman. GATB : nine aptitudes, US Employment Service. Attitude scales: - Thurstone (1928) : equal-appearing intervals, judges scale items 1 to 11. - Likert (1932) : summated rating, typically 5-point. - Guttman (1944) : cumulative; endorsing a stronger item implies endorsing weaker ones. - Bogardus : social distance. - Osgood semantic differential : bipolar adjectives, 3 factors (evaluation, potency, activity). Interest inventories: - Strong Interest Inventory : Holland themes (RIASEC) plus occupational scales. - Kuder Career Search : forced-choice triads. - Holland Self-Directed Search : RIASEC (Realistic, Investigative, Artistic, Social, Enterprising, Conventional).

chunks.heading: 8. Psychiatric rating scales, the clinical-tool family
chunks.text: 8. Psychiatric rating scales, the clinical-tool family These come up constantly. Memorize what each scale measures and whether it is clinician-rated or self-rated. Scale Measures Type BDI-II Depression Self, 21 items HAM-D / HDRS Depression Clinician, 17-21 items MADRS Depression Clinician, 10 items PHQ-9 Depression Self, 9 items BAI Anxiety Self, 21 items HAM-A Anxiety Clinician, 14 items GAD-7 Anxiety Self, 7 items Y-BOCS OCD severity (gold standard) Clinician, 10 items PANSS Schizophrenia symptoms (positive + negative) Clinician, 30 items BPRS Brief psychiatric symptoms Clinician, 18 items YMRS Mania Clinician, 11 items MMSE Cognitive screening (general) 30 points, cutoff 23-24 MoCA Mild cognitive impairment 30 points, cutoff 25, more sensitive than MMSE C-SSRS Suicide severity — CAPS-5 PTSD Clinician AUDIT Alcohol use Self The chronic confusions: - Y-BOCS is OCD specifically , not anxiety in general. If a question mentions “obsessive-compulsive severity gold standard”, the answer is Y-BOCS. - PANSS is schizophrenia , covers both positive and negative symptoms. BPRS is briefer and more general. - MMSE has 30 points with a cutoff in the 23-24 range. Frequently asked.

chunks.heading: 9. Educational measurement basics
chunks.text: 9. Educational measurement basics Three distinctions worth knowing: Achievement measures what you have learned (past). Examples: WIAT, school finals. Aptitude measures what you can learn (future). Examples: DAT, SAT. Intelligence measures general cognitive capacity. Examples: WAIS, SB. Scoring frame: - Norm-referenced : compare student to peer group (ranking, selection). - Criterion-referenced : compare student to absolute standard (mastery, licensing). Timing: - Formative : during learning, low-stakes feedback. - Summative : end of unit, high-stakes outcome.

chunks.heading: 10. The 10 traps to memorize cold
chunks.text: 10. The 10 traps to memorize cold Validity has a ceiling at sqrt(reliability). Unreliable tests cannot be strongly valid. Negative discrimination index = miskeyed item. Discard immediately. Cronbach alpha is not unidimensionality. High alpha can mask multiple factors. Wechsler IQ uses SD 15. Old Stanford-Binet used SD 16. Stanine has SD 2, range 1 to 9. Predictive = future criterion. Concurrent = same-time criterion. Face validity is the weakest form. Content validity is expert-judgment of domain coverage. MMPI-2 has 10 clinical scales (Hs D Hy Pd Mf Pa Pt Sc Ma Si). Rorschach = 10 inkblots. TAT = 31 total cards (20 per admin). Y-BOCS = OCD. PANSS = schizophrenia. MMSE = 30 points, cutoff 23-24.

chunks.heading: 11. How to use this primer
chunks.text: 11. How to use this primer Read this top to bottom, even the sections you think you know. Then sit the Bio + Testing 60Q drill at /quiz/bio-testing-paper/ — 30 of those questions are pure assessment. Tag every guess. Anything you miss, jump back to the relevant section here and re-read it. After the drill, you will know roughly which 3-5 facts are not sticking. Tell me which Q numbers you missed and I will hammer those specifically next session. Sihan MET 2026 Prep · Generated 2026-04-25

chunks.heading: Biopsychology — the full chapter, from scratch
chunks.text: Biopsychology — the full chapter, from scratch Read this like a textbook, not a cheatsheet. Every system explained from first principles, then the names, numbers and traps. Anchored to your Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology (11th ed.) , walked through chapter by chapter in book order, prioritised for NIMHANS clinical neuropsychology. Divisions of biopsychology · evolution & genetics · neuroanatomy · neural conduction & synapses · research methods · vision · audition & other senses · sensorimotor · development · brain damage & plasticity · memory & amnesia · hunger · hormones & sex · sleep · addiction & reward · lateralisation & language · emotion & stress · psychiatric disorders · Built 2026-05-05 · Rewritten as a full teaching chapter 2026-05-24 · Expanded to full depth 2026-05-24 (added the landmark experiments walked through step by step, an extended concept bank covering every remaining Pinel term per chapter, an A–Z glossary, and a by-chapter self-test) How to use this page. It is built to learn from , not just revise. Each system has: (1) the problem it solves / what it is for, (2) the core mechanism in plain language with an everyday example, (3) the parts unpacked one by one, then the tables, and (4) a coloured box recapping the exam-testable fact and the trap. Amber boxes = the intuition / why it matters. Green = the line to lock. Red = the MCQ trap. Purple = NIMHANS-speci

chunks.heading: 1. Biopsychology as a neuroscience (Pinel ch. 1)
chunks.text: 1. Biopsychology as a neuroscience (Pinel ch. 1) The one idea behind the whole book. Biopsychology is the scientific study of the biology of behaviour : it asks how the nervous system produces what we think, feel and do. It is one branch of neuroscience (the larger study of the nervous system), the branch that keeps behaviour at the centre. Pinel's recurring lesson is that mind and brain are not two things: every thought is a physical event in tissue.

chunks.heading: The six divisions of biopsychology
chunks.text: The six divisions of biopsychology Pinel splits the field by what you study and how . Learn each by its defining method, because the paper tests "which division does X?". Division What it studies Typical method Physiological psychology Neural mechanisms of behaviour Direct manipulation of the brain in controlled experiments (lesions, stimulation), usually in lab animals Psychopharmacology Effects of drugs on behaviour and the brain Manipulate behaviour with drugs; develop therapeutic drugs Neuropsychology Psychological effects of brain damage in human patients Case studies + standardised tests; the most applied division (NIMHANS leans here) Psychophysiology Relation between physiology and behaviour using non-invasive body measures in healthy humans EEG, heart rate, skin conductance (GSR), pupil size Cognitive neuroscience Neural bases of cognition (thought, memory, attention) Mainly functional brain imaging (fMRI, PET) in humans Comparative psychology Behaviour across species, evolution, genetics, ethology Cross-species comparison, naturalistic + lab study TRAP — psychophysiology vs physiological psychology. Both have "physiolog" in the name. Physiological psychology = invasive manipulation of the brain, usually in animals . Psychophysiology = non-invasive recording from the surface of healthy humans . And neuropsychology = the study of human brain-damaged patients.

chunks.heading: Kinds of research, kinds of inference
chunks.text: Kinds of research, kinds of inference Pure vs applied. Pure = curiosity-driven knowledge; applied = solving a practical problem. Most real work is a blend. Experiments vs non-experiments. Only a true experiment (the researcher manipulates an independent variable and randomly assigns) can support a causal claim. Quasi-experiments and case studies cannot fully rule out confounds. Converging operations. Because every single method is flawed, biopsychology trusts a conclusion only when several different methods point the same way . This is Pinel's signature methodological value. The Morgan's Canon / law of parsimony spirit: prefer the simplest explanation that fits, and do not attribute a higher mental process when a lower one will do. Lock it: human brain-damaged patients = neuropsychology ; drugs = psychopharmacology ; non-invasive measures in healthy humans = psychophysiology ; imaging of cognition = cognitive neuroscience ; animal brain manipulation = physiological psychology ; across species = comparative . Recap §1. Biopsychology = biology of behaviour, six divisions sorted by method. Causation needs a true experiment. Converging operations: trust the conclusion many methods agree on.

chunks.heading: 2. Evolution, genetics & experience (Pinel ch. 2)
chunks.text: 2. Evolution, genetics & experience (Pinel ch. 2) The problem this chapter fixes. The old "nature versus nurture" question is a false dichotomy. Pinel's "nature-nurture done right" is that genes and experience are not rival causes adding up to 100%; they interact continuously. A trait is the product of a genetic program read out in an environment. You cannot say a behaviour is "60% genetic" for an individual, only how much variation in a population is associated with genetic variation (heritability).

chunks.heading: Evolution of the brain
chunks.text: Evolution of the brain Natural selection (Darwin): heritable traits that improve fitness (reproductive success) spread. Behaviour evolves too. Larger brains are not automatically "better"; what matters is brain size relative to body size and the expansion of specific regions, especially the cerebral cortex in primates. Convergent evolution = similar traits arise independently (analogous structures). Homologous structures share a common ancestor. Do not read similarity as shared ancestry. Spandrels & exaptations: not every trait is a direct adaptation; some are by-products later co-opted for new uses.

chunks.heading: Mendelian genetics & the molecular layer
chunks.text: Mendelian genetics & the molecular layer Gene = a stretch of DNA on a chromosome. We have 23 pairs; the 23rd is the sex pair (XX female, XY male). Dominant vs recessive alleles; homozygous vs heterozygous ; genotype (the genes) vs phenotype (the expressed trait). Dizygotic (fraternal) twins share ~50% of genes (like ordinary siblings); monozygotic (identical) twins share ~100%. Comparing them is the classic heritability tool. Central dogma: DNA → (transcription) → mRNA → (translation) → protein.

chunks.heading: Epigenetics: experience changes which genes are read
chunks.text: Epigenetics: experience changes which genes are read Why this matters. Epigenetics is the mechanism that finally dissolves nature-vs-nurture. The DNA sequence does not change, but experience can switch genes on or off via chemical tags, especially DNA methylation (silences genes) and histone modification . These marks can persist and even be inherited. So early experience literally edits gene expression: that is how environment becomes biology.

chunks.heading: Ontogeny vs phylogeny
chunks.text: Ontogeny vs phylogeny Term Meaning Everyday handle Ontogeny Development of the individual across its own lifespan One person growing up Phylogeny Evolutionary history of the species/lineage The family tree of life TRAP: Ontogeny = individual development; phylogeny = species evolution. The mnemonic "ontogeny recapitulates phylogeny" (Haeckel) is largely discredited, but examiners still test which word means which. Also: heritability is a population statistic, not a personal percentage. Recap §2. Genes × experience interact (epigenetics is the bridge: methylation silences genes). Natural selection acts on fitness. Ontogeny = the individual; phylogeny = the species. MZ twins ~100%, DZ ~50%.

chunks.heading: 3. Anatomy of the nervous system (Pinel ch. 3)
chunks.text: 3. Anatomy of the nervous system (Pinel ch. 3) Before any function makes sense you need the map and the cells that build it. We start with the cells, then the divisions, then the protective wrappings, the directions, and finally the brain regions.

chunks.heading: The neuron, part by part
chunks.text: The neuron, part by part Dendrites receive input; surface area is multiplied by spines . Soma (cell body) integrates input; holds nucleus, ribosomes, mitochondria. Axon hillock is the trigger zone; it decides whether threshold is reached. Axon conducts the action potential; may be myelinated. Axon terminals (buttons) release neurotransmitter at the synapse.

chunks.heading: Neuron types by function
chunks.text: Neuron types by function Sensory (afferent) — periphery → CNS. Often pseudounipolar. Motor (efferent) — CNS → muscles/glands. Multipolar. Interneurons — local processing inside the CNS; the most numerous.

chunks.heading: Glia — the six you must know
chunks.text: Glia — the six you must know Cell Location Function Oligodendrocyte CNS Myelinates many axons (one cell, many segments) Schwann cell PNS Myelinates one axon segment per cell; aids PNS regeneration Astrocyte CNS Blood-brain barrier, K⁺ buffering, NT recycling, structural support Microglia CNS Immune defence, phagocytosis Ependymal cell Ventricles Produces and circulates CSF Satellite cell PNS ganglia Supports cell bodies in the PNS TRAP: CNS myelination = oligodendrocyte ; PNS myelination = Schwann cell . And Schwann cells, not oligodendrocytes, support axonal regeneration (see §10).

chunks.heading: The divisions: CNS and PNS
chunks.text: The divisions: CNS and PNS Nervous System ├── CNS (brain + spinal cord) └── PNS ├── Somatic NS (voluntary, skeletal muscle; afferent + efferent) └── Autonomic NS ├── Sympathetic ("fight/flight") — thoracolumbar, NE ├── Parasympathetic ("rest/digest") — craniosacral, ACh └── Enteric ("gut brain")

chunks.heading: Autonomic contrasts
chunks.text: Autonomic contrasts Sympathetic Parasympathetic Origin T1–L2 (thoracolumbar) CN III, VII, IX, X + S2–S4 (craniosacral) Pre/post-ganglionic NT ACh / NE ACh / ACh Heart ↑ rate ↓ rate (vagus) Pupil Dilate Constrict GI motility ↓ ↑ Sweat glands ACh (exception) —

chunks.heading: Meninges, CSF and ventricles
chunks.text: Meninges, CSF and ventricles The CNS is protected by three membranes, the meninges , from outside in: dura mater (tough outer), arachnoid mater (web-like middle), pia mater (delicate, hugs the brain). Between arachnoid and pia is the subarachnoid space , filled with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) . CSF cushions the brain, removes waste, and lets it float (reducing effective weight). It is produced by the choroid plexus in the ventricles. Ventricles: two lateral → third → cerebral aqueduct → fourth → central canal / subarachnoid space. Blockage causes hydrocephalus .

chunks.heading: Directional terms (orient yourself before lesions)
chunks.text: Directional terms (orient yourself before lesions) Term Means Anterior / rostral Toward the front (nose) Posterior / caudal Toward the back (tail) Dorsal Toward the back/top (in the brain, top) Ventral Toward the belly/bottom Medial / lateral Toward / away from the midline Ipsilateral / contralateral Same side / opposite side

chunks.heading: Forebrain, midbrain, hindbrain
chunks.text: Forebrain, midbrain, hindbrain Region Structures Function Forebrain (prosencephalon) Cerebral cortex, basal ganglia, limbic system, thalamus, hypothalamus Higher cognition, emotion, motor planning, autonomic control Midbrain (mesencephalon) Tectum (superior + inferior colliculi), tegmentum, substantia nigra, red nucleus, PAG Visual/auditory reflexes, motor control, pain modulation Hindbrain (rhombencephalon) Pons, medulla, cerebellum Vital functions (breathing, heart rate), balance, fine motor coordination Quick handle for the colliculi: S uperior colliculus = S ight (visual reflexes/orienting); I nferior colliculus = " I hear" (auditory). The brainstem = midbrain + pons + medulla, the part keeping you alive.

chunks.heading: Cortex — the four lobes
chunks.text: Cortex — the four lobes Lobe Key areas Lesion produces Frontal Motor cortex (precentral gyrus), prefrontal, Broca's (L) Paralysis, executive deficits, Broca's aphasia, personality change (Phineas Gage) Parietal Somatosensory cortex (postcentral gyrus), association cortex Hemispatial neglect if right, Gerstmann's syndrome if left, agnosia Temporal Primary auditory, Wernicke's (L), hippocampus, amygdala Wernicke's aphasia, anterograde amnesia, Klüver-Bucy Occipital Primary visual (V1), visual association Cortical blindness, visual agnosia, prosopagnosia (fusiform) The cortex is mostly six-layered neocortex . The deep grey matter and limbic structures sit below it.

chunks.heading: Subcortical structures
chunks.text: Subcortical structures Thalamus — sensory relay for all senses except smell . LGN (vision), MGN (hearing), VPL (body touch), VPM (face). Hypothalamus — homeostasis, hormones, the "4 Fs" (feeding, fighting, fleeing, mating). VMH lesion = hyperphagia + obesity; LH lesion = aphagia; suprachiasmatic nucleus = circadian clock; supraoptic → ADH; paraventricular → oxytocin + CRH. Basal ganglia — caudate, putamen, globus pallidus, subthalamic nucleus, substantia nigra. Red nucleus is NOT basal ganglia (it is midbrain tegmentum). Function: motor initiation/selection. Lesions: Parkinson's (SN), Huntington's (caudate/putamen), hemiballismus (subthalamic). Limbic system — hippocampus (memory), amygdala (fear), cingulate (emotion/attention), fornix, mammillary bodies, septum. Cerebellum — coordination, timing, motor learning. Lesions: ataxia, dysmetria, intention tremor.

chunks.heading: Hemisphere specialisation (overview; full treatment in §16)
chunks.text: Hemisphere specialisation (overview; full treatment in §16) Left: language (Broca, Wernicke), logic, sequential processing, calculation. Right: spatial, music, faces, holistic, emotional prosody. Corpus callosum — the major commissure; severance produces the split-brain (Sperry, Gazzaniga).

chunks.heading: The 12 cranial nerves
chunks.text: The 12 cranial nerves # Name Type Function I Olfactory S Smell. Only CN that does NOT relay through the thalamus. II Optic S Vision. Decussates at the optic chiasm . III Oculomotor M Most extraocular muscles, levator palpebrae, pupillary constriction. IV Trochlear M Superior oblique only. Smallest CN. V Trigeminal B Face sensation, mastication. VI Abducens M Lateral rectus only. VII Facial B Facial expression, taste (anterior 2/3 tongue), salivation, lacrimation. VIII Vestibulocochlear S Hearing + balance. IX Glossopharyngeal B Taste (posterior 1/3), pharynx, parotid. X Vagus B Parasympathetic to thorax/abdomen, larynx, pharynx. XI Spinal accessory M SCM and trapezius. XII Hypoglossal M Tongue movement. Mnemonic: "Some Say Marry Money But My Brother Says Big Brains Matter Most" → S = sensory, M = motor, B = both, in order I–XII. Recap §3. CNS + PNS (somatic + autonomic). Meninges DAP (dura-arachnoid-pia), CSF from choroid plexus through ventricles. Forebrain/midbrain/hindbrain. Thalamus relays all but smell; hypothalamus runs homeostasis. Glia: oligo (CNS) vs Schwann (PNS).

chunks.heading: 4. Neural conduction & synaptic transmission (Pinel ch. 4)
chunks.text: 4. Neural conduction & synaptic transmission (Pinel ch. 4) Full primer: action potential page . Here is the teaching version.

chunks.heading: The resting potential: why a neuron sits charged
