chunks.text: The resting potential: why a neuron sits charged An unstimulated neuron holds its inside about −70 mV negative to the outside. Three forces set this up: the Na⁺/K⁺ pump (pushes 3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in, using ATP), leaky K⁺ channels (K⁺ drifts out down its gradient), and large negative proteins trapped inside. The membrane is a charged battery waiting to discharge.

chunks.heading: The action potential, step by step
chunks.text: The action potential, step by step Threshold ~ −55 mV must be reached at the axon hillock. Depolarisation: voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open → Na⁺ rushes in → spike to ~ +30 mV. Repolarisation: Na⁺ channels inactivate; voltage-gated K⁺ channels open → K⁺ flows out. Hyperpolarisation (undershoot): K⁺ channels close slowly → dips below −70 mV briefly. All-or-none law: once threshold is reached the AP fires at constant amplitude . Stimulus intensity is coded by frequency of firing, never by spike size.

chunks.heading: Refractory periods
chunks.text: Refractory periods Absolute refractory period — Na⁺ channels inactivated; no stimulus, however strong, can fire another AP. This sets the maximum firing rate and forces the AP to travel one way. Relative refractory period — membrane is hyperpolarised; a stronger-than-usual stimulus can fire one.

chunks.heading: Saltatory conduction
chunks.text: Saltatory conduction In myelinated axons the AP regenerates only at the Nodes of Ranvier and "jumps" between them. This is faster and far more energy-efficient than continuous conduction. Demyelination (as in MS ) destroys this and slows or blocks conduction.

chunks.heading: The synapse: step by step
chunks.text: The synapse: step by step AP arrives at the terminal. Voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels open; Ca²⁺ enters. Vesicles fuse with the presynaptic membrane (SNARE proteins) and release NT. NT crosses the cleft and binds postsynaptic receptors. EPSP (depolarising) or IPSP (hyperpolarising); spatial + temporal summation at the axon hillock decides if a new AP fires. NT is cleared by reuptake , enzymatic breakdown , or diffusion . Receptors come in two styles: ionotropic (ligand-gated ion channels, fast, e.g. nicotinic ACh, GABA-A, AMPA/NMDA) and metabotropic (G-protein-coupled, slower, longer-lasting, e.g. muscarinic ACh, most dopamine receptors). Autoreceptors on the presynaptic terminal sense the cell's own NT and provide feedback.

chunks.heading: The seven neurotransmitter families (high-yield)
chunks.text: The seven neurotransmitter families (high-yield) NT Class Made from Cleared by Clinical link Acetylcholine (ACh) Quaternary amine Choline + acetyl-CoA Acetylcholinesterase Alzheimer's (low ACh), myasthenia gravis (anti-AChR), NMJ Dopamine Catecholamine Tyrosine → DOPA → DA Reuptake, MAO, COMT ↑ mesolimbic = +ve schizophrenia. Low nigrostriatal = Parkinson's. Reward / addiction. Norepinephrine Catecholamine DA + β-hydroxylase Reuptake, MAO Arousal, sympathetic. Locus coeruleus. Low in depression. Serotonin (5-HT) Indolamine Tryptophan Reuptake (SERT), MAO Mood, sleep, appetite. Low → depression, OCD. Raphe nuclei. Glutamate Amino acid Glutamine Reuptake by astrocytes Main excitatory NT. NMDA, AMPA, kainate. LTP, learning. Excess = excitotoxicity. GABA Amino acid Glutamate (via GAD) Reuptake Main inhibitory NT. GABA-A = ionotropic, target of benzos, alcohol, barbiturates. Endorphins Peptide POMC Peptidases Pain modulation, runner's high. μ, κ, δ receptors. TRAP: LTP in hippocampus depends on NMDA receptors. NMDA = a coincidence detector : it needs glutamate AND postsynaptic depolarisation to displace its Mg²⁺ block. Ca²⁺ entry through NMDA triggers LTP; AMPA carries the fast EPSP. Dopamine is built from tyrosine , serotonin from tryptophan , do not swap the precursors. Recap §4. Rest −70 mV (Na/K pump + leaky K⁺) → threshold −55 → Na⁺ in (depolarise) → K⁺ out (repolarise). All-or

chunks.heading: 5. Research methods of biopsychology (Pinel ch. 5)
chunks.text: 5. Research methods of biopsychology (Pinel ch. 5) Every claim about brain and behaviour rests on a method, and every method answers a different question. Pinel groups them into lesion, recording, imaging, and stimulation.

chunks.heading: Lesion / ablation methods
chunks.text: Lesion / ablation methods Ablation / lesion: remove or destroy tissue and observe the behavioural deficit (the oldest approach). Aspiration (suction), radio-frequency / electrolytic lesions, knife cuts , and chemical excitotoxic lesions (kainic acid spares fibres of passage, killing only cell bodies). Reversible lesions: cooling or local anaesthetic (lidocaine) temporarily knock out a region, then it recovers, a cleaner causal test. Stereotaxic surgery: the stereotaxic atlas + instrument lets you reach a deep target by 3-D coordinates from the bregma landmark on the skull. This is how electrodes and cannulae are placed.

chunks.heading: Recording methods
chunks.text: Recording methods Method What it records Strength Single-unit recording Firing of one neuron via a microelectrode Best spatial + temporal resolution (one cell) EEG Summed cortical electrical activity from scalp electrodes Excellent temporal resolution; poor spatial. Used for sleep stages, seizures, ERPs Event-related potential (ERP) EEG time-locked and averaged to a stimulus Tracks the timing of cognitive processing (e.g. P300, N400)

chunks.heading: Imaging methods
chunks.text: Imaging methods Method What it shows Note CT (CAT) X-ray structural image Fast, good for bleeds/fractures; uses radiation MRI Structural image from magnetic fields Higher resolution than CT, no radiation fMRI Function: the BOLD signal (blood oxygenation) Good spatial resolution, slower temporal; the workhorse of cognitive neuroscience PET Function: metabolism/blood flow via radioactive tracer (e.g. 2-DG, or ligands for receptors) Can map neurotransmitter receptors; uses radiation DTI White-matter tracts (diffusion of water) Maps connectivity TRAP — structure vs function and resolution. CT/MRI = structure ; fMRI/PET = function . EEG = great timing, poor location; fMRI = great location, poorer timing. Examiners pair these opposites. BOLD is the fMRI signal.

chunks.heading: Stimulation methods
chunks.text: Stimulation methods Electrical brain stimulation (ESB): drive a region and see the evoked behaviour (Penfield's cortical mapping; Olds & Milner's reward stimulation). Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS): a magnetic pulse non-invasively excites or transiently disrupts a cortical area, a "virtual lesion" in healthy humans, and a treatment for depression. Optogenetics (newer): light switches genetically modified neurons on/off with millisecond precision.

chunks.heading: Psychophysiological measures (non-invasive, on the body)
chunks.text: Psychophysiological measures (non-invasive, on the body) Skin conductance (SCR/GSR) — sympathetic arousal via sweat; used in lie detection and emotion research. ECG / heart rate , EMG (muscle), EOG (eye movement), pupillometry . Lock the pairings: deep target by coordinates = stereotaxic ; one neuron = single-unit ; timing of cognition = ERP/EEG ; non-invasive virtual lesion = TMS ; receptor mapping = PET ; structure = CT/MRI; function = fMRI/PET. Recap §5. Lesion (incl. reversible) + stereotaxic placement; recording (single-unit, EEG, ERP); imaging (CT/MRI structure, fMRI/PET function); stimulation (ESB, TMS, optogenetics); psychophysiology (SCR, HR, EMG, EOG).

chunks.heading: 6. The visual system (Pinel ch. 6)
chunks.text: 6. The visual system (Pinel ch. 6) Vision is the model sensory system in Pinel because we know its wiring best. The job: turn patterns of light into a neural representation of the world.

chunks.heading: The retina: where light becomes neural signal
chunks.text: The retina: where light becomes neural signal Light passes through the retina's layers to reach the photoreceptors at the back, so the retina is "inside out". Rods — peripheral, very light-sensitive, no colour, low acuity (night/scotopic vision). Cones — concentrated at the fovea , colour, high acuity (day/photopic vision). Cones are densest at the fovea centralis. The optic disc (where the optic nerve leaves) has no photoreceptors = the blind spot . Signal flow within the retina: photoreceptors → bipolar cells → retinal ganglion cells (whose axons form the optic nerve), with horizontal and amacrine cells doing lateral interaction. Lateral inhibition sharpens edges (Mach bands).

chunks.heading: The retina-geniculate-striate pathway
chunks.text: The retina-geniculate-striate pathway Retina → optic nerve → optic chiasm (nasal fibres cross, so the left visual field of both eyes goes right) → optic tract → LGN of the thalamus → optic radiations → primary visual cortex (V1 / striate cortex) in the occipital lobe. The map is retinotopic (neighbouring retina → neighbouring cortex). Hubel & Wiesel found V1 cells are feature detectors (simple, complex, hypercomplex cells tuned to edges and orientation).

chunks.heading: Two cortical streams: what vs where
chunks.text: Two cortical streams: what vs where Stream Route Job Lesion Ventral ("what") V1 → temporal lobe Object and face recognition Visual agnosia, prosopagnosia Dorsal ("where / how") V1 → parietal lobe Spatial location, visually guided action Optic ataxia, neglect

chunks.heading: Theories of colour vision (these are complementary, not rivals)
chunks.text: Theories of colour vision (these are complementary, not rivals) Trichromatic (Young-Helmholtz) — three cone types (S/M/L, "blue/green/red"); colour = ratio of their activity. Operates at the receptor (retinal) level . Opponent-process (Hering) — colour coded in opposing pairs: red-green, blue-yellow, black-white. Operates after the retina (ganglion cells, LGN). Explains negative afterimages and why we never see "reddish-green". TRAP: the two colour theories are both right at different stages : trichromatic at the cones, opponent-process downstream. Negative afterimages = opponent-process evidence. Rods do not code colour. Dorsal = where/how (parietal), Ventral = what (temporal): "dorsal is up and points to where". Recap §6. Rods (dim, no colour) vs cones (fovea, colour). Pathway: retina → chiasm → LGN → V1. Dorsal = where (parietal), ventral = what (temporal). Colour = trichromatic at cones + opponent-process after.

chunks.heading: 7. Mechanisms of perception: audition & the other senses (Pinel ch. 7)
chunks.text: 7. Mechanisms of perception: audition & the other senses (Pinel ch. 7)

chunks.heading: Audition
chunks.text: Audition Path: outer ear → middle ear ossicles ( malleus, incus, stapes ) → inner ear cochlea . Hair cells on the basilar membrane → CN VIII → cochlear nuclei → superior olive → inferior colliculus → MGN of thalamus → primary auditory cortex ( Heschl's gyrus , temporal lobe).

chunks.heading: How is pitch coded? Three theories
chunks.text: How is pitch coded? Three theories Theory Mechanism Best for Place theory (von Békésy) Different frequencies peak at different places on the basilar membrane: high at the base , low at the apex High frequencies Frequency (temporal) theory The whole membrane fires at the rate of the sound's frequency Low frequencies (< ~500 Hz) Volley principle Groups of neurons fire in rotating "volleys" to track frequencies above any single neuron's limit Mid-range (bridges the two) TRAP: Place = high frequency (base of cochlea), frequency theory = low , volley = middle . Loudness is coded by firing rate + number of hair cells, not by place.

chunks.heading: Somatosensation: two ascending highways
chunks.text: Somatosensation: two ascending highways Dorsal column–medial lemniscus (DCML) Anterolateral / spinothalamic Carries Fine touch, vibration, proprioception Pain, temperature, crude touch Decussates In the medulla (high up) At the spinal level of entry (immediately) Speed/fibres Fast, large myelinated Slower, small fibres Why the decussation level matters clinically. Because the two systems cross at different levels, a one-sided spinal cord lesion ( Brown-Séquard ) loses fine touch/proprioception on the same side (DCML crosses later, up in the medulla) but pain/temperature on the opposite side (spinothalamic crossed immediately). That dissociation is a favourite exam item. Pain & gate control (Melzack & Wall): non-painful input (rubbing) can "close a gate" in the dorsal horn and reduce pain; descending signals from the PAG (periaqueductal grey), via endorphins, also dampen pain.

chunks.heading: Chemical senses
chunks.text: Chemical senses Taste (gustation): five basics, sweet, salty, sour, bitter, umami. CN VII (anterior 2/3 tongue), IX (posterior 1/3), X (epiglottis). Insula = primary gustatory cortex. Smell (olfaction): olfactory epithelium → olfactory bulb → piriform cortex , with no thalamic relay (the exception). Direct limbic ties explain odour-evoked emotional memory.

chunks.heading: Attention
chunks.text: Attention Perception is selective. Cocktail-party effect : you track one voice in a crowd, yet your own name still breaks through (so unattended channels are partly processed). The posterior parietal cortex and frontal eye fields shift spatial attention; damage to the right parietal causes hemispatial neglect (§19). Pinel distinguishes endogenous (goal-driven, top-down) from exogenous (stimulus-driven, bottom-up) attention. Recap §7. Audition: ossicles → cochlea → basilar membrane → MGN → Heschl's gyrus; place=high, frequency=low, volley=mid. Touch: DCML (fine touch, crosses in medulla) vs spinothalamic (pain/temp, crosses at entry). Smell skips the thalamus. Attention: endogenous vs exogenous.

chunks.heading: 8. The sensorimotor system (Pinel ch. 8)
chunks.text: 8. The sensorimotor system (Pinel ch. 8) The organising idea: a hierarchy. Movement is planned top-down and executed bottom-up. High levels set goals; low levels handle the muscle detail; sensory feedback flows back up. The chain runs: association cortex (intention) → secondary motor cortex (SMA + premotor, the plan) → primary motor cortex M1 (the command) → brainstem & spinal circuits → muscle , with the basal ganglia and cerebellum tuning it from the side.

chunks.heading: Pyramidal tract (corticospinal)
chunks.text: Pyramidal tract (corticospinal) Origin: primary motor cortex (M1, Brodmann area 4) and premotor. Path: internal capsule → cerebral peduncle → pons → medullary pyramids. Decussates at the pyramids of the medulla (~85–90%) → lateral corticospinal tract (fine, distal, voluntary movement). The remaining 10–15% form the anterior corticospinal tract and decussate at the spinal segment.

chunks.heading: Extrapyramidal pathways
chunks.text: Extrapyramidal pathways Rubrospinal — from the red nucleus; flexor bias. Vestibulospinal — postural extensors, balance. Reticulospinal — locomotion, posture, gross movements. Tectospinal — head/neck orienting to stimuli.

chunks.heading: Who does what in the hierarchy (NIMHANS swap-traps)
chunks.text: Who does what in the hierarchy (NIMHANS swap-traps) Structure Job Lock the trap Posterior parietal association cortex Integrates body position + external space to form the intention to move and guide reaching. Lesion → apraxia, neglect. Premotor cortex Plans externally / sensory-cued movement: you see something and reach for it. Preps posture and muscle groups before M1 fires. Premotor = external / cue-driven . SMA (supplementary motor area) Plans internally generated, self-initiated movement; sequencing complex moves from memory + bimanual coordination. SMA = internal / from within . (premotor vs SMA = external vs internal, that one distinction is half the question) Primary motor cortex (M1) Issues the movement command; somatotopically organised (the motor homunculus ). Lesion → contralateral weakness/paralysis. Basal ganglia Initiate / select movement and gate it (move or not). Set the vigour : scale force and amplitude . Bradykinesia in Parkinson's is this failing. "Scales force / amplitude / vigour" → basal ganglia . Lesions go two ways: Parkinson's (hypokinetic, resting tremor) and Huntington's / chorea (hyperkinetic). Cerebellum Coordination, timing, balance, error correction, motor learning. Compares intended vs actual and smooths speed/accuracy while the movement is happening . "Timing / smoothing / coordination" → cerebellum . Lesions = ataxia, intention tremor, dysmet

chunks.heading: Upper vs lower motor neuron signs
chunks.text: Upper vs lower motor neuron signs UMN lesion LMN lesion Tone Spasticity (↑) Flaccidity (↓) Reflexes Hyperreflexia, clonus, + Babinski Hyporeflexia / areflexia Atrophy Mild, late (disuse) Severe, early Fasciculations Absent Present Lock it: UMN = spastic, hyperreflexic, Babinski up, no fasciculations. LMN = flaccid, areflexic, atrophy + fasciculations. (ALS strikes both.) Recap §8. Hierarchy: association cortex → SMA (internal) / premotor (external) → M1 → brainstem/spinal → muscle. Pyramidal crosses at the medullary pyramids. Basal ganglia = force/gating (resting tremor); cerebellum = timing/coordination (intention tremor). UMN spastic vs LMN flaccid.

chunks.heading: 9. Development of the nervous system (Pinel ch. 9)
chunks.text: 9. Development of the nervous system (Pinel ch. 9) The question: how does a single fertilised cell become a brain with ~86 billion neurons wired into the right circuits? Pinel walks five phases, then myelination and pruning. Neural tube formation (neurulation): the ectoderm folds into the neural tube (~week 3–4); its hollow centre becomes the ventricles, the anterior end becomes the brain. Failure = spina bifida / anencephaly (folic acid protects). Proliferation: cells in the ventricular zone divide to produce neurons and glia. Migration: new neurons travel to their destinations, many guided along radial glia ; the cortex is built inside-out (deep layers first). Differentiation & axon growth: neurons take on their type; the growth cone navigates by chemical cues (chemoaffinity, Sperry). Synaptogenesis: synapses form, in huge excess at first. Then two sculpting processes refine the over-built brain: Neural death (apoptosis) & synaptic pruning: ~50% of neurons die, and unused synapses are eliminated. Neurotrophins (e.g. NGF) keep useful connections alive: "use it or lose it". Myelination: continues for years after birth (the prefrontal cortex finishes myelinating in the early–mid 20s, which is why mature judgement comes late). Critical / sensitive periods. Some circuits must get the right experience within a time window or they wire abnormally for life. Hubel & Wiesel's monocular

chunks.heading: 10. Brain damage & neuroplasticity (Pinel ch. 10)
chunks.text: 10. Brain damage & neuroplasticity (Pinel ch. 10)

chunks.heading: Causes of brain damage
chunks.text: Causes of brain damage Cause Key facts Tumours (neoplasms) Encapsulated/benign (meningioma) vs infiltrating/malignant (glioma); metastatic from elsewhere. Cerebrovascular (stroke) Ischaemic (clot: thrombosis/embolism) vs haemorrhagic (bleed). Penumbra = salvageable tissue. Excitotoxic glutamate cascade kills neurons. Traumatic brain injury (TBI) Closed-head: contusions, contrecoup injury, concussion. Repeated TBI → chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) . Infections Encephalitis, meningitis, abscess; neurosyphilis. Neurotoxins Heavy metals (lead, mercury), MPTP (causes Parkinsonism), alcohol. Genetic / programmed See the genetic-disorders table below and the dementias.

chunks.heading: Degeneration & regeneration
chunks.text: Degeneration & regeneration Anterograde degeneration = the cut axon segment away from the cell body dies. Retrograde = the segment toward the cell body (and sometimes the cell) degenerates. Regeneration is much better in the PNS than the CNS, largely because Schwann cells (PNS) guide and support regrowth, whereas CNS oligodendrocytes /glial scarring inhibit it.

chunks.heading: Plasticity & recovery of function
chunks.text: Plasticity & recovery of function The brain rewires. "Plasticity" means the brain changes its structure and connections with experience and after injury. Mechanisms of recovery: cortical reorganisation (neighbouring areas take over), collateral sprouting , redundant circuits, and behaviourally driven relearning (the basis of rehabilitation). Adult neurogenesis occurs in the hippocampal dentate gyrus and the olfactory bulb/SVZ, but is limited.

chunks.heading: The major neurological disorders & dementias (NIMHANS-weighted)
chunks.text: The major neurological disorders & dementias (NIMHANS-weighted) Disorder Pathology Hallmark Alzheimer's disease Amyloid-β plaques + tau neurofibrillary tangles ; loss of cholinergic neurons (nucleus basalis of Meynert) Progressive anterograde memory loss first; treated with cholinesterase inhibitors + memantine (NMDA) Parkinson's disease Loss of dopamine neurons in substantia nigra (pars compacta) ; Lewy bodies (α-synuclein) Resting tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, postural instability; L-DOPA Huntington's disease Caudate/putamen atrophy; CAG expansion (HTT, chr 4), autosomal dominant Chorea + cognitive decline + psychiatric change; anticipation across generations Multiple sclerosis (MS) Autoimmune demyelination of CNS white matter Relapsing-remitting deficits; slowed conduction (loss of saltatory conduction) Epilepsy Hypersynchronous neuronal discharge Generalised (e.g. tonic-clonic, absence) vs focal/partial; aura, ictal, post-ictal

chunks.heading: Genetic disorders (retained, high-yield)
chunks.text: Genetic disorders (retained, high-yield) Disorder Genetics Notes Huntington's disease Autosomal dominant; CAG trinucleotide expansion on chromosome 4 (HTT gene) Anticipation across generations. Caudate atrophy, chorea, dementia, onset age 30–50. Down syndrome Trisomy 21 Intellectual disability, characteristic features, ↑ Alzheimer's risk. Fragile X X-linked CGG expansion (FMR1) Most common inherited cause of intellectual disability. PKU Autosomal recessive Phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency. Diet treatable; untreated → intellectual disability. Klinefelter XXY Male, hypogonadism, mild learning issues. Turner XO Female, short stature, gonadal dysgenesis. TRAP: Alzheimer's = plaques (amyloid) + tangles (tau) , memory-first. Parkinson's = substantia nigra dopamine loss + Lewy bodies , movement-first. Huntington's = caudate, CAG, dominant . Adult neurogenesis happens mainly in the hippocampal dentate gyrus . PNS (Schwann) regenerates better than CNS. Recap §10. Damage from tumour/stroke (ischaemic vs haemorrhagic)/TBI/infection/toxin. PNS regenerates better (Schwann). Plasticity drives recovery; neurogenesis in dentate gyrus. Dementias: Alzheimer's (plaques+tangles), Parkinson's (SN/Lewy), Huntington's (caudate/CAG), MS (demyelination).

chunks.heading: 11. Learning, memory & amnesia (Pinel ch. 11)
chunks.text: 11. Learning, memory & amnesia (Pinel ch. 11) The landmark case that built the field. Patient H.M. had both medial temporal lobes (including the hippocampus) removed in 1953 to stop seizures. He could no longer form new long-term explicit memories (severe anterograde amnesia ) yet kept old memories, normal IQ, and could still learn new motor skills (mirror drawing) without remembering having practised. This single dissociation proved (1) the hippocampus is needed to form new declarative memories but is not the storehouse, and (2) declarative and procedural memory are separate systems.

chunks.heading: The taxonomy of memory
chunks.text: The taxonomy of memory Type Subtype Brain region Declarative (explicit) Episodic (events) Hippocampus + medial temporal lobe Semantic (facts) Temporal neocortex Non-declarative (implicit) Procedural (skills, habits) Striatum / basal ganglia Classical conditioning (motor) Cerebellum Emotional conditioning Amygdala Patient K.C. lost episodic memory (could not re-experience events) but kept semantic knowledge, dissociating the two. Amygdala = emotional memory and fear conditioning; cerebellum = conditioned motor responses (eyeblink); striatum = habit/procedural learning.

chunks.heading: Long-term potentiation (LTP): the synaptic mechanism
chunks.text: Long-term potentiation (LTP): the synaptic mechanism LTP = a long-lasting strengthening of a synapse after high-frequency stimulation, the leading cellular model of learning, first shown in the hippocampus. It depends on the NMDA receptor , a coincidence detector: it opens only when glutamate binds and the postsynaptic cell is already depolarised (relieving its Mg²⁺ block). Ca²⁺ then floods in and drives AMPA receptor insertion , making the synapse stronger. This is the molecular face of Hebb's rule: "neurons that fire together wire together." LTD (long-term depression) is the opposite, weakening unused synapses; both enable plasticity.

chunks.heading: Amnesias
chunks.text: Amnesias Anterograde = cannot form new memories after the event (H.M.). Retrograde = lost memories from before the event. Ribot's law: recent memories are more vulnerable than remote ones. Korsakoff's syndrome = thiamine (B1) deficiency , usually from chronic alcoholism; damages the mammillary bodies + dorsomedial thalamus . Hallmark: dense anterograde amnesia + confabulation . The acute precursor is Wernicke's encephalopathy (confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia), together Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome (see §19). The engram = the physical memory trace; Lashley searched for it (mass action / equipotentiality), Richard Semon coined the term, and modern work locates engram cells in the hippocampus. TRAP: H.M. = bilateral medial temporal/hippocampus → anterograde amnesia, intact procedural learning. Korsakoff = thiamine , mammillary bodies + thalamus, confabulation . Hippocampus forms declarative memory but is not the permanent store. LTP needs NMDA ; AMPA carries the fast current. Recap §11. H.M. → hippocampus forms new declarative memory; procedural is separate (striatum/cerebellum/amygdala). LTP via NMDA + Ca²⁺ → AMPA insertion = Hebbian learning. Korsakoff = thiamine + mammillary bodies + confabulation.

chunks.heading: 12. Hunger, eating & health (Pinel ch. 12)
chunks.text: 12. Hunger, eating & health (Pinel ch. 12) The classic theory and its limits. The old dual-centre hypothalamic hypothesis said the lateral hypothalamus (LH) is the "hunger/go" centre and the ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH) is the "satiety/stop" centre. Lesion evidence: VMH lesion → hyperphagia + obesity (the rat overeats); LH lesion → aphagia (the rat stops eating). True but oversimplified, eating is regulated by a network and many peptides, not two switches.

chunks.heading: The hormonal signals
chunks.text: The hormonal signals Signal Source Effect on appetite Leptin Adipose (fat) tissue ↓ appetite (long-term adiposity signal); acts via the arcuate nucleus Ghrelin Stomach (empty) ↑ appetite (the "hunger hormone") Insulin Pancreas ↑ satiety; glucose uptake CCK Duodenum ↑ short-term satiety (meal termination) PYY Intestine ↓ appetite after eating

chunks.heading: Two competing frameworks for regulation
chunks.text: Two competing frameworks for regulation Set-point theory: the body defends a fixed weight/energy level like a thermostat; you eat to correct a deficit. Explains homeostasis but not why we eat when full or why obesity is rising. Positive-incentive theory (Pinel favours this): we eat largely because of the anticipated pleasure of food (its incentive value), shaped by taste, learning, and availability, not just internal depletion. Explains overeating in a food-rich world.

chunks.heading: Disorders of eating
chunks.text: Disorders of eating Obesity: mismatch between an evolved drive to store energy and an environment of cheap palatable food; leptin resistance in many cases. Anorexia nervosa (restriction, low weight, body-image disturbance) and bulimia nervosa (binge-purge); high mortality for anorexia. TRAP: VMH = satiety (lesion → obese); LH = feeding (lesion → aphagia). Leptin from fat lowers appetite; ghrelin from the stomach raises it (do not swap). Pinel argues positive-incentive beats pure set-point. Recap §12. VMH satiety / LH hunger. Leptin (fat) ↓ appetite via arcuate; ghrelin (stomach) ↑; insulin/CCK/PYY ↑ satiety. Set-point vs positive-incentive (Pinel prefers incentive).

chunks.heading: 13. Hormones & sex (Pinel ch. 13)
chunks.text: 13. Hormones & sex (Pinel ch. 13) The endocrine system is the body's slow, broadcast signalling system: glands release hormones into the blood to act on distant targets. The brain commands it through the hypothalamus → pituitary link.

chunks.heading: The endocrine map
chunks.text: The endocrine map Gland Hormone Action Hypothalamus CRH, TRH, GHRH, GnRH, somatostatin, dopamine Releasing/inhibiting factors to the anterior pituitary Anterior pituitary ACTH, TSH, GH, FSH/LH, prolactin Trophic hormones Posterior pituitary ADH (vasopressin), oxytocin Made in hypothalamus, stored/released by posterior pituitary. ADH → water reabsorption. Oxytocin → labour, milk ejection, bonding. Adrenal cortex Cortisol, aldosterone, DHEA Stress, salt/water, sex precursor Adrenal medulla Epinephrine, NE Sympathetic surge Thyroid T3, T4, calcitonin Metabolism, Ca regulation Pineal Melatonin Circadian rhythm Pancreas Insulin, glucagon Glucose regulation Gonads Testosterone (testes), estradiol + progesterone (ovaries) Reproduction, sexual differentiation TRAP: ADH and oxytocin are made in the hypothalamus (supraoptic + paraventricular nuclei) and merely released by the posterior pituitary , which makes no hormones of its own. ADH = water reabsorption.

chunks.heading: The HPG axis & sexual differentiation
chunks.text: The HPG axis & sexual differentiation The hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal (HPG) axis: hypothalamus → GnRH → pituitary → FSH/LH → gonads → sex steroids. Development of sex: Genetic sex set at fertilisation (XX/XY). The SRY gene on the Y triggers the gonads to become testes; without it they become ovaries. Testes secrete testosterone (masculinises the Wolffian ducts) and anti-Müllerian hormone (regresses the female ducts). Pinel's principle: development defaults toward female unless androgens intervene ("add testosterone to masculinise").

chunks.heading: Organizational vs activational effects (the key distinction)
chunks.text: Organizational vs activational effects (the key distinction) Organizational Activational When Early (perinatal) critical period Later (puberty onward), reversible What it does Permanently wires the brain/body along male or female lines Switches on behaviours in already-organised tissue (e.g. testosterone boosting libido in an adult) Lock it: organizational = early + permanent structuring; activational = later + reversible switching. SRY → testes → testosterone; the default body plan is female. Recap §13. Hypothalamus → pituitary → targets. Posterior pituitary only stores ADH/oxytocin. HPG: GnRH → FSH/LH → gonads. SRY makes testes; default is female. Organizational (early, permanent) vs activational (later, reversible) hormone effects.

chunks.heading: 14. Sleep, dreaming & circadian rhythms (Pinel ch. 14)
chunks.text: 14. Sleep, dreaming & circadian rhythms (Pinel ch. 14) Full primer: sleep page .

chunks.heading: The stages of sleep (read off the EEG)
chunks.text: The stages of sleep (read off the EEG) NREM 1 — theta waves, easy to wake, hypnic jerks. NREM 2 — sleep spindles + K-complexes ; ~50% of total sleep. NREM 3 — delta (slow-wave) sleep. Deep, restorative, growth hormone, sleepwalking/night terrors arise here. REM — desynchronised low-voltage EEG resembling waking, rapid eye movements, muscle atonia , vivid dreams, genital arousal. This is the "paradoxical" stage. NOT delta-dominant. The cycle: ~90 minutes; NREM 3 dominates the first third of the night, REM periods lengthen toward morning.

chunks.heading: Circadian rhythms & the clock
chunks.text: Circadian rhythms & the clock The master clock is the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) of the hypothalamus, entrained ("set") by light via the retinohypothalamic tract. The SCN drives the pineal gland to release melatonin in darkness, signalling night. Circadian rhythms are free-running (~24.x h) without light cues.

chunks.heading: Neural mechanisms of sleep/wake
chunks.text: Neural mechanisms of sleep/wake Reticular activating system (ARAS) in the brainstem maintains wakefulness/arousal. The VLPO (ventrolateral preoptic nucleus) promotes sleep (GABAergic "off switch"). Orexin/hypocretin neurons (lateral hypothalamus) stabilise wakefulness; their loss causes narcolepsy. REM is generated by pontine circuits (REM-on/REM-off cells); the flip-flop switch model explains rapid state transitions.

chunks.heading: Sleep disorders
chunks.text: Sleep disorders Disorder Core feature Narcolepsy Sleep attacks + cataplexy; loss of orexin/hypocretin Insomnia Difficulty initiating/maintaining sleep Sleep apnea Breathing stops repeatedly; fragmented sleep REM sleep behaviour disorder Atonia fails → acting out dreams; linked to Parkinson's/Lewy pathology Sleep paralysis REM atonia spills into wakefulness TRAP: REM = mixed/low-voltage EEG (like waking), not delta; delta = NREM 3 . Sleep spindles/K-complexes = NREM 2. SCN = the clock ; melatonin from the pineal . Narcolepsy = orexin loss. Sleepwalking is a NREM (deep sleep) event, not a REM one. Recap §14. NREM1 theta, NREM2 spindles/K, NREM3 delta, REM paradoxical + atonia. ~90-min cycles, REM grows toward morning. SCN clock + pineal melatonin; orexin loss = narcolepsy.

chunks.heading: 15. Drug use, addiction & reward circuits (Pinel ch. 15)
chunks.text: 15. Drug use, addiction & reward circuits (Pinel ch. 15)

chunks.heading: Core concepts
chunks.text: Core concepts Tolerance = needing more drug for the same effect (the dose-response curve shifts). Withdrawal = the opposite, aversive symptoms when the drug stops (often the mirror image of the drug's effects). Together they define physical dependence . Sensitisation = the reverse of tolerance: increased response to a drug with repetition (often for its incentive/wanting component). Conditioned tolerance / drug environment: tolerance is partly learned, cued by the setting, which is why a usual dose in a novel environment can become an overdose (Siegel).

chunks.heading: The mesolimbic dopamine reward pathway
chunks.text: The mesolimbic dopamine reward pathway The final common path of reward. Nearly all addictive drugs converge on one circuit: dopamine neurons in the ventral tegmental area (VTA) projecting to the nucleus accumbens (with the prefrontal cortex). Olds & Milner's rats pressed a lever endlessly for electrical stimulation here. Drugs hijack this "wanting" system. Incentive-sensitisation theory (Robinson & Berridge) splits "wanting" (dopamine, craving) from "liking" (opioid pleasure), explaining why addicts crave drugs they no longer enjoy.

chunks.heading: The classic drugs
chunks.text: The classic drugs Drug Mechanism Class Cocaine / amphetamine ↑ dopamine (block reuptake / force release) Stimulant Nicotine Nicotinic ACh agonist → ↑ dopamine Stimulant Alcohol ↑ GABA-A, ↓ glutamate (NMDA) Depressant Opioids (heroin, morphine) μ-opioid receptor agonist; ↑ dopamine indirectly Narcotic / depressant Cannabis (THC) CB1 cannabinoid receptor agonist — Caffeine Adenosine antagonist Stimulant TRAP: the reward pathway is VTA → nucleus accumbens (mesolimbic dopamine) . Tolerance and sensitisation are opposites (less vs more response). "Wanting" (dopamine) is dissociable from "liking" (opioids). Withdrawal symptoms typically mirror the drug's acute effects. Recap §15. Tolerance ↓ effect, withdrawal opposite, sensitisation ↑ effect. Reward = mesolimbic dopamine (VTA → nucleus accumbens). Wanting vs liking. Stimulants raise DA; alcohol/opioids depress.

chunks.heading: 16. Lateralisation, language & the split brain (Pinel ch. 16)
chunks.text: 16. Lateralisation, language & the split brain (Pinel ch. 16) Two hemispheres, different jobs. Most functions are bilateral, but some are lateralised . In ~90% of people language sits in the left hemisphere; the right is biased toward spatial processing, faces, music and emotional prosody.

chunks.heading: The split-brain studies (Sperry & Gazzaniga)
chunks.text: The split-brain studies (Sperry & Gazzaniga) Cutting the corpus callosum (to stop severe epilepsy) leaves two hemispheres that cannot talk to each other. Because each visual field projects to the opposite hemisphere, an object flashed to the left visual field → right hemisphere cannot be named (language is on the left), yet the left hand (right hemisphere) can pick it out by touch. Sperry won the Nobel for this; it proved functional lateralisation directly. Dichotic listening (Kimura): different sounds to each ear; the right-ear advantage for words reflects left-hemisphere language dominance. The Wada test (inject sodium amobarbital into one carotid to anaesthetise one hemisphere) clinically establishes the language-dominant hemisphere before surgery.

chunks.heading: The aphasias
chunks.text: The aphasias Aphasia Lesion Fluency Comprehension Repetition Broca's (expressive) Left inferior frontal (Broca's area) Non-fluent, effortful Intact Impaired Wernicke's (receptive) Left superior temporal (Wernicke's area) Fluent but meaningless Impaired Impaired Conduction Arcuate fasciculus Fluent Intact Impaired (the hallmark) Global Large left perisylvian Non-fluent Impaired Impaired Transcortical Around (sparing) the language zones Varies Varies Intact (preserved) TRAP: Broca = non-fluent but comprehends ("broken" speech); Wernicke = fluent but does not comprehend (word salad). Conduction aphasia = the one with intact fluency and comprehension but poor repetition (arcuate fasciculus). Transcortical aphasias spare repetition. Language is left in ~90%, even in most left-handers. Recap §16. Left = language, right = spatial/faces/prosody. Split-brain (Sperry/Gazzaniga): right hemisphere can't name. Dichotic listening = right-ear advantage. Wada test localises language. Broca non-fluent (comprehends), Wernicke fluent (no comprehension), conduction = bad repetition.

chunks.heading: 17. Emotion, stress & health (Pinel ch. 17)
chunks.text: 17. Emotion, stress & health (Pinel ch. 17)

chunks.heading: The neural circuitry of emotion
chunks.text: The neural circuitry of emotion Papez circuit (the early "emotion loop"): hippocampus → fornix → mammillary bodies → anterior thalamus → cingulate → entorhinal → back to hippocampus. The limbic system (MacLean) extended this. Amygdala = the hub of fear and threat detection; central to fear conditioning. Klüver-Bucy syndrome (bilateral amygdala/temporal lesion) = hyperorality, hypersexuality, placidity (tameness), visual agnosia. LeDoux's two roads to fear: a fast "low road" (thalamus → amygdala, crude but quick) and a slower "high road" (thalamus → cortex → amygdala, accurate).

chunks.heading: Theories of emotion (the must-know set)
chunks.text: Theories of emotion (the must-know set) Theory Claim One-liner James-Lange Body response comes first ; emotion is the perception of it "We feel afraid because we tremble" Cannon-Bard Bodily arousal and emotion occur simultaneously (thalamic theory) Body + feeling fire together Schachter-Singer Two-factor: arousal + a cognitive label for it Arousal + interpretation = emotion Lazarus Cognitive appraisal precedes and causes emotion Think first, then feel Lock the order: James-Lange = body → emotion. Cannon-Bard = body & emotion at once. Schachter-Singer = arousal + label. Lazarus = appraisal first.

chunks.heading: Stress, the HPA axis & immunity
chunks.text: Stress, the HPA axis & immunity HPA axis: stress → hypothalamus releases CRH → anterior pituitary releases ACTH → adrenal cortex releases cortisol ; negative feedback to the hypothalamus + pituitary. Chronically elevated in MDD, PTSD, Cushing's. The fast arm is the SAM axis (sympathetic-adrenal-medullary): epinephrine/NE for immediate fight-or-flight. Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS): alarm → resistance → exhaustion . Prolonged cortisol suppresses immune function and can damage the hippocampus; this is the basis of psychoneuroimmunology . TRAP: GAS = alarm, resistance, exhaustion (Selye). HPA endpoint = cortisol ; the fast sympathetic surge is epinephrine (SAM). James-Lange (body first) vs Cannon-Bard (simultaneous) is the most-swapped pair. Amygdala = fear; bilateral amygdala lesion = Klüver-Bucy. Recap §17. Papez/limbic loop; amygdala = fear (Klüver-Bucy if bilateral). Emotion theories: James-Lange (body first), Cannon-Bard (simultaneous), Schachter-Singer (arousal+label), Lazarus (appraisal). Stress: HPA → cortisol; Selye GAS = alarm/resistance/exhaustion.

chunks.heading: 18. Biopsychology of psychiatric disorders (Pinel ch. 18)
chunks.text: 18. Biopsychology of psychiatric disorders (Pinel ch. 18) The chapter that ties neurotransmitters to clinical conditions and their treatments. Learn each disorder by its leading biological hypothesis plus the drug that follows from it.

chunks.heading: Schizophrenia
chunks.text: Schizophrenia Dopamine hypothesis: positive symptoms (hallucinations, delusions) arise from excess dopamine activity in the mesolimbic pathway ; supported because antipsychotics are D2 antagonists and amphetamine (a DA agonist) can mimic psychosis. Refinement: negative/cognitive symptoms link to low dopamine in the mesocortical (prefrontal) pathway, plus glutamate/NMDA hypofunction (PCP/ketamine, NMDA blockers, mimic the full syndrome).

chunks.heading: Depression & bipolar
chunks.text: Depression & bipolar Monoamine hypothesis: depression reflects a deficit of serotonin and/or norepinephrine (the basis of SSRIs, SNRIs, TCAs, MAOIs). Limitations: drugs raise monoamines in hours but lift mood in weeks, so neuroplasticity/BDNF and HPA dysregulation matter too. Bipolar disorder: mood cycles between mania and depression; first-line mood stabiliser is lithium .

chunks.heading: Anxiety disorders
chunks.text: Anxiety disorders Linked to GABA (benzodiazepines enhance GABA-A) and serotonin (SSRIs are first-line for chronic anxiety/OCD); the amygdala is overactive in fear circuits.

chunks.heading: The treatment / psychopharmacology map (retained)
chunks.text: The treatment / psychopharmacology map (retained) Drug class Mechanism Used in SSRI (fluoxetine, sertraline) Block 5-HT reuptake Depression, OCD, anxiety SNRI (venlafaxine, duloxetine) Block 5-HT + NE reuptake Depression, GAD, neuropathic pain Tricyclic (TCA) Block 5-HT + NE reuptake; many side effects Depression (older), pain MAOI Block monoamine breakdown; tyramine diet Atypical/refractory depression Typical antipsychotic (haloperidol, chlorpromazine) D2 antagonist Positive symptoms of schizophrenia. Side effects: EPS, tardive dyskinesia. Atypical antipsychotic (clozapine, risperidone, olanzapine) D2 + 5-HT2A antagonist Schizophrenia (positive + some negative). Clozapine = agranulocytosis risk. Benzodiazepines GABA-A positive modulator Anxiety, insomnia, status epilepticus Lithium Unclear (inositol depletion) Bipolar mania prophylaxis Stimulants (methylphenidate, amphetamine) ↑ DA + NE ADHD, narcolepsy TRAP: schizophrenia positive symptoms = too much mesolimbic dopamine (treated by D2 antagonists ); depression = too little serotonin/NE. Typical antipsychotics block D2 → EPS/tardive dyskinesia; clozapine → agranulocytosis. Lithium = bipolar, not depression alone. Recap §18. Schizophrenia = ↑ mesolimbic dopamine (+ glutamate/NMDA hypofunction); D2 antagonists treat positive symptoms. Depression = ↓ monoamines (SSRI/SNRI/TCA/MAOI). Anxiety = GABA/5-HT. Bipolar = lithium.

chunks.heading: 19. Clinical neuropsychology: syndromes & assessment (NIMHANS focus)
chunks.text: 19. Clinical neuropsychology: syndromes & assessment (NIMHANS focus) NIMHANS-heavy. Neuropsychology is weighted far more here than in MET. They test named clinical syndromes, the lesion behind each, and the assessment batteries by name. Slow down and over-learn this section.

chunks.heading: Lesion syndromes (high-yield, retained + expanded)
chunks.text: Lesion syndromes (high-yield, retained + expanded) Lesion Syndrome Broca's area (L inferior frontal) Non-fluent aphasia, comprehension intact Wernicke's area (L superior temporal) Fluent but meaningless speech, poor comprehension Arcuate fasciculus Conduction aphasia (poor repetition) Bilateral hippocampus / medial temporal Anterograde amnesia (H.M.) Mammillary bodies + dorsomedial thalamus (thiamine) Wernicke-Korsakoff: confabulation, amnesia Right inferior parietal Left hemispatial neglect (ignores the left side of space) Left parietal (angular gyrus) Gerstmann's syndrome: agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia, left-right disorientation Bilateral amygdala / anterior temporal Klüver-Bucy: hyperoral, hypersexual, placid, visual agnosia Substantia nigra Parkinson's: bradykinesia, rigidity, resting tremor Caudate / putamen Huntington's: chorea, dementia Subthalamic nucleus Hemiballismus (violent flinging of one side) Cerebellum Ataxia, dysmetria, intention tremor, dysdiadochokinesia Frontal lobe (orbitofrontal) Disinhibition, personality change (Phineas Gage) Fusiform face area (ventral occipitotemporal) Prosopagnosia (cannot recognise familiar faces)

chunks.heading: The named clinical syndromes (learn each by its one defining symptom)
chunks.text: The named clinical syndromes (learn each by its one defining symptom) Syndrome Defining feature Locus Prosopagnosia Cannot recognise faces (objects ok) Fusiform face area (bilateral/right occipitotemporal) Capgras delusion Belief a loved one is replaced by an identical impostor Disconnect: face recognition intact but emotional/limbic response lost Hemispatial neglect Ignores one side of space (usually left) Right parietal Gerstmann's syndrome Agraphia + acalculia + finger agnosia + L-R disorientation (the tetrad) Left angular gyrus Klüver-Bucy Hyperorality, hypersexuality, placidity, visual agnosia Bilateral amygdala / temporal Anosognosia Denial / unawareness of one's own deficit (e.g. of a paralysed limb) Right parietal often Wernicke-Korsakoff Wernicke (confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia) → Korsakoff (amnesia + confabulation) Thiamine deficiency; mammillary bodies + thalamus

chunks.heading: The "A" deficits: agnosia, apraxia, aphasia
chunks.text: The "A" deficits: agnosia, apraxia, aphasia Family Definition Examples Agnosia Failure to recognise despite intact basic sensation Visual object agnosia, prosopagnosia (faces), associative vs apperceptive agnosia, astereognosis (touch) Apraxia Inability to perform learned skilled movements despite intact strength/comprehension Ideomotor, ideational, constructional, dressing apraxia (often left parietal) Aphasia Impaired language (production/comprehension) Broca, Wernicke, conduction, global, transcortical (see §16) TRAP — the three "A"s: agnosia = can't recognise (a perceptual-knowledge failure), apraxia = can't do a learned movement (a motor-planning failure), aphasia = can't language . And anosognosia (denial of deficit) is different again. Capgras = "replaced by impostor"; prosopagnosia = "can't recognise the face at all".

chunks.heading: Neuropsychological assessment batteries
chunks.text: Neuropsychological assessment batteries Battery What it is Halstead-Reitan Battery Fixed, comprehensive battery (Category Test, Tactual Performance, Trail Making, etc.); yields an impairment index for brain damage Luria-Nebraska Battery Standardised battery based on Luria's qualitative approach; scales for motor, rhythm, tactile, language, memory, etc. NIMHANS Neuropsychological Battery India-developed, normed for the Indian population; assesses attention, executive function, memory, language, visuospatial domains (must-know for this exam) Bender-Gestalt Test Copying geometric designs; screens visuomotor integration and organic impairment Wisconsin Card Sorting Test Frontal/executive function, set-shifting (perseveration = frontal damage) Wechsler Memory Scale Standardised memory assessment NIMHANS extra. Know that the NIMHANS Neuropsychological Battery exists and is normed for Indians; pair Halstead-Reitan = fixed quantitative battery and Luria-Nebraska = standardised version of Luria's qualitative method. Bender-Gestalt = visuomotor screen. Perseveration on the WCST = frontal lobe. Recap §19. Right parietal → left neglect + anosognosia; left angular gyrus → Gerstmann; fusiform → prosopagnosia; bilateral amygdala → Klüver-Bucy; Capgras = "impostor". Three A's: agnosia (recognise) / apraxia (do) / aphasia (language). Batteries: Halstead-Reitan, Luria-Nebraska, NIMHANS battery,

chunks.heading: 20. The MCQ traps, collected
chunks.text: 20. The MCQ traps, collected Divisions: human brain-damage = neuropsychology; non-invasive healthy-human measures = psychophysiology; animal brain manipulation = physiological psychology; imaging of cognition = cognitive neuroscience; drugs = psychopharmacology. Genetics: ontogeny = the individual, phylogeny = the species. Heritability is a population statistic. Epigenetics (methylation) silences genes. MZ ~100%, DZ ~50%. Glia: CNS myelin = oligodendrocyte; PNS myelin = Schwann (and Schwann aids regeneration). Action potential: all-or-none, frequency codes intensity. Absolute refractory = Na⁺ inactivated (no spike possible); relative = needs a stronger stimulus. NT precursors: dopamine from tyrosine, serotonin from tryptophan. LTP needs NMDA (coincidence detector); AMPA carries the fast EPSP. Methods: CT/MRI = structure, fMRI/PET = function. EEG = good timing/poor location; fMRI = good location/poorer timing. Stereotaxic = deep coordinates. TMS = non-invasive virtual lesion. Vision: cones densest at fovea; pathway retina → chiasm → LGN → V1. Dorsal = where (parietal), ventral = what (temporal). Trichromatic (cones) + opponent-process (after retina, afterimages). Audition: place theory = high frequency (base), frequency theory = low, volley = mid. Smell skips the thalamus. Somatosensation: DCML (fine touch/proprioception, crosses in medulla) vs spinothalamic (pain/temp, crosses

chunks.heading: 21. The landmark studies / classic experiments, walked through
chunks.text: 21. The landmark studies / classic experiments, walked through NIMHANS and MET stems love to describe a biopsych experiment and ask you to name it, its author, or its conclusion, and the favourite trick is the who-did-what swap (pairing the right finding with the wrong name). Here each landmark is walked through in the same shape: what they did , what they found , why it matters , and the trap . Learn the procedure, not just the headline, because the design ("a cat's visual cortex cell fired only to a bar at one angle" vs "a rat pressed a lever for brain stimulation") is the giveaway.

chunks.heading: Hubel & Wiesel (1959 onward) — feature detectors in the visual cortex
chunks.text: Hubel & Wiesel (1959 onward) — feature detectors in the visual cortex What: recorded from single cells in the cat (and monkey) primary visual cortex (V1) while showing bars and edges of light at various orientations and positions. Found: V1 neurons are feature detectors tuned to specific stimulus properties: simple cells respond to an edge/bar of a particular orientation in a particular location; complex cells respond to that orientation anywhere in their field and often to a direction of movement; hypercomplex (end-stopped) cells add length/corner tuning. They also mapped ocular dominance columns and orientation columns (the columnar organisation of cortex). Monocular deprivation in kittens showed a critical period : an eye sutured shut early lost its cortical representation permanently (amblyopia), but the same deprivation in an adult did not. Matters: founded the modern understanding of cortical receptive fields and experience-dependent plasticity; Nobel Prize 1981 (with Sperry). Trap: simple → orientation + position; complex → orientation regardless of position (+ motion); hypercomplex → adds length. Critical-period plasticity (deprivation amblyopia) is Hubel & Wiesel, not Sperry. Do not confuse "feature detector" (Hubel & Wiesel) with "grandmother cell" (the caricature of one cell per object).

chunks.heading: Olds & Milner (1954) — intracranial self-stimulation and the "pleasure centres"
chunks.text: Olds & Milner (1954) — intracranial self-stimulation and the "pleasure centres" What: implanted stimulating electrodes in rat brains and let the rat press a lever to deliver a brief electrical pulse to its own brain. Found: with electrodes in the septal area and the medial forebrain bundle / lateral hypothalamus , rats pressed the lever thousands of times an hour, choosing it over food, water, even crossing electrified grids, the discovery of brain reward / "pleasure" centres (electrical self-stimulation, ICSS). Matters: identified the substrate later mapped onto the mesolimbic dopamine reward pathway (VTA → nucleus accumbens) that all addictive drugs hijack (§15). Trap: the classic original site is the septal area (and medial forebrain bundle); the modern "reward pathway" name is VTA → nucleus accumbens. Olds & Milner = self-stimulation reward , not memory (that is the other Milner, Brenda, with H.M.).

chunks.heading: Scoville & Milner (1957) — patient H.M., the medial temporal lobe and memory
chunks.text: Scoville & Milner (1957) — patient H.M., the medial temporal lobe and memory What: surgeon William Scoville removed the medial temporal lobes bilaterally (including most of the hippocampus , plus amygdala and entorhinal cortex) to control intractable epilepsy in Henry Molaison (H.M.); Brenda Milner studied him for decades. Found: profound anterograde amnesia (could not form new long-term declarative memories) with relatively preserved remote memory, intact IQ, intact short-term/working memory, and crucially intact procedural learning , he improved at mirror-drawing across days while denying he had ever done the task. Matters: proved (1) the hippocampus/MTL is required to form new declarative memories but is not the permanent store, and (2) declarative and procedural memory are separate systems with separate substrates. The single most cited case in memory neuroscience. Trap: H.M. = bilateral medial temporal / hippocampus → anterograde amnesia, spared procedural (mirror-drawing) . The neurosurgeon was Scoville ; the neuropsychologist who tracked him was Brenda Milner (the mirror-drawing demonstration is hers). Do not confuse with Korsakoff (thiamine, mammillary bodies, confabulation).

chunks.heading: Brenda Milner — mirror tracing & procedural memory
chunks.text: Brenda Milner — mirror tracing & procedural memory What: had H.M. trace a star while viewing only its mirror image (a skill that is awkward at first). Found: his tracing got faster and more accurate over successive days even though, each day, he had no memory of ever having done it before . Matters: the cleanest single demonstration that skill (procedural) learning is dissociable from conscious (declarative) memory , and that the hippocampus is not needed for the former. Trap: "improved at a motor skill but had no memory of practising" = Milner's mirror-tracing in H.M.; the motor/procedural system here is the striatum + cerebellum , not the hippocampus.

chunks.heading: Sperry & Gazzaniga (1960s) — the split brain and lateralisation
chunks.text: Sperry & Gazzaniga (1960s) — the split brain and lateralisation What: studied patients whose corpus callosum had been severed (commissurotomy) to halt severe epilepsy. Stimuli were flashed to one visual field (hence one hemisphere) and responses tested by naming vs the hand. Found: an object shown to the left visual field → right hemisphere could not be named (speech is left-hemisphere) yet the left hand (right hemisphere) could select it by touch; the left hemisphere ("the interpreter," Gazzaniga) confabulated explanations for actions the right hemisphere initiated. Matters: direct proof of functional lateralisation and that the two hemispheres can operate independently; Sperry shared the 1981 Nobel. Trap: right hemisphere can't name but can point/select with the left hand ; left = language, right = spatial. Sperry (senior, Nobel) and Gazzaniga (the "interpreter" idea) go together; do not swap with Wada (a clinical test, not the split-brain study) or with Kimura (dichotic listening).

chunks.heading: Lashley (1929) — the search for the engram (equipotentiality & mass action)
chunks.text: Lashley (1929) — the search for the engram (equipotentiality & mass action) What: Karl Lashley trained rats in mazes, then made cortical lesions of varying size and location , hunting for the seat of the memory trace (the engram ). Found: the memory deficit depended on the amount of cortex removed, not its specific location, so he could not find a single engram site. Matters: yielded two principles, mass action (learning/memory impairment is proportional to the total mass of tissue destroyed) and equipotentiality (within an area, any part can substitute for any other in supporting the function). Now seen as overstated (memory is partly localised) but historically pivotal. Trap: Lashley = mass action + equipotentiality and the failed search for the engram. The term engram was coined by Richard Semon . Lashley's student Donald Hebb then proposed the opposite-spirited cell assembly .

chunks.heading: Hebb (1949) — cell assemblies and "fire together, wire together"
chunks.text: Hebb (1949) — cell assemblies and "fire together, wire together" What: Donald Hebb (Lashley's student) proposed a theory rather than a single experiment: repeatedly co-active neurons strengthen their connections, forming cell assemblies and phase sequences that are the physical basis of memory. Found / claimed: Hebb's rule , "when an axon of cell A repeatedly takes part in firing cell B, some growth process strengthens A's efficiency," popularised as "neurons that fire together wire together." Matters: the conceptual parent of long-term potentiation (LTP) , discovered later (Bliss & Lømo, 1973, in the hippocampus), the cellular mechanism that vindicated Hebb. Trap: Hebb = the theory (cell assembly, fire-together-wire-together); LTP is the experimental mechanism that confirmed it, and it depends on the NMDA receptor as a coincidence detector. Lashley (engram search, mass action) vs Hebb (cell assemblies) is a classic contrast pair.

chunks.heading: Penfield (1930s–50s) — cortical stimulation mapping and the homunculus
chunks.text: Penfield (1930s–50s) — cortical stimulation mapping and the homunculus What: Wilder Penfield electrically stimulated the cortex of awake epilepsy patients during surgery (only local anaesthesia; the brain feels no pain) and recorded what they felt or did. Found: systematic stimulation of the precentral gyrus produced movements and of the postcentral gyrus produced sensations, mapped out as the motor and sensory homunculi (distorted little men with huge hands/lips). Temporal-lobe stimulation sometimes evoked vivid "experiential" memories. Matters: established somatotopic organisation of the cortex and the homuncular map. Trap: the homunculus and cortical stimulation mapping = Penfield ; the disproportion reflects density of innervation (hands, lips, tongue are huge), not body size. Penfield = stimulation in humans; Hubel & Wiesel = recording in cats.

chunks.heading: Phineas Gage (1848) — the frontal lobe and personality
chunks.text: Phineas Gage (1848) — the frontal lobe and personality What: a railway tamping iron blasted through Gage's left frontal lobe (orbitofrontal/ventromedial prefrontal region). He survived. Found: his intellect and memory were largely intact but his personality changed, he became impulsive, profane, socially disinhibited, unable to plan ("no longer Gage"). Matters: the first dramatic evidence that the frontal lobes govern personality, social conduct and executive control / inhibition. Trap: Gage = frontal (orbitofrontal/ventromedial) → personality change, disinhibition, intact basic cognition . It is a frontal case, not a memory case. Damasio's later reconstruction (Hanna Damasio, 1994) placed the damage in ventromedial PFC, the region tied to emotion-guided decision-making (somatic marker hypothesis).

chunks.heading: Patient K.C. and Clive Wearing — episodic vs semantic memory
chunks.text: Patient K.C. and Clive Wearing — episodic vs semantic memory What: K.C. (studied by Tulving) had extensive medial temporal/hippocampal damage from a motorcycle accident; Clive Wearing , a musician, suffered herpes simplex encephalitis destroying hippocampi and temporal lobes. Found: K.C. lost episodic memory (could not mentally re-experience any personal event, past or imagined future) while retaining semantic knowledge (facts, vocabulary, how the world works). Clive Wearing had dense anterograde and retrograde amnesia with a ~7–30 second memory span, yet could still play piano and conduct (preserved procedural/musical memory) and recognised his wife. Matters: dissociate episodic (Tulving's "mental time travel," hippocampus-dependent) from semantic (temporal neocortex) and both from procedural . Trap: K.C. = lost episodic , kept semantic (Tulving's distinction). Clive Wearing = encephalitis, "the man with the 7-second memory," spared music/procedural. Both contrast with H.M., who showed the declarative/procedural split.

chunks.heading: O'Keefe (1971) & the Morris water maze — place cells and the cognitive map
chunks.text: O'Keefe (1971) & the Morris water maze — place cells and the cognitive map What: John O'Keefe recorded hippocampal neurons in freely moving rats; Richard Morris devised the Morris water maze (a hidden platform in opaque water that the rat must locate using room cues). Found: O'Keefe discovered place cells , hippocampal neurons that fire only when the animal is in a specific location , the neural substrate of a cognitive map (O'Keefe & Nadel). In the water maze, hippocampal lesions abolish the spatial (place) strategy. Later, the Mosers found grid cells in entorhinal cortex; O'Keefe and the Mosers shared the 2014 Nobel. Matters: ties the hippocampus to spatial memory and navigation , complementing its role in declarative memory. Trap: place cells = hippocampus = O'Keefe ; grid cells = entorhinal cortex = the Mosers. The Morris water maze is the standard spatial-memory / hippocampal behavioural test (Morris); do not confuse with the radial-arm maze (Olton).

chunks.heading: Kandel — Aplysia, habituation, sensitisation and the synapse
chunks.text: Kandel — Aplysia, habituation, sensitisation and the synapse What: Eric Kandel used the sea slug Aplysia (large, few, identifiable neurons) and its gill-withdrawal reflex to study the cellular basis of learning. Found: habituation (a decrease in response to repeated harmless stimulation) reflects reduced neurotransmitter release at the sensory-motor synapse; sensitisation (an enhanced response after a noxious stimulus) reflects increased release, via serotonin → cyclic AMP → more transmitter. Long-term memory (unlike short-term) requires new protein synthesis and gene expression (CREB) and the growth of new synaptic connections. Matters: showed that learning is a physical change at the synapse and bridged short- vs long-term memory mechanisms; Nobel 2000. Trap: Kandel = Aplysia , habituation (less transmitter) vs sensitisation (more transmitter), long-term memory needs protein synthesis / CREB . Habituation is non-associative learning, not fatigue and not adaptation.

chunks.heading: McGaugh & LeDoux — emotional memory and the amygdala
chunks.text: McGaugh & LeDoux — emotional memory and the amygdala What: James McGaugh studied how emotional arousal strengthens memory consolidation; Joseph LeDoux mapped fear conditioning circuits. Found: emotionally arousing events are remembered better because stress hormones (epinephrine, cortisol) and the basolateral amygdala modulate consolidation in the hippocampus, β-blockers can blunt this. LeDoux showed fear conditioning runs through the amygdala via a fast subcortical "low road" (thalamus → amygdala) and a slower cortical "high road" (thalamus → cortex → amygdala) . Matters: explains flashbulb memories and PTSD intrusions; the amygdala is the hub of emotional/fear memory (vs hippocampus for the declarative content). Trap: amygdala modulates emotional memory strength (McGaugh) and is the fear-conditioning hub (LeDoux's two roads); the hippocampus stores the facts of the event, the amygdala adds the emotional charge .

chunks.heading: Cannon & Bard, and Papez — the emotion circuits
chunks.text: Cannon & Bard, and Papez — the emotion circuits What / found: Walter Cannon (with Philip Bard) challenged James-Lange by showing that decorticate animals still display "sham rage," and argued the thalamus (later hypothalamus) triggers emotion and bodily arousal simultaneously (the Cannon-Bard thalamic theory , §17). James Papez (1937) proposed the Papez circuit (hippocampus → fornix → mammillary bodies → anterior thalamus → cingulate → entorhinal → hippocampus) as the anatomical loop of emotion; Paul MacLean extended it into the limbic system concept. Matters: the historical backbone of emotion neuroanatomy. Trap: Cannon-Bard = simultaneous body + emotion (thalamic); James-Lange = body first . Papez = the circuit/loop ; MacLean = the limbic system umbrella; Klüver-Bucy = bilateral amygdala/temporal lesion (hyperorality, hypersexuality, placidity).

chunks.heading: Early lesion physiology — Magendie, Bell, Broca, Brown-Séquard
chunks.text: Early lesion physiology — Magendie, Bell, Broca, Brown-Séquard What / found: the Bell-Magendie law established that the dorsal (posterior) spinal roots are sensory and the ventral (anterior) roots are motor , the founding dissociation of sensory vs motor pathways. Paul Broca (1861) studied patient "Tan," who could understand but only say "tan," and on autopsy found damage to the left inferior frontal gyrus, Broca's area , the first solid evidence of localisation of language in the left hemisphere; Carl Wernicke later localised comprehension to the left superior temporal gyrus. Brown-Séquard syndrome (hemisection of the spinal cord) gives the classic dissociation: ipsilateral loss of fine touch/proprioception/motor (DCML and corticospinal cross higher up) and contralateral loss of pain/temperature (spinothalamic crosses at entry; §7). Matters: these are the bedrock localisation findings. Trap: dorsal root = sensory, ventral root = motor (Bell-Magendie). Broca = production/non-fluent (left frontal, patient "Tan"); Wernicke = comprehension/fluent (left temporal). Brown-Séquard = ipsilateral touch/motor loss + contralateral pain/temp loss.

chunks.heading: Bouchard — the Minnesota twin study and heritability
chunks.text: Bouchard — the Minnesota twin study and heritability What: Thomas Bouchard's Minnesota Study of Twins Reared Apart compared monozygotic twins raised separately with those raised together (and with dizygotic twins). Found: MZ twins reared apart were strikingly similar on IQ and many personality traits, yielding high heritability estimates (IQ heritability often quoted ~0.5–0.7 in adults). Matters: the landmark behaviour-genetics evidence that individual differences have a substantial genetic component, while still leaving room for environment. Trap: heritability is a population statistic (the proportion of variance in a population due to genetic variance), not a personal "% genetic." MZ ≈ 100% shared genes, DZ ≈ 50%. Twins-reared-apart = Bouchard (Minnesota). Recap §21. Hubel & Wiesel (feature detectors, ocular dominance columns, visual critical period) · Olds & Milner (ICSS reward, septal area/MFB) · Scoville & (Brenda) Milner — H.M. (bilateral MTL → anterograde amnesia, spared mirror-drawing) · Sperry & Gazzaniga (split brain, lateralisation, "interpreter") · Lashley (failed engram search → mass action + equipotentiality) vs Hebb (cell assemblies, fire-together-wire-together) · Penfield (awake cortical stimulation → homunculus) · Phineas Gage (frontal → personality) · K.C./Tulving + Clive Wearing (episodic vs semantic; spared music) · O'Keefe place cells + Morris water maze (h

chunks.heading: 22. Extended concept bank (the rest of Pinel, chapter by chapter)
chunks.text: 22. Extended concept bank (the rest of Pinel, chapter by chapter) The sections above are the spine. This bank picks up the remaining named terms, structures, transmitters and syndromes Pinel uses that an MCQ can still pull, organised in the same chapter order so you can slot each into its home section. Every entry is the kind of one-line definition a distractor is built from.

chunks.heading: More on neuroanatomy & cells (§3)
chunks.text: More on neuroanatomy & cells (§3) Term What it is Nissl substance (Nissl bodies) Rough endoplasmic reticulum in the soma; stains reveal cell bodies (Nissl stain). Golgi stain Silver stain that fills a few entire neurons black (let Ramón y Cajal draw single cells; Golgi vs Cajal, the reticular vs neuron doctrine). Neuron doctrine Cajal's principle that the neuron is the discrete signalling unit (won over Golgi's reticular theory). Gyri / sulci / fissures Ridges / grooves / deep grooves of the cortex (folding increases surface area). Corpus callosum, anterior commissure, massa intermedia Commissures connecting the hemispheres (callosum is the largest). Decussation A crossing of fibres to the opposite side (e.g. pyramids, optic chiasm). Tract / nerve / nucleus / ganglion Bundle of axons in CNS / in PNS; cluster of cell bodies in CNS / in PNS. White vs grey matter Myelinated axons (white) vs cell bodies + dendrites (grey). Reticular formation Brainstem network for arousal, sleep-wake, muscle tone, vital reflexes (the ARAS lives here). Substantia gelatinosa Dorsal-horn region central to the pain gate (Melzack & Wall). Area postrema Medullary "vomiting centre"; one of the circumventricular organs lacking a blood-brain barrier. Blood-brain barrier Tight endothelial junctions + astrocyte end-feet keeping many bloodborne molecules out of the brain.

chunks.heading: More on conduction & synapses (§4)
chunks.text: More on conduction & synapses (§4) Term What it is Graded (postsynaptic) potentials EPSPs/IPSPs that vary in size and decay with distance, unlike the all-or-none AP. Spatial vs temporal summation Adding inputs from different synapses (spatial) vs rapid repeats at one synapse (temporal) at the axon hillock. Nernst / equilibrium potential The voltage at which an ion's electrical and chemical gradients balance (K⁺ ≈ −90 mV). Neuromodulator A transmitter that tunes many neurons diffusely/slowly rather than carrying a point-to-point signal. Gap junction (electrical synapse) Direct cytoplasmic channel for ultra-fast, bidirectional transmission (no neurotransmitter). Co-transmission / Dale's principle A neuron can release more than one transmitter; Dale's original "one neuron one transmitter" is now qualified. Nitric oxide (NO) & endocannabinoids Gaseous / lipid retrograde messengers that signal backward from postsynaptic to presynaptic cell. Agonist vs antagonist A drug that mimics/boosts a transmitter's action vs one that blocks it. Acetylcholinesterase Enzyme that degrades ACh in the cleft; inhibitors raise ACh (Alzheimer's, myasthenia, nerve agents). MAO & COMT Enzymes that break down monoamines; MAOIs treat depression, COMT clears synaptic dopamine.

chunks.heading: More on research methods (§5)
chunks.text: More on research methods (§5) Term What it is Bregma Skull landmark (where coronal & sagittal sutures meet) used as the zero point for stereotaxic coordinates. Cresyl violet / autoradiography / immunocytochemistry Histological labels for cell bodies / radioactive molecules / specific proteins. 2-deoxyglucose (2-DG) autoradiography Maps which brain regions were metabolically active (radioactive glucose analogue trapped in active cells). In situ hybridisation Locates specific mRNA (which cells are expressing a gene). Microdialysis & voltammetry Measure neurotransmitter concentration in the extracellular fluid of a living brain. Knockout / knock-in / transgenic Genetically engineered animals lacking (or carrying an extra) gene to test its behavioural role. Magnetoencephalography (MEG) Records magnetic fields from cortical activity; superb temporal + better spatial than EEG. Lordosis quotient, conditioned place preference, radial-arm/Morris maze Standard behavioural assays (sexual receptivity / drug reward / spatial memory).

chunks.heading: More on vision & the other senses (§6–7)
chunks.text: More on vision & the other senses (§6–7) Term What it is Rhodopsin / photopigments Light-absorbing molecules in photoreceptors (rod = rhodopsin); bleaching starts transduction. Duplexity theory Rods (scotopic, dim, no colour) vs cones (photopic, colour) are two separate systems. Purkinje shift In dim light sensitivity shifts toward blue (reds darken first at dusk) as vision goes rod-dominated. Receptive field / centre-surround The retinal area a cell responds to; ganglion cells have antagonistic on-centre/off-surround organisation (Kuffler). Lateral inhibition / Mach bands Neighbouring cells inhibit each other to sharpen edges (horizontal cells); produces the Mach band illusion. Magno vs parvo (M/P) LGN layers Magnocellular = motion/contrast/coarse; parvocellular = colour/detail (feeds dorsal vs ventral streams). Scotoma / blindsight A blind area from cortical damage; in blindsight patients respond to stimuli they deny seeing (subcortical routes). Tonotopic organisation Frequency-to-place mapping along the basilar membrane and auditory cortex (parallels retinotopy). Conductive vs sensorineural deafness Outer/middle-ear transmission failure vs cochlea/CN VIII damage. Tympanic membrane / oval window / organ of Corti Eardrum / cochlear entry / the receptor organ with hair cells on the basilar membrane. Vestibular system Semicircular canals (rotation) + otolith organs (utricle/sacc

chunks.heading: More on the sensorimotor system (§8)
chunks.text: More on the sensorimotor system (§8) Term What it is Muscle spindle vs Golgi tendon organ Senses muscle length/stretch (spindle, drives the stretch reflex) vs muscle tension (GTO, protective). Alpha vs gamma motor neurons Drive the main (extrafusal) muscle fibres vs set the sensitivity of the spindle (intrafusal). Monosynaptic stretch reflex The knee-jerk: spindle → one synapse → motor neuron (the simplest reflex arc). Reciprocal innervation Contracting one muscle automatically relaxes its antagonist. Central pattern generators (CPGs) Spinal circuits producing rhythmic output (walking) without ongoing cortical command. Motor unit / motor pool One motor neuron + all the fibres it innervates; recruitment grades force. Betz cells Giant pyramidal output cells of primary motor cortex (layer V) feeding the corticospinal tract. Mirror neurons Premotor/parietal cells firing both when acting and when watching the same act (Rizzolatti). Direct vs indirect basal-ganglia pathways "Go" (facilitates movement, D1) vs "no-go" (suppresses, D2); imbalance underlies Parkinson's/Huntington's. Apraxia (sensorimotor) Loss of skilled learned movement despite intact strength (often left parietal; see §19).

chunks.heading: More on development & plasticity (§9–10)
chunks.text: More on development & plasticity (§9–10) Term What it is Neural crest Cells migrating from the tube edges to form the PNS, adrenal medulla and other tissues. Radial glia Scaffold along which migrating neurons climb to the cortex (also a neural stem cell). Growth cone & chemoaffinity (Sperry) The motile axon tip navigating by chemical gradients to its target. Neurotrophins (NGF, BDNF) Target-derived survival factors; cells that fail to get enough die ("neurotrophic" competition). Apoptosis vs necrosis Programmed, tidy cell death vs messy injury-triggered death with inflammation. Long-term depression (LTD) Activity-dependent weakening of synapses; partner to LTP in plasticity. Kindling Repeated subthreshold stimulation progressively lowers seizure threshold (a plasticity model of epilepsy). Excitotoxicity Glutamate flooding (via NMDA/Ca²⁺) kills neurons after stroke/injury (the penumbra cascade). Diaschisis Dysfunction of an intact area distant from a lesion because it lost its input; recovers over time. Constraint-induced therapy Forcing use of the affected limb drives cortical reorganisation in rehab. Adult neurogenesis sites Hippocampal dentate gyrus (SGZ) and the subventricular zone → olfactory bulb.

chunks.heading: More on hunger, hormones & sex (§12–13)
chunks.text: More on hunger, hormones & sex (§12–13) Term What it is Arcuate nucleus: NPY/AgRP vs POMC/CART neurons The hypothalamic appetite hub: orexigenic ("eat") vs anorexigenic ("stop") populations leptin/ghrelin act on. Set point vs settling point A defended fixed weight vs a level where opposing forces simply balance (Pinel prefers settling point). Sham eating / VMH "finickiness" Classic feeding experiments: food not reaching the gut; VMH-lesioned rats over-eat palatable food but reject bad-tasting food. Cephalic phase Anticipatory digestive/insulin responses to the sight/smell of food before eating. Steroid vs peptide hormones Lipid-soluble, act on intracellular receptors / gene transcription (steroids) vs water-soluble, surface receptors (peptides). Releasing vs tropic hormones Hypothalamic releasing factors (GnRH, CRH, TRH) drive pituitary tropic hormones (LH/FSH, ACTH, TSH). Pulsatile & cyclic GnRH Female pattern is cyclic (drives the menstrual/estrous cycle); male is tonic. Aromatization hypothesis Testosterone is converted to estradiol in the brain to masculinise it (in rodents). Androgen insensitivity syndrome (AIS / testicular feminisation) XY with non-functional androgen receptors → female external phenotype (shows the "default female" rule). Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) Excess fetal androgens masculinise an XX individual (a natural test of organisational effects). 5

chunks.heading: More on sleep, addiction & emotion (§14–15, 17)
chunks.text: More on sleep, addiction & emotion (§14–15, 17) Term What it is PGO waves Pontine-geniculate-occipital waves heralding REM onset. Adenosine Builds up with wakefulness to drive sleep pressure; caffeine blocks its receptors. Process S & Process C Borbély's two-process model: homeostatic sleep debt (S) × circadian rhythm (C). Zeitgeber An external time-cue (chiefly light) that entrains the circadian clock. Free-running rhythm The ~24.2 h cycle the SCN runs on without time cues. Recuperation vs adaptation (circadian) theories of sleep Sleep to restore the body vs sleep to keep us safely inactive at the wrong times. Fatal familial insomnia Prion disease destroying the thalamus → progressive untreatable insomnia. Incentive-sensitisation theory Robinson & Berridge: addiction sensitises "wanting" (dopamine) apart from "liking" (opioids). Conditioned (Siegel) tolerance Drug-paired cues trigger compensatory responses; the same dose in a novel setting can overdose. Delta-FosB A transcription factor accumulating with chronic drug use, a molecular switch for addiction. Sham rage / decortication Cannon & Bard: decorticate animals show exaggerated rage, implicating subcortical control. Polygraph / GSR Measures autonomic arousal (skin conductance, HR, respiration); detects arousal, not lying per se. Display rules / facial feedback hypothesis Cultural rules for showing emotion; and the idea tha

chunks.heading: More on psychiatric biopsychology (§18)
chunks.text: More on psychiatric biopsychology (§18) Term What it is Diathesis-stress model A disorder appears when a biological/genetic vulnerability meets environmental stress. Glutamate / NMDA-hypofunction hypothesis Schizophrenia model: NMDA blockers (PCP, ketamine) reproduce positive + negative + cognitive symptoms. Mesolimbic vs mesocortical dopamine Excess mesolimbic DA → positive symptoms; deficient mesocortical DA → negative/cognitive symptoms.
