Typical vs atypical antipsychotics D2 blockers (EPS/tardive dyskinesia) vs D2 + 5-HT2A blockers (clozapine: agranulocytosis). Neurotrophic / BDNF hypothesis of depression Depression involves reduced hippocampal BDNF and neurogenesis; antidepressants restore them (explains the weeks-long delay). HPA dysregulation / dexamethasone suppression test Hypercortisolaemia and failed cortisol suppression in melancholic depression. Ketamine / esketamine Rapid-acting antidepressant via NMDA antagonism and glutamatergic plasticity. ECT, rTMS, DBS, VNS Somatic treatments: electroconvulsive therapy, repetitive TMS, deep-brain stimulation, vagus-nerve stimulation. Tardive dyskinesia / extrapyramidal side effects Involuntary movements from chronic D2 blockade (a classic typical-antipsychotic harm). Serotonin (SERT) & OCD circuit Cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical loop overactivity; SSRIs first-line. NIMHANS angle. Pair each disorder with its hypothesis and its

chunks.heading: 23. Fast glossary (one line each, A–Z)
chunks.text: 23. Fast glossary (one line each, A–Z) Last-mile recall: every nameable term, structure, transmitter, syndrome and theorist on this page reduced to a single line (and who gave it where relevant), alphabetical so you can self-test by covering the right column. If a name fires but the definition doesn't, that is the gap to drill. Term One-line definition (and who/where) Acetylcholine (ACh) NMJ + parasympathetic + memory transmitter; low in Alzheimer's; cleared by acetylcholinesterase. Action potential All-or-none spike: Na⁺ in (depolarise) → K⁺ out (repolarise); intensity coded by frequency. Adenosine Sleep-pressure molecule; caffeine is its antagonist. Agnosia Failure to recognise despite intact sensation (e.g. prosopagnosia for faces). Amygdala Fear/threat hub and emotional-memory modulator; bilateral lesion → Klüver-Bucy. Anosognosia Denial/unawareness of one's own deficit (often right parietal). Anterograde amnesia Inability to form new memories after an event (H.M.). Aphasia Impaired language: Broca (non-fluent), Wernicke (fluent, no comprehension), conduction (bad repetition). Aplysia Sea slug Kandel used to show habituation/sensitisation at the synapse. Apraxia Loss of skilled learned movement despite intact strength (often left parietal). Arcuate nucleus Hypothalamic appetite hub (NPY/AgRP "eat" vs POMC/CART "stop") where leptin and ghrelin act. ARAS (reticular activating

chunks.heading: 24. Self-test (active recall, by chapter)
chunks.text: 24. Self-test (active recall, by chapter) Recall beats re-reading. Cover the answers, ask yourself each question aloud, then check. If you miss one, jump back to its section. The answer follows in green .

chunks.heading: §1 Field & §2 evolution/genetics
chunks.text: §1 Field & §2 evolution/genetics Which division studies human brain-damaged patients, and which studies non-invasive measures in healthy humans? Neuropsychology (patients) vs psychophysiology (non-invasive, healthy). Why is heritability not a personal percentage? It is the proportion of population variance due to genetic variance, not how "genetic" one individual's trait is. Ontogeny vs phylogeny? Development of the individual vs evolutionary history of the species. What is the epigenetic mechanism that silences genes? DNA methylation (also histone modification).

chunks.heading: §3 Anatomy
chunks.text: §3 Anatomy Which glia myelinate in the CNS vs PNS, and which aids regeneration? Oligodendrocyte (CNS) vs Schwann cell (PNS); Schwann aids regeneration. Name the meninges outer to inner. Dura → arachnoid → pia. Which sense bypasses the thalamus? Smell (olfaction). VMH vs LH; superior vs inferior colliculus? VMH satiety / LH feeding; superior = sight, inferior = hearing.

chunks.heading: §4 Conduction & synapses
chunks.text: §4 Conduction & synapses What sets the resting potential, and what value? Na⁺/K⁺ pump + leaky K⁺ channels; about −70 mV. How is stimulus intensity coded if the AP is all-or-none? By the frequency of firing, never spike amplitude. What triggers neurotransmitter release at the terminal? Ca²⁺ influx through voltage-gated channels. Precursors of dopamine and serotonin? Tyrosine (dopamine) and tryptophan (serotonin). Which receptor is the coincidence detector behind LTP? The NMDA receptor (needs glutamate + depolarisation; AMPA carries the fast EPSP).

chunks.heading: §5 Methods
chunks.text: §5 Methods Structure vs function imaging? CT/MRI = structure; fMRI/PET = function (BOLD is the fMRI signal). Which method has great timing but poor location, and which the reverse? EEG = great timing/poor location; fMRI = great location/poorer timing. What is a TMS pulse used for experimentally? A non-invasive "virtual lesion" (and to treat depression).

chunks.heading: §6–7 Vision, audition & senses
chunks.text: §6–7 Vision, audition & senses Trace the retina-to-cortex pathway. Retina → optic nerve → chiasm → optic tract → LGN → V1 (striate cortex). Which colour theory operates at the cones and which after the retina? Trichromatic (Young-Helmholtz) at cones; opponent-process (Hering) after, explaining afterimages. Place vs frequency vs volley theory, best for which frequencies? Place = high, frequency = low, volley = mid. Which somatosensory tract crosses where, and what does Brown-Séquard show? DCML (fine touch) crosses in the medulla; spinothalamic (pain/temp) at entry → ipsilateral touch loss + contralateral pain loss.

chunks.heading: §8 Sensorimotor
chunks.text: §8 Sensorimotor SMA vs premotor cortex? SMA = internally generated/self-initiated; premotor = externally cued movement. Where does the pyramidal tract decussate? At the pyramids of the medulla (~85–90%). Resting vs intention tremor, which structure? Resting = basal ganglia (Parkinson's); intention = cerebellum. UMN vs LMN signs? UMN: spastic, hyperreflexic, Babinski up, no fasciculations. LMN: flaccid, areflexic, atrophy + fasciculations.

chunks.heading: §9–10 Development & plasticity
chunks.text: §9–10 Development & plasticity Give the developmental sequence. Proliferation → migration (inside-out, on radial glia) → differentiation → synaptogenesis → cell death/pruning → myelination. Where does adult neurogenesis mainly occur? Hippocampal dentate gyrus (and the SVZ → olfactory bulb). Match: Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, Huntington's to their pathology. Amyloid plaques + tau tangles; substantia-nigra dopamine loss + Lewy bodies; caudate/putamen atrophy (CAG, dominant).

chunks.heading: §11 Memory
chunks.text: §11 Memory What did H.M.'s case prove, and what surgery caused it? Bilateral medial-temporal (hippocampal) removal → anterograde amnesia with spared procedural memory; hippocampus forms but doesn't store declarative memory. Korsakoff: cause, locus, hallmark sign? Thiamine (B1) deficiency; mammillary bodies + dorsomedial thalamus; confabulation. Lashley vs Hebb? Lashley = failed engram search → mass action + equipotentiality; Hebb = cell assemblies ("fire together wire together"). What dissociation do K.C. and Clive Wearing illustrate? Episodic loss with spared semantic (K.C., Tulving); dense amnesia with spared music/procedural (Clive Wearing).

chunks.heading: §12–13 Hunger & hormones
chunks.text: §12–13 Hunger & hormones Leptin vs ghrelin, source and effect? Leptin from fat lowers appetite; ghrelin from the stomach raises it. Which framework does Pinel favour for eating? Positive-incentive (pleasure of food) over pure set-point. Where are ADH and oxytocin made and released? Made in the hypothalamus, released by the posterior pituitary. Organisational vs activational hormone effects? Early + permanent wiring vs later + reversible switching; SRY → testes, default is female.

chunks.heading: §14–15 Sleep & addiction
chunks.text: §14–15 Sleep & addiction What EEG features mark NREM 2 and NREM 3, and is REM delta? NREM 2 = spindles + K-complexes; NREM 3 = delta; REM is low-voltage, NOT delta. What is the master clock and what loss causes narcolepsy? The suprachiasmatic nucleus; loss of orexin/hypocretin causes narcolepsy. Name the reward pathway and the wanting/liking split. VTA → nucleus accumbens (mesolimbic dopamine); "wanting" = dopamine, "liking" = opioids. Tolerance vs sensitisation? Opposites: decreased vs increased response with repetition.

chunks.heading: §16 Lateralisation & language
chunks.text: §16 Lateralisation & language In split-brain patients, why can't an object in the left visual field be named? It projects to the right hemisphere, which lacks speech; the left hand can still select it. Broca vs Wernicke vs conduction aphasia? Broca = non-fluent, comprehends; Wernicke = fluent, no comprehension; conduction = fluent + comprehends but poor repetition (arcuate fasciculus). What does the Wada test establish? The language-dominant hemisphere (carotid amobarbital).

chunks.heading: §17 Emotion & stress
chunks.text: §17 Emotion & stress Order the four emotion theories by their claim. James-Lange (body first) → Cannon-Bard (simultaneous) → Schachter-Singer (arousal + label) → Lazarus (appraisal first). Trace the HPA axis to its endpoint. Hypothalamus (CRH) → pituitary (ACTH) → adrenal cortex (cortisol). Selye's three GAS stages? Alarm → resistance → exhaustion. Bilateral amygdala lesion produces what syndrome? Klüver-Bucy (hyperorality, hypersexuality, placidity, visual agnosia).

chunks.heading: §18 Psychiatric disorders
chunks.text: §18 Psychiatric disorders Dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia, and the drug class that supports it? Positive symptoms from excess mesolimbic dopamine; D2 antagonists (antipsychotics). Monoamine hypothesis of depression and its limitation? Deficit of serotonin/NE; but drugs raise monoamines in hours yet lift mood in weeks (neuroplasticity/BDNF matters). First-line treatment for bipolar disorder? Lithium. Match side effects: typical antipsychotics vs clozapine. Typicals → EPS/tardive dyskinesia; clozapine → agranulocytosis.

chunks.heading: §19 Clinical neuropsychology
chunks.text: §19 Clinical neuropsychology Right parietal lesion produces what two signs? Left hemispatial neglect and anosognosia. Name Gerstmann's tetrad and its locus. Agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia, L-R disorientation; left angular gyrus. Distinguish the three "A"s. Agnosia = can't recognise; apraxia = can't perform a learned movement; aphasia = can't language. Capgras vs prosopagnosia? Capgras = "loved one replaced by impostor" (emotional disconnect); prosopagnosia = can't recognise the face at all (fusiform). Pair the batteries: Halstead-Reitan, Luria-Nebraska, NIMHANS, Bender-Gestalt, WCST. Fixed quantitative battery; standardised Luria qualitative; India-normed battery; visuomotor screen; frontal set-shifting.

chunks.heading: §21 Landmark studies
chunks.text: §21 Landmark studies Who found visual-cortex feature detectors and the visual critical period? Hubel & Wiesel. Who discovered intracranial self-stimulation, and where was the classic electrode? Olds & Milner; septal area / medial forebrain bundle. Who discovered place cells and which test probes hippocampal spatial memory? O'Keefe (place cells); the Morris water maze. What did Kandel show in Aplysia? Habituation (less transmitter) vs sensitisation (more); long-term memory needs new protein synthesis (CREB). State the Bell-Magendie law. Dorsal spinal roots are sensory, ventral roots are motor. Recap §24. If you can answer these cold, you have the systems, the named layer and the discriminations. Re-test the ones you missed, then run the §20 traps and §23 glossary once more the night before. That sequence (recall → trap discrimination → glossary sweep) is the highest-yield last-mile routine for biopsychology. Companion pages: deeper primers on the action potential and sleep ; the compact cross-topic version sits in the general-psych notes ; the one-line testable list is in the textbook's Rapid Recall . chunks.heading: 1. Variables and Measurement Scales
chunks.text: 1. Variables and Measurement Scales Scale Property Example Stats allowed Nominal Categories, no order Diagnosis, gender Mode, frequency, chi-square Ordinal Ordered categories, unequal intervals Likert, ranks, IQ classification Median, percentile, Spearman, Mann-Whitney Interval Equal intervals, no true zero Temperature °C, IQ score Mean, SD, t-test, ANOVA, Pearson r Ratio Equal intervals, true zero Reaction time, weight All of the above + ratios Variable types: independent (manipulated), dependent (measured), control, extraneous, confounding (covaries with IV and DV).

chunks.heading: 2. Descriptive Statistics
chunks.text: 2. Descriptive Statistics

chunks.heading: Central tendency
chunks.text: Central tendency Mean — arithmetic average. Pulled by outliers. Median — middle value. Robust to outliers, best for skewed data. Mode — most frequent. Only measure for nominal data.

chunks.heading: Dispersion
chunks.text: Dispersion Range = max − min. IQR = Q3 − Q1. Used in box plots. Variance (σ²) = mean of squared deviations. Standard deviation (σ) = √variance. Same units as data. SEM = σ / √n. SD of the sampling distribution of the mean.

chunks.heading: Shape
chunks.text: Shape Skewness : positive (right tail; mean > median > mode), negative (left tail; mean < median < mode), zero (symmetric). Kurtosis : leptokurtic (peaked), mesokurtic (normal), platykurtic (flat).

chunks.heading: The normal distribution (mock-1 Q6)
chunks.text: The normal distribution (mock-1 Q6) Symmetric, bell-shaped. Mean = median = mode. Empirical rule: ±1 SD covers ≈ 68% ; ±2 SD covers ≈ 95%; ±3 SD covers ≈ 99.7%. z-score = (X − μ) / σ. Standardises any score. T-score : M=50, SD=10. T=70 → +2 SD → 97.5th percentile (MMPI clinical cutoff). Stanine : M=5, SD=2, range 1–9. Sten : M=5.5, SD=2, range 1–10.

chunks.heading: 3. Probability + Sampling
chunks.text: 3. Probability + Sampling

chunks.heading: Sampling methods
chunks.text: Sampling methods Method How Note Simple random Every unit equal probability Gold standard, requires sampling frame Systematic Every k-th unit from a list Risk if list has periodicity Stratified Divide into strata (e.g., gender), random sample within each Increases precision when strata differ on the variable Cluster Randomly select naturally occurring groups (schools, villages); often sample all units within (mock-1 Q5) Cheaper, less precise. Two-stage cluster samples within clusters. Multistage Combination of above National surveys Convenience Whoever is available Non-probability, biased Snowball Existing subjects recruit more Hidden populations, e.g. drug users Purposive / quota Investigator selects to fit categories Non-probability MCQ trap (mock-1 Q5): stratified divides population into strata then random samples within ; cluster randomly picks groups then samples all or many units per cluster. Both are probability methods.

chunks.heading: 4. Hypothesis Testing
chunks.text: 4. Hypothesis Testing

chunks.heading: Setup
chunks.text: Setup H0 (null) = no effect / no difference / status quo. H1 (alternative) = effect exists. Two-tailed (any direction) vs one-tailed (specific direction). α = type I error rate (false positive). Conventionally 0.05. β = type II error rate (false negative). Power = 1 − β. Conventionally ≥ 0.80.

chunks.heading: Errors
chunks.text: Errors H0 true H0 false Reject H0 Type I (α, false +) Correct (power) Retain H0 Correct Type II (β, false −) Mock-1 Q1 trap: Type I = wrongly rejecting a TRUE null. (Wrongly retaining a false null = Type II.)

chunks.heading: p-value
chunks.text: p-value Probability of obtaining the observed result or more extreme if H0 were true. NOT the probability that H0 is true. If p < α → reject H0 (mock-1 Q3: p=0.03 < α=0.05 → reject). Statistically significant ≠ practically important. Always report effect size.

chunks.heading: Power
chunks.text: Power Increases with: larger n, larger effect size, larger α, lower variability, one-tailed test. A priori power analysis sets sample size before data collection.

chunks.heading: Confidence intervals
chunks.text: Confidence intervals 95% CI: if we repeated the study many times, 95% of intervals would contain the true parameter. If 95% CI for a difference excludes 0 → significant at p < 0.05.

chunks.heading: 5. Effect Size
chunks.text: 5. Effect Size Statistic Used with Cohen's benchmarks Cohen's d Mean difference (t-tests) 0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large (mock-1 Q7) Pearson r Correlation 0.10 small, 0.30 medium, 0.50 large r² (or eta²) % variance explained 0.01 / 0.06 / 0.14 Odds ratio (OR) Categorical (case-control) 1.5 small, 2.5 medium, 4.3 large Hedges' g Like d, corrected for small n Same as d

chunks.heading: 6. Parametric Tests
chunks.text: 6. Parametric Tests Assumptions (all parametric): interval/ratio data, normality, homogeneity of variance, independence of observations. Test Used for Non-parametric equivalent z-test Mean vs known μ when σ known, large n — One-sample t-test Mean vs known μ, σ unknown Wilcoxon signed-rank (one sample) Independent t-test Two independent group means Mann-Whitney U (mock-1 Q2) Paired t-test Pre-post or matched pairs Wilcoxon signed-rank (paired) One-way ANOVA 3+ independent group means Kruskal-Wallis Repeated-measures ANOVA 3+ within-subject means Friedman Factorial ANOVA 2+ IVs with interaction — ANCOVA ANOVA + covariate adjustment — MANOVA Multiple DVs together — Pearson r Linear association, two interval vars Spearman ρ (rank correlation) Linear regression Predict Y from X(s) —

chunks.heading: 7. Non-Parametric Tests
chunks.text: 7. Non-Parametric Tests Use when: ordinal data, small n, non-normal data, or violated assumptions. Chi-square (χ²) : categorical variables. Goodness-of-fit (one variable) or test of independence (two variables, contingency table). Assumption: expected count ≥ 5 per cell. Fisher's exact test : like chi-square but for small expected counts (2×2 tables). McNemar's test : paired categorical (e.g., before/after). Mann-Whitney U : non-parametric independent two-sample (mock-1 Q2). Wilcoxon signed-rank : non-parametric paired test. Kruskal-Wallis : non-parametric one-way ANOVA. Friedman : non-parametric repeated-measures ANOVA. Spearman ρ / Kendall's τ : rank correlation.

chunks.heading: 8. Post-Hoc Tests (mock-1 Q8)
chunks.text: 8. Post-Hoc Tests (mock-1 Q8) If ANOVA F is significant, the omnibus result tells you that at least one mean differs but not which. Post-hoc pairwise tests localise differences while controlling family-wise error rate. Test When to use Conservatism Tukey HSD All pairwise, equal n Moderate Bonferroni Few planned comparisons Very conservative; α/k Scheffé Any contrasts, unequal n Most conservative LSD (Fisher) Only after significant F Liberal, no protection Dunnett Each group vs control Moderate Games-Howell Unequal variance Like Tukey

chunks.heading: 9. Correlation + Regression
chunks.text: 9. Correlation + Regression r ranges −1 to +1. 0 = no linear association. ±1 = perfect. Mock-1 Q9 trap: r = +0.90 means a strong positive linear association. r² = 0.81 → 81% of variance explained (NOT 90%). Correlation does NOT imply causation. Cohen's r benchmarks: 0.10 small, 0.30 medium, 0.50 large. Linear regression: Y = a + bX + ε. Least-squares fit minimises sum of squared residuals. Multiple regression : more predictors. Beware multicollinearity (VIF). Logistic regression : binary outcome. Reports odds ratios. Mediation (Baron-Kenny / Hayes PROCESS): X → M → Y. Moderation : X × M interaction term in regression.

chunks.heading: 10. Reliability + Validity (Measurement)
chunks.text: 10. Reliability + Validity (Measurement)

chunks.heading: Reliability (consistency)
chunks.text: Reliability (consistency) Test-retest — same test, two times. Susceptible to memory. Parallel forms — equivalent forms. Split-half (Spearman-Brown corrected). Internal consistency — Cronbach's α (≥0.7 acceptable; ≥0.8 good). KR-20 for dichotomous items. Inter-rater — Cohen's κ (categorical), ICC (continuous).

chunks.heading: Validity (accuracy)
chunks.text: Validity (accuracy) Content — covers domain (face validity = informal subset). Criterion — concurrent (now) vs predictive (future). Construct — convergent (correlates with similar measures), discriminant (doesn't with unrelated). Includes factorial validity. Validity ceiling: max validity = √reliability (assuming criterion is perfectly reliable). r_xx = 0.81 → max validity = 0.90.

chunks.heading: 11. Research Designs
chunks.text: 11. Research Designs

chunks.heading: Experimental hierarchy
chunks.text: Experimental hierarchy Design Random assignment? Control group? Internal validity True experiment Yes Yes High Quasi-experiment No (intact groups) Yes Moderate Pre-experimental No Often no Low Non-experimental (correlational) — — No causation

chunks.heading: Specific designs to know
chunks.text: Specific designs to know Pretest-posttest control group — classic two-group RCT. Posttest-only control group — avoids pretest sensitisation entirely. Solomon four-group (mock-1 Q4) — combines both. Two groups get pretest, two don't, half each get treatment. Detects + separates pretest sensitisation (interaction of pretest and treatment) from the treatment effect itself. Resource-heavy but most rigorous. Crossover design — every subject receives both conditions in different order. Factorial design — 2+ IVs, allows interaction analysis. Single-case (ABA, ABAB, multiple baseline) — used in behaviour analysis. Cohort study — follow exposed and unexposed groups forward; reports relative risk. Case-control — start with cases and controls, look back; reports odds ratio. Cross-sectional — single point in time; reports prevalence.

chunks.heading: 12. RCT + Clinical Trial Phases
chunks.text: 12. RCT + Clinical Trial Phases Phase Purpose n Phase 0 Microdosing in humans, pharmacokinetics ~10 Phase I Safety, tolerability, dose-finding 20–100 Phase II Preliminary efficacy + side-effects 100–300 Phase III Confirmatory efficacy vs standard 1000+ Phase IV Post-marketing surveillance Open Blinding: single (subject), double (subject + experimenter), triple (+ analyst). Reduces bias. Allocation concealment ≠ blinding — concerns who knows the next assignment at the time of randomisation .

chunks.heading: 13. Threats to Validity
chunks.text: 13. Threats to Validity

chunks.heading: Internal validity (causation within study)
chunks.text: Internal validity (causation within study) History — external events during study. Maturation — natural change with time. Testing — pretest affects posttest (controlled by Solomon four-group). Instrumentation — measure changes mid-study. Regression to the mean — extreme scorers move toward mean. Selection bias — non-random group differences. Mortality / attrition — differential dropout. Diffusion of treatment — control group learns from experimental. Hawthorne effect — being observed changes behaviour. Demand characteristics — subjects guess hypothesis.

chunks.heading: External validity (generalisation)
chunks.text: External validity (generalisation) Population validity (sample → population). Ecological validity (lab → real life). Treatment variation, time of measurement, etc.

chunks.heading: Construct + statistical conclusion
chunks.text: Construct + statistical conclusion Construct: does the operationalisation match the construct? Statistical conclusion: is the inference about the relationship valid? Threats: low power, violated assumptions, p-hacking.

chunks.heading: 14. Reporting Standards (mock-1 Q10)
chunks.text: 14. Reporting Standards (mock-1 Q10) Acronym For CONSORT Randomised controlled trials PRISMA Systematic reviews + meta-analyses STARD Diagnostic accuracy studies STROBE Observational studies (cohort, case-control, cross-sectional) COREQ Qualitative research SPIRIT Trial protocols CARE Case reports TRIPOD Prediction model studies

chunks.heading: 15. Qualitative Methods (overview)
chunks.text: 15. Qualitative Methods (overview) Phenomenology — lived experience (Husserl, Giorgi, IPA). Grounded theory — Glaser-Strauss, theory built from data via constant comparison and theoretical sampling. Ethnography — culture/community, participant observation. Case study — in-depth single unit (Yin). Narrative analysis — life stories. Discourse / conversation analysis — language as social action. Thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke) — flexible coding for themes. Trustworthiness criteria (Lincoln-Guba): credibility, transferability, dependability, confirmability. Triangulation — data, investigator, theory, methodological.

chunks.heading: 16. Ethics
chunks.text: 16. Ethics Belmont Report (1979): respect for persons, beneficence, justice. Informed consent — capacity, voluntariness, disclosure, comprehension. IRB / Ethics Committee approval — required before data collection. Confidentiality, anonymity, debriefing . Special populations — children, prisoners, cognitively impaired, pregnant women. Major scandals to know: Tuskegee, Milgram, Stanford Prison, Nazi experiments → Nuremberg Code (1947), Declaration of Helsinki (1964 onwards). Indian context: ICMR National Ethical Guidelines (2017), New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules (2019).

chunks.heading: 17. Mock-1 Trap Recap (10 questions)
chunks.text: 17. Mock-1 Trap Recap (10 questions) Type I error = wrongly rejecting a true null (false positive). Mann-Whitney U = non-parametric independent t-test. p < α → reject H0. p-value is NOT P(H0 true). Solomon four-group controls + measures pretest sensitisation. Cluster = random groups, sample within. Stratified = strata, random within each. Normal distribution: ±1 SD ≈ 68%. Cohen's d: 0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large. Significant ANOVA → post-hoc (Tukey, Bonferroni) to localise. r = +0.90 = strong positive linear association; r² = 0.81 = 81% variance explained. CONSORT = RCT reporting. PRISMA = SR/meta. STARD = diagnostic. COREQ = qualitative. Sihan MET 2026 Prep · Biostats + Research Methods · Built 2026-05-05

chunks.heading: Bronfenbrenner, Ecological Systems Theory
chunks.text: Bronfenbrenner, Ecological Systems Theory Developmental Psychology · Exam-grade · Built 2026-05-05

chunks.heading: 1. Core Idea
chunks.text: 1. Core Idea Urie Bronfenbrenner (1917-2005), Russian-born American developmental psychologist. Development is shaped by ongoing interaction between the person and a set of nested environmental systems . Originally Ecological Systems Theory , "The Ecology of Human Development" (1979). Later renamed Bioecological Model (1994, refined 2005) to give biology more weight and add the PPCT mechanism. Co-founded the Head Start program (1965) in the US, applied use of the theory. One-line answer: Development = person × proximal processes × nested context × time.

chunks.heading: 2. The 5 Systems (innermost to outermost)
chunks.text: 2. The 5 Systems (innermost to outermost)

chunks.heading: 2.1 Microsystem
chunks.text: 2.1 Microsystem Immediate settings with direct face-to-face contact . Examples: family, school, peer group, neighbourhood, daycare, workplace (for adults). Influence is bidirectional : child shapes the environment, environment shapes the child. Most direct effect on development.

chunks.heading: 2.2 Mesosystem
chunks.text: 2.2 Mesosystem Interactions between two or more microsystems . Not a setting itself, a system of microsystems . Examples: parent-teacher communication, family-peer overlap, home-daycare links. Strong, supportive mesosystem links = better developmental outcomes.

chunks.heading: 2.3 Exosystem
chunks.text: 2.3 Exosystem Settings the child does not directly participate in , but which still affect them via the microsystem. Examples: parent's workplace, school board decisions, mass media, parent's social network, local government policy. TRAP: Exosystem ≠ no influence. Child isn't in it, but it shapes them through their microsystem (e.g. dad loses job → stress at home → child's development affected).

chunks.heading: 2.4 Macrosystem
chunks.text: 2.4 Macrosystem The overarching cultural blueprint , the "cultural envelope" around all the other systems. Examples: ideologies, customs, laws, religion, SES, cultural values, economic system, war/peace. Doesn't refer to a specific setting, refers to the cultural patterning that shapes all settings.

chunks.heading: 2.5 Chronosystem
chunks.text: 2.5 Chronosystem The time dimension . Added later (after the original 4 systems). Three flavours of "time" effects: Life transitions , normative (school entry, puberty) and non-normative (parents' divorce, death of parent). Historical events the person lives through (pandemic, war, recession). Sociohistorical conditions of the cohort (cohort effects). TRAP: Chronosystem was added later . Older textbooks list only 4 systems. If a question says "Bronfenbrenner originally proposed 5 systems" — false. Originally 4, chronosystem added later.

chunks.heading: 3. Quick-Reference Table
chunks.text: 3. Quick-Reference Table System What it is Examples Microsystem Direct, face-to-face settings Family, school, peers, daycare Mesosystem Interactions between microsystems Parent-teacher meetings, home-school link Exosystem Indirect settings, child not in them Parent's workplace, school board, media Macrosystem Cultural blueprint Ideology, laws, religion, SES, customs Chronosystem Time dimension Divorce, pandemic, historical era

chunks.heading: 4. PPCT Model (1994 refinement, often asked)
chunks.text: 4. PPCT Model (1994 refinement, often asked) Bronfenbrenner refined the theory into the Bioecological Model using the PPCT mechanism. This is the engine of the modern version.

chunks.heading: 4.1 Process — proximal processes
chunks.text: 4.1 Process — proximal processes The engine of development . Most important driver. Regular, reciprocal interactions over extended time between the person and people/objects/symbols in the immediate environment. Examples: parent-child play, reading together, sustained peer activity, learning a skill from a mentor. Must be regular and over long stretches of time to count as proximal processes (not one-off events).

chunks.heading: 4.2 Person — individual traits
chunks.text: 4.2 Person — individual traits Three sub-types: Sub-type Definition Examples Demand characteristics Visible traits that pull responses from others Age, gender, skin colour, physical appearance Resource characteristics Skills, abilities, experiences Intelligence, prior knowledge, social skills Force characteristics Temperament, motivation, persistence Curiosity, drive, distractibility, regulation

chunks.heading: 4.3 Context — the 5 nested systems
chunks.text: 4.3 Context — the 5 nested systems Micro / Meso / Exo / Macro / Chrono. Already covered above.

chunks.heading: 4.4 Time
chunks.text: 4.4 Time Micro-time : continuity vs interruption within an activity (e.g. uninterrupted reading session). Meso-time : consistency of activities across days and weeks. Macro-time : chronosystem level, sociohistorical change across the lifespan.

chunks.heading: 5. High-Yield Exam Pointers
chunks.text: 5. High-Yield Exam Pointers Originally 4 systems , chronosystem added later. Bidirectionality is a key examiner trigger word, especially in microsystem questions. Theory has two phases: Ecological Systems Theory (1979) → Bioecological Model (1994) with PPCT. Proximal processes are the engine , not the context. Context modifies how proximal processes operate. Mesosystem is not a setting , it's a system of relationships between settings .

chunks.heading: 6. Compare and Contrast (very high-yield)
chunks.text: 6. Compare and Contrast (very high-yield) Theorist Focus Mechanism Piaget Cognitive stages, internal Schemas, assimilation, accommodation Vygotsky Sociocultural ZPD, scaffolding (Bruner), more knowledgeable other Bronfenbrenner Ecological / multi-layered context Person × Process × Context × Time Erikson Psychosocial stages 8 crises across lifespan Bandura Social learning Observation, modeling, self-efficacy Rule of thumb: If the question stem mentions nested environments , cultural context , parent's workplace affecting child , or indirect influence → answer is Bronfenbrenner.

chunks.heading: 7. Applications
chunks.text: 7. Applications Child welfare policy — interventions at multiple system levels (family + school + community). Inclusive education — coordinating microsystems (home, school, peers). Public health — tobacco control, vaccination uptake (macro + exo levels). Family therapy — recognising that family microsystem sits inside larger systems. Head Start program (Bronfenbrenner co-founded) — early childhood intervention targeting micro + meso systems.

chunks.heading: 8. Critique
chunks.text: 8. Critique Hard to operationalise and test empirically — too many simultaneous variables. Originally underplayed biology (fixed in the bioecological revision via "Person" component). Criticised for being descriptive more than predictive , doesn't say which system dominates when. Cultural specificity is unclear — macrosystem treats "culture" as a single bucket.

chunks.heading: 9. One-line MCQ Traps
chunks.text: 9. One-line MCQ Traps Exosystem ≠ no influence. Child isn't in it, but it still affects them via the microsystem (e.g. parent loses job). Mesosystem is not a setting , it's the link between two settings the child is in. Chronosystem was added later , originally 4 systems. Bidirectionality is a microsystem feature (child also shapes parent), not a one-way arrow. Proximal processes are the engine of development, not the context. Context only shapes their effect. PPCT belongs to the Bioecological Model (1994) , not the original 1979 theory. Mass media affecting a child = exosystem , not macrosystem (media is a setting, not a cultural blueprint). "Culture, religion, ideology, SES" = macrosystem . Parent's workplace = classic exosystem example. Sibling fight at home = microsystem . Parent-teacher meeting = mesosystem .

chunks.heading: 10. 30-Second Recall Script
chunks.text: 10. 30-Second Recall Script Bronfenbrenner. Five nested systems, innermost out: Micro (direct, family/school, bidirectional), Meso (links between micros), Exo (indirect, parent's workplace), Macro (culture, laws, ideology), Chrono (time, life transitions, history, added later). 1979 Ecological Systems Theory → 1994 Bioecological Model with PPCT : P roximal P rocesses are the engine, C ontext = the 5 systems, T ime = micro/meso/macro time. Person split into demand, resource, force characteristics. Built 2026-05-05 from MET-grade Bronfenbrenner request. Pair with the dev psych cheatsheet for the wider section context. chunks.heading: Cognitive Psychology — the whole domain, named, in book order
chunks.text: Cognitive Psychology — the whole domain, named, in book order Built from Eysenck & Keane, Cognitive Psychology: A Student's Handbook , the book you listed for cognitive. Cognition spans perception, attention, memory, knowledge, language and thinking, so instead of hunting across pages this is the one cognitive page , laid out the way the book is, chapter by chapter. Every major named model with name → who → the one-line hook , plus trap boxes for the pairs they swap. Built 2026-05-24. Effects Phenomena Theories Theorists Social Psych Cognitive Lookalikes How cognitive is tested. (1) Name the model from its claim ("we store info in three stores" = multi-store). (2) Pin the model to its author (working memory = Baddeley & Hitch). (3) Tell rival models apart, that's where the distractor lives: Gregory vs Gibson, early vs late selection, episodic vs semantic, prototype vs exemplar, Broca vs Wernicke. Learn each in its contrast pair. Jump to: 1. Approaches 2. Visual perception 3. Object & face recognition 4. Attention 5. Short-term & working memory 6. Long-term memory 7. Forgetting & everyday memory 8. Concepts & knowledge 9. Language 10. Problem solving & expertise 11. Judgement & decision making 12. Reasoning

chunks.heading: 1. Approaches to human cognition
chunks.text: 1. Approaches to human cognition Approach Who What it is Experimental cognitive psychology — Studies cognition in healthy people via lab experiments (RT, accuracy); the oldest strand. Cognitive neuropsychology — Studies brain-damaged patients to infer normal architecture; assumes modularity (functions are separable). Cognitive neuroscience — Uses fMRI, PET, EEG/ERP, TMS to locate cognition in the brain (where and when). Computational cognitive science — Builds computer models that simulate cognition; includes connectionism / parallel distributed processing. Information-processing approach Broadbent (founding) The mind as stages of input → processing → output; the frame the whole book sits in. Bottom-up vs top-down runs through the whole book. Bottom-up (data-driven) = processing starts from the stimulus. Top-down (concept-driven) = expectations, context and stored knowledge shape it. Almost every debate below is "how much of each."

chunks.heading: 2. Visual perception
chunks.text: 2. Visual perception Theory / term Who What it is Constructivist theory Richard Gregory Perception is top-down: we build (construct) percepts by inference from incomplete data; explains illusions as wrong hypotheses. Direct perception / ecological theory James Gibson Perception is bottom-up: the rich optic array directly affords meaning, no inference needed ("affordances"). Computational theory (primal/2½-D/3-D sketch) David Marr Vision builds up in stages from edges to a viewer-centred (2½-D) then object-centred (3-D) representation. Gestalt grouping laws Wertheimer, Koffka, Köhler Proximity, similarity, closure, continuity, common fate, Prägnanz; "the whole is other than the sum of parts." Depth cues — Binocular (retinal disparity, convergence) + monocular/pictorial (linear perspective, interposition, texture gradient, motion parallax). Perceptual constancies — Size, shape, colour, brightness stay stable despite changing retinal image. Two visual systems (perception vs action) Milner & Goodale Ventral stream "what" (perception/recognition) vs dorsal stream "where/how" (visually guided action). Patient DF = damaged ventral. Gregory vs Gibson: Gregory = indirect/constructivist, top-down, perception is a hypothesis (great for illusions, poor light). Gibson = direct, bottom-up, info is in the array (great for rich real-world viewing). If the stem says "inference / hypothesis," it

chunks.heading: 3. Object & face recognition
chunks.text: 3. Object & face recognition Theory / term Who What it is Template theory — Match input to a stored whole template; fails on size/orientation/font variation. Feature theory / Pandemonium Selfridge Recognise by detecting component features ("demons" shout for the features they see). Recognition-by-components (geons) Irving Biederman Objects decomposed into ~36 basic 3-D shapes (geons); view-invariant recognition. Face recognition model Bruce & Young Separate routes: structural encoding → face recognition units → person identity nodes → name. Familiarity can come before the name. Prosopagnosia — Selective inability to recognise faces despite intact object recognition; ventral/fusiform damage (FFA). Visual agnosia Lissauer (apperceptive vs associative) Can't recognise objects despite intact vision. Apperceptive = can't form the percept; associative = percept formed but can't link it to meaning. Apperceptive vs associative agnosia: apperceptive can't copy the drawing (perception broken); associative can copy it but still can't say what it is (perception intact, meaning lost).

chunks.heading: 4. Attention
chunks.text: 4. Attention Model Who What it is Filter (early-selection) theory Donald Broadbent One channel; an early filter selects by physical features before meaning. Basis of dichotic listening. Attenuation theory Anne Treisman Unattended channel is turned down, not off; salient words (your name) still get through. Early but leaky filter. Late-selection theory Deutsch & Deutsch (extended by Norman) All input is processed for meaning; selection happens late , at response. Capacity / resource theory Daniel Kahneman Attention is a limited pool of effort allocated flexibly; explains dual-task interference. Spotlight / zoom-lens Posner; Eriksen Visual attention is a movable spotlight that can narrow or widen; Posner cueing measures it. Feature Integration Theory Anne Treisman Features (colour, shape) detected in parallel pre-attentively; attention is the "glue" that binds them into objects. Explains illusory conjunctions; pop-out vs serial search. Inattentional / change blindness Simons & Chabris; Rensink We miss the unexpected gorilla / the swapped person when attention is elsewhere. Automatic vs controlled processing Shiffrin & Schneider Automatic = fast, parallel, no capacity (Stroop interference); controlled = slow, serial, effortful. Early vs late selection: Broadbent = filter before meaning (early). Treisman = attenuate, not block (early but leaky). Deutsch-Norman = process everything,

chunks.heading: 5. Short-term & working memory
chunks.text: 5. Short-term & working memory Model / term Who What it is Multi-store model Atkinson & Shiffrin Sensory store → STM → LTM, linked by attention and rehearsal. The serial-position curve (primacy = LTM, recency = STM) supports it. Sensory memory (iconic / echoic) Sperling (iconic) Very brief, large-capacity modality store; partial-report shows iconic memory ~1/2 s, echoic ~2–4 s. Magic number 7 ± 2 George Miller STM holds ~7 chunks; capacity is set by chunks, not raw items, so chunking expands it. Working memory model Baddeley & Hitch Replaces unitary STM: central executive + phonological loop + visuospatial sketchpad (+ episodic buffer, added later). Phonological loop Baddeley Inner voice + inner ear; word-length & phonological-similarity effects, articulatory suppression. Episodic buffer Baddeley (2000) Limited store that binds info across systems into a unified episode, links to LTM. Levels of processing Craik & Lockhart Deeper (semantic) encoding → better retention than shallow (structural/phonemic); memory is a by-product of processing depth. Multi-store vs working memory: Atkinson-Shiffrin's STM is a single passive store; Baddeley-Hitch splits it into active components doing different jobs. Evidence for the split: you can do a verbal + visuospatial task at once but not two verbal tasks (separate subsystems).

chunks.heading: 6. Long-term memory
chunks.text: 6. Long-term memory Term Who What it is Declarative vs procedural Cohen & Squire Declarative (explicit, "knowing that") vs procedural (implicit, "knowing how," skills). Episodic vs semantic Endel Tulving Episodic = events tied to time/place ("my last birthday"); semantic = general facts ("Paris is the capital"). Both declarative. Encoding specificity principle Tulving & Thomson Retrieval is best when cues at recall match cues at encoding (basis of context- and state-dependent memory). Forgetting curve Hermann Ebbinghaus Steep early loss then levelling; pioneered nonsense syllables and savings method. Reconstructive memory / schema Frederic Bartlett "War of the Ghosts": recall is rebuilt to fit schemas, so it distorts toward the familiar. Consolidation Müller & Pilzecker; McGaugh New memories are fragile and stabilise over time; sleep and the hippocampus aid it. Patient H.M. Scoville & Milner Bilateral medial-temporal/hippocampal removal → dense anterograde amnesia but intact STM and procedural learning. Proof STM and LTM dissociate. Episodic vs semantic: if the fact is tied to when/where you learned it , episodic; if it's free-floating general knowledge, semantic. Amnesics often lose episodic while semantic survives. Anterograde vs retrograde amnesia: anterograde = can't form new memories after the injury (H.M.); retrograde = lost memories from before the injury.

chunks.heading: 7. Forgetting & everyday memory
chunks.text: 7. Forgetting & everyday memory Term Who What it is Decay theory — Memory trace fades with time if not used. Interference theory — Proactive = old learning blocks new; retroactive = new learning blocks old. Cue-dependent forgetting Tulving The trace is intact but the retrieval cue is missing (tip-of-the-tongue). Repression / motivated forgetting Freud Threatening memories pushed out of awareness (controversial). Misinformation effect Elizabeth Loftus Post-event misleading info reshapes eyewitness memory ("smashed" vs "hit" changes the speed estimate). Flashbulb memory Brown & Kulik Vivid, confident memory of a shocking event; vivid does not mean accurate. Weapon focus Loftus A weapon draws attention and narrows it, worsening memory for the rest of the scene. Prospective memory — Remembering to do something in the future (event- vs time-based), distinct from retrospective memory.

chunks.heading: 8. Concepts & knowledge representation
chunks.text: 8. Concepts & knowledge representation Theory / term Who What it is Defining-attribute (classical) view — A concept = a set of necessary & sufficient features; fails for fuzzy categories. Prototype theory Eleanor Rosch We judge category membership by similarity to a best/average example; basic-level categories & typicality effects ("robin" is a better bird than "penguin"). Exemplar theory Medin & Schaffer We store specific instances, not an average; categorise by similarity to remembered exemplars. Hierarchical semantic network Collins & Quillian Concepts in a tree with cognitive economy; predicts sentence-verification times by distance. Spreading activation Collins & Loftus Concepts linked by relatedness, not strict hierarchy; activation spreads → semantic priming. Schema / script Bartlett; Schank & Abelson (scripts) Organised knowledge packets that guide comprehension and inference (the "restaurant script"). Prototype vs exemplar: prototype = one abstracted average per category; exemplar = many stored individual instances. "Compare to the ideal bird" = prototype; "compare to all the birds I've seen" = exemplar.

chunks.heading: 9. Language
chunks.text: 9. Language Theory / term Who What it is Linguistic relativity (Whorf hypothesis) Sapir & Whorf Language shapes thought; strong (determinism) form rejected, weak (influence) form has some support. Language acquisition device / universal grammar Noam Chomsky Innate grammar; surface vs deep structure; transformational grammar. Against Skinner's behaviourist account. Garden-path model Frazier (minimal attachment) We parse a sentence one way and have to reanalyse ("The horse raced past the barn fell"). Dual-route model of reading Coltheart Lexical route (whole-word, for irregular words) + grapheme-phoneme route (sounding out). Surface vs phonological dyslexia map onto the two routes. Speech production model Willem Levelt Conceptualisation → formulation → articulation; speech errors (Spoonerisms, slips) reveal the stages. Categorical perception / McGurk effect McGurk & MacDonald Vision changes what speech sound you hear (see "ga," hear "ba" → perceive "da"); speech perception is multimodal. Cohort model Marslen-Wilson Spoken word recognition: all words matching the onset activate, then narrow as more sound arrives. Broca's aphasia Paul Broca Non-fluent, effortful, agrammatic speech; comprehension relatively spared. Lesion: left frontal. Wernicke's aphasia Carl Wernicke Fluent but meaningless "word salad," poor comprehension. Lesion: left temporal. Broca vs Wernicke: Broca = Broken s

chunks.heading: 10. Problem solving & expertise
chunks.text: 10. Problem solving & expertise Theory / term Who What it is Insight / restructuring Gestalt (Köhler, Wertheimer) Sudden reorganisation of the problem ("aha"); Köhler's chimp Sultan stacking boxes. Functional fixedness Karl Duncker Fixating on an object's usual use blocks the solution (the candle / box-of-tacks problem). Mental set (Einstellung) Abraham Luchins A strategy that worked before is applied rigidly even when a simpler one exists (water-jar task). Means–ends analysis Newell & Simon Reduce the gap between current and goal state via subgoals; General Problem Solver, Tower of Hanoi. Problem space Newell & Simon All states + operators between start and goal; solving = searching this space. Well- vs ill-defined problems — Well-defined have clear start/goal/operators (chess); ill-defined don't ("write a good essay"). Expertise & chunking de Groot; Chase & Simon Chess masters recall real board positions far better than novices, but not random ones, expertise = stored chunks, not raw memory. Analogical problem solving Gick & Holyoak We transfer a solution from a similar problem (radiation/fortress); surface similarity helps spot it.

chunks.heading: 11. Judgement & decision making
chunks.text: 11. Judgement & decision making Term Who What it is Heuristics & biases Tversky & Kahneman Availability (ease of recall), representativeness (resemblance to a prototype), anchoring & adjustment. Base-rate neglect Tversky & Kahneman Ignoring prior probabilities in favour of individuating detail (the "Tom W." / lawyer-engineer problem). Conjunction fallacy Tversky & Kahneman Judging "feminist bank teller" more likely than "bank teller" (the Linda problem); a conjunction can't exceed its parts. Prospect theory Kahneman & Tversky We value gains/losses from a reference point, not absolute wealth; losses loom larger (loss aversion); S-shaped value function. Framing effect Tversky & Kahneman The same choice framed as a gain vs a loss flips preference (the "Asian disease" problem). Bounded rationality / satisficing Herbert Simon Limited capacity → we settle for "good enough" rather than the optimal choice. Dual-process theory (System 1 / 2) Stanovich & West; Kahneman System 1 = fast, automatic, intuitive; System 2 = slow, effortful, analytic. Availability vs representativeness: availability = judging by how easily examples come to mind (overrate plane crashes). Representativeness = judging by how much it resembles the stereotype (Linda, Tom W.). The conjunction & base-rate fallacies both stem from representativeness.

chunks.heading: 12. Reasoning
chunks.text: 12. Reasoning Term Who What it is Deductive vs inductive — Deductive = certain conclusion from premises (syllogisms); inductive = probable generalisation from cases. Wason selection task Peter Wason The 4-card logic test people fail abstractly but pass when framed as a familiar social rule (drinking-age version). 2-4-6 task / confirmation bias Peter Wason People test rules by seeking confirming, not falsifying, evidence. Belief bias Evans, Barston & Pollard We accept invalid syllogisms whose conclusions we believe and reject valid ones we don't. Mental models theory Philip Johnson-Laird We reason by building mental models of possibilities; errors come from considering too few models. Atmosphere effect Woodworth & Sells The "mood" of the premises (some/all, no) biases which conclusion feels right in syllogisms. Pragmatic reasoning schemas Cheng & Holyoak We reason with context-bound rules (permission, obligation), not pure logic; explains Wason content effects. Wason's two tasks: the selection task (4 cards, P/not-P) tests conditional logic and is solved by familiar content. The 2-4-6 task tests hypothesis testing and exposes confirmation bias. Both are Wason, don't conflate them. That's the cognitive syllabus on one page, Eysenck & Keane in book order. Cover the middle column → name the author; cover the right column → name the model from its claim; and for every trap box, lear

chunks.heading: Cranial Nerves I–XII
chunks.text: Cranial Nerves I–XII What this is. The full I–XII table (name, type, function, common deficits) plus both mnemonics and the MCQ traps that hit every MET/NIMHANS paper. Spun out of the biopsych brain-anatomy note because you flagged it in Mock 1 and it deserves its own page. If you only memorise one biopsych side-page, make it this one. Full I–XII table Mnemonics Sensory vs motor vs both Parasympathetic carriers Brainstem nuclei map High-yield deficits MCQ traps Bedside testing

chunks.heading: Full I–XII table
chunks.text: Full I–XII table # Name Type Function Common deficit / MCQ hook I Olfactory Sensory Smell Only nerve that bypasses thalamus. Anosmia is first lost in Parkinson's and Alzheimer's. Trauma to cribriform plate shears it off. II Optic Sensory Vision CNS tract, not a true peripheral nerve (myelinated by oligodendrocytes, surrounded by meninges). Lesion at optic chiasm = bitemporal hemianopia (pituitary adenoma). III Oculomotor Motor (+parasym) Most extraocular muscles (SR, IR, MR, IO) + levator palpebrae + parasympathetic pupil constriction (Edinger-Westphal nucleus) + lens accommodation. Full palsy = ptosis + "down & out" eye + fixed dilated pupil. Uncal herniation compresses III early (blown pupil). IV Trochlear Motor Superior oblique (depresses + intorts adducted eye). Smallest CN. Only CN that decussates before exit AND only one to exit dorsally from brainstem. Vertical diplopia worse going down stairs; patient tilts head away from lesion. V Trigeminal Both Sensation of face (V1 ophthalmic, V2 maxillary, V3 mandibular) + cornea + ant ⅔ scalp + dura. Motor: muscles of mastication. Trigeminal neuralgia (tic douloureux) — V2/V3 most common. Corneal reflex afferent. Jaw deviates toward weak side on opening. VI Abducens Motor Lateral rectus (abduction). Longest intracranial course → first CN affected by raised ICP. False localising sign. Lesion = inability to abduct, horizontal diplop

chunks.heading: Mnemonics
chunks.text: Mnemonics Name mnemonic (the classic): " On Old Olympus' Towering Tops, A Finn And German Viewed Some Hops " → O lfactory, O ptic, O culomotor, T rochlear, T rigeminal, A bducens, F acial, A uditory (vestibulocochlear), G lossopharyngeal, V agus, S pinal accessory, H ypoglossal. Type mnemonic (Sensory / Motor / Both): " Some Say Marry Money, But My Brother Says Big Brains Matter More " → S, S, M, M, B, M, B, S, B, B, M, M (I–XII). Brainstem exit level: Midbrain: III, IV. Pons: V, VI, VII, VIII. Medulla: IX, X, XI, XII. (I + II are forebrain; everything else exits brainstem top-to-bottom in number order.)

chunks.heading: Sensory vs motor vs both
chunks.text: Sensory vs motor vs both Class CNs Memory hook Purely sensory I, II, VIII "1, 2, 8" — the special senses (smell, sight, hearing/balance). Purely motor III, IV, VI, XI, XII Five of them. Eye movement trio (III/IV/VI) + neck/tongue duo (XI/XII). Mixed (both) V, VII, IX, X The four "B"s in the mnemonic.

chunks.heading: Parasympathetic carriers
chunks.text: Parasympathetic carriers Only four CNs carry parasympathetic fibres. Memorise the four targets: CN Parasympathetic target Nucleus (preganglionic) Ganglion (postganglionic) III Pupil constriction + lens accommodation Edinger-Westphal Ciliary VII Lacrimal, submandibular, sublingual glands Superior salivatory Pterygopalatine + submandibular IX Parotid gland Inferior salivatory Otic X Heart, lungs, GI tract to splenic flexure Dorsal motor nucleus of X + nucleus ambiguus Intrinsic ganglia in target organs

chunks.heading: Brainstem nuclei map
chunks.text: Brainstem nuclei map Level CN nuclei present Midbrain III (oculomotor + Edinger-Westphal), IV (trochlear) Pons V (trigeminal motor + main sensory + spinal trigeminal — spinal V extends down to upper cord), VI (abducens), VII (facial motor + superior salivatory + solitary, taste), VIII (vestibular + cochlear) Medulla IX (nucleus ambiguus motor + inferior salivatory + solitary, taste/visceral), X (dorsal motor + ambiguus + solitary), XI (nucleus ambiguus + spinal accessory nucleus C1–C5), XII (hypoglossal) Sensory nuclei sit lateral, motor nuclei sit medial. Solitary nucleus (taste + visceral afferent) gets VII, IX, X.

chunks.heading: High-yield deficits to memorise
chunks.text: High-yield deficits to memorise CN III palsy — ptosis + "down and out" eye + fixed dilated pupil. Compressive cause (PCom aneurysm, uncal herniation) hits parasympathetic fibres first → pupil involved. Ischaemic cause (diabetes) often pupil-sparing. CN IV palsy — vertical diplopia, worse looking down (reading, stairs). Compensatory head tilt away from lesion (Bielschowsky sign). CN VI palsy — inability to abduct, horizontal diplopia worse on gaze to lesion side. First CN to fail in raised ICP — false localising sign. Bell's palsy (CN VII, LMN) — whole half-face including forehead, taste loss anterior ⅔ tongue, hyperacusis, dry eye. UMN (stroke) spares forehead because upper face has bilateral cortical input. Acoustic neuroma (CN VIII) — unilateral sensorineural hearing loss + tinnitus + vertigo. At cerebellopontine angle so later involves V and VII as it grows. Bulbar palsy — LMN lesion of IX, X, XI, XII (and sometimes V, VII). Flaccid, fasciculating tongue, nasal speech, dysphagia. Cause: MND (PMA variant), Guillain-Barré, brainstem stroke. Pseudobulbar palsy — UMN lesion of same CNs. Spastic tongue (can't protrude), brisk jaw jerk, emotional lability, "Donald Duck" speech. Cause: bilateral strokes, MS, MND (UMN variant). CN XII lesion — tongue deviates TOWARD lesion (LMN) — "the lick goes to the sick." UMN lesion deviates AWAY. CN X / vagus lesion — uvula deviates AWAY from l

chunks.heading: High-yield MCQ traps
chunks.text: High-yield MCQ traps "Which CN bypasses the thalamus?" — Olfactory (I). Every other sensory modality relays through thalamus. "Which CN exits dorsally from the brainstem?" — Trochlear (IV). Also the only one to decussate before exit. "First CN affected in raised ICP?" — Abducens (VI), longest intracranial course. "Which CN is most often a false localising sign?" — VI (raised ICP) and III (uncal herniation). "Bell's palsy spares the forehead?" — NO. Bell's is LMN, whole half-face. Forehead-sparing = UMN = stroke. "Tongue deviates which way in CN XII lesion?" — TOWARD the lesion (LMN). The weak side can't push the tongue out so the strong side pushes it across. "Uvula deviates which way in CN X lesion?" — AWAY from lesion. Opposite of tongue. Same logic: strong side pulls uvula across. "Gag reflex — afferent vs efferent?" — Afferent IX, efferent X. (Both, but knowing which limb is which is the trap.) "Smallest CN?" — Trochlear (IV). "Largest CN?" — Trigeminal (V). "CN with longest intracranial course?" — Abducens (VI). "Which CN carries taste from anterior ⅔ tongue?" — Facial (VII) via chorda tympani. Posterior ⅓ = IX. Epiglottis = X. "Acoustic neuroma associated with?" — NF2 (bilateral), CPA lesion, CN V/VII signs as it expands. "Argyll Robertson pupil" — accommodates but does NOT react to light. Neurosyphilis classic. "Prostitute's pupil — accommodates but doesn't react." "Marc

chunks.heading: Bedside testing (NIMHANS clinical viva)
chunks.text: Bedside testing (NIMHANS clinical viva) CN How to test I Smell coffee/cloves each nostril separately. (Often skipped in routine exam.) II Snellen chart, fields by confrontation, fundoscopy, pupillary light reflex (afferent), colour vision (Ishihara). III, IV, VI "H-pattern" eye movements, pupils (light + accommodation), look for ptosis, diplopia. V Light touch + pinprick V1/V2/V3 each side. Corneal reflex (afferent V, efferent VII). Clench teeth (masseter bulk). Jaw jerk. VII Raise eyebrows, screw eyes shut tight, show teeth, puff cheeks. Watch for forehead sparing. VIII Whisper test or finger-rub each ear. Rinne (tuning fork mastoid vs air) + Weber (forehead, lateralises to affected ear in conductive loss, away in sensorineural). IX, X Say "ahh" — uvula should rise midline. Gag reflex (touch posterior pharynx). Voice quality (hoarse = X). XI Shrug shoulders against resistance (trapezius). Turn head against resistance (SCM — turns to opposite side). XII Protrude tongue — note deviation, fasciculations, atrophy. Push against cheek from inside. One-line revision trick. The eye-movement trio (III, IV, VI) is tested together as an H-pattern, the lower-CN bulbar group (IX, X, XII) is tested together with "ahh" + tongue + voice, and VII gets its own block (eyebrows + eyes shut + teeth + cheeks). If you can run those three sub-exams from memory, you've covered 8 of the 12 CNs. Source:

chunks.heading: Developmental Psychology, Cheatsheet
chunks.text: Developmental Psychology, Cheatsheet MET 2026 + NIMHANS · Built 2026-05-05 · Patches the thin section, absorbs Bronfenbrenner write-up. How to use. This is the section-3 fleshing of dev psych. Read top-to-bottom once, then revise off the tables and the red TRAP boxes. Bronfenbrenner gets its own section here (5) since exam loves him; full primer at notes/bronfenbrenner if you want deeper.

chunks.heading: 1. Foundational Principles
chunks.text: 1. Foundational Principles Principle Meaning Example Cephalocaudal Head → toe Head control before walking Proximodistal Center → periphery Trunk control before fine finger Continuity vs Discontinuity Gradual growth vs stage jumps Vocab growth (continuous) vs Piaget stages (discontinuous) Nature vs Nurture Genes vs environment, modern view = interactionist Twin studies, behavioral genetics Critical period Rigid window, miss it and the capacity is lost Lorenz imprinting in geese Sensitive period Flexible window, learning easier but still possible later L1 acquisition, depth perception Stability vs Change Do traits persist or shift across life? Temperament (mostly stable), IQ (some plasticity) Active vs Passive child Does the child shape their own development? Bidirectionality (Bronfenbrenner, Bell) TRAP: Critical = rigid biological window (lost if missed). Sensitive = optimal but flexible. Lorenz's imprinting = critical. Language learning = sensitive (you can still learn L2 at 30, just harder).

chunks.heading: 2. Prenatal Development & Teratogens
chunks.text: 2. Prenatal Development & Teratogens

chunks.heading: Three prenatal stages
chunks.text: Three prenatal stages Stage Duration Key event Germinal 0-2 weeks Zygote → blastocyst → implantation Embryonic 2-8 weeks Organogenesis, most vulnerable to teratogens Fetal 8 weeks-birth Growth + refinement, viability ~24 weeks

chunks.heading: Teratogens (high-yield)
chunks.text: Teratogens (high-yield) Alcohol — Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder (FASD); FAS = facial anomalies, growth restriction, CNS damage. Most common preventable cause of intellectual disability. Tobacco — low birth weight, prematurity. Thalidomide — limb malformations (1950s-60s, classic teratogen exam case). Rubella — heart, eye, ear defects in 1st trimester. Lead, mercury — CNS damage. Zika — microcephaly. TRAP: Embryonic period (weeks 2-8) is most vulnerable, not the fetal period. Organs are forming. By the fetal period, organs already exist, growth is the main task.

chunks.heading: 3. Piaget, Cognitive Development
chunks.text: 3. Piaget, Cognitive Development

chunks.heading: 4 stages
chunks.text: 4 stages Stage Age Achievements Limits Sensorimotor 0-2 Object permanence (~8mo), goal-directed action, deferred imitation (end) No symbolic thought early on Preoperational 2-7 Symbolic thought, language, pretend play Egocentrism, animism, centration, no conservation Concrete Operational 7-11 Conservation, reversibility, classification, seriation, decentration Tied to concrete reality, abstract is shaky Formal Operational 11+ Abstract, hypothetico-deductive, propositional logic Adolescent egocentrism (imaginary audience, personal fable)

chunks.heading: Sensorimotor 6 substages (mini-list)
chunks.text: Sensorimotor 6 substages (mini-list) Reflexive schemes (0-1mo) Primary circular reactions (1-4mo, on own body) Secondary circular reactions (4-8mo, on objects) Coordination of secondary schemes (8-12mo, intentional, object permanence , A-not-B error) Tertiary circular reactions (12-18mo, experimentation) Mental representation (18-24mo, deferred imitation, symbolic thought)

chunks.heading: Key concepts
chunks.text: Key concepts Schema — mental framework for understanding the world. Assimilation — fitting new info into existing schema (a horse = a "doggie"). Accommodation — modifying schema for new info ("ok, that's a horse, not a doggie"). Equilibration — drive to balance assimilation + accommodation, engine of cognitive change. Egocentrism — preoperational, can't take another's perspective. Three Mountains task. Animism — preoperational, attributing life to objects. Centration — focus on one feature at a time, blocks conservation. Conservation — quantity stays same despite change in form (number, mass, volume). Order: number → mass → liquid → length → area → weight → volume (last, ~11). TRAP: Object permanence (sensorimotor, ~8mo) ≠ Conservation (concrete operational, ~7yr). Different stages, different concepts. TRAP: "Egocentrism" in dev psych ≠ narcissism. It's a cognitive limit, not a personality trait.

chunks.heading: Critiques of Piaget
chunks.text: Critiques of Piaget Underestimated infants (modern habituation studies show object permanence earlier). Stages less discrete than he claimed (horizontal décalage = uneven within a stage). Underplayed culture (Vygotsky's main attack). Not everyone reaches formal operational, especially for unfamiliar content.

chunks.heading: 4. Vygotsky, Sociocultural
chunks.text: 4. Vygotsky, Sociocultural ZPD (Zone of Proximal Development) — gap between what child can do alone vs with help from a more knowledgeable other (MKO). Scaffolding — temporary tailored support, withdrawn as competence grows. Bruner's term , applied to Vygotsky's framework. Private speech — kids talk to themselves while problem-solving. Becomes inner speech, guides cognition. Piaget called this "egocentric speech" and dismissed it; Vygotsky said it's central. Tools of thought — language is the master tool, internalized from social interaction. Higher mental functions are socially mediated . Cultural specificity — cognitive development depends on the cultural tools available (counting systems, writing, schooling). TRAP: "Scaffolding" = Bruner , not Vygotsky. Vygotsky's own terms are ZPD and MKO. Piaget vs Vygotsky in one line: Piaget = child as lone scientist (development → learning). Vygotsky = child as apprentice (learning → development, mediated by culture).

chunks.heading: 5. Bronfenbrenner, Ecological Systems / Bioecological
chunks.text: 5. Bronfenbrenner, Ecological Systems / Bioecological Full standalone primer with PPCT details: notes/bronfenbrenner . Cheatsheet version below is exam-grade.

chunks.heading: Core idea
chunks.text: Core idea Urie Bronfenbrenner (1917-2005). Development = ongoing interaction between the person and a set of nested environmental systems . Ecological Systems Theory (1979) → renamed Bioecological Model (1994) with the PPCT mechanism. Co-founded Head Start (1965).

chunks.heading: The 5 systems (innermost → outermost)
chunks.text: The 5 systems (innermost → outermost) System What it is Examples Microsystem Direct, face-to-face settings; bidirectional Family, school, peers, daycare Mesosystem Interactions between microsystems (a system of microsystems , not a setting itself) Parent-teacher meeting, home-school link, family-peer overlap Exosystem Settings the child does not directly participate in but which still affect them Parent's workplace, school board, mass media, parent's social network Macrosystem Cultural blueprint, the "envelope" around all other systems Ideologies, customs, laws, religion, SES, cultural values Chronosystem Time dimension. Added later (originally 4 systems) Divorce, parental death, pandemic, sociohistorical era

chunks.heading: PPCT (1994 refinement, often asked)
chunks.text: PPCT (1994 refinement, often asked) P rocess — proximal processes , the engine of development. Regular, reciprocal interactions over extended time (parent-child play, reading together). P erson — individual traits in 3 sub-types: Demand (visible: age, gender, appearance) Resource (skills, intelligence, prior knowledge) Force (temperament, motivation, persistence) C ontext — the 5 nested systems above. T ime — micro-time (within an activity), meso-time (across days/weeks), macro-time (chronosystem level).

chunks.heading: High-yield pointers
chunks.text: High-yield pointers Bidirectionality is a microsystem feature, examiner trigger word. Originally 4 systems , chronosystem added later. Two phases of theory: Ecological Systems (1979) → Bioecological with PPCT (1994) . Mesosystem is not a setting , it's the link between two settings. Proximal processes are the engine , context only modifies their effect. TRAP 1: Exosystem ≠ no influence. Child isn't in it, but it shapes them via the microsystem (e.g. dad loses job → stress at home → child affected). TRAP 2: Mass media affecting a child = exosystem , not macrosystem. Media is a setting, not a cultural blueprint. TRAP 3: "Culture, religion, ideology, SES" = macrosystem . "Parent's workplace" = exosystem . "Sibling fight" = microsystem . "Parent-teacher meeting" = mesosystem . If the stem mentions: nested environments, cultural context, parent's workplace, indirect influence → answer is Bronfenbrenner .

chunks.heading: 6. Erikson, 8 Psychosocial Stages
chunks.text: 6. Erikson, 8 Psychosocial Stages Age Conflict Virtue (if resolved) Bad outcome 0-1.5 Trust vs Mistrust Hope Suspicion, withdrawal 1.5-3 Autonomy vs Shame/Doubt Will Compulsive self-doubt 3-6 Initiative vs Guilt Purpose Inhibition 6-12 Industry vs Inferiority Competence Inertia, low self-worth 12-18 Identity vs Role Confusion Fidelity Identity crisis 18-40 Intimacy vs Isolation Love Loneliness 40-65 Generativity vs Stagnation Care Self-absorption 65+ Integrity vs Despair Wisdom Regret, fear of death Mnemonic: " T rust A utonomy I nitiative I ndustry I dentity I ntimacy G enerativity I ntegrity" — TAIIIIGI roughly tracks the stages.

chunks.heading: 7. Marcia, Identity Statuses (Erikson stage 5 expansion)
chunks.text: 7. Marcia, Identity Statuses (Erikson stage 5 expansion) Status Crisis explored? Commitment made? Description Diffusion No No Drifting, uncommitted Foreclosure No Yes Commitment without exploration (handed down by parents) Moratorium Yes (in progress) No Active exploration, no commitment yet Achievement Yes (resolved) Yes Explored + committed

chunks.heading: 8. Freud, Psychosexual Stages
chunks.text: 8. Freud, Psychosexual Stages Age Stage Erogenous zone / theme Fixation traits 0-1 Oral Mouth, feeding Smoking, overeating, dependency 1-3 Anal Bowel control Anal-retentive (orderly, stingy) or anal-expulsive (messy) 3-6 Phallic Genitals; Oedipus / Electra; superego forms Vanity, recklessness 6-12 Latency Sexual urges dormant, same-sex friendships, school focus (no fixation classically) 12+ Genital Mature sexuality, healthy adult relationships (if all prior resolved)

chunks.heading: 9. Kohlberg, Moral Development
chunks.text: 9. Kohlberg, Moral Development Level Stage Driver Preconventional (self-interest) 1. Punishment-obedience Avoid punishment 2. Instrumental exchange Self-benefit, "what's in it for me" Conventional (social rules) 3. Good boy / good girl Approval of others 4. Law and order Maintain social order, duty Postconventional (abstract principles) 5. Social contract Laws as agreed contracts, can be changed 6. Universal ethical principles Internal moral compass, e.g. justice, dignity TRAP: Gilligan's critique = Kohlberg's stages reflect a male "justice" orientation ; women often reason via "ethics of care" (relationships, responsibility). Gilligan added a parallel orientation, didn't replace Kohlberg. Methodology = Heinz dilemma (steal drug to save wife?). Stage = reasoning , not the choice itself.

chunks.heading: 10. Attachment, Bowlby + Ainsworth + Main
chunks.text: 10. Attachment, Bowlby + Ainsworth + Main

chunks.heading: Bowlby's 4 phases
chunks.text: Bowlby's 4 phases Age Phase Behavior 0-6 wk Pre-attachment Indiscriminate signals (cry, smile) 6 wk-8 mo Attachment-in-the-making Prefers familiar caregivers, no clear protest at separation yet 8 mo-18 mo Clear-cut attachment Separation anxiety + stranger anxiety peak; secure base behavior 18-24 mo+ Reciprocal relationships Internal working model; goal-corrected partnership

chunks.heading: Ainsworth's Strange Situation, 4 styles
chunks.text: Ainsworth's Strange Situation, 4 styles Style Sep behavior Reunion behavior Caregiver pattern Secure (B, ~60%) Distressed Easily comforted, returns to play Sensitive, responsive Avoidant (A, ~20%) Little distress Avoids/ignores caregiver Rejecting, unresponsive Resistant / Ambivalent (C, ~10%) Very distressed Seeks + resists contact, can't be soothed Inconsistent Disorganized (D) Confused, freezing, contradictory Approach + avoid, dazed Frightening / abusive / unresolved trauma TRAP: Disorganized (D) was added by Main & Solomon , not Ainsworth. Ainsworth's original 3 = A/B/C.

chunks.heading: Adult attachment (Main, AAI)
chunks.text: Adult attachment (Main, AAI) Secure-Autonomous (corresponds to B) Dismissing (corresponds to A) Preoccupied (corresponds to C) Unresolved / disorganized (corresponds to D)

chunks.heading: Foundational attachment experiments
chunks.text: Foundational attachment experiments Harlow — wire vs cloth mother monkeys. Contact comfort > food. Demolished pure drive-reduction view of attachment. Lorenz — imprinting in geese, classic critical period example. Bowlby's WHO Report (1951) — "maternal deprivation hypothesis," institutional rearing harms development. Influenced post-WWII childcare policy.

chunks.heading: 11. Baumrind, Parenting Styles
chunks.text: 11. Baumrind, Parenting Styles High demand Low demand High warmth Authoritative (best outcomes) Permissive / Indulgent Low warmth Authoritarian Neglectful / Uninvolved Authoritative — high warmth + high demand, clear limits, explanations. Best child outcomes (competence, self-regulation, school). Authoritarian — high demand, low warmth, "because I said so." Linked to lower self-esteem, more anxiety. Permissive — high warmth, few demands. Linked to impulsivity, lower achievement. Neglectful — low on both (added by Maccoby & Martin , 4th style). Worst outcomes. TRAP: Authoritative ≠ Authoritarian. Authoritative = warm + firm (good). Authoritarian = cold + harsh (bad). Words look similar, opposite outcomes.

chunks.heading: 12. Temperament, Thomas & Chess
chunks.text: 12. Temperament, Thomas & Chess Easy (~40%) — regular routines, positive mood, adapts to change. Difficult (~10%) — irregular, intense reactions, slow to adapt. Slow-to-warm-up (~15%) — low activity, mild reactions, gradual to adapt. Remaining ~35% don't fit cleanly. Goodness of fit (Thomas & Chess) — match between temperament and environmental demands predicts adjustment, not temperament alone.

chunks.heading: 13. Language Development
chunks.text: 13. Language Development Age Milestone 0-2 mo Crying, reflexive sounds 2-4 mo Cooing (vowels) 6 mo Babbling (consonants + vowels, "bababa") 10-14 mo First word; holophrastic speech (one word = whole thought) 18-24 mo Two-word / telegraphic speech ("more milk") 2-3 yr Vocab burst, simple sentences, overregularization ("goed", "foots") 3-5 yr Complex grammar, ~2000 words by 5

chunks.heading: Theories of language acquisition
chunks.text: Theories of language acquisition Theorist School Mechanism Skinner Behaviorist Operant conditioning, imitation, reinforcement Chomsky Nativist LAD , Universal Grammar, poverty of stimulus argument Vygotsky / Bruner Social-interactionist Language emerges from social interaction; LASS (Bruner) Piaget Cognitive Thought before language; language reflects cognition TRAP: Overregularization ("goed", "mouses") is a sign of rule learning , not regression. The child has learned the past-tense rule and is over-applying it.

chunks.heading: 14. Theorist Hooks (1-line each)
chunks.text: 14. Theorist Hooks (1-line each) Theorist Hook Piaget 4 cognitive stages, schemas, equilibration Vygotsky ZPD, MKO, sociocultural, language as tool Bruner Scaffolding, modes of representation (enactive/iconic/symbolic), LASS Erikson 8 psychosocial conflicts across life Freud 5 psychosexual stages, id/ego/superego Bowlby Attachment as biological survival system, IWM Ainsworth Strange Situation, A/B/C styles Main & Solomon Disorganized (D) Harlow Wire vs cloth mother, contact comfort > food Lorenz Imprinting, critical period Kohlberg 3 levels, 6 stages of moral reasoning, Heinz dilemma Gilligan Ethics of care, gendered critique Baumrind Parenting styles (3, then 4 with Maccoby & Martin) Bandura Social learning, observation, Bobo doll, self-efficacy Bronfenbrenner Ecological systems, PPCT, micro/meso/exo/macro/chrono Thomas & Chess Temperament types, goodness of fit Marcia 4 identity statuses Gesell Maturation, normative milestones Hall Adolescence as "storm and stress" Skinner Operant theory of language Chomsky LAD, Universal Grammar

chunks.heading: 15. Adolescence (compact)
chunks.text: 15. Adolescence (compact) Puberty — primary (gonads) + secondary (hair, voice) sex characteristics. Girls typically 1-2 yr earlier than boys. Adolescent egocentrism (Elkind) — imaginary audience (everyone is watching) + personal fable (I am unique, immune to harm). Identity — central task (Erikson stage 5); Marcia's 4 statuses. Risk-taking — limbic system matures before prefrontal cortex (dual systems model). Storm and stress (G. Stanley Hall) — older view, modern data shows most adolescents are not in chronic conflict.

chunks.heading: 16. Aging & Late Adulthood
chunks.text: 16. Aging & Late Adulthood Primary aging — biological (sensory decline, slower processing). Secondary aging — disease, lifestyle (preventable). Crystallized intelligence — preserved or improves with age (vocab, knowledge). Fluid intelligence — declines (processing speed, novel problem-solving). Cattell-Horn-Carroll model. Socioemotional selectivity theory (Carstensen) — older adults prioritize emotionally meaningful goals as time horizon shrinks. Kübler-Ross 5 stages of dying — denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance. Often misunderstood as universal/linear, she didn't claim that.

chunks.heading: 17. Top 15 MCQ Traps (Dev Psych)
chunks.text: 17. Top 15 MCQ Traps (Dev Psych) Object permanence (sensorimotor) ≠ Conservation (concrete operational). Critical period (rigid, biological) vs Sensitive period (flexible). Authoritative ≠ Authoritarian. One word, opposite outcomes. Disorganized attachment was Main & Solomon, not Ainsworth. "Scaffolding" is Bruner's term, applied to Vygotsky's ZPD. Bronfenbrenner exosystem = child not in it, but still affected (parent's workplace). Bronfenbrenner mesosystem = link between microsystems, not a setting itself. Chronosystem was added later, originally 4 systems. PPCT = Bioecological Model (1994), not the original 1979 theory. Gilligan added "ethics of care," didn't replace Kohlberg. Overregularization ("goed") is rule-learning, not regression. Embryonic period (weeks 2-8) is most teratogen-vulnerable, not fetal. FAS / FASD = most common preventable cause of intellectual disability. Egocentrism (Piaget) = cognitive limit, not a personality trait. Goodness of fit (Thomas & Chess) — outcome depends on temperament × environment match.

chunks.heading: 18. 30-Second Recall Script
chunks.text: 18. 30-Second Recall Script Dev psych core: Piaget (4 cognitive stages, equilibration), Vygotsky (ZPD, MKO, sociocultural), Bronfenbrenner (5 nested systems + PPCT, exosystem trap), Erikson (8 psychosocial conflicts), Bowlby/Ainsworth/Main (4 attachment styles, B/A/C/D), Baumrind (4 parenting styles, authoritative is best), Kohlberg (3 levels × 2 stages, Gilligan adds care), Thomas & Chess (temperament + goodness of fit), Chomsky vs Skinner on language. Critical vs sensitive period. Conservation ≠ object permanence. Built 2026-05-05 to patch the dev psych section, integrates the Bronfenbrenner exam-grade write-up. Pair with the Bronfenbrenner deep-dive and the high-yield abn+dev sheet. Last sweep before MET. Sihan MET 2026 + NIMHANS Prep
