chunks.heading: Lookalikes — telling two close terms apart on the options
chunks.text: Lookalikes — telling two close terms apart on the options For when plain definitions aren't enough and the trap is a near-identical distractor. Each block is one confusable pair: what's the same (why both look right), what differs (line by line), and the one tell — the single thing in the stem that splits them. Read the tell, not the whole block, on exam day. Built 2026-05-25. Effects Phenomena Theories Theorists Social Psych Cognitive Lookalikes How to use it. The examiner picks two real, correct-sounding terms and bets you can't split them. Don't re-derive both definitions. Find the tell word in the stem (added vs removed? up vs down? before vs after? thought vs act?) and the option falls out. These are the pairs that actually bleed marks on MET/NIMHANS. Jump to: 1. Learning & conditioning 2. Developmental 3. Sensation & perception 4. Memory & cognition 5. Stats & research 6. Abnormal / clinical 7. Defense mechanisms 8. Therapy 9. Social 10. Intelligence

chunks.heading: 1. Learning & conditioning
chunks.text: 1. Learning & conditioning Classical conditioning vs Operant conditioning Same: both are associative learning; both show acquisition, extinction, spontaneous recovery, generalisation and discrimination. Classical (Pavlov) Operant (Skinner) Behaviour Involuntary, reflexive (salivation, fear) Voluntary, emitted (lever press) Association Stimulus → stimulus (CS–US) Behaviour → consequence (response–reinforcer) Learner Passive, responds to a cue Active, operates on the environment Reinforcer timing Comes before/with the response Comes after the response The tell: Is the behaviour automatic and triggered by a cue that comes first (classical), or voluntary and shaped by what happens after (operant)? Any "reward / consequence / punishment" in the stem → operant. Negative reinforcement vs Punishment Same: both are operant procedures and both usually involve an aversive/unpleasant stimulus, so they read alike. Negative reinforcement Punishment Effect on behaviour Increases it Decreases it What happens Removes an aversive stimulus (take painkiller → pain gone) Adds aversive (positive) or removes pleasant (negative) "Negative" means Subtraction, not "bad" — The tell: Did the behaviour go up or down ? Up = reinforcement (negative = the bad thing was taken away ). Down = punishment. "Negative" is about removal, never about being unpleasant. Positive punishment vs Negative punishment Same: b

chunks.heading: 2. Developmental
chunks.text: 2. Developmental Assimilation vs Accommodation (Piaget) Same: the twin processes of adaptation ; both are how a schema deals with new information. Assimilation Accommodation Schema Stays the same — new info forced into it Changes / a new one is created to fit reality Example Calls a whale a "fish" Learns a whale is a mammal, makes a new category The tell: Did the existing schema stay put (assimilation) or did it have to change (accommodation)? If the child updated their mental category, it's accommodation. Piaget vs Vygotsky Same: both constructivists; both say the child actively builds knowledge rather than passively absorbing it. Piaget Vygotsky Engine of development The individual child exploring; cognition leads language Social/cultural interaction; language leads cognition Signature terms Stages, schema, assimilation/accommodation, egocentrism ZPD, scaffolding, More Knowledgeable Other, private speech The tell: Is the driver the child alone (Piaget) or a guiding social other / ZPD (Vygotsky)? Any "scaffolding" or "zone of proximal development" → Vygotsky.

chunks.heading: 3. Sensation & perception
chunks.text: 3. Sensation & perception Sensation vs Perception Same: both are stages of taking in stimulus information. Sensation Perception What it is Raw detection by sense organs + transduction Brain's organisation & interpretation of it Direction Bottom-up (data in) Top-down (meaning added) The tell: Detecting the raw signal at the receptor (sensation) vs making sense of / recognising it (perception). Interpretation, meaning, recognition → perception. Absolute threshold vs Difference threshold (JND) Same: both are psychophysics thresholds (Weber/Fechner). Absolute threshold Difference threshold (JND) Detects Minimum intensity to detect a stimulus 50% of the time Smallest detectable change between two stimuli Law — Weber's law: JND is a constant proportion The tell: Detecting that one stimulus is present (absolute) vs detecting a difference between two (difference / JND). "Just noticeable difference" → difference threshold.

chunks.heading: 4. Memory & cognition
chunks.text: 4. Memory & cognition Proactive interference vs Retroactive interference Same: both are forgetting caused by interference between old and new learning. Proactive Retroactive Direction Old blocks new (forward) New blocks old (backward) What you forget The new material The old material Example Old password keeps coming up New password wipes the old one The tell: Which is forgotten? Forget the new → proactive (" pro = prior learning interferes forward"). Forget the old → retroactive. Recall vs Recognition Same: both are measures of retrieval from long-term memory. Recall Recognition Task Produce the info with little/no cue (essay, free recall) Identify the correct item among options (MCQ) Difficulty Harder Easier — the answer is in front of you The tell: Generate it from scratch (recall) vs pick it out of choices (recognition). A multiple-choice exam tests recognition. Anterograde amnesia vs Retrograde amnesia Same: both are memory loss, usually after brain injury, defined relative to the moment of injury. Anterograde Retrograde Lost memories Can't form new memories after the event Lost old memories from before the event Time direction Forward from injury Backward from injury The tell: " Antero = after" — no new memories form. Retrograde = the past is gone. (H.M. = classic anterograde.) Explicit (declarative) vs Implicit (non-declarative) memory Same: both are long-term memory sys

chunks.heading: 5. Stats & research methods
chunks.text: 5. Stats & research methods Type I error vs Type II error Same: both are wrong decisions in null-hypothesis testing. Type I (α) Type II (β) Mistake Reject a true null = false positive Fail to reject a false null = false negative In words Claim an effect that isn't there Miss a real effect The tell: False alarm = Type I (α). Miss = Type II (β). "Type I = I see something that isn't there." Reliability vs Validity Same: both are desirable psychometric properties of a test or measure. Reliability Validity Question it answers Is it consistent / repeatable? Does it measure what it's supposed to? Relationship Can be reliable but not valid (consistently wrong) Validity requires reliability, not vice versa The tell: Consistency = reliability; accuracy/measures-the-right-thing = validity. Same spot every time = reliable; the bullseye = valid. Independent variable vs Dependent variable Same: both are the variables defined in an experiment. Independent (IV) Dependent (DV) Role Manipulated — the presumed cause Measured — the outcome (depends on the IV) The tell: What the experimenter changes = IV; what they measure as the result = DV.

chunks.heading: 6. Abnormal / clinical
chunks.text: 6. Abnormal / clinical Delusion vs Hallucination Same: both are psychotic symptoms; both appear in schizophrenia. Delusion Hallucination Disturbance of Thought content — a false, fixed belief Perception — a false sensory experience Example "The FBI is tracking me" Hearing voices with no one there The tell: A wrong belief (delusion) vs a wrong perception (hallucination). If there's a sensory experience, it's a hallucination. Illusion vs Hallucination Same: both are perceptual disturbances. Illusion Hallucination External stimulus? Yes — a real stimulus is misperceived No — perception with no stimulus at all Example A shadow looks like an intruder Seeing a person who isn't there The tell: Is there a real object being misread (illusion) or nothing there to begin with (hallucination)? Obsession vs Compulsion Same: both are core to OCD; both are distressing and unwanted. Obsession Compulsion Type Intrusive thought , image or urge (mental) Repetitive act or ritual (behaviour) Function Causes the anxiety Done to relieve the anxiety The tell: The thought that intrudes (obsession) vs the act done to neutralise it (compulsion). Hand-washing = compulsion; the fear of germs = obsession. Affect vs Mood Same: both describe emotional state in a mental status exam. Affect Mood Timescale Momentary, observable expression Sustained, pervasive feeling Analogy The weather The climate The tell: Shor

chunks.heading: 7. Defense mechanisms
chunks.text: 7. Defense mechanisms Repression vs Suppression Same: both push distressing material out of awareness. Repression Suppression Awareness Unconscious, involuntary Conscious, deliberate The tell: Done unknowingly (repression) vs on purpose (suppression). "Decided not to think about it" = suppression. Displacement vs Sublimation Same: both redirect an unacceptable impulse onto a new target. Displacement Sublimation New target A safer but still similar target A socially valued, productive outlet Example Yell at the kids instead of the boss Channel aggression into sport or surgery The tell: Just a safer target (displacement) vs a constructive, socially-approved channel (sublimation). Sublimation is the mature one. Projection vs Reaction formation Same: both defend against one's own unacceptable feelings. Projection Reaction formation Strategy Attribute your impulse to someone else Act the opposite of your impulse Example "He hates me" (when you hate him) Hating someone → being overly nice to them The tell: Pin the feeling on someone else (projection) vs flip to the opposite behaviour (reaction formation).

chunks.heading: 8. Therapy
chunks.text: 8. Therapy Transference vs Countertransference Same: both are displaced feelings inside the psychodynamic therapeutic relationship. Transference Countertransference Whose feelings The client's , redirected onto the therapist The therapist's , redirected onto the client The tell: Client → therapist = transference. Therapist → client = countertransference.

chunks.heading: 9. Social
chunks.text: 9. Social Conformity vs Compliance vs Obedience Same: all three are behaviour change due to social influence. Conformity Compliance Obedience Source of pressure Implicit group norm A direct request An order from authority Study Asch (lines) Foot-in-the-door Milgram (shocks) The tell: Group norm with no one asking (conformity) vs someone requests (compliance) vs an authority commands (obedience). Stereotype vs Prejudice vs Discrimination Same: all three are components of intergroup bias and constantly swapped in options. Stereotype Prejudice Discrimination Component (ABC) Cognition — a belief Affect — a negative attitude Behaviour — an action The tell: Thought = stereotype, feeling = prejudice, action = discrimination. Map it to A ffect / B ehaviour / C ognition.

chunks.heading: 10. Intelligence
chunks.text: 10. Intelligence Fluid intelligence vs Crystallised intelligence (Cattell) Same: both are Cattell's components of general intelligence (Gf–Gc). Fluid (Gf) Crystallised (Gc) What it is Reasoning with novel problems, independent of knowledge Accumulated knowledge, vocabulary, learned skills With age Declines earlier Holds up / keeps rising The tell: On-the-spot novel reasoning (fluid) vs stored, learned knowledge (crystallised). If age makes it better , it's crystallised. That's the lookalikes set. If a pair you keep missing isn't here, send it and I'll add a block. Related sweeps: Phenomena , Effects , Theories , Theorists . Sihan MET 2026 + NIMHANS prep · /notes/differentiators/ · built 2026-05-25

chunks.heading: Genetic, Chromosomal & Metabolic Disorders
chunks.text: Genetic, Chromosomal & Metabolic Disorders High-yield for MET 2026 + NIMHANS · Built 2026-05-16 Why this page. NIMHANS and MET both ask "which disorder is associated with which gene / chromosome / enzyme / behaviour." The MCQ traps are almost always trisomy number, sex chromosome count, inheritance pattern, or the one giveaway feature (musical ear, self-mutilation, happy puppet, etc.). Memorise the table, then the traps. Three things to know per disorder: (1) genetic mechanism, (2) one physical or biochemical sign, (3) one behavioural / cognitive sign. That's the MCQ unit.

chunks.heading: 1. Master one-line table (memorise this)
chunks.text: 1. Master one-line table (memorise this) Disorder Mechanism One-line ID IQ / behaviour Down syndrome Trisomy 21 (47,XX/XY+21) Flat face, epicanthal folds, single palmar crease, hypotonia IQ 30-70; sociable, "Prince Charming"; early-onset Alzheimer's after 40 Edwards syndrome Trisomy 18 Clenched fists with overlapping fingers, rocker-bottom feet Severe ID; <10% survive 1 year Patau syndrome Trisomy 13 Cleft lip/palate, polydactyly, holoprosencephaly Severe ID; <10% survive 1 year Klinefelter 47,XXY (extra X in males) Tall, gynecomastia, small testes, infertility Mild ID or normal; verbal < performance IQ; shy, immature Turner 45,X0 (missing X in females) Short stature, webbed neck, shield chest, amenorrhoea Normal verbal IQ, poor visuospatial; social difficulty XYY 47,XYY Tall males, normal phenotype Mild ID, impulsivity; old "criminal chromosome" myth (disproved) Triple X 47,XXX Tall females, normal phenotype Mild language delay, normal IQ Fragile X CGG repeat on FMR1, X-linked Long face, large ears, macroorchidism (post-puberty) Most common inherited ID; hand-flapping, ASD overlap Williams Microdeletion 7q11.23 (elastin gene) Elfin face, supravalvular aortic stenosis Mild-mod ID; hypersocial , "cocktail party" speech, musical affinity Prader-Willi Paternal 15q11-13 deletion (or maternal UPD) Hypotonia in infancy, hyperphagia later, obesity Mild ID, compulsive eating, skin-pick

chunks.heading: 2. Chromosomal disorders — deeper dive
chunks.text: 2. Chromosomal disorders — deeper dive

chunks.heading: 2.1 Down syndrome (Trisomy 21)
chunks.text: 2.1 Down syndrome (Trisomy 21) Most common chromosomal cause of ID . Incidence ~1 in 700 live births overall. Mechanism (95%) : maternal non-disjunction at meiosis I. Risk rises sharply with maternal age (1/1500 at 20, 1/100 at 40, 1/30 at 45). Other 5% : Robertsonian translocation (14;21) — inheritable, recurrence risk much higher; mosaicism — milder phenotype. Physical : brachycephaly, upslanting palpebral fissures, epicanthal folds, Brushfield spots on iris, flat nasal bridge, protruding tongue, single transverse palmar crease (simian), short fifth finger (clinodactyly), sandal-gap toe. Medical : congenital heart defect (AV septal defect, ~50%), duodenal atresia, hypothyroidism, atlantoaxial instability, leukaemia risk. Cognitive/behavioural : IQ commonly 30-70 (mild to moderate ID), sociable temperament, language < comprehension, mosaic Down syndrome milder. Early-onset Alzheimer's by 40s (extra APP gene on chr 21). Screen : triple test (low AFP, high hCG, low estriol). Confirmed by karyotype. TRAP: "Translocation Down" can be inherited from a carrier parent. Non-disjunction Down is not inherited and increases with maternal age. Know which.

chunks.heading: 2.2 Klinefelter (47,XXY)
chunks.text: 2.2 Klinefelter (47,XXY) Most common sex-chromosome aneuploidy (~1 in 600 males). Tall stature, long limbs, small firm testes, gynecomastia, sparse body hair, infertility (azoospermia). Cognitive: verbal IQ typically below performance IQ, language delay, reading difficulties; IQ often normal or borderline. Behavioural: shy, immature, anxious; increased risk of depression and breast cancer. Treatment: testosterone replacement at puberty.

chunks.heading: 2.3 Turner (45,X0)
chunks.text: 2.3 Turner (45,X0) Only viable monosomy in humans (~1 in 2,500 females). Short stature, webbed neck, low posterior hairline, shield chest with widely spaced nipples, cubitus valgus, lymphoedema of hands/feet in newborn. Streak ovaries → primary amenorrhoea, infertility; coarctation of aorta. Cognitive: verbal IQ usually normal, visuospatial deficit (right hemisphere pattern), nonverbal learning disorder. Behavioural: social immaturity, difficulty reading social cues; not generally ID.

chunks.heading: 2.4 Fragile X (FMR1, CGG repeat)
chunks.text: 2.4 Fragile X (FMR1, CGG repeat) Most common inherited cause of ID (Down is most common overall but mostly sporadic). X-linked; full mutation = >200 CGG repeats on FMR1 → silencing of FMRP protein. Males more severely affected; females show variable, milder picture (X-inactivation). Phenotype: long narrow face, prominent jaw and forehead, large protruding ears, post-pubertal macroorchidism, joint hyperlaxity. Cognitive/behavioural: mild-to-severe ID, ADHD, hand-flapping, gaze aversion, autism features (~30% meet ASD criteria). Premutation carriers (55-200 repeats) → FXTAS (tremor/ataxia) in older males, POI in females. TRAP: "Most common inherited ID" = Fragile X . "Most common chromosomal ID" = Down . Don't swap these.

chunks.heading: 2.5 Williams (7q11.23 deletion)
chunks.text: 2.5 Williams (7q11.23 deletion) Microdeletion includes elastin gene → supravalvular aortic stenosis, joint laxity, hoarse voice. Elfin facies: broad forehead, periorbital fullness, short upturned nose, wide mouth, full lips, small chin. Cognitive: mild-to-moderate ID with classic strength in verbal expressiveness, weakness in visuospatial . Behavioural: hypersocial , overfriendly with strangers, "cocktail party" personality, anxiety, strong affinity for music. Hypercalcaemia in infancy.

chunks.heading: 2.6 Prader-Willi vs Angelman (15q11-13, genomic imprinting)
chunks.text: 2.6 Prader-Willi vs Angelman (15q11-13, genomic imprinting) Prader-Willi Angelman Missing copy Paternal 15q11-13 Maternal 15q11-13 Mechanism ~70% paternal deletion, ~25% maternal uniparental disomy ~70% maternal deletion, UBE3A mutation, paternal UPD Infancy Severe hypotonia, poor feeding, "floppy baby" Normal at birth, feeding difficulty, jerky movements Later Hyperphagia, obesity, short stature, small hands/feet, hypogonadism Microcephaly, ataxic gait, seizures, almost no speech Behaviour Skin-picking, temper outbursts, OCD-like food obsessions "Happy puppet": frequent laughter, hand-flapping, easily excitable IQ Mild-moderate ID Severe ID Memory hook: P aternal = P rader , M aternal = a M elman (Angelman). Same locus, opposite parent of origin, opposite phenotypes — classic imprinting example.

chunks.heading: 2.7 Cri-du-chat (5p−)
chunks.text: 2.7 Cri-du-chat (5p−) Deletion of short arm of chromosome 5. Newborn cry resembles a cat's meow (laryngeal abnormality) — pathognomonic. Microcephaly, hypertelorism (wide-set eyes), epicanthal folds, low-set ears, round "moon face". Severe ID, motor and language delay.

chunks.heading: 2.8 22q11.2 deletion (DiGeorge / Velocardiofacial)
chunks.text: 2.8 22q11.2 deletion (DiGeorge / Velocardiofacial) Most common microdeletion syndrome (~1 in 4,000). CATCH-22: Cardiac (conotruncal), Abnormal facies, Thymic hypoplasia (T-cell immunodeficiency), Cleft palate, Hypocalcaemia (parathyroid hypoplasia), 22q11. Mild-moderate ID, learning disability, nonverbal < verbal pattern. Highest single-gene risk factor for schizophrenia known (~25× general population).

chunks.heading: 3. Inborn errors of metabolism (deeper)
chunks.text: 3. Inborn errors of metabolism (deeper)

chunks.heading: 3.1 PKU (Phenylketonuria) — exam favourite
chunks.text: 3.1 PKU (Phenylketonuria) — exam favourite Enzyme : Phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH) deficiency. Autosomal recessive, chromosome 12. Biochemistry : phenylalanine cannot convert to tyrosine → Phe accumulates, neurotoxic; tyrosine deficiency → low melanin (fair skin, blue eyes, blond hair) and low dopamine/NE. Clinical : untreated → severe ID, seizures, microcephaly, eczema, musty/mousy body odour (phenylacetate in urine/sweat). Screening : Guthrie test (heel-prick at 48-72 hrs of life, blood Phe by bacterial inhibition assay). Now mostly tandem mass spectrometry. Treatment : low-phenylalanine diet (avoid aspartame, meat, dairy, eggs) for life; ideally lifelong. Maternal PKU — mother off diet during pregnancy → fetal damage even if fetus is heterozygote (Phe crosses placenta). Outcome with treatment : normal IQ if started in first 3 weeks of life. TRAP: PKU is the textbook example of preventable ID . The biochemistry (Phe → Tyr block) is the most common single-line MCQ stem. "Musty smell + fair child + ID" = PKU.

chunks.heading: 3.2 Tay-Sachs
chunks.text: 3.2 Tay-Sachs Enzyme : Hexosaminidase A deficiency → GM2 ganglioside accumulates in neurons. Autosomal recessive, HEXA gene chr 15. High carrier rate in Ashkenazi Jews (~1/30). Normal at birth; regression starts at 3-6 months: loss of motor skills, exaggerated startle to sound, progressive paralysis, blindness. Cherry-red spot on macula (pathognomonic when paired with neurodegeneration). Death by 3-5 years. No effective treatment.

chunks.heading: 3.3 Lesch-Nyhan
chunks.text: 3.3 Lesch-Nyhan Enzyme : HGPRT deficiency → cannot recycle purines → uric acid build-up. X-linked recessive (males). Hyperuricaemia → gout, kidney stones in childhood. Self-mutilation is the unique behavioural sign — biting lips, fingertips, head-banging. Compulsive, not psychotic; child is distressed by it. Choreoathetosis, spasticity, ID. TRAP: Self-mutilation in a male child + gout-like features = Lesch-Nyhan . Self-mutilation in a Rett girl = stereotyped hand-mouthing, different. Self-injury in autism is common but is not lip-biting in the classical Lesch-Nyhan pattern.

chunks.heading: 3.4 Galactosaemia
chunks.text: 3.4 Galactosaemia GALT enzyme deficiency. Autosomal recessive. Newborn vomits / fails to thrive after milk; jaundice, hepatomegaly, cataracts, E. coli sepsis. Untreated → ID, ovarian failure. Treat with lactose-free diet.

chunks.heading: 3.5 Maple syrup urine disease
chunks.text: 3.5 Maple syrup urine disease BCKD (branched-chain α-keto acid dehydrogenase) deficiency. Build-up of leucine, isoleucine, valine. Sweet/maple-syrup smelling urine, neonatal lethargy, seizures, coma if untreated.

chunks.heading: 3.6 Wilson's disease
chunks.text: 3.6 Wilson's disease ATP7B mutation → copper accumulates in liver, brain (basal ganglia), cornea. Kayser-Fleischer rings (copper in Descemet's membrane), hepatic dysfunction, parkinsonism, dysarthria. Psychiatric: personality change, depression, psychosis — can mimic primary psychiatric illness. Treat with penicillamine / zinc — psychiatric features reverse.

chunks.heading: 3.7 Hurler vs Hunter (mucopolysaccharidoses)
chunks.text: 3.7 Hurler vs Hunter (mucopolysaccharidoses) Hurler (MPS I) Hunter (MPS II) Enzyme α-L-iduronidase Iduronate-2-sulfatase Inheritance Autosomal recessive X-linked recessive (males) Cornea Corneal clouding Clear cornea Severity More severe, earlier Slower, milder Memory hook: H unter goes h unting → needs clear vision → clear cornea. Hurler is hurt early → corneas cloud.

chunks.heading: 4. Other developmental disorders worth knowing
chunks.text: 4. Other developmental disorders worth knowing

chunks.heading: 4.1 Rett syndrome
chunks.text: 4.1 Rett syndrome MECP2 gene, X-linked dominant. Almost exclusively in girls (lethal in males). Normal development 6-18 months, then deceleration of head growth. Stereotyped hand-wringing / midline hand movements after loss of purposeful hand use. Loss of speech, gait apraxia, breathing irregularities, seizures. Was in DSM-IV PDD section; removed from DSM-5 (now a medical condition with neurodevelopmental features, not a separate ASD subtype).

chunks.heading: 4.2 Fetal Alcohol Syndrome (FAS)
chunks.text: 4.2 Fetal Alcohol Syndrome (FAS) Most common preventable cause of ID (alongside iodine deficiency globally). Facial: short palpebral fissures, smooth philtrum, thin upper lip, low nasal bridge. Growth retardation, microcephaly, ADHD, learning disability. Threshold dose unknown; first trimester exposure most damaging to face.

chunks.heading: 4.3 Congenital hypothyroidism (Cretinism)
chunks.text: 4.3 Congenital hypothyroidism (Cretinism) Iodine deficiency or thyroid dysgenesis in fetal life. Coarse features, large tongue, umbilical hernia, hypotonia, jaundice, lethargic feeding. Untreated → severe ID, short stature. Preventable by neonatal screening + thyroxine.

chunks.heading: 4.4 Neurofibromatosis 1 (NF1)
chunks.text: 4.4 Neurofibromatosis 1 (NF1) NF1 gene, chromosome 17, autosomal dominant. High new-mutation rate. ≥6 café-au-lait spots (>5 mm pre-puberty, >15 mm post), axillary/inguinal freckling, Lisch nodules (iris hamartomas), neurofibromas, optic glioma. Learning disability in ~50%, ADHD overlap, normal IQ usually.

chunks.heading: 4.5 Tuberous sclerosis (TSC)
chunks.text: 4.5 Tuberous sclerosis (TSC) TSC1 (chr 9) or TSC2 (chr 16), autosomal dominant. Ash-leaf hypopigmented macules, facial angiofibromas (adenoma sebaceum), shagreen patch, cortical tubers. Infantile spasms / epilepsy, ID in ~50%, ASD in ~50%.

chunks.heading: 4.6 Huntington's disease
chunks.text: 4.6 Huntington's disease CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion on chromosome 4 (HTT gene), autosomal dominant. Anticipation (earlier onset in successive generations, esp. paternal transmission). Onset 30-50 yrs. Chorea (involuntary jerky movements), caudate + putamen atrophy on imaging. Subcortical dementia (slow processing, executive dysfunction, preserved language) — contrast with cortical dementia of Alzheimer's. Psychiatric: depression, irritability, psychosis, very high suicide risk , may precede motor signs by years.

chunks.heading: 5. Inheritance patterns at a glance
chunks.text: 5. Inheritance patterns at a glance Pattern Examples MCQ giveaway Autosomal dominant Huntington's, NF1, TSC, Marfan Every generation; ~50% offspring affected Autosomal recessive PKU, Tay-Sachs, Wilson's, Galactosaemia, MSUD, Hurler Carrier parents, consanguinity, skips generations X-linked recessive Lesch-Nyhan, Hunter, DMD, Hemophilia A/B Males affected, female carriers, no male-to-male transmission X-linked dominant Rett (MECP2), Fragile X (often grouped here despite repeat) Affects both sexes, lethal in males for Rett Trinucleotide repeat Huntington (CAG), Fragile X (CGG), Friedreich (GAA), Myotonic (CTG) Anticipation Imprinting Prader-Willi (paternal), Angelman (maternal) Same locus, opposite parent of origin, opposite phenotype Chromosomal (numerical) Down (T21), Edwards (T18), Patau (T13), Klinefelter (XXY), Turner (X0) Karyotype Microdeletion Williams (7q11), Prader/Angelman (15q11), DiGeorge (22q11), Cri-du-chat (5p) FISH or microarray to detect

chunks.heading: 6. Twenty MCQ traps
chunks.text: 6. Twenty MCQ traps "Most common chromosomal cause of ID" → Down. "Most common inherited cause of ID" → Fragile X. Single palmar crease + flat face + early Alzheimer's → Down. Tall male, gynecomastia, small testes, infertility → Klinefelter (47,XXY). Short female, webbed neck, amenorrhoea → Turner (45,X0). Cat-like cry → Cri-du-chat (5p−). Elfin face + hypersocial + heart murmur → Williams (7q11 elastin). Hyperphagia + obesity + hypotonic infant → Prader-Willi (paternal 15q). Happy puppet, inappropriate laughter, ataxia → Angelman (maternal 15q). 22q11.2 deletion → CATCH-22 + highest schizophrenia risk. Normal girl → regression at 1 yr + hand-wringing → Rett (MECP2). Self-mutilation + gout in boy → Lesch-Nyhan (HGPRT, X-linked). Musty urine + fair child + ID → PKU (PAH deficiency). Cherry-red macula + Ashkenazi + regression → Tay-Sachs (HexA). Chorea + dementia + family hx → Huntington (CAG, AD). KF rings + tremor + liver → Wilson's (ATP7B, AR). Café-au-lait ≥6 + neurofibromas → NF1. Ash-leaf macules + infantile spasms → tuberous sclerosis. FAS triad → smooth philtrum, thin upper lip, short palpebral fissures. Down: 95% non-disjunction (maternal age), 5% translocation (inheritable). Get the percentages. Maternal PKU: mother off diet during pregnancy damages a heterozygote fetus. Tested in MCQs as "PKU genetics in pregnancy". What to do next. Re-read the master table top to bott

chunks.heading: Effects — every named "____ effect," who gave it, the one-line hook
chunks.text: Effects — every named "____ effect," who gave it, the one-line hook First of the four category sweeps. The bucket is "named effects." NIMHANS / MET love to give you a name and ask "who proposed it" OR describe the situation and ask you to name the effect. So each row pairs the effect → person → what it is . Read it once for the pairings, re-pass with the right column covered. Built 2026-05-24. Effects Phenomena Theories Theorists Social Psych Cognitive Lookalikes How to use it. If the stem names "the ___ effect," the answer is usually a person (who coined it). If the stem describes a scene with no name, the answer is usually the effect . This page drills both directions. The trap is always a same-family effect (halo↔horn, Pygmalion↔Golem, primacy↔recency), so learn each in its pair. Jump to: 1. Memory & learning 2. Attention & perception 3. Social & expectancy 4. Judgment & decision 5. Persuasion & media 6. Biological & clinical

chunks.heading: 1. Memory & learning effects
chunks.text: 1. Memory & learning effects Effect Who What it is Zeigarnik effect Bluma Zeigarnik Interrupted / unfinished tasks are remembered better than completed ones. Von Restorff (isolation) effect Hedwig von Restorff The odd-one-out item in a list stands out and is recalled best. Serial position effect Ebbinghaus (named by Murdock) First + last items in a list recalled best (= primacy + recency together). Primacy effect — First items recalled well (rehearsed into long-term store). Recency effect — Last items recalled well (still in short-term store). A delay/distractor kills recency, not primacy. Spacing (distributed practice) effect Ebbinghaus Spread-out study beats cramming for long-term retention. Testing effect — Retrieving (self-testing) cements memory better than re-reading. Generation effect Slamecka & Graf Info you generate yourself is remembered better than info you just read. Self-reference effect Rogers, Kuiper & Kirker Material related to yourself is encoded and recalled better. Misinformation effect Elizabeth Loftus Post-event misleading info distorts the original memory (eyewitness work). Picture superiority effect Paivio (dual-coding) Pictures are remembered better than words. Encoding-specificity / context effect Tulving & Thomson Recall is best when retrieval cues match the encoding context (state/context-dependent memory). Levels-of-processing effect Craik & Lockhart

chunks.heading: 2. Attention & perception effects
chunks.text: 2. Attention & perception effects Effect Who What it is Stroop effect J. Ridley Stroop Slower to name ink colour when the word spells a different colour (automatic reading interferes). Cocktail-party effect Colin Cherry Selective attention to one voice in a crowd, yet you still catch your own name. McGurk effect McGurk & MacDonald What you see the mouth do changes what you hear (audio-visual speech fusion). Ventriloquist effect — Sound is mislocated toward a plausible visual source. Troxler effect (fading) Troxler Fixate steadily and unchanging peripheral stimuli fade from awareness. Motion aftereffect (waterfall illusion) — After staring at motion, a static scene appears to drift the opposite way. Bouba/kiki effect Köhler (later Ramachandran) People map "bouba" to round shapes, "kiki" to spiky ones (sound symbolism). Tetris effect — Heavy repeated activity intrudes into imagery/dreams. NIMHANS angle: the phi phenomenon and autokinetic phenomenon are on the Phenomena page (they're called "phenomena," not "effects") — don't go looking for them here.

chunks.heading: 3. Social & expectancy effects
chunks.text: 3. Social & expectancy effects Effect Who What it is Halo effect Edward Thorndike One good trait (e.g. looks) bleeds into an overall positive judgement. Horn(s) effect — The negative mirror of halo: one bad trait darkens the whole impression. Pygmalion (Rosenthal) effect Rosenthal & Jacobson High teacher/leader expectations → the person actually performs better. Golem effect — Low expectations → worse performance (the dark twin of Pygmalion). Hawthorne effect Elton Mayo (Western Electric) People change behaviour because they know they're being observed. John Henry effect Saretsky A control group tries extra hard because it knows it's the comparison (a research artefact). Mere-exposure effect Robert Zajonc Repeated exposure alone increases liking. Bystander effect Latané & Darley More onlookers → less likely any one helps (diffusion of responsibility). After Kitty Genovese. Ringelmann effect Max Ringelmann Per-person effort drops as group size grows (precursor to social loafing). Pratfall effect Elliot Aronson A competent person becomes more likeable after a small blunder. Spotlight effect Thomas Gilovich Overestimating how much others notice you. False-consensus effect Lee Ross Overestimating how many people share your views. Lake Wobegon / above-average effect — Most people rate themselves above average (illusory superiority). Cheerleader effect — Faces look more attractive in

chunks.heading: 4. Judgment & decision effects
chunks.text: 4. Judgment & decision effects Effect Who What it is Barnum / Forer effect Bertram Forer Accepting vague, general descriptions as uniquely true of you (horoscopes, cold reading). Dunning–Kruger effect Dunning & Kruger Low-skill people overestimate their own competence. Anchoring effect Tversky & Kahneman First number seen drags later estimates toward it. Framing effect Tversky & Kahneman Same facts, different wording (gain vs loss) flips the choice. Endowment effect Richard Thaler You value a thing more just because you own it. IKEA effect Norton, Mochon & Ariely You over-value things you partly built yourself. Decoy (asymmetric dominance) effect Huber et al. A third inferior option nudges choice between the other two. Bandwagon effect — Adopting a belief because many others hold it. Actor–observer effect Jones & Nisbett Your own acts blamed on the situation, others' on their character. Recency / availability in judgment Tversky & Kahneman Easily recalled examples seem more frequent than they are (availability heuristic). Pollyanna effect Matlin & Stang Positive items are processed and recalled more readily than negative. NIMHANS angle: anchoring, framing and availability are also written up as cognitive biases — if the stem says "bias," check the Phenomena page; if it says "effect," it's here. Same content, two labels.

chunks.heading: 5. Persuasion, media & population effects
chunks.text: 5. Persuasion, media & population effects Effect Who What it is Sleeper effect Carl Hovland (Yale) A message from a low-credibility source persuades more over time once you forget the source. Mere-exposure effect Zajonc (Also a persuasion lever: familiarity breeds liking.) Werther effect David Phillips Spike in copycat suicides after a publicised one. Papageno effect Niederkrotenthaler Responsible media coverage of coping can reduce suicide (the protective opposite of Werther). Mozart effect Rauscher et al. A brief, small spatial-reasoning bump after Mozart (popularly overstated). Flynn effect James Flynn Population IQ scores have risen generation on generation (forces test re-norming). Matthew effect Robert Merton "Rich get richer": early advantage compounds (reading, science credit). Kuleshov effect Lev Kuleshov Viewers read emotion into a neutral face based on the adjacent shot (film editing).

chunks.heading: 6. Biological & clinical effects
chunks.text: 6. Biological & clinical effects Effect Who What it is Placebo effect — Improvement from an inert treatment driven by expectation. Nocebo effect — Negative symptoms from an inert treatment (the dark twin of placebo). Garcia effect (taste aversion) John Garcia One-trial conditioned aversion to a taste; biological preparedness; defies classic CC timing rules. Coolidge effect Frank Beach (named it) Renewed sexual interest when a novel partner is introduced. Westermarck effect Edvard Westermarck Reverse sexual imprinting: people raised together in early childhood feel no attraction (incest avoidance). Kindling effect Goddard (seizure model) Repeated sub-threshold stimulation lowers the threshold for episodes (used for mood/seizure recurrence). Tolerance / sensitisation — Same drug dose gives less effect (tolerance) or more (sensitisation) with repetition. Placebo vs nocebo, Werther vs Papageno, Pygmalion vs Golem, halo vs horn, primacy vs recency, tolerance vs sensitisation — six "good twin / bad twin" pairs. If you only learn one of each, the distractor will be the other. That's the effects bucket. Cover the middle column and name the person; cover the right column and name the effect from the description. The other three sweeps: Phenomena , Theories , Theorists . chunks.heading: Ethics in Practice — the terms they test
chunks.text: Ethics in Practice — the terms they test Each principle + what it actually looks like in the clinic room · Built 2026-05-22 How they ask this. Either straight definition ("non-maleficence means ___") or a vignette ("a clinician does X, which principle is violated?"). The 4 big ones are Beauchamp & Childress's principles . The rest are the day-to-day rules that fall out of them. For each, learn the one-line definition and the in-practice example, because the vignette items only give you the scenario.

chunks.heading: The 4 core principles (Beauchamp & Childress)
chunks.text: The 4 core principles (Beauchamp & Childress) Mnemonic: "A-B-N-J" / "Auto Brings No Justice." Autonomy · Beneficence · Non-maleficence · Justice. Principle One line In practice Autonomy Respect the client's right to decide for themselves Informed consent · right to refuse treatment · not coercing Beneficence Act for the client's good Choosing the treatment most likely to help · promoting wellbeing Non-maleficence "First, do no harm" ( primum non nocere ) Not using unproven/harmful methods · staying within competence Justice Fairness — treat like cases alike, distribute resources fairly No discrimination · fair access to care · equitable waitlists The classic swap: beneficence = do good , non-maleficence = avoid harm . They're a pair but separate principles. "Withholding a harmful drug" = non-maleficence. "Giving a helpful one" = beneficence.

chunks.heading: What falls under Autonomy
chunks.text: What falls under Autonomy Informed consent: client understands the nature, risks, benefits, and alternatives, and agrees voluntarily and with capacity . Three pillars: disclosure · capacity · voluntariness. Assent: agreement from someone who can't legally consent (a minor) — you still get their assent alongside the parent's consent . Right to refuse / withdraw at any time without penalty. Paternalism = overriding a competent person's choice "for their own good." It's the violation of autonomy. Only justified when the person lacks capacity.

chunks.heading: Confidentiality and its limits
chunks.text: Confidentiality and its limits Confidentiality: not disclosing client information. Privacy = the client's right; confidentiality = your duty to protect it; privileged communication = the legal protection in court. Limits / when you must break it: risk of serious harm to self or others · suspected child/elder abuse ( mandatory reporting ) · court order. Duty to warn / protect (Tarasoff): if a client makes a credible threat against an identifiable person, the therapist must act to protect that person. This is where non-maleficence/beneficence to a third party overrides confidentiality. Very common vignette.

chunks.heading: The other named terms
chunks.text: The other named terms Term Means Fidelity Loyalty, keeping promises, being trustworthy and reliable to the client Veracity Truth-telling — being honest with the client (e.g. about diagnosis, prognosis) Competence Practising only within the limits of your training; refer out otherwise Dual / multiple relationship Having a second role with a client (friend, business, romantic) — a boundary violation Duty of care The legal/ethical obligation to act in the client's best interest Negligence Falling below the accepted standard of care, causing harm (basis of malpractice) Capacity / competence to consent Whether the person can understand and reason about the decision Vulnerability Extra protection owed to those who can't fully protect their own interests (children, severe MI)

chunks.heading: Indian context (worth a line)
chunks.text: Indian context (worth a line) RCI (Rehabilitation Council of India) licenses clinical psychologists and has its own code of ethics . Mental Healthcare Act 2017 codifies advance directives, nominated representative, right to confidentiality, and consent for persons with mental illness, plus decriminalises suicide attempt. APA Ethics Code is the international reference (the 5 general principles: beneficence/non-maleficence, fidelity/responsibility, integrity, justice, respect for rights & dignity).

chunks.heading: Match the scenario to the principle
chunks.text: Match the scenario to the principle Cover the right column, name the principle violated or upheld. Scenario Principle Therapist uses a technique they're not trained in and the client worsens Non-maleficence (+ competence) Clinician forces medication on a competent, refusing adult Autonomy violated (paternalism) Psychologist dates a current client Fidelity / dual relationship — boundary violation Therapist tells a client's threat to the named target Upholds duty to warn (Tarasoff); breaks confidentiality lawfully Same waitlist priority regardless of caste/income Justice Choosing the most evidence-based treatment for the client Beneficence Hiding a poor prognosis from the client Veracity violated Sharing case details at a party Confidentiality violated Getting a 14-year-old's agreement alongside the parent's consent Assent (+ consent)

chunks.heading: The traps
chunks.text: The traps Beneficence vs non-maleficence. Do good vs avoid harm. If the answer is about stopping/avoiding something harmful, it's non-maleficence. Privacy vs confidentiality vs privilege. Privacy = the right · confidentiality = your duty · privileged communication = court protection. Consent vs assent. Adults with capacity give consent ; minors give assent (parent gives consent). Autonomy vs paternalism. Overriding a competent refusal "for their good" violates autonomy. Only ok if capacity is genuinely absent. Confidentiality is not absolute. Harm to self/others, abuse reporting, and court orders override it. Tarasoff is the headline case. chunks.heading: General Psychology — detailed notes
chunks.text: General Psychology — detailed notes Perception · attention · memory · learning · emotion · motivation · intelligence · cognition · landmark experiments · Built 2026-05-22 What this is. The detailed standalone general-psychology notes you asked for, one section per area, each with the named theories, the people behind them, and the traps. This is the depth; the Rapid Recall block is the one-line version for the cab. Use this to read, that one to test yourself. Jump to: 1. Perception 2. Attention 3. Memory 4. Learning 5. Emotion 6. Motivation 7. Intelligence 8. Cognition 9. Landmark experiments 10. Personality 11. Social psychology 12. Developmental 13. Consciousness & sleep 14. Stress & coping 15. Schools & history

chunks.heading: 1. Perception & Sensation
chunks.text: 1. Perception & Sensation Sensation is detecting raw stimulus energy at the receptors; perception is the brain organising and interpreting it. Transduction is the conversion of stimulus energy into neural signals.

chunks.heading: Psychophysics (thresholds)
chunks.text: Psychophysics (thresholds) Concept Meaning Absolute threshold Smallest intensity detectable 50 percent of the time Difference threshold (JND) Smallest change between two stimuli that is detectable 50 percent of the time Weber's law The JND is a constant proportion of the stimulus, not a fixed amount Fechner's law Sensation grows with the logarithm of stimulus intensity Stevens' power law Sensation is a power function of intensity (often fits better than Fechner) Subliminal / priming Stimuli below the absolute threshold can still prime responses

chunks.heading: Signal detection theory
chunks.text: Signal detection theory Detection is a decision under uncertainty, not a fixed threshold. Four outcomes: hit , miss , false alarm , correct rejection . d-prime (d') measures true sensitivity; beta is the response criterion (how willing you are to say "yes"). Motivation and expectation shift beta, not sensitivity.

chunks.heading: Theories of perception
chunks.text: Theories of perception The two camps: Gibson's direct / bottom-up theory (the stimulus itself carries enough information, perception is data-driven) versus Gregory's constructivist / top-down theory (perception is an active hypothesis built from prior knowledge and inference). Most modern views combine both.

chunks.heading: Gestalt laws of organisation
chunks.text: Gestalt laws of organisation "The whole is greater than the sum of its parts." Proximity, similarity, closure, continuity (good continuation), common fate, figure-ground, pragnanz (simplicity). Founders: Wertheimer, Koffka, Kohler.

chunks.heading: Depth & constancy
chunks.text: Depth & constancy Binocular cues: retinal disparity, convergence. Monocular cues: relative size, interposition, linear perspective, texture gradient, motion parallax, aerial perspective. Perceptual constancies: size, shape, colour, brightness, the object looks stable despite changing retinal image. Feature integration theory (Treisman): a preattentive stage detects individual features in parallel, then focused attention binds them into a whole object. Failure of binding produces illusory conjunctions.

chunks.heading: Pattern recognition & perceptual set
chunks.text: Pattern recognition & perceptual set Template, prototype, and feature-detection theories of how we recognise patterns; Biederman's recognition-by-components (geons) builds objects from basic 3D primitives. Perceptual set / expectancy: context, motivation, culture, and prior knowledge bias what we perceive (top-down). Illusions: Müller-Lyer, Ponzo, Ames room, moon illusion, the Kanizsa triangle (illusory contours), the McGurk effect (vision alters what we hear). Illusions reveal the brain's interpretive shortcuts.

chunks.heading: 2. Attention
chunks.text: 2. Attention Attention is the selective allocation of limited processing capacity. The big debate: where in the stream does selection happen (early vs late), and how much capacity is there (bottleneck vs flexible resources).

chunks.heading: Bottleneck / filter models (where does selection happen?)
chunks.text: Bottleneck / filter models (where does selection happen?) Model Claim Broadbent (1958, early selection) A single filter blocks unattended input early , based on physical features (pitch, location), before meaning is processed. Based on Cherry's dichotic-listening / shadowing work. Treisman (1964, attenuation) The filter attenuates (turns down) unattended input rather than fully blocking it; high-priority words with low thresholds (your name, "fire") still break through. Deutsch & Deutsch / Norman (late selection) All input is fully processed for meaning; selection happens late , at the response/awareness stage, not at perception. Johnston & Heinz (multimode) Selection is flexible: it can occur early or late depending on task demands, but later selection costs more capacity.

chunks.heading: Capacity / resource models (how much is there?)
chunks.text: Capacity / resource models (how much is there?) Model Claim Kahneman (1973, single capacity) Attention is one limited pool of effort/resources allocated across tasks; arousal changes the size of the pool; an allocation policy decides where it goes. Wickens (multiple resources) There are several separate resource pools (e.g. visual vs auditory, verbal vs spatial). Two tasks interfere most when they draw on the same pool, which is why you can drive and listen but not read and listen. Norman & Bobrow Data-limited (limited by poor stimulus quality) vs resource-limited (limited by available attention) performance. Lavie (perceptual load theory) Under high perceptual load selection is early (no spare capacity, distractors filtered out); under low load spare capacity spills onto distractors, so selection is late. Reconciles the early/late debate.

chunks.heading: Spatial / visual attention
chunks.text: Spatial / visual attention Spotlight model (Posner): attention is a movable "spotlight" that enhances processing wherever it points. Zoom-lens (Eriksen): the spotlight can widen or narrow, trading area for resolution. Posner cueing paradigm: a valid cue speeds detection, an invalid one slows it. Endogenous (voluntary, goal-driven, central cue) vs exogenous (reflexive, stimulus-driven, peripheral cue) orienting. Phases of orienting: disengage → move → engage. Feature Integration Theory (Treisman): a preattentive stage registers features (colour, orientation) in parallel across the field; focused attention then binds them into objects. Feature search ("pop-out") is parallel and fast; conjunction search is serial. Failed binding = illusory conjunctions . Guided search (Wolfe): a refinement of FIT, top-down knowledge guides attention toward likely targets.

chunks.heading: Types & control
chunks.text: Types & control Selective (focus on one source), divided (split across tasks), sustained (vigilance over time), alternating/switching (toggle between tasks, with a switch cost). Automatic vs controlled (Schneider & Shiffrin): automatic is fast, parallel, effortless, hard to suppress (Stroop interference happens because reading is automatic); controlled is slow, serial, effortful, flexible. Practice automatises a skill. Supervisory Attentional System (Norman & Shallice): routine action runs on automatic "schemas" via contention scheduling; the SAS (frontal) intervenes only for novel or risky situations. Failures → action slips / capture errors.

chunks.heading: Key phenomena
chunks.text: Key phenomena Cocktail-party effect (Cherry): you can follow one voice in a crowd yet still detect your own name in an ignored stream. Stroop effect: naming the ink colour of a colour-word is slowed because reading is automatic. Classic interference / automaticity demo. Inattentional blindness (Simons & Chabris invisible-gorilla) and change blindness : without attention, even large changes go unnoticed, so attention is needed for conscious perception. Attentional blink: in rapid serial visual presentation, a second target is missed if it appears ~200-500 ms after the first, attention is briefly "used up". Vigilance decrement (Mackworth's clock test): sustained-attention performance declines over time, faster when signals are rare. Psychological refractory period: a second response is delayed when two stimuli arrive close together, evidence for a central bottleneck. Spatial neglect: right-parietal damage leaves patients ignoring the left side of space, a clinical breakdown of spatial attention. TRAP: Cocktail-party effect (hearing your name in an unattended conversation) supports late /attenuation selection, NOT Broadbent's early filter, this is the most common attention MCQ. Broadbent = early/physical; Treisman = attenuation; Deutsch-Norman = late/meaning; Lavie = depends on load. Feature search pops out (parallel); conjunction search is serial.

chunks.heading: 3. Memory
chunks.text: 3. Memory

chunks.heading: Multi-store model (Atkinson-Shiffrin)
chunks.text: Multi-store model (Atkinson-Shiffrin) Sensory memory → short-term/working memory → long-term memory, with attention and rehearsal as the gates. Store Capacity / duration Sensory: iconic (visual) large; about 0.25 to 1 second (Sperling's partial-report) Sensory: echoic (auditory) about 2 to 4 seconds Short-term memory 7 plus or minus 2 items (Miller), about 15 to 30 seconds; chunking expands it Long-term memory effectively unlimited, durable

chunks.heading: Working memory (Baddeley & Hitch)
chunks.text: Working memory (Baddeley & Hitch) Four parts: central executive (control), phonological loop (verbal/acoustic), visuospatial sketchpad (visual/spatial), and the episodic buffer (added 2000, integrates information across systems).

chunks.heading: Types of long-term memory
chunks.text: Types of long-term memory Explicit / declarative (conscious): episodic (events, "what I did") and semantic (facts, meanings). Implicit / non-declarative (unconscious): procedural (skills), priming, classical conditioning.

chunks.heading: Processes, forgetting & distortion
chunks.text: Processes, forgetting & distortion Encoding → storage → retrieval. Levels of processing (Craik & Lockhart): deep semantic encoding beats shallow. Forgetting: decay; interference (proactive = old disrupts new; retroactive = new disrupts old); cue-dependent / retrieval failure; encoding failure. Ebbinghaus forgetting curve: rapid early loss then levelling; spacing and overlearning slow it. Serial position effect: primacy (LTM) + recency (STM). A delay wipes recency, not primacy. Reconstructive memory: Bartlett (schemas distort recall, "War of the Ghosts"); Loftus (misinformation effect, leading questions reshape memory). Amnesia: anterograde (cannot form new memories, e.g. H.M.) vs retrograde (cannot recall old). Korsakoff = thiamine deficiency + confabulation.

chunks.heading: Retrieval, cues & enhancement
chunks.text: Retrieval, cues & enhancement Encoding specificity (Tulving): retrieval is best when cues at recall match those at encoding. Context-dependent (same place/environment) and state-dependent (same mood/physiological state) memory; mood-congruent recall. Recall vs recognition vs relearning (savings) as measures of retention; recognition is usually easier than recall. Flashbulb memories: vivid, confident memories of shocking events, felt accurate but still prone to distortion. Tip-of-the-tongue state = retrieval failure with partial access. Spacing effect and testing effect : spaced practice and active retrieval beat massed re-reading. Consolidation: the hippocampus binds new memories; sleep aids consolidation; reconsolidation makes reactivated memories briefly editable.

chunks.heading: 4. Learning
chunks.text: 4. Learning

chunks.heading: Classical conditioning (Pavlov)
chunks.text: Classical conditioning (Pavlov) A neutral stimulus paired with an unconditioned stimulus (UCS) becomes a conditioned stimulus (CS) that triggers a conditioned response (CR). Phases: acquisition, extinction, spontaneous recovery, generalisation, discrimination, higher-order conditioning. Watson's Little Albert = conditioned fear. Garcia effect = taste aversion learned in one trial over long delay (biological preparedness).

chunks.heading: Operant conditioning (Thorndike, Skinner)
chunks.text: Operant conditioning (Thorndike, Skinner) Thorndike's law of effect : responses followed by satisfaction are stamped in. Skinner formalised it. Add (positive) Remove (negative) Increase behaviour (reinforcement) Positive reinforcement (give a reward) Negative reinforcement (remove an aversive) Decrease behaviour (punishment) Positive punishment (add an aversive) Negative punishment (remove a reward) Schedules of reinforcement: Fixed Ratio, Variable Ratio, Fixed Interval, Variable Interval. Variable Ratio gives the highest, steadiest response rate and is the most resistant to extinction (gambling). Ratio schedules beat interval; variable beats fixed. Shaping = reinforcing successive approximations. Premack principle = a high-frequency behaviour reinforces a low-frequency one ("eat your vegetables, then dessert").

chunks.heading: Cognitive & observational learning
chunks.text: Cognitive & observational learning Tolman: latent learning + cognitive maps (rats learned the maze without reinforcement). Kohler: insight learning (chimps solved problems suddenly, the "aha"). Bandura: observational learning / modelling (Bobo doll); steps = attention, retention, reproduction, motivation. Seligman: learned helplessness; biological constraints (preparedness) limit what can be conditioned. Rescorla-Wagner model: conditioning depends on surprise/prediction error , not mere pairing. The CS must reliably predict the UCS. Explains blocking (a new cue learns nothing if an existing cue already predicts the UCS) and the contingency (not just contiguity) requirement, Rescorla showed the CS must signal information. More terms: stimulus generalisation vs discrimination ; spontaneous recovery of an extinguished CR; overshadowing (a salient cue overshadows a weak one); latent inhibition (a pre-exposed stimulus is harder to condition). In operant work: escape vs avoidance learning, discriminative stimulus (signals when a response pays off), extinction burst , and the partial-reinforcement extinction effect (intermittently reinforced behaviour resists extinction).

chunks.heading: 5. Emotion
chunks.text: 5. Emotion Theory Sequence James-Lange Stimulus → body arousal → you label the emotion ("I tremble, therefore I am afraid") Cannon-Bard Stimulus → arousal AND emotion at the same time (thalamus routes both) Schachter-Singer (two-factor) Arousal + a cognitive label = emotion; same arousal, different label, different emotion Lazarus (appraisal) Cognitive appraisal comes first, then emotion Zajonc Some emotional reactions occur before/without cognition ("preferences need no inferences") Facial feedback hypothesis Facial expressions feed back and intensify the felt emotion Ekman: six basic universal emotions (happiness, sadness, anger, fear, surprise, disgust). Components of emotion: physiological arousal, expressive behaviour, conscious experience. Yerkes-Dodson law: performance peaks at moderate arousal (inverted U); harder tasks peak at lower arousal. Plutchik's wheel: eight primary emotions in opposing pairs that blend into secondary emotions (e.g. joy + trust = love). Dimensional models: Russell's circumplex maps emotion on valence (pleasant-unpleasant) × arousal (high-low). LeDoux's two roads to fear: a fast "low road" (thalamus → amygdala) for quick reaction and a slower "high road" (via cortex) for accurate appraisal. Cognitive appraisal detail (Lazarus): primary appraisal (is it relevant/threatening?) then secondary (can I cope?). Display rules: culturally learned norms fo

chunks.heading: 6. Motivation
chunks.text: 6. Motivation Instinct theory: behaviour driven by innate biological programs. Drive-reduction (Hull): a need creates a drive; behaviour reduces the drive to restore homeostasis. Arousal theory: we seek an optimal level of arousal (links to Yerkes-Dodson). Incentive theory: external rewards pull behaviour. Maslow's hierarchy: physiological → safety → love/belonging → esteem → self-actualisation (later: cognitive, aesthetic, transcendence). Intrinsic vs extrinsic: intrinsic = for its own sake; extrinsic = for a reward. The overjustification effect : paying for an already-enjoyed activity can reduce intrinsic motivation. Self-determination theory (Deci & Ryan): autonomy, competence, relatedness. McClelland: needs for achievement, affiliation, power (measured via the TAT). ERG theory (Alderfer): Maslow condensed to Existence, Relatedness, Growth; allows movement up and down (frustration-regression). Expectancy theory (Vroom): motivation = expectancy × instrumentality × valence. Goal-setting theory (Locke & Latham): specific, challenging, accepted goals drive performance. Approach-avoidance conflict (Lewin): approach-approach, avoidance-avoidance, and approach-avoidance conflicts. Specific drives: hunger (lateral hypothalamus starts eating, ventromedial stops it; the set-point/leptin idea); arousal/sensation-seeking; achievement motivation (need for achievement vs fear of failure).

chunks.heading: 7. Intelligence
chunks.text: 7. Intelligence Theorist Model Spearman (1904) Two-factor: general intelligence g + specific s ; invented factor analysis Thurstone (1938) 7 Primary Mental Abilities (no single g) Cattell & Horn Fluid intelligence (Gf, reasoning) vs crystallised (Gc, learned knowledge) Guilford Structure of Intellect (up to 180 cells); convergent vs divergent thinking Gardner (1983) Multiple intelligences (8): linguistic, logical-mathematical, spatial, musical, bodily-kinaesthetic, interpersonal, intrapersonal, naturalist Sternberg Triarchic: analytical, creative, practical Carroll / CHC Three-stratum hierarchy (g → broad → narrow); the dominant modern model Tests: Wechsler (WAIS/WISC, deviation IQ, SD 15), Stanford-Binet (SD 16, SB-5 uses 15), Raven's Progressive Matrices (culture-reduced g). Ratio IQ = (mental age / chronological age) × 100. Flynn effect = rising IQ scores across generations. Heritability estimates are population statistics, not individual destiny. Vernon's hierarchical model and Cattell-Horn-Carroll (CHC) integrate g, broad, and narrow abilities, the basis of most modern tests. Galton (first to study individual differences, hereditary genius), Binet & Simon (first practical test, the concept of mental age), Terman (Stanford-Binet, longitudinal study of gifted "Termites"). Emotional intelligence (Goleman) and Sternberg's successful intelligence broaden the construct beyond ac

chunks.heading: 8. Cognition (thinking, problem-solving, language)
chunks.text: 8. Cognition (thinking, problem-solving, language) Concepts & prototypes: we categorise by comparison to a best example (prototype). Problem solving: algorithms (guaranteed, slow) vs heuristics (fast rules of thumb). Barriers: fixation, mental set, functional fixedness. Heuristics & biases (Tversky & Kahneman): representativeness, availability, anchoring; confirmation bias; framing effect; overconfidence. Decision making: System 1 (fast, intuitive) vs System 2 (slow, deliberate). Language: phonemes → morphemes → syntax → semantics → pragmatics. Stages: cooing, babbling, one-word (~12 mo), telegraphic (~24 mo). Chomsky: language acquisition device + universal grammar (nativist). Skinner: language is learned by reinforcement (behaviourist), demolished by Chomsky's review. Whorf: linguistic relativity (language shapes thought). Critical/sensitive period (Lenneberg); the case of Genie. Reasoning: deductive (general → specific, logically certain) vs inductive (specific → general, probabilistic); confirmation bias and belief bias distort it. More heuristics & effects: gambler's fallacy, sunk-cost fallacy, hindsight bias, base-rate neglect, the conjunction fallacy (Linda problem), loss aversion and prospect theory (Kahneman & Tversky). Mental imagery: Shepard & Metzler's mental rotation, imagery is analog and spatial. Concept structure: classical (defining features) vs prototype vs ex

chunks.heading: 9. Landmark experiments (the detail)
chunks.text: 9. Landmark experiments (the detail) Study Method & finding Milgram (1963) obedience Participants gave what they thought were escalating shocks on an experimenter's orders; 65 percent went to the maximum 450 V. Obedience to authority over conscience. Asch (1951) conformity Line-judgement task with confederates giving wrong answers; about 75 percent conformed at least once. Normative social influence. Zimbardo (1971) Stanford Prison Students randomly assigned guard/prisoner roles; the situation produced abusive behaviour, stopped early. Power of roles and situation (deindividuation). Darley & Latane (1968) bystander The more bystanders present, the less likely and slower any one person helps. Diffusion of responsibility (sparked by the Kitty Genovese case). Festinger & Carlsmith (1959) dissonance People paid 1 dollar to lie about a boring task later rated it more enjoyable than those paid 20 dollars. Less external justification → more attitude change. Sherif (1954) Robbers Cave Boys' camp; competition created intergroup hostility, shared superordinate goals reduced it. Realistic conflict theory. Tajfel (1971) minimal group Arbitrary group labels alone produced in-group favouritism. Social identity theory. Bandura (1961) Bobo doll Children who watched an adult hit a doll imitated the aggression. Observational learning. Harlow (1958) monkeys Infant monkeys preferred a soft cloth "

chunks.heading: 10. Personality
chunks.text: 10. Personality Full version: this is the compact pass. The dedicated Personality Theories page has all of it in depth — every defence mechanism, the neo-Freudians side by side, type theories, assessment pairings, and the collected MCQ traps.

chunks.heading: Psychodynamic (Freud)
chunks.text: Psychodynamic (Freud) Structure: id (pleasure principle), ego (reality principle), superego (morality/conscience). Topographic: conscious, preconscious, unconscious. The iceberg. Psychosexual stages: oral → anal → phallic (Oedipus/Electra) → latency → genital. Fixation at a stage shapes the adult personality. Defence mechanisms: repression, denial, projection, displacement, reaction formation, rationalisation, sublimation, regression. (Anna Freud catalogued these.)

chunks.heading: Neo-Freudians
chunks.text: Neo-Freudians Jung: collective unconscious, archetypes, introversion/extraversion. Adler: inferiority complex, striving for superiority, birth order. Horney: basic anxiety, womb envy (countered Freud). Erikson: psychosocial stages (see Development).

chunks.heading: Trait theories
chunks.text: Trait theories Theorist Model Allport Cardinal, central, secondary traits Cattell 16 Personality Factors (16PF), via factor analysis Eysenck Three dimensions: extraversion, neuroticism, psychoticism (PEN) Costa & McCrae Big Five / OCEAN: Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism

chunks.heading: Humanistic & social-cognitive
chunks.text: Humanistic & social-cognitive Rogers: self-concept, congruence (real vs ideal self), unconditional positive regard, the fully functioning person. Maslow: self-actualisation (see Motivation). Bandura: reciprocal determinism (behaviour ↔ person ↔ environment), self-efficacy. Rotter: locus of control (internal vs external). Assessment: projective tests (Rorschach inkblots, TAT) tap the unconscious; objective inventories (MMPI, 16PF, NEO-PI) are self-report and standardised.

chunks.heading: 11. Social psychology (concepts)
chunks.text: 11. Social psychology (concepts) Attribution: dispositional vs situational. Fundamental attribution error = overweighting disposition for others' behaviour. Actor-observer bias , self-serving bias (credit success, blame the situation). Attitudes & persuasion: ABC components (affective, behavioural, cognitive). Elaboration Likelihood Model (Petty & Cacioppo): central route (argument quality) vs peripheral route (cues). Cognitive dissonance (Festinger): conflicting cognitions create discomfort that drives attitude change. Conformity & obedience: normative (to fit in) vs informational (to be right) influence. Compliance techniques: foot-in-the-door, door-in-the-face, low-balling. Group processes: social facilitation (others improve easy tasks, worsen hard ones), social loafing, deindividuation, groupthink (Janis), group polarisation, risky shift. Prejudice: stereotype (cognitive), prejudice (affective), discrimination (behavioural). Realistic conflict theory; social identity theory (Tajfel); contact hypothesis (Allport) reduces it. Prosocial & aggression: bystander effect + diffusion of responsibility; altruism vs reciprocity. Frustration-aggression hypothesis; social learning of aggression. Attraction: proximity, similarity, mere-exposure effect, reciprocity, physical attractiveness; matching hypothesis; Sternberg's triangular theory of love (intimacy, passion, commitment). Self

chunks.heading: 12. Developmental psychology
chunks.text: 12. Developmental psychology Theorist Stages / idea Piaget (cognitive) Sensorimotor (0-2, object permanence) → preoperational (2-7, egocentrism, no conservation) → concrete operational (7-11, conservation) → formal operational (11+, abstract). Schemas, assimilation, accommodation. Erikson (psychosocial) 8 stages, each a crisis: trust v mistrust → autonomy v shame → initiative v guilt → industry v inferiority → identity v role confusion → intimacy v isolation → generativity v stagnation → integrity v despair. Kohlberg (moral) Preconventional (punishment/reward) → conventional (social approval, law and order) → postconventional (social contract, universal ethics). Vygotsky (sociocultural) Zone of proximal development, scaffolding, the social origin of thought (more-knowledgeable other). Freud (psychosexual) See Personality. Attachment (Bowlby; Ainsworth's Strange Situation): secure, insecure-avoidant, insecure-resistant/ambivalent, and disorganised (Main & Solomon). Harlow = contact comfort. Temperament (Thomas & Chess): easy, difficult, slow-to-warm-up. Nature vs nurture & epigenetics; maturation vs learning; continuous vs stage (discontinuous) views; critical vs sensitive periods. Theory of mind (false-belief / Sally-Anne task, ~4 yrs); Vygotsky vs Piaget on private speech and the social origin of thought. Parenting styles (Baumrind): authoritative, authoritarian, permissive, n

chunks.heading: 13. States of consciousness & sleep
chunks.text: 13. States of consciousness & sleep Sleep stages: NREM 1 (theta, hypnagogic) → NREM 2 (sleep spindles, K-complexes) → NREM 3 (delta, deep/slow-wave) → REM (paradoxical: brain active, body paralysed, dreaming). ~90-minute cycles; REM lengthens toward morning. Circadian rhythm: ~24-hour cycle, governed by the suprachiasmatic nucleus; melatonin from the pineal gland. Dream theories: Freud (wish fulfilment, manifest vs latent content); activation-synthesis (Hobson & McCarley, brain makes sense of random REM activity); information-processing/consolidation. Sleep disorders: insomnia, narcolepsy, sleep apnoea, night terrors (NREM) vs nightmares (REM), somnambulism. Altered states: hypnosis, meditation, and psychoactive drugs (depressants, stimulants, hallucinogens, opioids) altering consciousness via neurotransmitters. Theories of hypnosis: Hilgard's neodissociation ("hidden observer") vs the social-cognitive/role-enactment view. Functions of sleep: restoration, energy conservation, memory consolidation; sleep deprivation effects. Drug concepts: tolerance, dependence, withdrawal, the reward pathway (dopamine, nucleus accumbens). Consciousness debates: the "hard problem"; the cognitive unconscious; global workspace theory.

chunks.heading: 14. Stress, coping & health
chunks.text: 14. Stress, coping & health Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome: alarm → resistance → exhaustion. Lazarus & Folkman: primary appraisal (is it a threat?) then secondary appraisal (can I cope?). Problem-focused coping (change the stressor) vs emotion-focused coping (manage the feeling). Physiology: the HPA axis and sympathetic "fight-or-flight" (Cannon); cortisol as the chronic-stress hormone. Type A (competitive, hostile, time-urgent) vs Type B; hostility links to heart disease. Buffers: social support, perceived control, optimism, hardiness (Kobasa: commitment, control, challenge). Stressors: Holmes & Rahe Social Readjustment Rating Scale (life-change units); daily hassles vs uplifts (Lazarus); acute vs chronic stress. Tend-and-befriend (Taylor): an alternative to fight-or-flight, oxytocin-linked, more often described in women. Health: psychoneuroimmunology (stress suppresses immunity); the biopsychosocial model; learned optimism (Seligman).

chunks.heading: 15. Schools & history of psychology
chunks.text: 15. Schools & history of psychology School Core idea & figures Structuralism Break consciousness into elements via introspection. Wundt (first lab, 1879), Titchener. Functionalism What is the mind for ? Adaptive function of behaviour. William James, influenced by Darwin. Psychoanalysis Unconscious drives and early experience. Freud. Behaviourism Only observable behaviour; learning by conditioning. Watson, Pavlov, Skinner. Gestalt The whole differs from the sum of parts. Wertheimer, Koffka, Kohler. Humanistic ("third force") Free will, growth, self-actualisation. Maslow, Rogers. Cognitive Mental processes as information processing; the "cognitive revolution" (1950s-60s). Neisser, Miller. Biological / evolutionary Behaviour rooted in the brain, genes, and adaptation. Companion: the one-line testable version of all of this is in the textbook's Section 9, Rapid Recall . Read this page once for understanding, then drill the Rapid Recall block. Sihan MET 2026 + NIMHANS prep · /notes/general-psych/
