chunks.heading: High-Yield Revision Sheet
chunks.text: High-Yield Revision Sheet Abnormal + Developmental Psychology · Built 2026-05-04 · 19 days to MET How to use this sheet. One pass tonight, full read. One pass tomorrow morning, only the red TRAP boxes and the tables. Anything you blank on, mark it and re-read the corresponding cheatsheet section. Don't try to memorize this in one sitting, target the gaps.

chunks.heading: 1. Abnormal Psychology
chunks.text: 1. Abnormal Psychology

chunks.heading: 1.1 The 4 Ds (definition of abnormality)
chunks.text: 1.1 The 4 Ds (definition of abnormality) Deviance — statistical or social norm violation Distress — subjective suffering Dysfunction — impairs daily life / role functioning Danger — risk to self or others TRAP: Deviance alone ≠ abnormal. A genius IQ is statistically deviant but not pathological. Always need distress or dysfunction with it.

chunks.heading: 1.2 Historical conceptions, one-line
chunks.text: 1.2 Historical conceptions, one-line Era Model Key name Ancient Supernatural (demons, possession) Trephination Greek Biological, four humors Hippocrates Middle Ages Demonological return, witch trials Malleus Maleficarum Renaissance Asylum reform begins Pinel (moral treatment), Tuke 19th c. Biological / classification Kraepelin (dementia praecox), Bleuler (renamed schizophrenia) 20th c. Psychological Freud (psychoanalysis), Watson (behaviorism), Beck (CBT)

chunks.heading: 1.3 DSM-5 vs ICD-11, must-knows
chunks.text: 1.3 DSM-5 vs ICD-11, must-knows DSM-5 (2013) / DSM-5-TR (2022) ICD-11 (2019) Publisher APA, US WHO, global Sections 3 sections, 22 chapters, no axes (axes dropped from DSM-IV) Chapter 6 = mental, behavioral, neurodev OCD Own chapter (separated from anxiety) Own chapter too PTSD Own chapter (Trauma-related) Own chapter, adds Complex PTSD Schizophrenia subtypes Removed in DSM-5 (no more paranoid/catatonic/etc.) Removed in ICD-11 too Mental Retardation Renamed Intellectual Developmental Disorder Disorders of Intellectual Development Asperger's Folded into ASD Folded into ASD Bereavement exclusion (MDD) Removed Still cautious TRAP: Multi-axial system was DSM-IV. DSM-5 dropped it. If a question says "Axis I disorder" it is testing pre-DSM-5 vocabulary.

chunks.heading: 1.4 Mental Status Examination (MSE), order matters
chunks.text: 1.4 Mental Status Examination (MSE), order matters ABS-MTPCIJ : Appearance, Behavior, Speech, Mood/affect, Thought (form + content), Perception, Cognition, Insight, Judgment. Mood = subjective ("how do you feel"). Affect = observed (range, congruence). Thought form = how thoughts flow (loose, tangential, flight of ideas, circumstantial). Thought content = what (delusions, suicidal, obsessions). Insight = awareness of illness. Judgment = decision-making in real situations.

chunks.heading: 1.5 Approaches to psychopathology
chunks.text: 1.5 Approaches to psychopathology Approach Cause Treatment Biological Genes, neurotransmitters, brain Meds, ECT Psychodynamic Unconscious conflict, early experience Psychoanalysis, free association Behavioral Maladaptive learning Conditioning, exposure, reinforcement Cognitive Distorted thoughts, schemas CBT, cognitive restructuring (Beck, Ellis) Humanistic Blocked self-actualization Person-centered (Rogers), Gestalt (Perls) Sociocultural Family, culture, stigma Family therapy, community Biopsychosocial All three interact (Engel, 1977) Integrative

chunks.heading: 1.6 Anxiety disorders, distinguishing features
chunks.text: 1.6 Anxiety disorders, distinguishing features Disorder Core feature Time GAD Excessive worry, multiple domains, hard to control ≥ 6 months Panic Disorder Recurrent unexpected panic attacks + worry about more Attack peaks in 10 min Specific Phobia Fear of one object/situation ≥ 6 months Social Anxiety Fear of scrutiny, judgment in social situations ≥ 6 months Agoraphobia Fear of places where escape is hard (≥ 2 of 5 situations) ≥ 6 months Separation Anxiety Excessive fear of separation from attachment figure ≥ 4 wks (kids), 6 mo (adults) TRAP: OCD is NOT in the anxiety chapter in DSM-5. It has its own chapter (OCD and related). Same for PTSD (Trauma- and stressor-related).

chunks.heading: 1.7 OCD and related, hoard the list
chunks.text: 1.7 OCD and related, hoard the list OCD Body Dysmorphic Disorder (BDD) Hoarding Disorder (new in DSM-5) Trichotillomania (hair-pulling) Excoriation (skin-picking, new in DSM-5)

chunks.heading: 1.8 Mood disorders
chunks.text: 1.8 Mood disorders Disorder Episode Duration MDD ≥ 5 of 9 SIG-E-CAPS, must include depressed mood OR anhedonia ≥ 2 weeks Persistent Depressive Disorder (Dysthymia) Chronic low-grade depression ≥ 2 yrs (1 yr kids) Bipolar I ≥ 1 manic episode (depression not required) Mania ≥ 1 wk Bipolar II Hypomania + at least one MDE, no full mania ever Hypomania ≥ 4 days Cyclothymia Hypomanic + depressive symptoms, never full episode ≥ 2 yrs PMDD Severe mood symptoms premenstrually Most cycles in last yr Disruptive Mood Dysregulation Disorder Severe temper outbursts in kids Onset before 10, dx 6-18 SIG-E-CAPS for MDD: Sleep, Interest (anhedonia), Guilt, Energy, Concentration, Appetite, Psychomotor, Suicidal ideation. + depressed mood = 9 total. DIG-FAST for mania: Distractibility, Indiscretion, Grandiosity, Flight of ideas, Activity increase, Sleep decrease, Talkativeness.

chunks.heading: 1.9 Suicide risk, SAD PERSONS
chunks.text: 1.9 Suicide risk, SAD PERSONS S ex (male), A ge (<19 or >45), D epression, P revious attempt, E thanol/drugs, R ational thinking loss, S ocial supports lacking, O rganized plan, N o spouse, S ickness. TRAP: Strongest single predictor of completed suicide = previous attempt . Most common method globally = hanging. Highest-risk diagnosis = MDD with comorbid substance use.

chunks.heading: 1.10 Schizophrenia (Schneider, Bleuler, DSM-5)
chunks.text: 1.10 Schizophrenia (Schneider, Bleuler, DSM-5) Bleuler's 4 As : Associations (loose), Affect (flat), Ambivalence, Autism (withdrawal). Schneider's First-Rank Symptoms : thought insertion/withdrawal/broadcasting, audible thoughts, voices commenting/arguing, made impulses/actions, somatic passivity, delusional perception. Suggestive but not diagnostic alone. Positive symptoms : hallucinations, delusions, disorganized speech, disorganized behavior. Negative symptoms : flat affect, alogia, avolition, anhedonia, asociality. DSM-5 criteria : ≥ 2 of (delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, grossly disorganized/catatonic behavior, negative symptoms), at least one from first three. Active phase ≥ 1 month, total disturbance ≥ 6 months. Disorder Duration Brief Psychotic Disorder 1 day to < 1 month Schizophreniform 1 month to < 6 months Schizophrenia ≥ 6 months Schizoaffective Mood episode + psychosis, but ≥ 2 wks of psychosis without mood symptoms Delusional Disorder ≥ 1 month delusions only, no other psychotic symptoms TRAP: Kraepelin coined dementia praecox . Bleuler renamed it schizophrenia (split mind, not split personality). Don't confuse with DID.

chunks.heading: 1.11 Dissociative disorders
chunks.text: 1.11 Dissociative disorders Dissociative Amnesia — gaps in autobiographical memory, often after trauma. Specifier: with dissociative fugue. DID (Dissociative Identity Disorder) — ≥ 2 distinct identities, recurrent gaps in recall. Strongly linked to severe early trauma. Depersonalization / Derealization Disorder — feeling unreal/detached from self or surroundings, reality testing intact.

chunks.heading: 1.12 Somatic symptom and related (DSM-5 renamed from somatoform)
chunks.text: 1.12 Somatic symptom and related (DSM-5 renamed from somatoform) Somatic Symptom Disorder — distressing somatic symptoms + excessive thoughts/behaviors about them. Illness Anxiety Disorder — preoccupation with having illness, few/no somatic symptoms (replaces hypochondriasis). Conversion Disorder (Functional Neurological Symptom) — neuro symptoms without medical explanation. La belle indifférence is a soft sign. Factitious Disorder — intentional faking for sick role. Munchausen = on self; Munchausen by proxy = on another. Malingering — faking for external gain (money, avoiding work). NOT a mental disorder, V-code. TRAP: Conversion + factitious + malingering are easy to mix. Conversion = unconscious, no gain. Factitious = conscious symptom production, sick role gain. Malingering = conscious, external gain.

chunks.heading: 1.13 Personality disorders (3 clusters)
chunks.text: 1.13 Personality disorders (3 clusters) Cluster Theme Disorders A Odd / eccentric Paranoid, Schizoid, Schizotypal B Dramatic / emotional Antisocial, Borderline, Histrionic, Narcissistic C Anxious / fearful Avoidant, Dependent, Obsessive-Compulsive PD TRAP: OCPD ≠ OCD. OCPD = perfectionism, rigid, ego-syntonic personality style. OCD = ego-dystonic obsessions/compulsions. Different chapters in DSM-5.

chunks.heading: 1.14 Substance use disorder (DSM-5)
chunks.text: 1.14 Substance use disorder (DSM-5) ≥ 2 of 11 criteria in 12 months. Severity: 2-3 mild, 4-5 moderate, ≥ 6 severe. DSM-5 collapsed abuse + dependence into one spectrum (no more "abuse vs dependence").

chunks.heading: 1.15 Childhood / neurodevelopmental disorders
chunks.text: 1.15 Childhood / neurodevelopmental disorders IDD (Intellectual Developmental Disorder) — onset in dev period, deficits in intellectual + adaptive functioning. Severity by adaptive function, not just IQ. ASD — social communication deficits + restricted/repetitive behaviors. DSM-5 merged Asperger's, PDD-NOS, autistic disorder into one spectrum. ADHD — inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity ≥ 6 months, onset before 12, ≥ 2 settings. Specific Learning Disorder — reading (dyslexia), writing (dysgraphia), math (dyscalculia). Tic disorders — Tourette's = motor + vocal tics ≥ 1 yr, onset before 18.

chunks.heading: 2. Developmental Psychology
chunks.text: 2. Developmental Psychology

chunks.heading: 2.1 Principles of development
chunks.text: 2.1 Principles of development Cephalocaudal — head to toe Proximodistal — center to periphery Continuity vs discontinuity (gradual vs stages) Nature vs nurture (genes vs environment, now interactionist consensus) Critical periods (rigid window) vs sensitive periods (preferred but flexible window)

chunks.heading: 2.2 Piaget, 4 stages
chunks.text: 2.2 Piaget, 4 stages Stage Age Achievement Sensorimotor 0-2 Object permanence (~8 mo), goal-directed action Preoperational 2-7 Symbolic thought, egocentrism, animism, lacks conservation Concrete Operational 7-11 Conservation, reversibility, classification, seriation Formal Operational 11+ Abstract, hypothetico-deductive reasoning Sensorimotor 6 substages : Reflexes (0-1mo) → Primary circular reactions (1-4mo, on body) → Secondary CR (4-8mo, on objects) → Coordination of secondary (8-12mo, intentional, object permanence) → Tertiary CR (12-18mo, experimentation) → Mental representation (18-24mo, deferred imitation). TRAP: Conservation ≠ object permanence. Object permanence = sensorimotor (~8mo). Conservation = concrete operational (~7yr). Easy mix-up.

chunks.heading: 2.3 Piaget key concepts
chunks.text: 2.3 Piaget key concepts Schema — mental framework Assimilation — fitting new info into existing schema Accommodation — modifying schema for new info Equilibration — drive to balance assimilation + accommodation Egocentrism — preoperational, can't take others' view (Three Mountains task) Animism — preoperational, attributing life to objects Centration — focus on one feature, blocks conservation

chunks.heading: 2.4 Vygotsky, sociocultural
chunks.text: 2.4 Vygotsky, sociocultural ZPD (Zone of Proximal Development) — gap between what child can do alone vs with help Scaffolding — temporary support from more knowledgeable other (MKO) Private speech — self-talk that becomes inner speech, guides thinking Tools of thought — language is the master tool, internalized from social interaction TRAP: Scaffolding term is Bruner's , applied to Vygotsky's ZPD. Vygotsky himself talked about MKO and ZPD, didn't use "scaffolding" word.

chunks.heading: 2.5 Erikson, 8 psychosocial stages
chunks.text: 2.5 Erikson, 8 psychosocial stages Age Conflict Virtue 0-1.5 Trust vs Mistrust Hope 1.5-3 Autonomy vs Shame/Doubt Will 3-6 Initiative vs Guilt Purpose 6-12 Industry vs Inferiority Competence 12-18 Identity vs Role Confusion Fidelity 18-40 Intimacy vs Isolation Love 40-65 Generativity vs Stagnation Care 65+ Integrity vs Despair Wisdom

chunks.heading: 2.6 Freud, 5 psychosexual stages
chunks.text: 2.6 Freud, 5 psychosexual stages Age Stage Erogenous zone / fixation 0-1 Oral Mouth, dependency, smoking, eating 1-3 Anal Bowel control; anal-retentive (orderly) or anal-expulsive (messy) 3-6 Phallic Genitals; Oedipus / Electra; superego forms 6-12 Latency Sexual urges dormant, same-sex friends 12+ Genital Mature sexuality

chunks.heading: 2.7 Kohlberg, moral development
chunks.text: 2.7 Kohlberg, moral development Level Stages Driver Preconventional 1. Punishment-obedience 2. Instrumental exchange Self-interest Conventional 3. Good boy / good girl 4. Law and order Social approval, rules Postconventional 5. Social contract 6. Universal ethical principles Abstract principles TRAP: Gilligan's critique = Kohlberg's stages reflect male "justice" orientation; women often reason via "ethics of care." Don't say Gilligan replaced Kohlberg, she added a parallel orientation.

chunks.heading: 2.8 Attachment, Bowlby + Ainsworth
chunks.text: 2.8 Attachment, Bowlby + Ainsworth Bowlby phases : Pre-attachment (0-6 wk) → Attachment-in-the-making (6 wk - 8 mo) → Clear-cut attachment (8 mo - 18 mo, separation anxiety + stranger anxiety peak) → Reciprocal relationships (18-24 mo+). Ainsworth's Strange Situation (4 styles): Style Behavior on separation Behavior on reunion Caregiver pattern Secure (B, ~60%) Distressed Easily comforted, returns to play Sensitive, responsive Avoidant (A, ~20%) Little distress Avoids/ignores caregiver Rejecting, unresponsive Resistant / Ambivalent (C, ~10%) Very distressed Seeks + resists contact, can't be soothed Inconsistent Disorganized (D, Main & Solomon) Confused, freezing, contradictory Approach + avoid, dazed Frightening / abusive / unresolved trauma TRAP: Disorganized was added by Main & Solomon, not Ainsworth. Ainsworth's original three were A/B/C.

chunks.heading: 2.9 Baumrind's parenting styles (2 axes)
chunks.text: 2.9 Baumrind's parenting styles (2 axes) High demand Low demand High warmth Authoritative (best outcomes) Permissive / Indulgent Low warmth Authoritarian Neglectful / Uninvolved (Maccoby & Martin added this 4th) TRAP: Authoritative ≠ Authoritarian. Authoritative = high warmth + high demand (the good one). Authoritarian = low warmth + high demand (the harsh one).

chunks.heading: 2.10 Language development, milestones
chunks.text: 2.10 Language development, milestones Age Milestone 0-2 mo Crying, reflexive sounds 2-4 mo Cooing (vowels) 6 mo Babbling (consonants + vowels) 10-14 mo First word; holophrastic speech (one word = whole thought) 18-24 mo Two-word / telegraphic speech ("more milk") 2-3 yr Vocab burst, simple sentences, overregularization ("goed", "foots") 3-5 yr Complex grammar, ~2000 words by 5 Theories : Skinner = behaviorist (operant, imitation). Chomsky = nativist (LAD, Universal Grammar, poverty of stimulus). Vygotsky / Bruner = social-interactionist. Piaget = cognitive (thought before language).

chunks.heading: 2.11 Theorists, 1-line hooks
chunks.text: 2.11 Theorists, 1-line hooks Theorist Hook Piaget 4 cognitive stages, schemas, equilibration Vygotsky ZPD, scaffolding, sociocultural, language as tool Erikson 8 psychosocial conflicts across life Freud 5 psychosexual stages, unconscious, id/ego/superego Bowlby Attachment as biological survival system, internal working model Ainsworth Strange Situation, A/B/C styles Main & Solomon Added disorganized (D) Harlow Wire vs cloth mother, contact comfort > food Lorenz Imprinting in geese, critical period Kohlberg 3 levels, 6 stages of moral reasoning, Heinz dilemma Gilligan Ethics of care, gendered critique of Kohlberg Baumrind Parenting styles (3, then 4) Bandura Social learning, observation, Bobo doll, self-efficacy Bronfenbrenner Ecological systems (micro/meso/exo/macro/chrono) Thomas & Chess Temperament, easy / difficult / slow-to-warm Marcia Identity statuses (diffusion, foreclosure, moratorium, achievement) Gesell Maturation, normative milestones Hall Adolescence as "storm and stress"

chunks.heading: 2.12 Bronfenbrenner's ecological systems
chunks.text: 2.12 Bronfenbrenner's ecological systems Full exam-grade primer: Bronfenbrenner, Ecological Systems Theory . Microsystem — direct, face-to-face settings (family, school, peers). Bidirectional influence. Mesosystem — interactions between microsystems (parent-teacher meetings, home-school link). Not a setting itself. Exosystem — settings the child isn't in but which still affect them (parent's workplace, school board, mass media). Macrosystem — cultural blueprint (ideology, laws, religion, SES, customs). Chronosystem — the time dimension (divorce, pandemic, sociohistorical era). Added later , originally 4 systems. 1979 Ecological Systems Theory → 1994 Bioecological Model with PPCT : P roximal P rocesses (engine of development, regular reciprocal interactions over time), P erson (demand / resource / force traits), C ontext (the 5 systems), T ime (micro / meso / macro time). TRAP: Exosystem ≠ no influence. Child isn't in it, but it shapes them via the microsystem (e.g. dad loses job → stress at home). If the stem mentions: nested environments, cultural context, parent's workplace affecting child, indirect influence → answer is Bronfenbrenner .

chunks.heading: 2.13 Marcia's identity statuses (Erikson stage 5 expansion)
chunks.text: 2.13 Marcia's identity statuses (Erikson stage 5 expansion) Crisis explored? Commitment made? Diffusion No No Foreclosure No Yes (handed down) Moratorium Yes (in progress) No Achievement Yes (resolved) Yes

chunks.heading: 3. Top 20 MCQ Traps, mixed
chunks.text: 3. Top 20 MCQ Traps, mixed Object permanence vs conservation, different stages. OCD is NOT in the anxiety chapter (DSM-5). Authoritative ≠ Authoritarian. Conversion (unconscious) ≠ Factitious (conscious, sick role) ≠ Malingering (conscious, external gain). OCPD ≠ OCD. Bipolar I needs mania ≥ 1 wk; Bipolar II is hypomania + MDE, never full mania. Schizophrenia = Bleuler. Dementia praecox = Kraepelin. Schizophrenia ≠ DID (split personality). Disorganized attachment was Main & Solomon, not Ainsworth. Scaffolding is Bruner's term (applied to Vygotsky). Schizophreniform = 1-6 mo. Brief Psychotic = < 1 mo. Schizophrenia = ≥ 6 mo. DSM-5 dropped axes; multi-axial is DSM-IV. Strongest predictor of completed suicide = previous attempt. MDD needs ≥ 5 of 9 SIG-E-CAPS, must include depressed mood OR anhedonia. Egocentrism is preoperational (Piaget), not narcissism. Critical period (rigid) vs sensitive period (flexible). Gilligan added "ethics of care," didn't replace Kohlberg. Asperger's no longer a separate dx (folded into ASD in DSM-5). Hoarding and Excoriation are NEW disorders in DSM-5. Bereavement exclusion was REMOVED in DSM-5 (you can dx MDD even within 2 mo of loss). Sheet built 2026-05-04 for last 19 days before MET. Pair with the abnormal and dev cheatsheets for the full picture. Papers (full primers) coming next. Sihan MET 2026 + NIMHANS Prep

chunks.heading: HPA Axis — Stress Endocrinology
chunks.text: HPA Axis — Stress Endocrinology Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Adrenal axis · Built 2026-05-16 Why this matters. HPA shows up in MET + NIMHANS papers under at least four hats: (1) biopsych "draw the axis," (2) abnormal psych "HPA in MDD/PTSD/Cushing's," (3) stress/health psych "Selye + allostatic load," (4) assessment "dexamethasone suppression test." One page, all four. Three things to know cold: CRH → ACTH → cortisol, the negative feedback loop, and which psychiatric disorder shows what kind of HPA dysregulation.

chunks.heading: 1. The axis in one diagram
chunks.text: 1. The axis in one diagram STRESSOR (physical, psychological, immune) ↓ HYPOTHALAMUS (paraventricular nucleus, PVN) → releases CRH (Corticotropin-Releasing Hormone) + AVP (vasopressin, synergistic) ↓ (via portal blood, infundibular stalk) ANTERIOR PITUITARY (corticotroph cells) → releases ACTH (Adrenocorticotropic Hormone) from POMC precursor ↓ (via systemic circulation) ADRENAL CORTEX — zona fasciculata → releases CORTISOL (glucocorticoid) + small DHEA, weak aldosterone ↓ TARGET TISSUES : liver, muscle, fat, immune, brain NEGATIVE FEEDBACK : cortisol inhibits both hypothalamus (↓CRH) and pituitary (↓ACTH). This loop shuts the response off when the stressor ends. In MDD and PTSD it breaks.

chunks.heading: 1.1 Anatomy details to memorise
chunks.text: 1.1 Anatomy details to memorise Paraventricular nucleus (PVN) of hypothalamus — the brain origin of stress. CRH = 41-amino-acid peptide, half-life ~60 min. Co-secreted with AVP (potentiates). Anterior pituitary corticotrophs make POMC → cleaved to ACTH + β-endorphin + MSH. Adrenal cortex layers (outside in): G lomerulosa (aldosterone), F asciculata (cortisol), R eticularis (androgens — DHEA). Memory: " GFR , salt-sugar-sex deeper you go". Adrenal medulla (inner) makes adrenaline / noradrenaline via SAM axis — fast, "fight-or-flight". HPA is the slower, sustained arm.

chunks.heading: 2. The two stress systems (compare and contrast)
chunks.text: 2. The two stress systems (compare and contrast) SAM (Sympatho-Adrenal Medullary) HPA Onset Seconds Minutes Hormones Adrenaline, noradrenaline Cortisol (with CRH, ACTH) Source Adrenal medulla, sympathetic neurons Adrenal cortex, via hypothalamus + pituitary Effect ↑HR, ↑BP, pupil dilation, bronchodilation, blood to muscle ↑glucose, ↑BP sustained, ↓immune, ↑gluconeogenesis, ↑lipolysis Role Immediate fight-or-flight Sustained mobilisation + recovery Cannon vs Selye Cannon's "fight or flight" Selye's GAS, "stress" coined

chunks.heading: 3. Cortisol — what it actually does
chunks.text: 3. Cortisol — what it actually does Metabolic : ↑gluconeogenesis, ↑glycogenolysis, ↑lipolysis, ↑proteolysis (catabolic). Raises blood glucose. Immune : suppresses inflammation, decreases lymphocytes, neutrophilia. That's why glucocorticoids are anti-inflammatory drugs. Cardiovascular : maintains vascular tone, permissive for catecholamines. CNS : alertness, attention. At chronic high levels: hippocampal atrophy, memory deficits, mood changes. GI : ↑gastric acid (chronic stress → ulcers). Bone : ↑resorption, ↓formation → osteoporosis with chronic excess.

chunks.heading: 3.1 Cortisol's diurnal rhythm
chunks.text: 3.1 Cortisol's diurnal rhythm Peak : ~30 min after waking ("cortisol awakening response", CAR). Trough : around midnight. Tightly tied to SCN (suprachiasmatic nucleus) circadian rhythm via the hypothalamus. Disrupted in shift workers, depression, chronic insomnia, jet lag.

chunks.heading: 4. HPA dysregulation in psychiatric disorders
chunks.text: 4. HPA dysregulation in psychiatric disorders

chunks.heading: 4.1 Major Depressive Disorder (MDD)
chunks.text: 4.1 Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) Hyperactive HPA axis is one of the most replicated biological findings in MDD. Elevated baseline cortisol; blunted diurnal variation; flattened cortisol awakening response. Enlarged adrenal glands on imaging. Dexamethasone Suppression Test (DST) : give 1 mg dex at 11 pm, measure cortisol next morning. In healthy subjects → cortisol suppressed. In ~50% of melancholic / psychotic depression → non-suppression . Sensitivity ~40-50%, specificity ~80-90%, not used diagnostically but historically big in NIMHANS papers (Carroll DST). Mechanism: impaired glucocorticoid receptor feedback → cortisol cannot turn the axis off → sustained CRH drive. Reduces hippocampal BDNF, contributes to volume loss. SSRIs and CBT both normalise HPA over weeks of treatment.

chunks.heading: 4.2 PTSD — paradox
chunks.text: 4.2 PTSD — paradox PTSD shows low basal cortisol (often) but enhanced negative feedback (super-suppression on low-dose DST). Elevated CRH in CSF. Theory: hypersensitive glucocorticoid receptors → over-suppression of cortisol after stressor. Contrast with MDD: depressed = hypercortisolaemic with failed feedback; PTSD = hypocortisolaemic with exaggerated feedback. Frequent MCQ trap.

chunks.heading: 4.3 Cushing's syndrome / disease
chunks.text: 4.3 Cushing's syndrome / disease Excess cortisol from any cause. Cushing's disease = pituitary ACTH-secreting adenoma (most common endogenous cause). Cushing's syndrome = the broader phenotype, often iatrogenic (exogenous steroids). Physical: central obesity, moon face, buffalo hump, purple striae, hirsutism, hypertension, hyperglycaemia, thin skin, easy bruising. Psychiatric: depression in 50-80% , irritability, anxiety, insomnia, occasional psychosis or mania. Treating the Cushing's often resolves the depression — pure example of endocrine psychiatry.

chunks.heading: 4.4 Addison's disease
chunks.text: 4.4 Addison's disease Primary adrenal insufficiency — cortisol and aldosterone deficient. Fatigue, weight loss, hyperpigmentation (high ACTH stimulates MSH), hypotension, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia. Psychiatric: apathy, depression, occasional psychosis. Reverses with hydrocortisone replacement.

chunks.heading: 4.5 Anxiety disorders, panic, OCD
chunks.text: 4.5 Anxiety disorders, panic, OCD Findings are mixed. Panic disorder shows mild HPA activation during attacks but normal baselines. GAD: subtle blunting of CAR, elevated evening cortisol. OCD: no clear HPA signature — less examinable than mood / PTSD.

chunks.heading: 4.6 Schizophrenia
chunks.text: 4.6 Schizophrenia HPA hyperactivity at first episode, especially with poor outcome. Cortisol rises before psychotic relapse in some prospective studies. Linked to dopamine sensitisation theory ("threat → cortisol → mesolimbic DA").

chunks.heading: 4.7 Eating disorders
chunks.text: 4.7 Eating disorders Anorexia nervosa: hypercortisolaemia, loss of diurnal variation, often DST non-suppression even without depression. Restoration of weight partly normalises HPA.

chunks.heading: 4.8 Early life stress / abuse
chunks.text: 4.8 Early life stress / abuse Childhood maltreatment → durable HPA dysregulation in adulthood (often blunted reactivity + altered glucocorticoid receptor methylation). Mediator for later depression, PTSD, addiction risk. McGowan / Meaney rat studies — maternal licking ↑ glucocorticoid receptor in hippocampus → calmer adult. Classic epigenetics MCQ.

chunks.heading: 5. Stress theory — Selye and beyond
chunks.text: 5. Stress theory — Selye and beyond

chunks.heading: 5.1 Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS)
chunks.text: 5.1 Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS) Stage What happens HPA state Alarm "Fight or flight": SAM activation first, then HPA kicks in Cortisol rises sharply Resistance Body adapts, mobilises resources, performance can rise Cortisol elevated and sustained Exhaustion Resources depleted, disease onset (ulcers, infection, depression) HPA dysregulation — high or low Memory: A-R-E (Alarm, Resistance, Exhaustion). Selye called the non-specific response to demand "stress" and the trigger "stressor". His rat experiments (1936) launched the field.

chunks.heading: 5.2 Cannon — "fight or flight" (1915)
chunks.text: 5.2 Cannon — "fight or flight" (1915) Walter Cannon coined "fight or flight" — the immediate SAM response. Predates Selye; describes the acute phase only. " Homeostasis " is also Cannon's term — keeping internal milieu constant.

chunks.heading: 5.3 Allostasis and allostatic load (McEwen, 1993+)
chunks.text: 5.3 Allostasis and allostatic load (McEwen, 1993+) Allostasis = achieving stability through change (active adaptation, not just returning to a setpoint). Allostatic load = the wear-and-tear from chronic activation of adaptive systems (HPA, SAM, immune). Allostatic overload = the load becomes pathology: cardiovascular disease, depression, metabolic syndrome, immune dysfunction. Updates Selye's "exhaustion" with a cumulative, multi-system model. Bruce McEwen — high-yield name for any "modern stress theory" MCQ.

chunks.heading: 5.4 Lazarus & Folkman — cognitive appraisal (1984)
chunks.text: 5.4 Lazarus & Folkman — cognitive appraisal (1984) Stress is the relationship between person and environment appraised as exceeding resources . Primary appraisal : is this event harmful/threatening/challenging? Secondary appraisal : can I cope with it? Coping styles: problem-focused vs emotion-focused . Transactional model — bridges biology with cognition; what activates HPA depends on appraisal, not the event alone.

chunks.heading: 6. Measuring the HPA axis
chunks.text: 6. Measuring the HPA axis Salivary cortisol — non-invasive, captures diurnal rhythm and CAR. Used in research. 24-hour urinary free cortisol — best for Cushing's screening. Midnight serum cortisol — should be low; non-suppression suggests Cushing's. Dexamethasone Suppression Test (DST) : Low-dose (1 mg overnight) — screen for Cushing's; non-suppression abnormal. High-dose (8 mg) — distinguishes pituitary Cushing's (suppresses) from ectopic ACTH (no suppression). In psychiatry: Carroll DST in depression — non-suppression suggests melancholic depression. CRH stimulation test — distinguishes hypothalamic vs pituitary defects. Trier Social Stress Test (TSST) — laboratory stressor (mock interview + arithmetic). Reliably activates HPA in healthy controls; blunted in many psychiatric groups. Highly cited.

chunks.heading: 7. HPA + neuroplasticity — why chronic cortisol matters
chunks.text: 7. HPA + neuroplasticity — why chronic cortisol matters Hippocampus is densely packed with glucocorticoid receptors. Chronic cortisol → dendritic atrophy in CA3, suppression of neurogenesis in dentate gyrus, hippocampal volume loss (MRI in MDD, PTSD, Cushing's). Cortisol ↓ BDNF (brain-derived neurotrophic factor) → less synaptic plasticity. Antidepressants reverse this over weeks. Prefrontal cortex also atrophies; amygdala often hypertrophies or hyperreacts → fear bias. This biology underpins the "neurotrophic hypothesis of depression" : stress → ↑cortisol → ↓BDNF → ↓hippocampal plasticity → depressive phenotype. Reversed by antidepressants and exercise.

chunks.heading: 8. One-page exam summary
chunks.text: 8. One-page exam summary Element Answer in 1 line Source of CRH Paraventricular nucleus of hypothalamus Source of ACTH Anterior pituitary corticotrophs (from POMC) Source of cortisol Adrenal cortex, zona fasciculata Feedback target Hypothalamus + pituitary (negative) Cortisol peak / trough Peak 30 min post-waking (CAR), trough ~midnight Fast vs slow stress SAM (seconds, adrenaline) vs HPA (minutes, cortisol) Selye's stages Alarm → Resistance → Exhaustion Allostatic load McEwen — wear and tear of chronic adaptation MDD HPA Hyper-cortisol, blunted rhythm, DST non-suppression PTSD HPA Hypo-cortisol, exaggerated feedback (paradox) Cushing's ↑cortisol, depression in 50-80%, central obesity, striae Addison's ↓cortisol, hyperpigmentation, apathy/depression Hippocampal effect Chronic cortisol → atrophy, ↓BDNF, ↓neurogenesis Test for HPA in research Salivary CAR, TSST, low-dose DST

chunks.heading: 9. Top 10 MCQ traps
chunks.text: 9. Top 10 MCQ traps "Releasing hormone for cortisol" → CRH , not ACTH. ACTH is the pituitary hormone downstream of CRH. Adrenal cortex layers: GFR → glomerulosa (aldosterone) / fasciculata (cortisol) / reticularis (androgens). Medulla = adrenaline. MDD = hyper -cortisol with failed suppression. PTSD = hypo -cortisol with super-suppression. Don't mix these up. DST non-suppression has poor sensitivity — not diagnostic, only suggestive of melancholic depression. Cushing's disease = pituitary adenoma. Cushing's syndrome = any cause of hypercortisolism (often iatrogenic steroids). Addison's hyperpigmentation is from MSH (made from same POMC precursor as ACTH). "Stress" was coined by Selye , "fight or flight" by Cannon , "allostatic load" by McEwen , "cognitive appraisal" by Lazarus & Folkman . Cortisol awakening response peaks ~30 minutes after waking , not at waking. Chronic cortisol → hippocampal atrophy (memory complaints in depression, Cushing's). Glucocorticoid receptor methylation (Meaney) is the headline epigenetics finding linking early life care to adult stress reactivity. chunks.heading: ICD — the full breakdown
chunks.text: ICD — the full breakdown International Classification of Diseases: who owns it, how it's built, ICD-10 vs ICD-11, the F-codes for mental disorders, and every place it differs from DSM. Built 2026-05-24. Read the boxes and tables; the prose is just glue. One-line frame. The ICD is the WHO's global classification of all diseases, not just mental ones. Mental disorders sit in one chapter of it. DSM (American Psychiatric Association) only does mental disorders. So: ICD = whole-body, global, free, used for official health stats; DSM = mental-only, US, paywalled, used heavily in research. NIMHANS/India officially uses ICD . Jump to: 1. What ICD is & who owns it 2. Version history 3. Where mental disorders live 4. ICD-10 F-codes (F00–F99) 5. ICD-11 & what changed 6. ICD vs DSM 7. Exam traps

chunks.heading: 1. What ICD is & who owns it
chunks.text: 1. What ICD is & who owns it Question Answer Full name International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems Who publishes it WHO (World Health Organization). DSM is APA, the contrast they love. Scope All diseases and health conditions, every body system. Mental & behavioural disorders are just one chapter . Purpose Global standard for mortality & morbidity statistics , billing, epidemiology. It's the official tool for cause-of-death and disease reporting worldwide. Cost Free , multilingual. DSM is copyrighted and sold by APA. Used where ~194 WHO member states, including India . DSM dominates US clinical research.

chunks.heading: 2. Version history (the dates they ask)
chunks.text: 2. Version history (the dates they ask) Version Year Note ICD-6 1949 First edition to include a section on mental disorders. Common MCQ. ICD-8 1965 ICD-9 1975 US used a clinical modification, ICD-9-CM , for decades. ICD-10 1990 endorsed, 1992 in use The one still tested. Mental disorders = Chapter V (F-codes) . Alphanumeric coding introduced here. ICD-11 Adopted 2019, in force 1 Jan 2022 Fully digital, "foundation" architecture. Mental disorders = Chapter 06 . Lock: ICD-6 (1949) = first mental-disorder section · ICD-10 (1992) = F-codes · ICD-11 (in force 2022) = current.

chunks.heading: 3. Where mental disorders live
chunks.text: 3. Where mental disorders live ICD-10 ICD-11 Chapter Chapter V Chapter 06 Title Mental and Behavioural Disorders Mental, Behavioural or Neurodevelopmental Disorders Code prefix F (F00–F99) Alphanumeric 6 -codes (e.g. 6A20 for schizophrenia) Companion text "Blue Book" (Clinical Descriptions & Diagnostic Guidelines) + "Green Book" (research criteria) CDDR (Clinical Descriptions and Diagnostic Requirements) Why "F"? No mnemonic meaning, it's just the letter assigned to the mental-disorders chapter (Chapter V) in ICD-10's alphanumeric scheme. If asked "F-codes refer to," answer mental and behavioural disorders .

chunks.heading: 4. ICD-10 F-codes — the F00–F99 blocks (memorise the ranges)
chunks.text: 4. ICD-10 F-codes — the F00–F99 blocks (memorise the ranges) Range Block Examples F00–F09 Organic, incl. symptomatic, mental disorders Dementia (Alzheimer's, vascular), delirium F10–F19 Mental/behavioural due to psychoactive substance use Alcohol, opioids, cannabis dependence F20–F29 Schizophrenia , schizotypal & delusional disorders Schizophrenia (F20), delusional disorder F30–F39 Mood (affective) disorders Mania, bipolar, depression, recurrent depressive F40–F48 Neurotic, stress-related & somatoform Phobias, panic, GAD, OCD, PTSD, dissociative, somatoform F50–F59 Behavioural syndromes + physiological/physical factors Eating disorders, sleep disorders, sexual dysfunction F60–F69 Disorders of adult personality & behaviour Personality disorders, gender identity, habit/impulse F70–F79 Mental retardation (ICD-10 term; "intellectual disability" in ICD-11) Mild → profound F80–F89 Disorders of psychological development Speech/language, scholastic, autism (F84) F90–F98 Behavioural/emotional onset usually in childhood/adolescence ADHD/hyperkinetic (F90), conduct, tic disorders F99 Unspecified mental disorder Trap they set: In ICD-10, OCD and PTSD sit inside F40–F48 (neurotic/stress-related), NOT as standalone chapters. That's the opposite of DSM-5, which pulled OCD and trauma out into their own chapters. Know which manual the question is about. Fast recall: 0 organic · 1 substances · 2

chunks.heading: 5. ICD-11 — what actually changed
chunks.text: 5. ICD-11 — what actually changed Coding format changed. Mental disorders moved from F-codes to alphanumeric 6-codes (chapter 06). E.g. schizophrenia = 6A20 , bipolar type I = 6A60. Complex PTSD added. ICD-11 has PTSD AND Complex PTSD (PTSD core + the three "disturbances in self-organization": affect dysregulation, negative self-concept, relationship disturbance). DSM-5 does not have Complex PTSD. High-yield difference. Gaming disorder added as a formal diagnosis. "Mental retardation" → "Disorders of intellectual development." Gender incongruence moved out of the mental disorders chapter into a new sexual-health chapter (depathologised). Schizophrenia subtypes removed (paranoid, catatonic, etc. dropped), matching DSM-5. Rated by symptom dimensions instead. Bereavement → Prolonged grief disorder recognised. Neurodevelopmental added to the chapter title; autism + ADHD grouped here. Dimensional personality model: ICD-11 scrapped the categorical PD types and uses severity + five trait domains (negative affectivity, detachment, dissociality, disinhibition, anankastia) with one retained pattern, borderline .

chunks.heading: 6. ICD vs DSM — the side-by-side they ask
chunks.text: 6. ICD vs DSM — the side-by-side they ask ICD (ICD-11) DSM (DSM-5/5-TR) Body WHO APA (American Psychiatric Association) Scope All diseases; mental = 1 chapter Mental disorders only Reach Global, ~194 countries US-centric (heavy in research) Cost Free Sold/copyrighted Style Clinical guidelines (flexible, prototype-based) Explicit operational criteria (count symptoms, thresholds) Latest ICD-11, in force 2022 DSM-5 (2013), DSM-5-TR (2022) Complex PTSD Yes No Multiaxial? Never multiaxial DSM-IV had 5 axes; DSM-5 dropped axes NIMHANS angle: India officially codes on ICD . Expect "which body publishes ICD" (WHO), "ICD chapter for mental disorders" (V / F-codes in ICD-10), and an ICD-vs-DSM difference (Complex PTSD, free-vs-paid, global-vs-US, guidelines-vs-criteria).

chunks.heading: 7. Exam traps, fast
chunks.text: 7. Exam traps, fast WHO vs APA. ICD = WHO. DSM = APA. Swapping these is the #1 setup. F = mental. "F-codes" → mental & behavioural disorders (ICD-10 Chapter V). Don't overthink the letter. OCD/PTSD placement. ICD-10 buries them in F40–F48 (neurotic/stress). DSM-5 gave each its own chapter. ICD-11 also broke them out more. Complex PTSD is ICD-11 only. Not in DSM-5. First mental-disorders edition = ICD-6 (1949). Multiaxial was DSM-IV, not ICD. ICD has never been multiaxial; DSM-5 abolished its 5 axes. That's ICD end to end. If you remember nothing else: WHO owns it, it covers all disease, mental disorders are Chapter V/F-codes in ICD-10 and Chapter 06/6-codes in ICD-11, ICD-11 added Complex PTSD + gaming disorder and depathologised gender incongruence, and India codes on ICD. Sihan MET 2026 + NIMHANS prep · /notes/icd/ · built 2026-05-24

chunks.heading: Intelligence Tests, Deep Reference
chunks.text: Intelligence Tests, Deep Reference Built 2026-05-20, companion to the personality + projective deep reference . Same job, different test family: for every individual + group + infant intelligence scale in the MET/NIMHANS pool, lock the item/subtest count, scales/indices, scoring, author + year, and age range . Cross-link with the read-first primer (reliability/validity/IQ history) and the revision pack (one-page table). How MCQ-writers attack intelligence tests. Five recurring moves: (1) swap the SD between Wechsler (15) and old Binet (16); (2) swap subtest count between SPM/CPM/APM, or between Bhatia (5) and Army Beta (7); (3) swap the year (Binet-Simon 1905 vs Terman 1916 vs Stern's IQ formula 1912); (4) swap which index belongs to which Wechsler version (WAIS-IV has 4, WISC-V has 5); (5) swap a theorist with their model (Spearman g, Thurstone PMA, Guilford SOI, Gardner MI, Sternberg triarchic, Cattell-Horn Gf-Gc). Memorize those five swaps cold.

chunks.heading: 1. Stanford-Binet Family
chunks.text: 1. Stanford-Binet Family

chunks.heading: Origin: Binet-Simon (1905, France)
chunks.text: Origin: Binet-Simon (1905, France) Authors: Alfred Binet & Théodore Simon, commissioned by the French Ministry of Public Instruction to identify children needing special schooling. Year: 1905 (original 30-item scale), revised 1908 (introduced mental-age concept) and 1911 . Items: 30 tasks of graded difficulty in the 1905 version. Range from "follow a light with eyes" to "abstract definitions." Key contribution: the concept of mental age (MA) in the 1908 revision - child's performance level matched to the average chronological age that performs at that level. Did NOT yield IQ. Binet himself rejected a single global score; he wanted a clinical descriptive profile.

chunks.heading: Stanford revisions - the IQ-formula era
chunks.text: Stanford revisions - the IQ-formula era 1916 - Stanford-Binet, 1st edition. Lewis M. Terman, Stanford University. First English-language adaptation. Adopted William Stern's 1912 ratio IQ formula : IQ = (MA / CA) × 100. Mean ≈ 100. 1937 - SB-LM (2nd edition). Terman & Maud Merrill. Two equivalent forms L and M. Still ratio IQ. 1960 - SB-LM revised (3rd edition). Terman & Merrill. Switched from ratio IQ to deviation IQ (Pinneau's tables): M = 100, SD = 16 . Memorize this 16 - it is the classic Wechsler-vs-Binet trap. 1986 - SB-IV (4th edition). Thorndike, Hagen & Sattler. First time the test moved to a hierarchical structure with 4 area scores: Verbal Reasoning, Abstract/Visual Reasoning, Quantitative Reasoning, Short-Term Memory. 15 subtests. Age 2 to adult. 2003 - SB-5 (current edition). Gale H. Roid, Riverside Publishing. SD changed to 15 to align with Wechsler. Age range 2 to 85+ .

chunks.heading: SB-5 structure (the version exam-writers mean today)
chunks.text: SB-5 structure (the version exam-writers mean today) 10 subtests, 5 factors × 2 domains. 5 factors: Fluid Reasoning (FR), Knowledge (KN), Quantitative Reasoning (QR), Visual-Spatial Processing (VS), Working Memory (WM). Identical names across the verbal and nonverbal domains. 2 domains: Verbal (5 subtests) and Nonverbal (5 subtests). Each factor has one verbal + one nonverbal subtest. 3 IQ scores yielded: Full-Scale IQ (FSIQ), Verbal IQ (VIQ), Nonverbal IQ (NVIQ). All M = 100, SD = 15. Routing subtests: Object Series/Matrices (nonverbal) and Vocabulary (verbal) determine entry difficulty for the rest. Administration time: ~45–75 min full battery; 15–20 min abbreviated.

chunks.heading: 2. Wechsler Family
chunks.text: 2. Wechsler Family David Wechsler (Bellevue Hospital, NY) built his scales explicitly to fix two SB problems: (a) it was age-stratified and clunky for adults, and (b) ratio IQ broke down past age 16 because MA stops climbing linearly. His fix was the deviation IQ (1939) and a point-scale structure where every adult takes the same subtests.

chunks.heading: Edition lineage
chunks.text: Edition lineage Wechsler-Bellevue I (W-B I, 1939) - David Wechsler. First deviation-IQ test. 11 subtests. W-B II (1946) - alternate form. WAIS (1955) - adults 16–64. WAIS-R (1981) - restandardised. WAIS-III (1997) - added Processing Speed Index, 4-index structure introduced. WAIS-IV (2008) - current MET/NIMHANS reference; ages 16:0–90:11. WAIS-5 (2024) - rolled out in US/UK; exams still default to WAIS-IV unless otherwise specified. WISC (1949) → WISC-R (1974) → WISC-III (1991) → WISC-IV (2003) → WISC-V (2014 US, 2016 UK, 2019 India adaptation) . Ages 6:0–16:11. WPPSI (1967) → WPPSI-R (1989) → WPPSI-III (2002) → WPPSI-IV (2012) . Ages 2:6–7:7.

chunks.heading: WAIS-IV - the canonical exam answer
chunks.text: WAIS-IV - the canonical exam answer Age range: 16:0 to 90:11. Total subtests: 15 (10 core + 5 supplemental). 4 index scores (memorize): Verbal Comprehension (VCI), Perceptual Reasoning (PRI), Working Memory (WMI), Processing Speed (PSI). FSIQ derived from the 10 core subtests across these 4 indices. Subtest scaled scores: M = 10, SD = 3, range 1–19. FSIQ and index scores: M = 100, SD = 15. Administration time: ~60–90 minutes for FSIQ. WAIS-IV subtest map (core in bold, supplemental in italics): Index Subtests VCI Similarities, Vocabulary, Information , Comprehension PRI Block Design, Matrix Reasoning, Visual Puzzles , Figure Weights, Picture Completion WMI Digit Span, Arithmetic , Letter-Number Sequencing PSI Symbol Search, Coding , Cancellation

chunks.heading: WISC-V - the children's scale
chunks.text: WISC-V - the children's scale Age range: 6:0 to 16:11. Total subtests: 21 (10 primary + 11 secondary, including 5 complementary subtests scored separately). 5 primary indices: Verbal Comprehension (VCI), Visual Spatial (VSI), Fluid Reasoning (FRI), Working Memory (WMI), Processing Speed (PSI). The big WISC-IV → WISC-V change was splitting old PRI into VSI + FRI , giving 5 primary indices instead of 4. 5 ancillary indices: Quantitative Reasoning Index (QRI), Auditory Working Memory Index (AWMI), Nonverbal Index (NVI), General Ability Index (GAI), Cognitive Proficiency Index (CPI). 5 complementary subtests (CHC narrow abilities): Naming Speed Literacy, Naming Speed Quantity, Immediate Symbol Translation, Delayed Symbol Translation, Recognition Symbol Translation. WISC-V primary subtest map : Index Primary subtests VCI Similarities, Vocabulary VSI Block Design, Visual Puzzles FRI Matrix Reasoning, Figure Weights WMI Digit Span, Picture Span PSI Coding, Symbol Search Secondary subtests: Information, Comprehension, Picture Concepts, Arithmetic, Letter-Number Sequencing, Cancellation.

chunks.heading: WPPSI-IV - the preschool scale
chunks.text: WPPSI-IV - the preschool scale Age range: 2:6 to 7:7. Split into two batteries: 2:6–3:11 and 4:0–7:7. Ages 2:6 to 3:11: 7 subtests, 3 primary indices (VCI, VSI, WMI). No FRI or PSI at this age (cognitive abilities not yet differentiated). Ages 4:0 to 7:7: 15 subtests, 5 primary indices (VCI, VSI, FRI, WMI, PSI) - same structure as WISC-V. Primary subtests (4:0–7:7): Information, Similarities, Block Design, Object Assembly, Matrix Reasoning, Picture Concepts, Picture Memory, Zoo Locations, Bug Search, Cancellation.

chunks.heading: 3. Raven's Progressive Matrices
chunks.text: 3. Raven's Progressive Matrices Author: John C. Raven. Year: SPM published 1938 (developed 1936). CPM 1947. APM 1943. Nature: nonverbal, multiple-choice, pattern-completion. Targets Spearman's g via eductive (meaning-extracting) reasoning. "Culture-fair": commonly described that way because items are abstract shapes, but research shows cultural loading still exists (familiarity with paper-pencil format, formal schooling). Treat "culture-reduced" as the more honest phrasing. Version Items Sets Age / use Standard Progressive Matrices (SPM) 60 5 sets (A, B, C, D, E) of 12 each Ages 6 to 80+, general population Coloured Progressive Matrices (CPM) 36 3 sets (A, A b , B) of 12 each Ages 5–11, elderly, intellectually disabled Advanced Progressive Matrices (APM) 36 + 12 practice (Set I) Set I (12 practice) + Set II (36 scored) Above-average adolescents and adults; ceiling effect on SPM MCQ trap: SPM = 60, CPM = 36, APM (scored) = 36. The 36 on CPM and APM is the swap that wrecks people. Lock both.

chunks.heading: 4. Indian Intelligence Tests
chunks.text: 4. Indian Intelligence Tests

chunks.heading: Bhatia's Battery of Performance Tests of Intelligence
chunks.text: Bhatia's Battery of Performance Tests of Intelligence Author: Chandra Mohan Bhatia. Year: 1955. Age range: originally 11 to 16 years; extended use up to early adulthood. Subtests (5 - memorize the count): Koh's Block Design Test (10 designs) Alexander's Pass-Along Test (8 problems) Pattern Drawing Test (8 designs) Immediate Memory Test - digits forward + digits backward + sentence repetition Picture Construction Test (5 pictures) Use case: built specifically for the Indian context, suitable for illiterate and rural populations because of its performance (nonverbal) orientation. MCQ trap: the Pass-Along is Alexander's (1932), incorporated into Bhatia's battery. Don't say "Bhatia Pass-Along."

chunks.heading: Binet-Kamat Test (BKT)
chunks.text: Binet-Kamat Test (BKT) Author: V.V. Kamat. Year: 1934 (Marathi adaptation), later Kannada version. Age range: 3 to 22 years. Indian Binet adaptation, still used in NIMHANS clinical assessment for clinical IQ estimation in Indian children.

chunks.heading: Malin's Intelligence Scale for Indian Children (MISIC)
chunks.text: Malin's Intelligence Scale for Indian Children (MISIC) Author: Arthur J. Malin. Year: 1969. Age range: 6 to 15 years. Indian adaptation of WISC (the 1949 original, not WISC-R). 11 subtests in the original Indian version.

chunks.heading: Other Indian instruments
chunks.text: Other Indian instruments Mohsin General Intelligence Test (S.M. Mohsin, 1959) - verbal group test, Hindi. Jalota's Group Test of General Mental Ability (S. Jalota, 1972) - verbal, ages 13+, 100 items. Seguin Form Board (1907 origin, used in India for ages 3–7) - nonverbal performance, 10 cut-outs. Often misattributed to Indian authors; it is Edouard Seguin's, used in Indian developmental screening. Developmental Screening Test (DST) - Bharath Raj, 1977 - Indian developmental screen, ages 0–15. Vineland Social Maturity Scale, Indian adaptation (A.J. Malin, 1965) - Indian SQ (Social Quotient).

chunks.heading: 5. Kaufman Family
chunks.text: 5. Kaufman Family Authors: Alan S. Kaufman & Nadeen L. Kaufman. K-ABC (Kaufman Assessment Battery for Children, 1983) → KABC-II (2004) . Ages 3:0–18:11. Built on Luria's neuropsychological model (simultaneous + sequential processing) and updated in KABC-II to allow CHC interpretation . KABC-II yields two global scores: Mental Processing Index (MPI) for Luria-style use and Fluid-Crystallized Index (FCI) for CHC-style use. 5 scales: Sequential, Simultaneous, Planning, Learning, Knowledge. Designed to reduce verbal/cultural loading and detect minority and ESL children fairly. KAIT (Kaufman Adolescent & Adult Intelligence Test, 1993) : ages 11–85, separates Fluid IQ vs Crystallized IQ explicitly. KBIT-2 (Kaufman Brief Intelligence Test, 2004) : 2 subtests (Verbal Knowledge + Matrices), 20 min, screening tool.

chunks.heading: 6. Cattell's Culture Fair Intelligence Test (CFIT)
chunks.text: 6. Cattell's Culture Fair Intelligence Test (CFIT) Author: Raymond B. Cattell. Year: first published 1949; revised 1973. Purpose: measure fluid intelligence (Gf) per Cattell's Gf-Gc theory, with reduced cultural and language loading. 3 scales: Scale 1 : ages 4–8 and intellectually disabled adults. 8 subtests. Scale 2 : ages 8–13 and average adults. 4 subtests. Scale 3 : ages 14+ and above-average adults. 4 subtests. Scales 2 & 3 subtests (same 4): Series, Classifications, Matrices, Conditions (Topology). Form A + Form B available for retest reliability. Scoring: M = 100, SD = 24 in original; renormed editions use SD = 15 or 16 depending on manual.

chunks.heading: 7. Group Intelligence Tests
chunks.text: 7. Group Intelligence Tests

chunks.heading: Army Alpha (1917)
chunks.text: Army Alpha (1917) Chair / committee: Robert M. Yerkes (APA president, chair) with Arthur S. Otis, Lewis Terman, E.L. Thorndike, Henry Goddard, Walter V. Bingham, Guy Whipple. World War I, US Army. Items: 212 questions across 8 subtests . Subtests: Oral Directions, Arithmetic Problems, Practical Judgment, Synonym-Antonym, Disarranged Sentences, Number Series Completion, Analogies, Information. Population: literate, English-speaking recruits.

chunks.heading: Army Beta (1917)
chunks.text: Army Beta (1917) Same committee, Yerkes-led. 7 subtests: Maze, Cube Analysis, X-O Series, Digit Symbol, Number Checking, Pictorial Completion, Geometrical Construction. Population: illiterate or non-English-speaking recruits. Administered via pantomime and demonstration. Trap: Beta has 7 subtests, Alpha has 8 . Bhatia also has 5. Don't conflate.

chunks.heading: Other group tests
chunks.text: Other group tests Otis Self-Administering Tests of Mental Ability (Arthur S. Otis, 1922) - civilian descendant of Army Alpha; Otis was on the Yerkes committee. Otis-Lennon School Ability Test (OLSAT) - current K–12 group ability screen. Wonderlic Personnel Test (1937) - 50 items, 12 minutes , employment screening; famous for being used by the NFL combine. Multidimensional Aptitude Battery (MAB-II, Jackson, 1998) - group-administrable Wechsler-style. California Test of Mental Maturity (CTMM) , Henmon-Nelson Tests , Cognitive Abilities Test (CogAT) - older / current school-grade group ability tests.

chunks.heading: 8. Infant and Developmental Scales
chunks.text: 8. Infant and Developmental Scales Bayley Scales of Infant Development (BSID) - Nancy Bayley. BSID-I (1969), BSID-II (1993), Bayley-III (2006) , Bayley-4 (2019). Ages 1 to 42 months . Bayley-III has 5 scales: Cognitive, Language (Receptive + Expressive), Motor (Fine + Gross), Social-Emotional, Adaptive Behavior. Gesell Developmental Schedules - Arnold Gesell, 1940s. Ages 4 weeks to 6 years. 5 fields: Adaptive, Gross Motor, Fine Motor, Language, Personal-Social. Yields a Developmental Quotient (DQ) = (Developmental Age / Chronological Age) × 100. Cattell Infant Intelligence Scale (Psyche Cattell, 1940) - downward extension of Stanford-Binet, ages 2–30 months. Brunet-Lézine Scale (1951) - French infant scale. Mullen Scales of Early Learning (1995) - ages birth to 68 months. Denver Developmental Screening Test (DDST, 1967; Denver-II, 1992) - screening, not diagnostic; ages 0–6.

chunks.heading: 9. Special-Purpose and Nonverbal Scales
chunks.text: 9. Special-Purpose and Nonverbal Scales Leiter International Performance Scale - Russell G. Leiter, 1936 → Leiter-R (1997) → Leiter-3 (2013) . Fully nonverbal, no language required; used with deaf, ASD, non-English speakers. Ages 3–75+. Goodenough Draw-A-Man Test (Florence Goodenough, 1926) → Goodenough-Harris Drawing Test (Harris, 1963) . Children draw a man (and woman, and self in Harris); scored on 64+ body-detail criteria. Ages 3–15. Slosson Intelligence Test (SIT, Slosson, 1963; SIT-R3, 2002) - brief individual screen. Differential Ability Scales (DAS-II, Elliott, 2007) - ages 2:6–17:11; CHC-aligned, popular for LD identification. Woodcock-Johnson Tests of Cognitive Abilities (WJ-IV, 2014) - explicitly built on CHC theory; ages 2–90+. Stanford-Binet Intelligence Scales for Early Childhood (SB5: Early SB-5) - ages 2:0–7:3 abbreviated form. Comprehensive Test of Nonverbal Intelligence (CTONI-2, Hammill et al., 2009) . Universal Nonverbal Intelligence Test (UNIT-2, Bracken & McCallum, 2016) . Wide Range Intelligence Test (WRIT, Glutting et al., 2000) . Reynolds Intellectual Assessment Scales (RIAS-2, Reynolds & Kamphaus, 2015) .

chunks.heading: 10. Theories Behind the Tests
chunks.text: 10. Theories Behind the Tests Theorist Year Model One-liner Charles Spearman 1904 Two-factor: g + s All cognitive tests share a general factor g plus task-specific s . Computed via factor analysis (which Spearman invented for this). L.L. Thurstone 1938 Primary Mental Abilities (7 PMAs) Verbal Comprehension, Word Fluency, Number, Spatial, Memory, Perceptual Speed, Reasoning. Rejected single g . Raymond Cattell + John Horn 1966 Gf-Gc Fluid intelligence (Gf, novel reasoning) vs Crystallized intelligence (Gc, accumulated knowledge). Gf peaks early adulthood, Gc rises lifelong. Philip E. Vernon 1950 Hierarchical g → v:ed (verbal-educational) + k:m (spatial-mechanical) → minor group factors → specific. J.P. Guilford 1967 Structure of Intellect (SOI) Originally 5 operations × 6 products × 5 contents = 150 abilities ; later expanded to 180 . Introduced divergent vs convergent thinking. Howard Gardner 1983 (Frames of Mind) Multiple Intelligences Linguistic, Logical-Mathematical, Musical, Bodily-Kinesthetic, Spatial, Interpersonal, Intrapersonal. Naturalist added 1995. Existential proposed but not confirmed. Robert Sternberg 1985 Triarchic Theory (later Successful Intelligence, 1996) Analytical (componential), Creative (experiential), Practical (contextual). PASS / WICS extensions later. McGrew, Schneider, Carroll 1993 / 1997 / 2018 Cattell-Horn-Carroll (CHC) Integrative hierarchical mod

chunks.heading: 11. IQ Score Mechanics
chunks.text: 11. IQ Score Mechanics

chunks.heading: The formula history (memorize this sequence)
chunks.text: The formula history (memorize this sequence) Mental Age introduced by Binet, 1908 revision. Ratio IQ = (MA / CA) × 100 : William Stern, 1912. Applied by Terman in the Stanford-Binet 1916. Deviation IQ : Wechsler 1939 for adults. Compares the examinee to age-mates via standardized score, fixed mean and SD. Stanford-Binet switches to deviation IQ in 1960 (Pinneau's tables), SD = 16. SB-5 (2003) drops SD to 15 to match Wechsler.

chunks.heading: Intellectual disability severity (DSM-5 / ICD-11)
chunks.text: Intellectual disability severity (DSM-5 / ICD-11) Severity IQ range (approx) Adaptive profile Mild 50–69 ~85% of ID; academic skills to ~6th grade; often community-independent with support Moderate 35–49 ~10%; basic communication, supervised work, some self-care Severe 20–34 ~3–4%; limited speech, requires support for ADLs Profound < 20 ~1–2%; fully dependent DSM-5 specifically downplays IQ cutoffs in favour of adaptive functioning across conceptual, social, and practical domains; the IQ bands above are pedagogical, not hard cutoffs.

chunks.heading: 15. MCQ Traps and One-Line Stems
chunks.text: 15. MCQ Traps and One-Line Stems Trap 1: Wechsler SD = 15, old Stanford-Binet (1960–1986) SD = 16, SB-5 (2003+) SD = 15. The 16 still surfaces because textbooks lag. Trap 2: SPM = 60, CPM = 36, APM scored = 36 (don't include the 12 practice). Most common item-count swap on Indian PG papers. Trap 3: Bhatia has 5 subtests (Koh, Pass-Along, Pattern Drawing, Immediate Memory, Picture Construction). Army Beta has 7 . Army Alpha has 8 . Trap 4: WAIS-IV has 4 indices (VCI/PRI/WMI/PSI). WISC-V has 5 (VCI/VSI/FRI/WMI/PSI). The WISC-V split was: old PRI broke into VSI + FRI. Trap 5: Ratio IQ = (MA/CA)×100. Stern (1912) wrote the formula; Terman (1916) put it into Stanford-Binet. Don't credit Binet for the IQ formula - Binet rejected it. Trap 6: Stanford-Binet 1st edition = 1916, not 1905. 1905 = Binet-Simon (France). Trap 7: Cattell-Horn Gf-Gc is 1966. Cattell's CFIT is 1949. Raymond Cattell is also 16PF (1949). Three things by the same author. Trap 8: Gardner originally proposed 7 intelligences (1983), added Naturalist in 1995 → 8. Existential is proposed but not formally accepted. "9 intelligences" is debated and usually wrong on Indian exams. Trap 9: KABC-II yields two global indices (MPI and FCI) because it supports both Luria's model and CHC. The original K-ABC (1983) was pure Luria. Trap 10: Bayley-III is ages 1–42 months, NOT just infants. Gesell goes to 6 years. Stanford-Binet st

chunks.text: 17. Three-Pass Revision Plan for This Page First pass (60 min): read sections 1–9 in order. Don't skip the Wechsler subtest tables, that's where most index-swap traps live. Second pass (next day, ~20 min): read only the cross-comparison master table (§12) and the numbers cheatsheet (§13). Cover the right column and self-test. Third pass (exam week, 10 min daily): author-year speedround (§14) + MCQ traps (§15) + stems (§16) only. These three sections are the actual exam ammunition. Built 2026-05-20. chunks.heading: Learning & Conditioning — Full Terms Page
chunks.text: Learning & Conditioning — Full Terms Page Built 2026-05-16 because MET / NIMHANS love the operant-conditioning vocabulary as 1-mark definition traps. Every term has the same 3-row block: Definition · Classic example · MCQ trap . Skim once, then drill by closing the example/trap columns and self-quizzing on the term name.

chunks.heading: 0. Big picture — where each term sits
chunks.text: 0. Big picture — where each term sits Family Terms inside Classical (Pavlovian) phenomena Extinction, spontaneous recovery, generalization, discrimination, habituation, sensitization Operant (Skinnerian) shaping tools Shaping, chaining, fading, prompting Operant schedules FR, VR, FI, VI Cognitive / social learning Latent learning (Tolman), insight learning (Köhler), observational learning (Bandura) Implicit / cognitive priming Priming (semantic, perceptual, affective) Read this once: all of classical conditioning is about stimulus pairings , all of operant is about consequences shaping voluntary behaviour , priming is about one stimulus making a later stimulus easier to process , and habituation/sensitization are non-associative (single stimulus, no pairing). If a question mixes the families, the answer is almost always the term whose family matches the stem.

chunks.heading: 1. Priming
chunks.text: 1. Priming Definition Exposure to one stimulus (the prime ) unconsciously influences the response to a later stimulus (the target ), by activating related representations in memory. A form of implicit memory. Classic example You read the word NURSE . A moment later you identify DOCTOR faster than an unrelated word like BREAD . The semantic network around "medical" was pre-activated. MCQ trap Priming is not classical conditioning — there is no UCS, no reflex, no pairing. It is also not recall — the person doesn't consciously remember the prime. Tested on the implicit-vs-explicit memory split. Subtypes: semantic (NURSE → DOCTOR), perceptual (briefly flashed word → faster identification), affective (smiling face → positive judgement).

chunks.heading: 2. Shaping
chunks.text: 2. Shaping Definition Reinforcing successive approximations of a target behaviour the organism doesn't yet emit. Operant, Skinner. Classic example Training a rat to press a lever: first reinforce facing the lever, then approaching it, then touching it, then pressing it. Each step gets closer to the final behaviour. MCQ trap Shaping is for behaviours the organism cannot yet do . Don't confuse with chaining (linking behaviours the organism already does into a sequence) or prompting (cueing an existing behaviour). The reinforcement criterion changes across trials — that is the defining feature.

chunks.heading: 3. Chaining
chunks.text: 3. Chaining Definition Linking a sequence of already-learned behaviours into a longer chain, where each behaviour serves as the discriminative stimulus (S D ) for the next, and only the final link is reinforced. Classic example Brushing teeth: pick up brush → wet it → apply paste → brush → rinse → put brush away. Each step cues the next. Used heavily in ABA / autism skill training. MCQ trap Two variants — forward chaining teaches step 1 first; backward chaining teaches the last step first (so the learner always experiences the reinforcer at the natural endpoint). Backward chaining is often preferred clinically because the final reinforcer is reached immediately. Do not confuse with shaping — chaining links existing behaviours; shaping builds a new one.

chunks.heading: 4. Fading
chunks.text: 4. Fading Definition Gradually removing a prompt while transferring stimulus control to the natural cue, so the behaviour eventually occurs without the prompt. Classic example Teaching a child to say "ball" — start with full verbal model ("say ball"), fade to partial ("say buh…"), fade to just holding up the ball. The picture/object becomes the controlling stimulus. MCQ trap Fading is about removing the prompt , not the reinforcer . Removing the reinforcer is extinction . Fading transfers stimulus control; extinction eliminates the behaviour. Both can run side-by-side but they target different things.

chunks.heading: 5. Prompting
chunks.text: 5. Prompting Definition Providing an additional stimulus (verbal, gestural, physical, modelled, visual) that helps the learner emit the correct response in the presence of the natural cue. Classic example Therapist says "wave bye-bye" and physically guides the child's hand (physical prompt). Over trials, prompts are faded until the verbal cue alone works. MCQ trap Know the prompt hierarchy from most to least intrusive: physical → modelling → gestural → verbal → visual/positional . "Least-to-most" vs "most-to-least" prompting are common clinical-vignette distractors. Prompts are antecedent manipulations; reinforcement is a consequence — that distinction has been tested.

chunks.heading: 6. Extinction
chunks.text: 6. Extinction Definition Reduction and eventual disappearance of a conditioned response when reinforcement (operant) or the UCS (classical) is no longer presented. Classic example Classical: Pavlov's dog stops salivating to the bell once the bell is repeatedly presented without food. Operant: a child stops tantrumming after parents consistently ignore tantrums that previously got attention. MCQ trap Watch for the extinction burst — a temporary increase in the behaviour's frequency and intensity right after reinforcement is withdrawn, before it declines. Extinction does not erase the learning; the response can return as spontaneous recovery . Behaviours on variable schedules are most resistant to extinction (partial-reinforcement extinction effect).

chunks.heading: 7. Spontaneous Recovery
chunks.text: 7. Spontaneous Recovery Definition Reappearance of a previously extinguished conditioned response after a rest period, without any new conditioning trials. Classic example Pavlov extinguished salivation to a bell. He let the dog rest for several hours, presented the bell again, and the salivation came back (weaker than original, but real). MCQ trap Spontaneous recovery proves extinction is not unlearning — the original association is suppressed, not erased. The recovered response is typically weaker than the original. Re-extinction is also faster the second time (savings effect). Don't confuse with reinstatement (re-emergence after UCS-alone presentation) or renewal (re-emergence in a new context).

chunks.heading: 8. Generalization vs Discrimination
chunks.text: 8. Generalization vs Discrimination Generalization Discrimination Definition Responding similarly to stimuli that resemble the original CS / S D . Responding differently to stimuli that resemble the CS / S D but are not it — only the specific stimulus elicits the response. Classic example Little Albert (Watson) was conditioned to fear a white rat. He then also feared a white rabbit, cotton wool, a Santa beard — fear generalized to similar stimuli. A dog is reinforced for salivating to a 1000 Hz tone but not to a 1200 Hz tone. After training, only 1000 Hz produces salivation — the dog discriminates . MCQ trap Generalization gradient — response strength decreases with distance from the original CS. Stimulus generalization (similar CS) ≠ response generalization (different responses to same CS). Discrimination is taught by differential reinforcement : reinforce in presence of S D , withhold in presence of S Δ . Sharper gradient = better discrimination. Failure to discriminate is the mechanism behind many phobias. One-liner to memorize: generalization is the default , discrimination is trained .

chunks.heading: 9. The Four Reinforcement Schedules
chunks.text: 9. The Four Reinforcement Schedules Schedule Definition Response pattern Classic example MCQ trap Fixed Ratio (FR) Reinforcement after a fixed number of responses. High rate, brief post-reinforcement pause , then burst. Step-like cumulative record. Factory piece-work: paid per 10 units assembled. FR-10. The pause comes after the reinforcer, not before. Higher ratios = longer pauses. Ratio strain (work stops) if ratio is raised too fast. Variable Ratio (VR) Reinforcement after an average number of responses (unpredictable trial-to-trial). Highest, steadiest response rate of any schedule. Almost no pause. Slot machines, fishing, sales cold-calls. The schedule behind gambling addiction. Most resistant to extinction. Produces the most persistent behaviour. If a stem says "extremely hard to stop" or "addictive" → VR. Fixed Interval (FI) Reinforcement for the first response after a fixed time has elapsed. Scallop pattern — slow responding right after reinforcement, accelerating as the interval ends. Checking the mail when you know it arrives at 11 am. Studying right before a scheduled weekly quiz. FI gives the lowest overall rate among the four. Don't confuse with FR — FI is time -based, FR is response-count based. Variable Interval (VI) Reinforcement for the first response after a variable, unpredictable time interval. Steady, moderate rate. No scallop. Resistant to extinction. Chec

chunks.heading: 10. Latent Learning
chunks.text: 10. Latent Learning Definition Learning that occurs without reinforcement and without immediate behavioural expression ; it shows up later when reinforcement is introduced. Demonstrates that learning ≠ performance. Classic example Tolman & Honzik (1930) rat-in-maze experiment. Three groups: (a) reinforced every trial, (b) never reinforced, (c) unreinforced for 10 days, then reinforced from day 11. Group (c) immediately outperformed group (a) on day 12 — proving they had been learning the maze all along ("cognitive map") but not showing it. MCQ trap The buzzword is cognitive map (Tolman, 1948 "Cognitive Maps in Rats and Men"). Latent learning was the first big challenge to strict behaviourism — it showed mental representations form without external reinforcement. Don't confuse with insight learning (sudden problem-solving) or observational learning (via a model).

chunks.heading: 11. Insight Learning
chunks.text: 11. Insight Learning Definition Sudden understanding of a problem's solution, typically after a period of contemplation, without trial-and-error. Associated with the Gestalt school. Classic example Köhler's chimpanzee Sultan (1925). Sultan was placed in a cage with a banana out of reach and two short sticks that could be joined. After a period of inactivity, Sultan suddenly joined the sticks and retrieved the banana — the "aha!" moment. MCQ trap Linked to Wolfgang Köhler and the Gestalt psychologists (perceptual reorganization). It is cognitive , not behaviourist. Contrast with Thorndike's trial-and-error learning (law of effect, puzzle box cats). If the stem mentions "aha!", "sudden," or "no gradual improvement" → insight.

chunks.heading: 12. Observational Learning
chunks.text: 12. Observational Learning Definition Learning by watching others (the model ) and imitating their behaviour. No direct reinforcement of the learner is required — vicarious reinforcement of the model is enough. Classic example Bandura's Bobo doll experiment (1961). Children who watched an adult aggressively beat a Bobo doll later beat it themselves; controls did not. Aggression was learned by observation alone. MCQ trap Bandura's four processes are commonly tested: Attention → Retention → Reproduction → Motivation (ARRM). Vicarious reinforcement (seeing the model rewarded) and vicarious punishment (seeing the model punished) modulate motivation. Bandura's broader framework is Social Learning Theory (1977), later renamed Social Cognitive Theory (1986) — also home of self-efficacy and reciprocal determinism .

chunks.heading: 13. Habituation vs Sensitization
chunks.text: 13. Habituation vs Sensitization Habituation Sensitization Definition Decrease in response to a repeated, harmless stimulus. Non-associative learning. Increase in response to a stimulus after exposure to an intense or noxious stimulus. Also non-associative . Classic example You stop noticing the ticking of a wall clock after a few minutes. Aplysia (sea slug, Kandel) reduces gill-withdrawal reflex with repeated mild touch. After a sudden loud bang, you flinch harder at every subsequent door creak. Aplysia gill-withdrawal becomes stronger after a tail shock — even to mild touch. MCQ trap Habituation is stimulus-specific (a new stimulus restores the response → dishabituation). Do not confuse with sensory adaptation (receptor fatigue, peripheral) or with extinction (which requires a prior pairing). Habituation needs only one stimulus, no learning history. Mechanism (Kandel) Reduced neurotransmitter release at the sensory-motor synapse. Heterosynaptic facilitation via serotonergic interneurons → increased NT release. One-liner: habituation says "this is safe, ignore it"; sensitization says "the world is dangerous, react more." Both are the simplest forms of learning and were Kandel's 2000 Nobel Prize work.

chunks.heading: 14. Confusable-pairs cheat-table (read last)
chunks.text: 14. Confusable-pairs cheat-table (read last) Pair Distinguishing feature Shaping vs Chaining Shaping builds a new behaviour . Chaining links existing behaviours . Fading vs Extinction Fading removes the prompt . Extinction removes the reinforcer / UCS . Extinction vs Spontaneous recovery Extinction suppresses; spontaneous recovery shows the memory is still there. Generalization vs Discrimination Generalization is the default; discrimination is trained by differential reinforcement. FR vs FI FR = fixed responses . FI = fixed time . Both pause after reinforcement, but FI shows a scallop . VR vs VI VR = highest, most vigorous rate (gambling). VI = steady, moderate rate (checking phone). Latent vs Insight learning Latent = hidden until reinforced (Tolman, rats). Insight = sudden "aha" (Köhler, chimps). Observational learning vs Imitation Imitation is one component; observational learning is the whole 4-stage process (Bandura's ARRM). Habituation vs Sensory adaptation Habituation is in the CNS (learning). Sensory adaptation is in the receptor (fatigue). Habituation vs Extinction Habituation needs only one stimulus, no prior pairing. Extinction requires a previously conditioned association. Priming vs Classical conditioning Priming = implicit memory facilitation, no UCS. Classical = reflex paired with neutral stimulus.

chunks.heading: 15. Quick self-test (close the answers, write your own)
chunks.text: 15. Quick self-test (close the answers, write your own) A pigeon stops pecking when food is no longer delivered, then pecks again after a 24-hour rest. What is the second peck called? You praise a child for any sound that sounds like "ma" — over weeks she progresses to "ma-ma," then to "mama." Which procedure? Slot machines maintain behaviour on which schedule, and why is that schedule the hardest to extinguish? Tolman's rats had learned the maze even though they showed no improvement until food was introduced. What is this phenomenon called, and what concept did Tolman propose to explain it? A therapist holds a child's hand to help her wave bye-bye. Over sessions she removes the hand prompt and only the verbal cue remains. Name the two procedures involved. You stop hearing the air conditioner after 5 minutes. The cat suddenly jumps on the table and you immediately hear the AC again. Which two non-associative processes did you just experience? Show answers Spontaneous recovery. Shaping (successive approximations). Variable Ratio (VR). Highly resistant to extinction because the next response could always be the reinforced one. chunks.heading: Therapy technique → which school "more terms like Socratic"
chunks.text: Therapy technique → which school "more terms like Socratic" Technique / cue School Socratic questioning, guided discovery, thought records, cognitive triad CBT (Beck) ABC model, disputing irrational beliefs, "musturbation" REBT (Ellis) Empathy, unconditional positive regard, congruence, "real relationship" Person-centred (Rogers) Free association, transference, dream analysis, working through Psychoanalysis (Freud) Empty chair, top-dog/underdog Gestalt (Perls) Mindfulness / distress tolerance / emotion reg / interpersonal effectiveness DBT (Linehan) Hexaflex, cognitive defusion, values, committed action ACT (Hayes) Miracle question, scaling, exceptions SFBT Systematic desensitisation, reciprocal inhibition, fear hierarchy Behaviour therapy (Wolpe) Exposure & response prevention (ERP) For OCD (Foa) Paradoxical intention, dereflection Logotherapy (Frankl) You missed this: the approach that prefers "real relationship" + UPR over the term "therapeutic alliance" is Person-centred therapy . chunks.heading: Psychodynamic self & object relations Kohut — you said you don't know any of this
chunks.text: Psychodynamic self & object relations Kohut — you said you don't know any of this Kohut's self psychology. The self develops through 3 selfobject needs : Mirroring (being admired/validated → healthy ambition), Idealizing (merging with a calm, strong other → ideals), Twinship/alter-ego (feeling alike/belonging). Failure of mirroring → grandiosity + craving admiration (narcissistic pathology). Failure of mirroring + idealizing → a fragmented, empty self (emptiness, abandonment fears, unstable relationships). Object relations = the internalised mental representations of self and others and the relationship between them (Klein, Winnicott, Fairbairn, Mahler). Not the id/ego/superego, not defence mechanisms.

chunks.heading: Learning: escape vs avoidance you guessed this
chunks.text: Learning: escape vs avoidance you guessed this Escape learning = behaviour terminates an aversive stimulus that is already present (turn off a loud alarm). Avoidance learning = behaviour prevents the aversive stimulus from starting (leave before the alarm). Both are negative reinforcement. More: Psychotherapy cheatsheet · Learning & conditioning 6. A motor-control problem, not planning Agnosia Can't recognise objects/faces/sounds despite intact senses (e.g. prosopagnosia) Aphasia Language deficit — Broca's (non-fluent, comprehension intact), Wernicke's (fluent, poor comprehension) Alexia Acquired inability to read (with intact vision) Agraphia Acquired inability to write Anomia Can't name objects (word-finding)

chunks.heading: The 4 wrongs
chunks.text: The 4 wrongs m1_the01 Psychotherapy wrong The 'empty chair' technique is most associated with which approach? A) Cognitive Behaviour Therapy B) Gestalt therapy (Perls) ← correct C) Person-Centred Therapy ← you picked D) Psychoanalysis You: C Correct: B Why B. Fritz Perls' Gestalt therapy built the empty-chair technique: client dialogues with a disowned part of self (top-dog vs underdog) or an absent other (dead parent, ex-partner) by physically switching seats. Goal: integrate split parts of the self into present-moment awareness. Person-Centred (Rogers) is the trap because both are humanistic-existential, but Rogers' tools are reflection, unconditional positive regard, empathic understanding , not staged dialogue. Therapy → founder cheat row, learn this cold: Gestalt → Fritz Perls. Empty chair, top-dog/underdog, "now and how" not "why." Person-Centred / Client-Centred → Carl Rogers. Three core conditions: empathy, genuineness, unconditional positive regard . Logotherapy → Viktor Frankl. Meaning-seeking, paradoxical intention, dereflection. Existential → Yalom, May, Binswanger. Death, freedom, isolation, meaninglessness. Rational Emotive (REBT) → Albert Ellis. ABCDE model. Cognitive Therapy → Aaron Beck. Cognitive triad, automatic thoughts, schema.
