chunks.text: Sleep wave mnemonic You used elimination on Q14 ("REM is characterised by all EXCEPT…predominantly delta-wave EEG"). Here's the wave → stage table cold, plus a mnemonic for which wave goes where. Wave Frequency State What's happening Beta (β) 13–30 Hz Awake, alert, eyes open Active thinking, focused attention Alpha (α) 8–13 Hz Awake, eyes closed, relaxed Resting wakefulness, occipital dominant Theta (θ) 4–8 Hz NREM Stage 1 (N1), drowsy Transition into sleep, hypnagogic imagery Sleep spindles + K-complexes 11–16 Hz bursts NREM Stage 2 (N2) Spindles consolidate memory; K-complexes suppress arousal Delta (δ) 0.5–4 Hz NREM Stage 3 / 4 (N3, slow-wave sleep) Deepest sleep; growth hormone release; sleepwalking, night terrors, bed-wetting happen here Mixed / beta-like, low-voltage Fast, desynchronised REM EEG resembles waking but with atonia + rapid eye movements; vivid dreams Stages → waves mnemonic: "BATS Drink Blood." B eta — awake, alert A lpha — awake, eyes closed T heta — N1 S pindles + K-complexes — N2 (sometimes labelled "Sigma" in older books) D elta — N3, slow-wave sleep B eta-like / REM — paradoxical sleep, EEG looks awake Alternative (high → low frequency): " BAT-D + REM" — Beta > Alpha > Theta > Delta as you descend through stages, then REM jumps back up to look like awake. Frequency drops as depth increases, then REM rebounds. MCQ traps to lock in: REM EEG looks like awak

chunks.heading: Yalom's 11 therapeutic factors
chunks.text: Yalom's 11 therapeutic factors Irvin Yalom, group psychotherapy and existential psychotherapy. His 11 therapeutic factors are the curative mechanisms that operate in any group. Universality (Q16) is one of them — the realisation that you're not alone in your suffering. Factor One-line definition MCQ trigger phrase 1. Instillation of hope Seeing others improve gives you reason to expect your own improvement "hope from observing others recover" 2. Universality Realising others share your problems; you are not uniquely broken "not alone in suffering," "I'm not the only one" 3. Imparting of information Didactic instruction by therapist or other members; psychoeducation "teaching about the illness" 4. Altruism Helping others in the group restores self-worth; "I have something to give" "giving back to others" 5. Corrective recapitulation of the primary family group Group re-creates family dynamics, allowing them to be worked through "group as substitute family" 6. Development of socialising techniques Learning basic social skills through feedback and modelling "learning to communicate better" 7. Imitative behaviour Modelling on the therapist or successful members; "spectator therapy" "imitating peers' coping" 8. Interpersonal learning Insight into one's own interpersonal patterns through group feedback "how I come across to others," social microcosm 9. Group cohesiveness The "we-ness

chunks.heading: Theory of mind
chunks.text: Theory of mind Theory of mind (ToM) = the capacity to attribute mental states — beliefs, desires, intentions, knowledge — to oneself and to others, and to understand that others can hold mental states different from one's own . Term coined by Premack & Woodruff (1978) in a chimpanzee study. Critical milestone in social cognitive development.

chunks.heading: How it's tested
chunks.text: How it's tested Sally-Anne task (false-belief) — Wimmer & Perner (1983), popularised by Baron-Cohen, Leslie & Frith (1985). Sally puts marble in basket, leaves. Anne moves marble to box. Sally returns. "Where will Sally look for her marble?" Correct answer = basket (Sally's false belief). Passed reliably at ~4 years . Smarties / Maxi task — child is shown a Smarties tube containing pencils. "What will another child think is in here?" Pre-ToM: "pencils" (can't separate own knowledge from other's). Post-ToM: "Smarties." Second-order false belief — "What does Mary think John thinks?" Passed ~6–7 years. Tests recursive ToM. Reading the Mind in the Eyes — adult ToM test (Baron-Cohen), identify emotion from eye region only. Used in autism research.

chunks.heading: Developmental timeline
chunks.text: Developmental timeline ~18 months — joint attention, pointing to share, pretend play (precursors). ~2–3 years — understands desires drive behaviour (desire psychology). ~4 years — first-order false belief, Sally-Anne passed. ~6–7 years — second-order false belief, recursive mentalising. ~9–11 years — faux pas detection, irony, sarcasm, white lies.

chunks.heading: Clinical relevance
chunks.text: Clinical relevance Autism Spectrum Disorder — classic ToM deficit, especially on false-belief tasks. Baron-Cohen's "mindblindness" hypothesis (1995). Note this is one theory, not the whole story; ASD also involves weak central coherence and executive dysfunction. Schizophrenia — ToM impairment linked to delusions and social withdrawal (Frith). Frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD) — selective ToM loss with preserved IQ early on. Trap to avoid. Sally-Anne tests first-order false belief (what Sally thinks). It is NOT a test of empathy, perspective-taking in general, or appearance-reality distinction (that's the Smarties task variant).

chunks.heading: Korsakoff vs dissociative amnesia
chunks.text: Korsakoff vs dissociative amnesia You got Q8 right (dissociative amnesia) but asked "what would it be if it was Korsakoff?" The two get confused because both involve memory loss without a structural mass lesion. Here's the full split. Feature Korsakoff syndrome Dissociative amnesia Cause Thiamine (B1) deficiency, usually chronic alcoholism; also bariatric surgery, hyperemesis, malnutrition Psychological trauma; no medical/neurological cause Pathology Mammillary body atrophy, mediodorsal thalamic nuclei, hippocampal damage Functional disconnection; no structural lesion on imaging Memory affected Anterograde amnesia (can't form new memories) + variable retrograde; procedural memory preserved Retrograde, personal autobiographical, often selective for the traumatic period Hallmark feature Confabulation — fills gaps with plausible but false stories, no intent to deceive Localised or selective amnesia for traumatic events; sense of self may remain intact Insight Poor; patient unaware of memory failure Variable; often distressed by the gap Precedes Wernicke encephalopathy — acute triad of confusion + ataxia + ophthalmoplegia . Together: Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome Often preceded by an identifiable trauma or major stressor Other cognition Often preserved IQ + immediate memory; classic "amnesic syndrome with confabulation" Other cognition preserved; not a global cognitive disorder Treat

chunks.heading: p-value refresher
chunks.text: p-value refresher You got Q6 right but flagged "I forgot this concept. Knew it well before but need a detailed revision." Here's the clean version, plus the things examiners weaponise.

chunks.heading: The definition (one sentence, memorise it)
chunks.text: The definition (one sentence, memorise it) p-value = the probability of observing the obtained data (or more extreme), assuming the null hypothesis is true.

chunks.heading: What it does NOT mean
chunks.text: What it does NOT mean p is NOT the probability that H₀ is true. p is NOT the probability that H₁ is true. p is NOT the probability you're wrong. p is NOT the effect size — a small p with a tiny effect on a huge sample is statistically significant but clinically meaningless. p < 0.05 does NOT prove H₁; it just lets you reject H₀ at α = 0.05.

chunks.heading: Decision rule
chunks.text: Decision rule p < α (e.g., 0.03 < 0.05) → reject H₀. Result is "statistically significant." p ≥ α → fail to reject H₀. (Never "accept H₀" — absence of evidence ≠ evidence of absence.) α is set before the study, not chosen after seeing the data.

chunks.heading: The four-cell decision matrix (the foundation)
chunks.text: The four-cell decision matrix (the foundation) H₀ actually true H₀ actually false Reject H₀ Type I error (α) — false positive, you think there's an effect when there isn't Correct rejection (power = 1 − β) Fail to reject H₀ Correct retention (1 − α) Type II error (β) — false negative, you miss a real effect

chunks.heading: Common asks on MET / NIMHANS
chunks.text: Common asks on MET / NIMHANS α (alpha) = pre-set threshold, usually 0.05. Probability of Type I error. β (beta) = probability of Type II error. Usually 0.20. Power = 1 − β = probability of detecting a real effect. Aim for ≥ 0.80. Power depends on sample size, effect size, α, and variability. Effect size = magnitude of the effect, independent of n. Cohen's d (means), r (correlation), η² (ANOVA), OR/RR (epidemiology). Confidence interval at 95% complements p < 0.05: if the 95% CI for a mean difference excludes 0, p < 0.05. One-tailed vs two-tailed — directional vs non-directional H₁. One-tailed makes it easier to reject H₀ but you must pre-specify the direction. Bonferroni correction — adjust α when running multiple comparisons. α_new = α / k. p-hacking / multiple comparisons — running many tests inflates Type I error. Not a "scientific finding," it's a statistics failure. One-liner that always works in MCQ: "If p < α, reject H₀." If asked for the meaning of p, the safest answer is always "probability of the observed result (or more extreme) under the assumption that H₀ is true." Anything stronger than this is a distractor.

chunks.heading: Ainsworth's attachment styles
chunks.text: Ainsworth's attachment styles Mary Ainsworth, Strange Situation Procedure (1969–1978). Lab procedure with 8 episodes: mother + baby alone, stranger enters, mother leaves, stranger interacts, mother returns, etc. Classification is made primarily on reunion behaviour , not separation distress. Original three styles + a fourth added later by Main & Solomon (1986). Style Distress on separation? Behaviour on reunion (the key) Caregiver pattern Approx % Secure (B) Yes, moderate Seeks contact, is comforted, returns to play Sensitive, consistent, responsive ~60–65% Insecure-Avoidant (A) Little to none visible Avoids or ignores caregiver, continues play, treats stranger and parent similarly Emotionally unavailable, rejecting ~15–20% Insecure-Resistant / Ambivalent (C) High Seeks contact AND resists it (clings then pushes away); cannot be soothed Inconsistent — sometimes responsive, sometimes not ~10–15% Disorganised (D) (added 1986) Chaotic Contradictory behaviour: approaches then freezes, stares blankly, walks backward toward parent Frightened or frightening caregiver, often trauma/abuse ~5–10%

chunks.heading: How Q4 trapped you
chunks.text: How Q4 trapped you "Distress on separation but cannot be comforted on reunion and may resist contact" → this is the C (resistant/ambivalent) signature, not avoidant. Avoidant = doesn't even seek the parent on reunion. The trap was probably the word "resist" pulling you toward "resistant" — that's actually correct labelling, but you went the other way to "avoidant." Memorise: Avoidant = doesn't try to make contact. Resistant / Ambivalent = tries AND resists. Disorganised = no coherent strategy at all. Secure = upset on departure, comforted on return.

chunks.heading: Adult attachment (Hazan & Shaver, Bartholomew)
chunks.text: Adult attachment (Hazan & Shaver, Bartholomew) Infant style Adult parallel (Hazan & Shaver, 1987) Bartholomew 4-cat (1991) Secure Secure Secure (+self, +other) Avoidant Avoidant Dismissing (+self, −other) Resistant / Ambivalent Anxious-ambivalent Preoccupied (−self, +other) Disorganised (not in original H&S) Fearful (−self, −other) One-line MCQ trick. If the question describes the reunion behaviour, that's the answer. Separation distress alone doesn't distinguish secure from resistant — both show distress. Calm-on-departure = avoidant.

chunks.heading: Trinucleotide repeat disorder list
chunks.text: Trinucleotide repeat disorder list From Q17 (Huntington's, CAG on chromosome 4). Trinucleotide repeat expansions are the cause of a small but heavily-tested group of disorders. Three things to memorise per disorder: repeat (3 letters) , chromosome , inheritance pattern . Disorder Repeat Gene / Chromosome Inheritance Hallmark Huntington's disease CAG HTT, 4p16.3 Autosomal dominant Adult-onset chorea + cognitive decline + psychiatric sx Fragile X syndrome CGG FMR1, Xq27.3 X-linked Most common inherited intellectual disability; long face, large ears, macroorchidism Myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1) CTG DMPK, 19q13 Autosomal dominant Myotonia + frontal balding + cataracts + cardiac conduction defects Friedreich ataxia GAA FXN, 9q21 Autosomal recessive (the odd one out) Gait ataxia + hypertrophic cardiomyopathy + diabetes; onset childhood/adolescence Spinocerebellar ataxias (SCA 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 17) CAG Multiple genes Autosomal dominant Progressive cerebellar ataxia + variable extras Spinobulbar muscular atrophy (Kennedy disease) CAG AR (androgen receptor), Xq12 X-linked Adult-onset proximal weakness + gynaecomastia + reduced fertility Dentatorubral-pallidoluysian atrophy (DRPLA) CAG ATN1, 12p13 Autosomal dominant Ataxia + choreoathetosis + dementia + seizures; mostly Japanese populations Two facts that MET/NIMHANS love: Anticipation — repeat expansions grow across generations, so disea

chunks.heading: EMDR + trauma therapists
chunks.text: EMDR + trauma therapists From Q13. Francine Shapiro developed EMDR in 1987. You asked who Shapiro and Foa were — here's the trauma-therapy lineage.

chunks.heading: EMDR — Eye Movement Desensitisation and Reprocessing
chunks.text: EMDR — Eye Movement Desensitisation and Reprocessing Founder : Francine Shapiro, 1987. Mechanism (theoretical) : bilateral stimulation (eye movements, taps, tones) while recalling a traumatic memory facilitates reprocessing, hypothesised to mimic REM sleep memory consolidation. 8 phases : (1) history-taking, (2) preparation, (3) assessment, (4) desensitisation, (5) installation of positive cognition, (6) body scan, (7) closure, (8) re-evaluation. Indication : PTSD primary. Endorsed by APA (2017) and WHO (2013) as a first-line PTSD treatment alongside trauma-focused CBT. Controversy : whether the eye movements themselves are essential or just the exposure component. Component-dismantling studies are mixed.

chunks.heading: Trauma therapy lineage — who did what
chunks.text: Trauma therapy lineage — who did what Therapist Approach / contribution Trigger phrase in MCQs Francine Shapiro EMDR (1987) "eye movements + trauma reprocessing" Edna Foa Prolonged Exposure (PE) therapy for PTSD; also OCD treatment with Exposure & Response Prevention (ERP) "prolonged exposure," "imaginal + in vivo exposure for PTSD," "ERP for OCD" Patricia Resick Cognitive Processing Therapy (CPT) for PTSD, originally developed for sexual assault survivors "CPT," "stuck points," "Socratic dialogue PTSD" Judith Herman Concept of complex PTSD (1992); 3-stage trauma recovery model (safety → remembrance/mourning → reconnection) "complex trauma," "3-stage recovery" Bessel van der Kolk The Body Keeps the Score ; somatic + body-based trauma interventions; trauma-sensitive yoga "body-based trauma therapy" Peter Levine Somatic Experiencing , completing the freeze response "somatic experiencing" Marsha Linehan Dialectical Behaviour Therapy (DBT) — for borderline PD + chronic suicidality; also useful for PTSD with emotion-dysregulation features "DBT," "BPD" Pierre Janet Late-19th-century French psychiatrist; original theory of dissociation as trauma response; pre-Freud "dissociation, historical figure" One-line trap fixes: • Shapiro → E MDR (S e e + e ye movements; mnemonic: Shapiro Sees). • Foa → F locked exposure (Foa = Floods you with exposure to the trauma + OCD ERP). • Resick → CPT (

chunks.heading: Bonus quick hits, your other notes
chunks.text: Bonus quick hits, your other notes You also flagged seven smaller items in the dump. One-line fixes each:

chunks.heading: [2] MMPI T-score scoring — "don't know scoring of any test"
chunks.text: [2] MMPI T-score scoring — "don't know scoring of any test" T-scores have mean = 50, SD = 10 . T = 60 → +1 SD. T = 65 → conventional "elevated" cut-off on MMPI-2. T = 70 → +2 SD → clinically significant elevation . T = 80 → +3 SD, rare and extreme. Other standardised score systems to keep separate: Z-score : M = 0, SD = 1. Standard score / IQ : M = 100, SD = 15 (Wechsler) or 16 (Stanford-Binet 4th ed, older). Subtest scaled scores (WAIS/WISC) : M = 10, SD = 3. So scaled 7 = −1 SD, scaled 13 = +1 SD. Stanine : M = 5, SD ~ 2. Range 1–9. Percentile : rank 1–99, not a standardised score, NOT normally distributed.

chunks.heading: [5] WAIS IQ ranges — "what is dependent on edition"
chunks.text: [5] WAIS IQ ranges — "what is dependent on edition" The IQ range labels shifted between WAIS-III and WAIS-IV. Memorise the WAIS-IV (current) version: 130+ — Very Superior / Extremely High 120–129 — Superior 110–119 — High Average 90–109 — Average 80–89 — Low Average 70–79 — Borderline <70 — Extremely Low (DSM-5 requires concurrent adaptive deficits to call it intellectual disability) Older texts (WAIS-III, Wechsler-1955) sometimes used "Borderline" for 70–79 AND "Dull Normal" for 80–89. The WAIS-IV uses "Low Average / Borderline" depending on cut-point. Trap: if a question says "70–84 falls under…" with both "Low Average / Borderline (depending on edition)" and just "Borderline" as options, the more inclusive answer (edition-dependent) is safer.

chunks.heading: [9] Ellis ABC, "I was confused between A and C"
chunks.text: [9] Ellis ABC, "I was confused between A and C" REBT's ABC is: A — Activating event (not just "Antecedent" — that's Skinnerian). B — Beliefs (irrational, in REBT). C — Consequences (emotional + behavioural). D — Disputing (the irrational belief). Therapist's job. E — Effective new belief / Effect. The trap option in Q9 (option A: "Activating event, Behaviour, Consequence") looks right because it sounds like the operant ABC. But Ellis is cognitive — the middle term is Belief , not Behaviour. Skinner's three-term contingency is the look-alike: Antecedent → Behaviour → Consequence.

chunks.heading: [10] Basal ganglia, "I thought it was subthalamic first"
chunks.text: [10] Basal ganglia, "I thought it was subthalamic first" Basal ganglia = caudate, putamen, globus pallidus (internal + external), subthalamic nucleus, substantia nigra . Sometimes lumped as "striatum" (caudate + putamen) and "lentiform nucleus" (putamen + globus pallidus). Red nucleus is NOT basal ganglia — it's midbrain tegmentum, gives the rubrospinal tract. Subthalamic IS in the basal ganglia (lesion = hemiballismus, contralateral wild flinging movements). Red nucleus lesion = rubral tremor + ataxia.

chunks.heading: [11] Place theory + Bekesy
chunks.text: [11] Place theory + Bekesy Georg von Békésy, Nobel 1961. Place theory : pitch is encoded by the location of maximum basilar membrane displacement. High frequencies vibrate the basal (narrow, stiff) end of the cochlea; low frequencies vibrate the apical (wide, floppy) end. Best for high frequencies (above ~1 kHz). Frequency / Volley theory (Wever) handles low frequencies: groups of auditory neurons fire in volleys phase-locked to the sound wave. Above ~5 kHz, place theory does all the work.

chunks.heading: [12] LTP and NMDA, "completely forgot"
chunks.text: [12] LTP and NMDA, "completely forgot" Long-term potentiation = persistent strengthening of synapses with repeated stimulation. Bliss & Lomo, 1973, hippocampus. NMDA receptor is the coincidence detector: needs both glutamate binding AND postsynaptic depolarisation (to expel the Mg²⁺ block). Once both happen, Ca²⁺ floods in → triggers cascade → more AMPA receptors inserted into the membrane → synapse permanently stronger. AMPA is the workhorse for fast excitatory transmission; NMDA is the gate-keeper for plasticity. LTP is the cellular substrate of learning/memory. Hippocampus + NMDA + Ca²⁺ + LTP = memorise as a chain.

chunks.heading: What to do next
chunks.text: What to do next 3-step plan. Tonight (45 min) : read the top 4 topic blocks above (cranial nerves, sleep waves, Korsakoff vs dissociative, p-values). These are the highest-frequency items. Tomorrow (60 min) : read the remaining 5 (Yalom, ToM, Ainsworth, trinucleotide list, EMDR) + the bonus quick hits. By end of day you've closed every gap surfaced in the dump. Day after (90 min) : re-attempt MET Mock 1. Goal: cut the 47 skips to under 15. Even half-guessing on previously-skipped Qs at 33% accuracy nets you ~+30 to ~+45 marks. Target 240+ on this re-attempt. If you only have 20 minutes, read these three blocks in this order: Sleep waves (because Q14 had you eliminating), p-value (because you said you knew this and forgot), Ainsworth (because it cost you a wrong, not a skip). Everything else is recovery from blanks, not corrections to known knowledge. Open the auto-analysis dashboard → Retake MET Mock 1 → Consolidated revision pack →

chunks.heading: Biopsychology, 6 wrong
chunks.text: Biopsychology, 6 wrong Pattern: you keep losing points on where structures are and which side does what . Memorise the locations, then the lesions follow. m1_bio03 Biopsych The corticospinal tract decussates primarily at the: a) Optic chiasm b) Spinal cord at the level of entry c) Pons ← you picked d) Pyramids of the medulla ← correct You: c Correct: d Why d. 85-90% of corticospinal fibres cross at the pyramidal decussation in the lower medulla, forming the lateral corticospinal tract . The remaining ~10% stay ipsilateral as the anterior corticospinal tract and cross only at the spinal segmental level. Adjacent topics they will retest: Optic chiasm (option a) crosses only the nasal retinal fibres so each cortex sees the contralateral visual field. Sectioning it = bitemporal hemianopia . Sensory decussations: dorsal column / medial lemniscus (fine touch, proprioception) crosses at the medulla (internal arcuate fibres). Spinothalamic (pain, temp) crosses at the spinal cord level of entry , 1-2 segments up. Brown-Sequard syndrome = hemisection of cord. Ipsilateral motor + dorsal column loss below the lesion, contralateral pain/temp loss starting 1-2 segments below. UMN vs LMN signs: UMN lesion (above anterior horn) = spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski up. LMN = flaccid, atrophy, fasciculations, areflexia. m1_bio05 Biopsych guessed Damage to the ventromedial hypothalamus typically

chunks.heading: Language, 6 wrong
chunks.text: Language, 6 wrong Pattern: vocabulary + grammar fundamentals + RC tone reading. The grammar ones are pure rule-recall, fix the rule once and you stop bleeding marks here. m1_lang02 Language guessed Identify the antonym of 'GREGARIOUS': a) Sociable b) Reclusive ← correct c) Affable ← you picked d) Convivial You: c Correct: b Why b. Gregarious = fond of company, sociable. Antonym = withdrawn / solitary = reclusive . Sociable, affable, convivial are all synonyms (the trap: 3 of 4 options agreed with the word, you picked one of those instead of the outlier). Antonym/synonym pairs that show up on this exam style: Word Synonym Antonym Gregarious sociable, affable reclusive, solitary Garrulous talkative, loquacious taciturn, reticent Ephemeral fleeting, transient permanent, enduring Ubiquitous omnipresent scarce, rare Sanguine optimistic, cheerful morose, pessimistic Lucid clear, intelligible obscure, opaque Verbose wordy, prolix terse, concise Magnanimous generous petty, vindictive Pragmatic practical idealistic, dogmatic Equivocal ambiguous unequivocal, clear Trap rule for antonym MCQs: if 3 options are similar in meaning, the 4th is almost always the answer. Look for the outlier first. m1_lang03 Language Choose the correct preposition: 'The therapist insisted ___ a follow-up after two weeks.' a) for ← you picked b) with c) on ← correct d) to You: a Correct: c Why c. "Insist on " is

chunks.heading: Assessment, 4 wrong
chunks.text: Assessment, 4 wrong Pattern: IQ band names, projective trivia, normal-curve percentile-to-z conversions. All pure recall. m1_ass03 Assessment guessed In Wechsler's classification, an FSIQ in the range 70-84 falls under: a) Low average / borderline (depending on edition) ← correct b) Borderline ← you picked c) Average d) Mild intellectual disability You: b Correct: a Why a. 70-84 spans two Wechsler bands: 70-79 = borderline , 80-89 = low average . Option (a) acknowledges that. Picking just "borderline" misses half the range. WAIS-IV / WISC-V IQ classification, lock this exactly: FSIQ Classification 130 and above Very superior / Extremely high 120-129 Superior 110-119 High average 90-109 Average 80-89 Low average 70-79 Borderline 69 and below Extremely low / Intellectual disability (with adaptive deficits, per DSM-5) Adjacent traps: Stanford-Binet 5 uses M=100 but the older versions used SD=16 , not 15. Modern SB5 = SD 15. DSM-5 ID severity is now based on adaptive functioning , not IQ alone. (Old DSM-IV used IQ bands.) FSIQ alone doesn't diagnose ID without adaptive deficits in conceptual, social, or practical domains. m1_ass04 Assessment guessed Which projective test uses incomplete cartoon-style frames in which the respondent fills in what the depicted character is saying in a frustrating situation? a) TAT ← you picked b) Rosenzweig P-F Study ← correct c) Rorschach d) Sentence

chunks.heading: Therapy, 4 wrong
chunks.text: Therapy, 4 wrong Pattern: who-built-what attribution. Match the technique ↔ school ↔ founder. m1_the01 Therapy The 'empty chair' technique is most associated with which approach? a) Cognitive Behaviour Therapy b) Gestalt therapy (Perls) ← correct c) Person-Centred Therapy ← you picked d) Psychoanalysis You: c Correct: b Why b. Empty chair = Fritz Perls' Gestalt therapy . Client speaks to an imagined other (or a disowned part of self) sitting in an empty chair. Promotes integration of split-off parts. Person-centred (Rogers) uses reflection / unconditional positive regard, no role-play techniques. Therapy school ↔ founder ↔ signature technique: School Founder Signature techniques Psychoanalysis Freud Free association, dream interpretation, transference, resistance, slip analysis Analytical psychology Jung Active imagination, archetype work, word association, dream amplification Individual psychology Adler Lifestyle assessment, early recollections, "as if" technique Person-centred Rogers UPR, congruence, accurate empathy — no specific "techniques" Gestalt Perls Empty chair, two-chair, here-and-now awareness, exaggeration Existential Yalom, Frankl, May Confront givens (death, freedom, isolation, meaning); Frankl = logotherapy / paradoxical intention Behaviour therapy Wolpe, Skinner Systematic desensitisation, flooding, token economy, aversion CBT Beck, Ellis Cognitive restructurin

chunks.heading: Biostats, 3 wrong (and you guessed 5/10 here so the real number is shakier than 70%)
chunks.text: Biostats, 3 wrong (and you guessed 5/10 here so the real number is shakier than 70%) m1_bst02 Biostats guessed The Mann-Whitney U test is the non-parametric equivalent of the: a) Independent samples t-test ← correct b) Paired t-test ← you picked c) One-way ANOVA d) Chi-square test You: b Correct: a Why a. Mann-Whitney U works on ranks of two independent groups. Wilcoxon signed-rank is the paired-t equivalent. Don't conflate them. Parametric ↔ non-parametric pairing (memorise the table): Parametric Non-parametric Use Independent t-test Mann-Whitney U (Wilcoxon rank-sum) Compare 2 independent groups Paired t-test Wilcoxon signed-rank Compare 2 related/paired scores (pre-post) One-way ANOVA Kruskal-Wallis H 3+ independent groups Repeated-measures ANOVA Friedman test 3+ related conditions Pearson r Spearman rho (or Kendall tau) Correlation (none, categorical) Chi-square / Fisher's exact 2 categorical variables When to go non-parametric: data not normal, ordinal scale, small n, outliers, unequal variances. Tradeoff: non-parametric tests have less power if assumptions for parametric are met. m1_bst05 Biostats guessed Cluster sampling differs from stratified sampling primarily in that: a) Stratified samples randomly choose entire groups; cluster samples sample within groups ← you picked b) Both are non-probability methods c) Cluster sampling randomly chooses naturally occurring groups

chunks.heading: Developmental, 3 wrong
chunks.text: Developmental, 3 wrong m1_dev07 Developmental guessed The Visual Cliff experiment (Gibson & Walk, 1960) demonstrated that depth perception emerges: a) Only after age 2 ← you picked b) By the time infants can crawl (~6-8 months) ← correct c) At birth, fully developed d) After explicit verbal teaching You: a Correct: b Why b. 6-8-month-old crawlers refused to cross the "deep" side onto a glass surface. Newer heart-rate studies show even pre-crawlers perceive the cliff (HR drops on the deep side) but only crawlers act on it. Classic infant perception studies you should recognise: Visual cliff (Gibson & Walk, 1960) — depth perception by ~6-8 months. Fantz preferential looking (1961) — newborns prefer face-like patterns. Habituation paradigm — infants look longer at novel stimuli → used to test discrimination. Violation-of-expectation (Baillargeon) — suggests object permanence may emerge as early as 3.5 months, earlier than Piaget claimed. Still-face experiment (Tronick, 1975) — infants distress when caregiver becomes unresponsive → importance of contingent interaction. Sucking habituation / high-amplitude sucking (DeCasper & Fifer) — newborns prefer mother's voice + language heard prenatally. m1_dev09 Developmental Object permanence, in Piaget's theory, is fully achieved by approximately: a) 2 months ← you picked b) 18-24 months ← correct c) 8-12 months (with A-not-B error) d) 4 mo

chunks.heading: Abnormal, 2 wrong
chunks.text: Abnormal, 2 wrong m1_abn03 Abnormal guessed In DSM-5-TR, persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) requires depressed mood for at least: a) 6 months in adults b) 2 years in adults / 1 year in children ← correct c) 1 year in adults ← you picked d) 5 years You: c Correct: b Why b. PDD = 2 years adults / 1 year children-adolescents , depressed mood most of the day, more days than not, plus ≥2 of (poor appetite/overeating, sleep disturbance, low energy, low self-esteem, poor concentration, hopelessness). DSM-5 duration criteria, learn this whole table cold: Disorder Minimum duration Major depressive episode 2 weeks Manic episode 1 week (or any if hospitalised) Hypomanic episode 4 days Persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) 2 yr adults / 1 yr children Cyclothymia 2 yr adults / 1 yr children Schizophreniform 1-6 months Schizophrenia ≥6 months (incl. ≥1 month active) Brief psychotic disorder 1 day to 1 month Schizoaffective ≥6 months (with mood + psychotic) Generalised anxiety disorder 6 months Panic disorder persistent worry / behaviour change >1 month after attack Specific phobia / Social anxiety / Agoraphobia 6 months OCD >1 hour/day or distress (no minimum duration per se) PTSD >1 month post-trauma Acute stress disorder 3 days to 1 month Adjustment disorder within 3 months of stressor, ≤6 months after stressor ends Anorexia / Bulimia (BN binge frequency) BN ≥1×/week for 3 mon

chunks.heading: Compact cheats — print these
chunks.text: Compact cheats — print these

chunks.heading: Biopsych one-liners
chunks.text: Biopsych one-liners Corticospinal decussates at medullary pyramids . Spinothalamic at spinal level . Dorsal column at medulla . VMH = satiety (lesion → obesity). LH = hunger (lesion → aphagia). Basal ganglia = Caudate, Putamen, Globus pallidus, STN, SNc/SNr . Red nucleus is midbrain, not BG. Cones at fovea, rods at periphery, optic disc has neither. Right parietal lesion → left neglect. Right fusiform → prosopagnosia. Bilateral medial temporal → amnesia (HM). Huntington: CAG, chr 4, AD. Fragile X: CGG, X-linked. PKU: AR, chr 12.

chunks.heading: Language one-liners
chunks.text: Language one-liners 3-out-of-4-options-similar → the 4th is the antonym answer. Each / every / either / neither = singular verb . Insist on . Comprise (no "of"). Discuss (no "about"). RC main idea = most general statement supported. Avoid "always / every / never" options. Tone words: dismissive (rejects), polemical (attacks), didactic (teaches), supportive-but-qualified (positive with hedges).

chunks.heading: Assessment one-liners
chunks.text: Assessment one-liners Wechsler bands: 130+ Very Sup, 120-129 Sup, 110-19 High Avg, 90-109 Avg, 80-89 Low Avg, 70-79 Borderline, <70 Extremely Low. +1 SD = 84th percentile. +2 = 97.5. -1 = 16. Vineland: Communication, DLS, Socialisation, Motor (<7). NOT IQ. Rosenzweig P-F = cartoons of frustration. TAT = ambiguous photos. SCT = sentence stems. Reliability cap on validity: max validity = √r_xx.

chunks.heading: Therapy one-liners
chunks.text: Therapy one-liners Empty chair → Perls / Gestalt . UPR + congruence + empathy → Rogers. ABC model → Ellis (REBT). Cognitive triad → Beck. Family therapy: Minuchin = structural. Bowen = intergenerational / genogram. Satir = experiential. Haley = strategic. Yalom: Universality ≠ Instillation of hope ≠ Catharsis. Memorise the 11. Downward arrow = drill to core belief. Exposure hierarchy = anxiety treatment.

chunks.heading: Biostats one-liners
chunks.text: Biostats one-liners Mann-Whitney = independent t. Wilcoxon signed-rank = paired t. Kruskal-Wallis = ANOVA. Friedman = repeated-measures ANOVA. Spearman = Pearson. Stratified = sample within strata. Cluster = sample whole clusters. (Don't swap.) CONSORT = RCT. PRISMA = systematic review. STROBE = observational. STARD = diagnostic. COREQ = qualitative. Type I (alpha) = false positive. Type II (beta) = false negative. Power = 1 - beta.

chunks.heading: Developmental one-liners
chunks.text: Developmental one-liners Visual cliff (Gibson & Walk) = depth perception by 6-8 months crawl-age. Object permanence (Piaget) = 18-24 months. A-not-B error around 8-12 months. Sally-Anne false belief = ToM at ~age 4. Strange Situation = attachment, 12-18 months. Secure / insecure-avoidant (A) / resistant (C) / disorganised (D).

chunks.heading: Abnormal one-liners
chunks.text: Abnormal one-liners MDE 2 weeks. Mania 1 week (or any if hospitalised). Hypomania 4 days. Schizophreniform 1-6 mo. Schizophrenia 6 mo. PDD/dysthymia 2 yr adults, 1 yr kids. Cyclothymia same. GAD 6 months. PTSD >1 month. Acute stress 3d to 1 month. Adjustment within 3 mo, max 6 mo after stressor ends. PTSD = 4 clusters (B intrusion, C avoidance, D negative cog/mood, E arousal). Built from the 28 wrong answers on MET Mock 1 (2026-05-05). Sahil + Claude. Adjacent topics chosen by what the same paper-style is most likely to retest.

The other two weak sections (Therapy / Social, both 70%) are not strategy failures, they're trivia failures. Three takeaways: Biopsych is your single highest-yield fix. chunks.heading: Neuropsych / Biopsych, 6 wrong — the leak
chunks.text: Neuropsych / Biopsych, 6 wrong — the leak Score: 9/15 (60%) Solid: 8 Guessed-right: 1 Wrong: 6 Pattern: pituitary / hypothalamus axis, neurochemistry of metabolism, classic case studies, drug side-effect timelines . You're not weak on "biopsych" in general, you're weak on endocrine + neurology trivia . Three of six wrongs came from the same axis (anterior pituitary, hypothalamus, PKU). n1_bio01 Biopsych wrong NIMHANS 2025 In Phenylketonuria (PKU), the body fails to convert phenylalanine into which substance due to a deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase? A) Urea B) Tyrosine ← correct C) Tryptophan ← you picked D) Histidine You: C Correct: B Your note: "DOnt know this. need to learn" Why B. PKU = autosomal recessive deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH) . The enzyme normally converts phenylalanine → tyrosine . With PAH gone, phenylalanine piles up (toxic to brain in infancy) and tyrosine drops. The downstream consequence is intellectual disability, fair skin / hair (tyrosine is the precursor for melanin), and a musty body odour. Newborn screen catches it; treatment is a low-Phe diet for life. The amino-acid → neurotransmitter chain (memorise this entire row): Phenylalanine → Tyrosine → L-DOPA → Dopamine → Norepinephrine → Epinephrine. The whole catecholamine pathway. PKU breaks step 1. Parkinson's loses dopamine at step 4 (treat with L-DOPA, not dopamine, because dopam

chunks.heading: Research / Biostats, 3 wrong
chunks.text: Research / Biostats, 3 wrong Score: 12/15 (80%) Solid: 8 Guessed-right: 4 Wrong: 3 Pattern: sampling distinctions + reliability vocabulary + standard-score families . You're at the surface level. 4 guesses on 15 means real understanding is ~8/15, not 12/15. n1_bst01 Biostats guessed-right NIMHANS 2024 Risk ratio = 1.0 in a cohort study. Means: C) no difference in risk between groups ← correct, you guessed. Your note: "wtf is risk ratio?" Risk ratio (RR) = relative risk = incidence in exposed / incidence in unexposed. RR = 1 → no association (incidence equal in both groups). RR > 1 → exposure raises risk. RR = 2 means exposed group has twice the risk. RR < 1 → exposure protects. RR = 0.5 means exposed group has half the risk. Used in cohort studies and RCTs (you know who developed the outcome over time). RR vs OR vs HR, the trio that owns biostats MCQs: Measure What When used RR (risk ratio) incidence in exposed / incidence in unexposed Cohort, RCT OR (odds ratio) odds of exposure in cases / odds in controls Case-control (you can't compute incidence) HR (hazard ratio) instantaneous risk ratio over time Survival analysis, Cox regression ARR (absolute risk reduction) risk-unexposed minus risk-exposed RCTs NNT 1 / ARR How many you treat to prevent 1 outcome Rule of thumb: When outcome is rare (<10%), OR ≈ RR. When outcome is common, OR exaggerates the effect. n1_bst04 Biostats righ

Your conceptual base is solid; the misses are reference-table failures. n1_abn02 Abnormal wrong NIMHANS 2024 Phobia of pain: A) Nosophobia, B) Algophobia, C) Cynophobia, D) Hematophobia. Correct = B. You picked A. You: A (disease) Correct: B (pain) Algos = pain (Greek). Nosos = disease, so nosophobia = fear of disease (often confused with hypochondriasis but more specific to fear of illness rather than belief in having one). Cynos = dog. Haema = blood. chunks.heading: Developmental, 0 wrong — your notes only
chunks.text: Developmental, 0 wrong — your notes only Score: 10/10 (100%) Solid: 8 Guessed-right: 2 Wrong: 0 Perfect, but you flagged two with notes. Closing the gap here turns 2 guesses into 2 solids. n1_dev01 Dev guessed-right NIMHANS 2024 Thomas & Chess temperament: difficult child = B. You guessed. Your note: "Dont know this model" Thomas & Chess (NYLS, 1956 →). Studied 133 infants longitudinally. Identified 9 temperament dimensions : activity, rhythmicity, approach/withdrawal, adaptability, intensity, threshold, mood, distractibility, attention span/persistence. Clustered into three types (+ mixed): Easy (~40%): regular biological rhythms, approaches new situations positively, adapts quickly, positive mood. Difficult (~10%): irregular rhythms, withdraws from new, slow to adapt, negative mood, intense reactions. Slow-to-warm-up (~15%): low activity, mild reactions, slow adapt but adapts eventually, mildly negative at first. Mixed (~35%): don't fit cleanly. Goodness of fit : developmental outcome depends on match between child's temperament and the parenting/environmental demands. A "difficult" child with a patient, flexible parent → fine. The same child with a rigid parent → conduct + emotional problems. Temperament & attachment NIMHANS bundle: Kagan : behavioural inhibition (shy / fearful infants); 15-20% of toddlers. Stable temperament linked to amygdala reactivity. Rothbart : tempera

chunks.heading: Psych Assessment, 2 wrong
chunks.text: Psych Assessment, 2 wrong Score: 8/10 (80%) Solid: 7 Guessed-right: 1 Wrong: 2 Pattern: WAIS subtest structure + IQ history (ratio vs deviation) . Pure trivia, pure fixable in one sitting. n1_ass04 Assessment guessed-right NIMHANS 2024 WAIS-IV subtest scaled score of 10 → B) 50th percentile. You guessed. Your note: "Dont know shit about the scoring on this" Two parallel scales on the WAIS-IV: Subtest scaled score : Mean = 10, SD = 3. Range typically 1-19. Scaled score of 10 = mean = 50th percentile. 13 = +1 SD = 84th. 16 = +2 SD = 97.7th. 7 = −1 SD = 16th. 4 = −2 SD = 2.3rd. Index / composite score (VCI, PRI, WMI, PSI, FSIQ): Mean = 100, SD = 15. Same conversion logic. WAIS-IV structure, lock this entire thing: Index Core subtests Supplemental Verbal Comprehension (VCI) Similarities, Vocabulary, Information Comprehension Perceptual Reasoning (PRI) Block Design, Matrix Reasoning, Visual Puzzles Picture Completion, Figure Weights Working Memory (WMI) Digit Span, Arithmetic Letter-Number Sequencing Processing Speed (PSI) Symbol Search, Coding Cancellation Core total = 10 subtests = FSIQ. 3 VCI + 3 PRI + 2 WMI + 2 PSI = 10. That answers ass05 below. IQ classification (WAIS-IV) : ≥130 Very Superior · 120-129 Superior · 110-119 High Average · 90-109 Average · 80-89 Low Average · 70-79 Borderline · <70 ID range. n1_ass05 Assessment wrong NIMHANS 2025 WAIS-IV core subtests: VCI vs PRI

chunks.heading: Psychotherapy, 3 wrong
chunks.text: Psychotherapy, 3 wrong Score: 7/10 (70%) Solid: 5 Guessed-right: 2 Wrong: 3 Pattern: who founded what . Maxwell Jones, Ellis vs Beck, Linehan, Kernberg, BPD defenses. All school-attribution traps. None of them are conceptually hard, they're memorisation. n1_thr01 Therapy wrong NIMHANS 2024 Maxwell Jones pioneered: B) Therapeutic community ← correct. You picked C (group analysis). You: C (group analysis) Correct: B (therapeutic community) Why B. Maxwell Jones (1953, Henderson Hospital UK) developed the therapeutic community : hospital ward as a treatment medium itself, with democratic decision-making, communalism, permissiveness, reality confrontation, and social analysis (Rapoport's 4 themes). Patients participate in their own treatment, staff hierarchy is flattened. Group-modality founders, NIMHANS-grade: Modality Founder Key idea Therapeutic community Maxwell Jones Democratic ward, communalism, reality confrontation. Milieu therapy Bruno Bettelheim, Stanton & Schwartz Total environment as treatment. Broader than TC; TC is a sub-type. Group analysis S.H. Foulkes Psychoanalytic group work, group-as-a-whole, "matrix." T-groups / sensitivity training Kurt Lewin (NTL, 1947) Here-and-now feedback, organisational application. Encounter groups Carl Rogers (1960s) Humanistic, personal growth. Psychodrama J.L. Moreno Acting out conflicts, role reversal, doubling. Self-help groups (AA)

chunks.heading: Social Psych, 3 wrong
chunks.text: Social Psych, 3 wrong Score: 7/10 (70%) Solid: 5 Guessed-right: 2 Wrong: 3 Pattern: named-concept trivia : Kitty Genovese, Type D, anomie. These three would be solid if you'd read a 1-page social-psych summary. n1_soc02 Social wrong NIMHANS 2024 Bystander apathy paradigm was inspired by the murder of: B) Kitty Genovese ← correct. You picked C (Emmett Till). You: C Correct: B 1964, Queens NY. Catherine "Kitty" Genovese was murdered outside her apartment. NYT initially reported "38 neighbours saw the attack and did nothing." The figure is historically inflated (later investigation: most witnesses heard fragments, some did call police), but the narrative drove John Darley and Bibb Latané to design the bystander studies (1968-70) . Bystander phenomenon, the two-factor explanation (came up directly in soc01): Diffusion of responsibility : in a group, each individual feels less personal obligation to act. The more bystanders, the less likely any single one helps. (Smoke-filled-room experiment.) Pluralistic ignorance : each bystander privately thinks "this is an emergency" but reads others' inaction as evidence that it's not . Everyone defers to everyone else. Latané's 5 steps of helping : (1) notice the event → (2) interpret it as an emergency → (3) assume responsibility → (4) know how to help → (5) decide to help. Any step can break. Evaluation apprehension = fear of being judged if

chunks.heading: General / Cognitive, 2 wrong
chunks.text: General / Cognitive, 2 wrong Score: 8/10 (80%) Solid: 6 Guessed-right: 2 Wrong: 2 Pattern: Baddeley episodic buffer + Bandura careless miss . One was unknown content, one was a mis-click. The careless one is the most expensive type of wrong — it's already in your head. n1_gen01 General wrong NIMHANS 2024 Baddeley component that integrates phonological loop + sketchpad + LTM: B) Episodic buffer ← correct. You picked A (central executive). You: A Correct: B Why B. The central executive is the attentional controller — it allocates resources, switches tasks, supervises. It is not a store . The episodic buffer (added by Baddeley in 2000) is the limited-capacity multimodal store that binds information across the phonological loop (verbal), visuospatial sketchpad (visual), and long-term memory into a coherent episode. Baddeley's working memory model (full, this is high-yield): Component Role Capacity / type Central executive Attentional control, task-switching Modality-free, limited Phonological loop Verbal + acoustic info ~2 seconds; phonological store + articulatory rehearsal Visuospatial sketchpad Visual + spatial info "Inner eye"; can dissociate visual cache + inner scribe Episodic buffer (2000) Binds info from slave systems + LTM Limited multimodal store Connected models: Atkinson-Shiffrin (1968) : sensory → short-term store → long-term store. The classic "modal" model. Baddeley

chunks.heading: English / Reasoning, 1 wrong
chunks.text: English / Reasoning, 1 wrong Score: 4/5 (80%) Solid: 4 Wrong: 1 Pattern: antonym vocabulary . Fix with a 100-word antonym list. n1_eng01 English wrong GREGARIOUS : RECLUSIVE :: GARRULOUS : ? Answer: D) Taciturn. You picked C (Verbose). You: C (verbose) Correct: D (taciturn) The analogy is antonyms, not synonyms. Gregarious (sociable) is the OPPOSITE of reclusive (withdrawn). So the second pair must also be antonyms: garrulous (excessively talkative) ↔ taciturn (uncommunicative, silent by nature). Loquacious + verbose are both synonyms of garrulous, which is the trap. High-yield antonym pairs (NIMHANS / MET English): Word Means Antonym Gregarious Sociable, fond of company Reclusive, solitary Garrulous / Loquacious / Verbose Talkative Taciturn, laconic, reticent Magnanimous Generous in spirit Petty, vindictive Ephemeral Short-lived Perennial, enduring Ubiquitous Everywhere Rare, scarce Esoteric Known to few Exoteric, common Sycophant Flatterer Critic Pragmatic Practical Idealistic, dogmatic Lethargic Sluggish Vigorous, energetic Frugal Sparing Prodigal, profligate Capricious Unpredictable Steadfast, constant Erudite Learned Ignorant Indolent Lazy Industrious Verbose Wordy Concise, terse Mundane Ordinary Extraordinary Cogent Convincing Unconvincing, weak Belligerent Hostile Amicable, peaceful Obsequious Servile, fawning Domineering, assertive Vehement Forceful, passionate Apatheti

chunks.heading: NIMHANS PYQ Topic Breakdown — 2023 / 2024 / 2025
chunks.text: NIMHANS PYQ Topic Breakdown — 2023 / 2024 / 2025 What this is: A close read of 300 NIMHANS M.Phil Clinical Psych entrance questions across the 2023, 2024, and 2025 memory-based papers. Topics are tagged by repeat frequency so you know where the marks live. Use this to drive revision priority — not the raw textbook order. 300 PYQs analysed 3 Years (2023-25) ~38 Repeat topics Tier legend Tier 1 Repeated in all three years or asked multiple times within a year. Master cold. Tier 2 Repeated in two years . Solid working knowledge. Tier 3 Single appearance. Recognise + classify, don't memorise depth.

chunks.heading: Section weighting from PYQs (rolling 3-year average)
chunks.text: Section weighting from PYQs (rolling 3-year average) Section ~Q count / 100 Notes Therapy / Behaviour change ~19 Heaviest section. Reinforcement, conditioning, schools of therapy. Abnormal / Psychopathology ~16 Personality disorders, delusional syndromes (Capgras-family), schizophrenia. Biopsych / Neuropsych ~14 Aphasias, amnesia (HM), endocrine, EPS side effects, neurochemistry. Developmental ~12 Erikson + Piaget dominate. Bronfenbrenner & Marcia secondary. Research / Biostats ~12 Sampling, factor analysis, study designs, error types. Assessment ~10 Wechsler subtests, Rorschach scoring, Indian batteries, validity types. Social ~9 Bystander effect, just-world, attribution biases, Type D personality. General / Cognitive ~8 Memory models, defenses, Indian psychology (Triguna), heuristics. Calibrate effort to this distribution. Therapy + Abnormal + Biopsych = ~49% of marks. NIMHANS has no English / reasoning / general-aptitude section, so none of your time goes there.

chunks.heading: 1 · Research / Biostatistics
chunks.text: 1 · Research / Biostatistics

chunks.heading: Tier 1 — High repeat, master cold
chunks.text: Tier 1 — High repeat, master cold T1 Sampling methods 2023, 2024, 2025 : probability vs non-probability, simple random, stratified, cluster (multi-stage), quota, snowball, purposive, convenience. Know calculation of sampling error only for probability methods. T1 Factor analysis basics 2023, 2024 : scree plot, eigenvalues, Kaiser-Guttman rule (>1.0), elbow, EFA vs CFA, factor loadings, CFI/RMSEA fit indices. T1 Reliability types 2023, 2024 : test-retest (Pearson r), split-half, parallel forms, inter-rater (Cohen's κ), internal consistency (Cronbach α). Know which threat each addresses. T1 Type I vs Type II error 2024, 2025 : α (false positive, reject true H0), β (false negative), power = 1−β. Bonferroni correction logic.

chunks.heading: Tier 2 — Asked twice across the three years
chunks.text: Tier 2 — Asked twice across the three years T2 Study designs (cohort, case-control, cross-sectional, RCT) — pick best design for given scenario (rare outcome → case-control; rare exposure → cohort). T2 Reporting guidelines: PRISMA (sys reviews), CONSORT (RCTs), STROBE (observational), CARE (case reports). T2 Parametric vs nonparametric tests: t-test ↔ Mann-Whitney U; paired t ↔ Wilcoxon signed-rank; one-way ANOVA ↔ Kruskal-Wallis; repeated-measures ANOVA ↔ Friedman. T2 Validity types: face, content, construct (convergent + discriminant), criterion (concurrent + predictive).

chunks.heading: Tier 3 — Asked once each, recognise + classify
chunks.text: Tier 3 — Asked once each, recognise + classify T3 Levels of measurement (Stevens: nominal, ordinal, interval, ratio). T3 Z-score interpretation; normal distribution properties (mean=median=mode, AUC=1, kurtosis types: leptokurtic / platykurtic / mesokurtic). T3 df for chi-square (rows−1)(cols−1). T3 Multicollinearity in regression; ANCOVA covariate assumption (linear with DV). T3 Partial correlation, biserial correlation, Spearman rank correlation. T3 Factorial ANOVA for interaction effects. T3 Sociogram (sociometry); ethnographic methodology. T3 Intention-to-treat (ITT) principle; blinding levels.

chunks.heading: 2 · Neuropsychology / Biological Psychology
chunks.text: 2 · Neuropsychology / Biological Psychology

chunks.heading: Tier 1 — High repeat
chunks.text: Tier 1 — High repeat T1 Aphasias 2024 (multiple Qs) : Broca's (non-fluent, intact comprehension, agrammatism), Wernicke's (fluent, poor comprehension, word salad), conduction (arcuate fasciculus), global, anomic, transcortical. Plus angular gyrus = reading/writing. T1 Patient HM (Henry Molaison) 2024 (3+ Qs in one paper) : medial temporal lobectomy → anterograde amnesia, intact working memory, intact procedural (mirror tracing). Cornerstone case for hippocampus + memory consolidation. T1 Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome 2024, 2025 : thiamine (B1) deficiency in chronic alcohol use. Wernicke = confusion + ataxia + ophthalmoplegia. Korsakoff = anterograde amnesia + confabulation. Confabulation tested separately. T1 Reticular activating system (ARAS) 2023, 2024 : brainstem, regulates arousal/wakefulness/attention. Damage → coma.

chunks.heading: Tier 2 — Two-year repeats
chunks.text: Tier 2 — Two-year repeats T2 Antipsychotic side effects: tardive dyskinesia (chronic D2 blockade, oro-facial), akathisia (acute restlessness), acute dystonia, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, drug-induced parkinsonism. T2 Memory subtypes: episodic, semantic, procedural; anterograde vs retrograde amnesia; Ribot's law. T2 Endocrine — anterior vs posterior pituitary hormones; adrenal cortex (cortisol, aldosterone) vs medulla (adrenaline/noradrenaline); hypothalamus as integrator; thyroid (metabolism); pineal (melatonin).

chunks.heading: Tier 3
chunks.text: Tier 3 T3 Genetic disorders: PKU (phenylalanine → tyrosine block), Down (trisomy 21), Turner (XO), Huntington (chromosome 4, autosomal dominant CAG repeat). T3 Neuroimaging: EEG (electrical, ms-temporal, low-spatial), fMRI (BOLD, mm-spatial, ~s temporal), PET, MEG, structural CT/MRI. T3 Lateral ventricles (CSF), choroid plexus, ventricular system flow. T3 Myelin sheath → saltatory conduction (10-100× faster); demyelination → MS. T3 Synaptic plasticity (LTP, LTD); Karl Lashley's distributed memory storage view. T3 Neurodegenerative differential: Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, Huntington's, FTD, vascular dementia, Lewy body. T3 Apraxia, agnosia (incl. prosopagnosia, anosognosia, simultanagnosia), alexia, ataxia — know the difference cold. T3 Action potential mechanics, Na⁺/K⁺/Ca²⁺ channel roles. (See action potential primer .)

chunks.heading: 3 · Abnormal / Psychopathology
chunks.text: 3 · Abnormal / Psychopathology

chunks.heading: Tier 1 — Master cold
chunks.text: Tier 1 — Master cold T1 Schizophrenia 2023, 2024, 2025 : dementia praecox (Kraepelin) → schizophrenia (Bleuler, 4 As). Positive vs negative symptoms (5 As of negative: alogia, anhedonia, avolition, affective flattening, asociality). DSM-5 ≥6 months total / ICD-10 ≥1 month criterion. T1 Capgras-family delusional syndromes 2025 had 4+ Qs : Capgras (familiar = impostor), Fregoli (strangers = one disguised person), Othello (delusional jealousy), De Clérambault's / erotomania, Cotard (nihilistic / "I am dead"), Reduplicative paramnesia. Folie à deux (shared delusion) repeated 2023+2024. T1 Cluster B personality disorders 2023, 2024, 2025 : BPD (instability, splitting, abandonment fears), NPD (grandiosity, mirroring failure / Kohut), HPD (theatrical, attention-seeking, seductive), ASPD. Know how to differentiate when stem mentions admiration-seeking vs grandiosity. T1 OCD-related concepts : ego-dystonic vs ego-syntonic, intrusive thoughts, compulsions as safety/avoidance behaviours, Body Dysmorphic Disorder (DSM-5 OCRD chapter), thought-action fusion, magical thinking.

chunks.heading: Tier 2
chunks.text: Tier 2 T2 Dissociative disorders: DID, dissociative amnesia, fugue, depersonalization/derealization disorder. Trauma origin. T2 Conversion (Functional Neurological Symptom) Disorder + la belle indifférence ; differentiating from factitious and malingering. T2 Specific phobia naming: algophobia (pain), nosophobia (disease), cynophobia (dogs), hematophobia (blood), acrophobia (heights), agoraphobia (open/crowded spaces). T2 Mood disorders — DSM-5 specifiers for manic/depressive episodes (with anxious distress, mixed features, psychotic features, peripartum, seasonal). Note: "with limited prosocial emotions" is a Conduct Disorder specifier — common trap.

chunks.heading: Tier 3
chunks.text: Tier 3 T3 Chronic Fatigue Syndrome / SEID criteria (DSM/ICD). T3 Substance addictive liability ranking (nicotine highest in epi data); gateway theory (marijuana). T3 Eating disorders, somatic symptom disorder, illness anxiety disorder. T3 Treatment of acute mania (lithium, valproate, atypicals; SSRIs NOT first-line). T3 Mental Healthcare Act 2017 provisions (minors, nominated rep, Mental Health Review Board).

chunks.heading: 4 · Developmental Psychology
chunks.text: 4 · Developmental Psychology

chunks.heading: Tier 1 — Erikson + Piaget = ~70% of dev questions
chunks.text: Tier 1 — Erikson + Piaget = ~70% of dev questions T1 Erikson's 8 psychosocial stages + virtues 2023, 2024, 2025 (multi-Q each) : Trust vs Mistrust (0-1) → Hope Autonomy vs Shame/Doubt (1-3) → Will Initiative vs Guilt (3-6) → Purpose Industry vs Inferiority (6-12) → Competence Identity vs Role Confusion (12-18) → Fidelity Intimacy vs Isolation (18-40) → Love Generativity vs Stagnation (40-65) → Care Ego Integrity vs Despair (65+) → Wisdom Memorise the age range AND the virtue. Both have been asked. T1 Piaget's cognitive stages 2023, 2024, 2025 : Sensorimotor (0-2): object permanence (substage 4-5), circular reactions. Preoperational (2-7): egocentrism, animism, centration, lack of conservation. Concrete operational (7-11): conservation, classification, decentration; struggles with hypothetico-deductive. Formal operational (11+): abstract reasoning, hypothetical thinking, propositional logic. Plus: assimilation vs accommodation, equilibration; moral development (heteronomous → autonomous). T1 Marshmallow Test / delay of gratification 2023, 2024 : Mischel preschool paradigm, predicts later self-regulation.

chunks.heading: Tier 2
chunks.text: Tier 2 T2 Thomas & Chess temperament (NYLS): easy / difficult / slow-to-warm-up; goodness of fit. T2 Bandura observational learning — ARRM (Attention, Retention, Reproduction, Motivation). Reinforcement is NOT required (vicarious is enough). T2 Kohlberg moral development: pre-conventional / conventional / post-conventional, 6 stages.

chunks.heading: Tier 3
chunks.text: Tier 3 T3 Ainsworth attachment (Strange Situation): A/B/C/D types; Bowlby internal working models. T3 Marcia identity statuses: diffusion, foreclosure, moratorium, achievement (cross of exploration × commitment). T3 Baumrind parenting styles: authoritative > authoritarian / permissive / neglectful (warmth × control). T3 Bronfenbrenner's ecological/bioecological model — micro/meso/exo/macro/chrono + PPCT (covered in primer ; not yet a confirmed PYQ but exam-relevant). T3 Vineland Social Maturity Scale — adaptive behaviour assessment. T3 Visual cliff (depth perception in infants); Harlow attachment / contact comfort.

chunks.heading: 5 · Psychological Assessment
chunks.text: 5 · Psychological Assessment

chunks.heading: Tier 1
chunks.text: Tier 1 T1 Wechsler scales 2024, 2025 : WAIS-IV (4 indices: VCI, PRI, WMI, PSI; 3 core subtests each in VCI and PRI), WISC-V; scaled scores M=10 SD=3, composite M=100 SD=15. Letter-Number Sequencing in WAIS but not WISC-V. T1 Indian intelligence batteries 2024, 2025 : Bhatia's Battery of Performance Tests (illiterate / rural — performance only), MISIC (Malin), Binet-Kamat / ABKT, Seguin Form Board. T1 Rorschach scoring 2024, 2025 : F (Form), FC (Form-Color, with form dominant), CF (Color-Form, with color dominant), C (Pure Color), M (human movement), Cn (Color naming). Major systems: Beck, Klopfer, Piotrowski, Hertz, Rapaport, Exner Comprehensive, R-PAS. Murray = TAT, NOT a Rorschach system.

chunks.heading: Tier 2
chunks.text: Tier 2 T2 Stanford-Binet ratio IQ (MA/CA × 100) vs Wechsler deviation IQ (M=100 SD=15). T2 Personality inventories: MMPI (objective, empirically keyed, validity scales L/F/K), 16PF (Cattell, factor-analytic), NEO-PI-R (Big Five), MBTI (Jungian types). T2 Projectives: TAT (Murray, ambiguous pictures → narratives), Rorschach, Sentence Completion, Draw-a-Person, Children's Apperception Test. T2 Speed test vs power test distinction.

chunks.heading: Tier 3
chunks.text: Tier 3 T3 Raven's Progressive Matrices — culture-fair, fluid intelligence. T3 Vineland (adaptive behaviour), DSM/AAIDD intellectual disability levels (IQ 50-70 mild, 35-49 moderate, 20-34 severe, <20 profound). T3 BDI for depression severity; HAM-D / HAM-A. T3 Validity types: discriminant (low correlation with unrelated construct), convergent, predictive, criterion. T3 Allport personality theory — traits as basic units; cardinal / central / secondary.

chunks.heading: 6 · Psychotherapy / Behaviour Change
chunks.text: 6 · Psychotherapy / Behaviour Change

chunks.heading: Tier 1 — Repeated EVERY year, never miss these
chunks.text: Tier 1 — Repeated EVERY year, never miss these T1 Premack Principle 2023, 2024, 2025 : high-frequency behaviour reinforces low-frequency one. "Grandma's rule." Asked basically every NIMHANS year. T1 Reinforcement schedules 2023, 2024, 2025 (multi-Q) : continuous, FR (high rate, post-rein pause), FI (scallop pattern), VR (highest rate, gambling, most resistant to extinction), VI. Know what each pattern looks like. T1 Operant conditioning quadrants 2023, 2024 : Positive reinforcement: add desirable → ↑ behaviour Negative reinforcement: remove aversive → ↑ behaviour Positive punishment: add aversive → ↓ behaviour Negative punishment: remove desirable → ↓ behaviour. Time-out and response cost are negative punishment. T1 Three "schools" with named founders : REBT (Ellis, ABC model, musterbation, irrational beliefs), Cognitive Therapy (Beck, cognitive triad, automatic thoughts, Socratic questioning), Person-Centered (Rogers, three core conditions = UPR + congruence + empathy).

chunks.heading: Tier 2
chunks.text: Tier 2 T2 Exposure-based therapies: systematic desensitization (Wolpe; relaxation + graded hierarchy), flooding, implosion, prolonged exposure (PTSD), in-vivo vs imaginal. T2 Defense mechanism hierarchy (Vaillant): mature (sublimation, humour, suppression), neurotic (intellectualization, rationalization, repression, reaction formation), immature (acting out, projection, splitting, regression), psychotic (denial, distortion, delusional projection). Splitting = BPD hallmark (Klein, Kernberg). T2 Behavioural techniques: shaping (successive approximations), chaining, fading, prompting, response cost, covert sensitization, habit reversal training (HRT for tics).

chunks.heading: Tier 3
chunks.text: Tier 3 T3 DBT (Linehan, Zen mindfulness, 4 modules); ACT (Hayes, psychological flexibility); MBCT. T3 Logotherapy (Frankl, will to meaning); Existential therapy (Yalom's 4 ultimate concerns; May; Dasein in Heidegger/Boss/Binswanger; Umwelt/Mitwelt/Eigenwelt). T3 Therapeutic community (Maxwell Jones); milieu therapy; group therapy curative factors (Yalom's 11). T3 Reality therapy (Glasser, 5 needs: survival, love/belonging, power, freedom, fun); Transactional Analysis (Berne, Parent/Adult/Child ego states; injunctions, games). T3 Object relations therapy (Klein, Winnicott transitional objects, Kohut self-psychology with mirroring/idealizing/twinship); Narrative therapy (re-authoring); IPT (4 problem areas). T3 Affirmative therapy (LGBTQ+); ABA (autism, picture exchange). T3 Dodo Bird Verdict — common factors equivalence across therapies. T3 Defensive pessimism vs strategic optimism.

chunks.heading: 7 · Social Psychology
chunks.text: 7 · Social Psychology

chunks.heading: Tier 1
chunks.text: Tier 1 T1 Bystander effect + Kitty Genovese 2023, 2024 : Latané & Darley → diffusion of responsibility + pluralistic ignorance. T1 Just-world hypothesis 2023, 2024 : Lerner — belief that the world is fair → victim blaming. T1 Type A / Type D personality 2023, 2024 : Type A = hostility/competitiveness/time-urgency (CHD risk); Type D = negative affectivity + social inhibition (Denollet, doubles cardiac mortality).

chunks.heading: Tier 2
chunks.text: Tier 2 T2 Attribution biases: fundamental attribution error (Ross, dispositional over situational), actor-observer asymmetry, self-serving bias, false consensus effect. T2 Cooley's looking-glass self; Mead's symbolic interactionism; self-esteem (affective evaluation) vs self-concept (cognitive description). T2 Halo effect (Thorndike) and other impression-formation biases.

chunks.heading: Tier 3
chunks.text: Tier 3 T3 Conformity (Asch lines), obedience (Milgram, proximity effects), Sherif Robber's Cave (superordinate goals), social facilitation/loafing/deindividuation. T3 Cognitive dissonance (Festinger & Carlsmith $1 vs $20 study); persuasion (Cialdini's 6 principles; foot-in-the-door / door-in-the-face). T3 Glass ceiling, Matthew effect, Pygmalion / Rosenthal expectancy effects. T3 Reactance (Brehm); learned helplessness (Seligman) → depressive attributional style (internal-stable-global). T3 Anomie (Durkheim); disaffiliation; alienation; group polarization; groupthink (Janis). T3 Tajfel social identity theory; minimal group paradigm; contact hypothesis (Allport's 4 conditions).

chunks.heading: 8 · General / Cognitive Psychology
chunks.text: 8 · General / Cognitive Psychology

chunks.heading: Tier 1
chunks.text: Tier 1 T1 Memory models 2023, 2024, 2025 : Atkinson-Shiffrin (sensory → STM → LTM); Baddeley working memory (central executive, phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad, episodic buffer added 2000); episodic vs semantic vs procedural; backward digit span = working memory. T1 Defense mechanisms 2024, 2025 (multi-Q) : hierarchy (mature/neurotic/immature/psychotic), splitting (Klein/Kernberg), introjection, projection, sublimation, repression, displacement, intellectualization, regression. Linked with personality disorders.

chunks.heading: Tier 2
chunks.text: Tier 2 T2 Indian psychology: Triguna (Sattva, Rajas, Tamas); Ashtanga Yoga 8 limbs (Yama, Niyama, Asana, Pranayama, Pratyahara, Dharana, Dhyana, Samadhi — Karma is NOT a limb). T2 Beck's cognitive triad (self / world / future); cognitive distortions (catastrophising, all-or-nothing, overgeneralization, mind-reading, etc.). T2 Crystallized vs fluid intelligence (Cattell-Horn); Spearman g + s; Sternberg triarchic; Gardner multiple intelligences. T2 Maslow's hierarchy + peak experiences + plateau experiences.

chunks.heading: Tier 3
chunks.text: Tier 3 T3 Wallas creative process (Preparation → Incubation → Illumination → Verification); insight learning (Köhler chimps). T3 Heuristics: representative, availability, anchoring; algorithm vs heuristic; planning fallacy; thought-action fusion; magical thinking. T3 Carl Jung: collective unconscious, archetypes (Shadow, Anima/Animus, Self, Persona), individuation, synchronicity. Oedipus complex is Freud, not Jung. T3 Cathexis (Freud psychic energy investment); fixation; sublimation. T3 Allport's traits (cardinal/central/secondary); Cattell 16PF + global factors; Eysenck PEN. T3 Perception: Weber's law (ΔI/I = k), Fechner's law (logarithmic); signal detection theory (hit/miss/false-alarm/correct rejection); phi phenomenon; Gestalt principles (Prägnanz, proximity, similarity, continuity, closure, common fate). T3 Lashley distributed memory; Lewin's life space and force-field analysis; Sullivan's interpersonal theory (prototaxic / parataxic / syntaxic modes).

chunks.text: Week 4 — Tier 3 recognition + mock papers Run through Tier 3 lists with a recognition-only goal (no deep memorisation; just classify when you see the term). Take NIMHANS Mock 1 (PYQ-based) under timed conditions, then debrief every wrong + every guessed. Re-take NIMHANS Mock 1 a week later; gap should narrow.

chunks.heading: Watch-outs (NIMHANS specific)
chunks.text: Watch-outs (NIMHANS specific) "NOT" stems are heavy. ~20% of NIMHANS PYQs ask which is NOT a member of a category. Slow down on those. Year-tagged DSM/ICD criteria. If a stem says ICD-10 → 1 month for schizophrenia. If DSM-5 → 6 months total. Don't conflate. Fictional / clinical-vignette format. NIMHANS leans heavily on case stems (more than MET). Practice extracting the diagnostic core from a paragraph fast. Distractors that swap one well-known concept for another. Capgras vs Fregoli, FAE vs actor-observer, negative reinforcement vs negative punishment, Type A vs Type D. Keep a contrast-pairs list in the relevant cheatsheets. Length of options is no longer a tell on the actual paper. Don't lean on it for guessing — practice on real PYQs.
