Trap: Type A → heart disease ; the most cardiotoxic component is hostility . Type = discrete category (the older, body-/pattern-based tradition), unlike a continuous trait.

chunks.heading: Seligman — learned helplessness → learned optimism
chunks.text: Seligman — learned helplessness → learned optimism Question: what does uncontrollable aversive experience do to motivation? What: Seligman & Maier gave dogs inescapable shock; later, in a box where escape was easy (just jump the barrier), these dogs failed to even try , unlike dogs that had earlier been able to escape. Found: learned helplessness — having learned that responses don't matter, the organism stops responding and shows deficits resembling depression . Reformulation (with Abramson): whether helplessness follows depends on the person's explanatory / attributional style along three axes — internal–external, stable–unstable, global–specific . The depressive/pessimist explains bad events as internal, stable, global ("it's me, it always happens, it ruins everything"). Matters: a leading cognitive model of depression; flipped into learned optimism and launched positive psychology (PERMA, signature strengths). Trap: the pessimistic style for bad events = internal + stable + global. Learned helplessness / optimism / positive psychology all = Seligman .

chunks.heading: Rotter — locus of control & the I-E Scale
chunks.text: Rotter — locus of control & the I-E Scale Question: do people differ in whether they believe they control their own outcomes? What: from his social-learning theory (behaviour potential = expectancy × reinforcement value ), Julian Rotter built the Internal-External (I-E) Scale , a forced-choice self-report. Found: people array along a dimension from internal locus (outcomes flow from my own actions/ability) to external locus (outcomes flow from luck, fate, powerful others). Internals generally show better coping, achievement, health behaviour and stress resistance. Matters: one of the most-used constructs in clinical and health psychology. Trap: locus of control = Rotter , about the source of outcomes ("who controls what happens"); contrast Bandura's self-efficacy ("can I perform this task"). Both sound like "belief about control".

chunks.heading: The Minnesota Study of Twins Reared Apart (Bouchard) — heritability
chunks.text: The Minnesota Study of Twins Reared Apart (Bouchard) — heritability Question: how much of personality is genetic? What: Thomas Bouchard's Minnesota study assessed identical ( MZ ) and fraternal ( DZ ) twins, crucially including pairs reared apart , on personality inventories and other measures. Found: MZ twins reared apart were strikingly similar on the major personality traits — heritability estimates of roughly 40–60% for the big trait dimensions — and shared environment contributed surprisingly little (the non-shared environment matters more than the shared family environment). Matters: the empirical backbone for the biological/trait camp (Eysenck, McCrae & Costa) and the "Part Eleven" perspective chapter's heritability figure. Trap: lock ~40–60% heritability ; and note the counter-intuitive finding that the shared family environment explains little — siblings differ largely because of non-shared experiences.

chunks.heading: Eysenck's factor-analytic & arousal studies
chunks.text: Eysenck's factor-analytic & arousal studies Question: are there a few biologically based super-dimensions, and what causes them? What: Hans Eysenck factor-analysed large samples to extract the PEN dimensions (Psychoticism, Extraversion, Neuroticism), then tested their biological basis with arousal measures (lemon-juice salivation tests, EEG, conditioning studies). Found: introverts show higher baseline cortical arousal (a more active reticular activating system) and so avoid extra stimulation, while extraverts are chronically under-aroused and seek stimulation; neuroticism reflects an over-reactive limbic/autonomic system. Traits showed high heritability . Matters: the model of a causal, biological trait theory (says why , not just what ). Trap: Eysenck = 3 dimensions (PEN), biological, arousal-based ; introverts are over -aroused (hence stimulation-shy). Contrast Cattell's 16 and the descriptive Big Five. Reward/punishment sensitivity in a stem = Gray (BIS/BAS) , not Eysenck.

chunks.heading: Cattell's lexical/factor work — the 16PF
chunks.text: Cattell's lexical/factor work — the 16PF Question: how many basic source traits underlie personality? What: Raymond Cattell started from the lexical pool, reduced thousands of trait words to clusters, and applied factor analysis to three data sources — L-data (life records), Q-data (questionnaires) and T-data (objective tests). Found: he distilled personality to 16 source traits (the deep causal factors) beneath the visible surface traits , operationalised as the 16PF questionnaire. He also separated fluid from crystallised intelligence. Matters: the prototypical factor-analytic trait programme and a direct ancestor of the Big Five (re-analyses of his variables kept yielding five higher-order factors). Trap: Cattell = 16 source traits, 16PF, factor analysis ; surface trait (visible cluster) vs source trait (underlying cause).

chunks.heading: McCrae & Costa — cross-cultural stability of the Five-Factor Model
chunks.text: McCrae & Costa — cross-cultural stability of the Five-Factor Model Question: are the Big Five universal and stable? What: Paul Costa & Robert McCrae administered the NEO-PI-R across many languages and cultures and re-tested adults longitudinally. Found: the same five factors ( OCEAN ) replicated broadly across cultures, and individual trait levels are largely stable after about age 30 (with small normative shifts — neuroticism and openness tend to decline, agreeableness and conscientiousness to rise, with age, the "maturity principle"). Matters: evidence that the FFM taps something cross-culturally real and trait-like, feeding the Five-Factor Theory (heritable basic tendencies → culturally shaped characteristic adaptations ). Trap: FFM = 5 (OCEAN), NEO-PI-R, descriptive, stable after ~30, cross-cultural . The Big Five describes what traits exist; Eysenck's PEN explains why .

chunks.heading: Murray's TAT & McClelland's need for achievement
chunks.text: Murray's TAT & McClelland's need for achievement Question: can hidden motives ("needs") be read from imaginative fantasy? What: Henry Murray (with Christiana Morgan ) built the Thematic Apperception Test (TAT) — ambiguous picture cards the person tells stories about — as a window onto his system of needs (achievement, affiliation, power, etc.) meeting environmental press (his theory: personology ). David McClelland then scored TAT stories for need for achievement (nAch) and linked high nAch to entrepreneurial striving and even economic growth, plus need for power and affiliation. Found: projective fantasy reliably elicits implicit motives that self-report misses. Matters: the projective-test lineage and the motive-measurement tradition. Trap: TAT = Murray (& Morgan) ; need for achievement run hard by McClelland . TAT is projective (apperception of pictures); don't confuse with the Rorschach (inkblots).

chunks.heading: Allport & Odbert (1936) — the lexical study
chunks.text: Allport & Odbert (1936) — the lexical study Question: how many trait words does the language hold? What: Gordon Allport & Henry Odbert combed an unabridged English dictionary and extracted about 18,000 person-describing words, sorting them into stable traits, temporary states, evaluative terms, etc. Found: the sheer size of the lexicon, taken as support for the lexical hypothesis — if an individual difference matters to human life, language will have coined a word for it. Matters: the starting point for the whole trait/lexical tradition that Cattell and then the Big Five mined. Trap: the ~18,000 figure and the lexical hypothesis = Allport & Odbert ; but note Allport himself was idiographic and did not use factor analysis (Cattell did the reduction).

chunks.heading: Harlow's monkeys — contact comfort & the roots of attachment
chunks.text: Harlow's monkeys — contact comfort & the roots of attachment Question: do infants bond for food or for comfort? What: Harry Harlow raised infant rhesus monkeys with two surrogate "mothers": a bare wire mother that dispensed milk and a soft cloth mother that gave none. Found: the monkeys clung to the cloth mother for comfort and ran to her when frightened, going to the wire mother only to feed, decisively contradicting the drive-reduction/"cupboard-love" view that attachment is learned through feeding. Total isolation produced lasting social and emotional damage. Matters: "contact comfort" showed love/attachment is a primary need, not a by-product of feeding, undercutting both behaviourist and orthodox Freudian (oral-stage) accounts and supporting object-relations/attachment theory. Trap: the monkeys preferred the cloth (comfort) mother over the wire (feeding) mother — comfort, not food, drives bonding. (Maslow began his career studying monkeys with Harlow.)

chunks.heading: Bowlby & Ainsworth — attachment and the Strange Situation
chunks.text: Bowlby & Ainsworth — attachment and the Strange Situation Question: what is the bond between infant and caregiver, and how is it measured? What: John Bowlby proposed attachment as an innate, evolved system: the infant seeks a secure base , builds an internal working model ("are others reliable? am I worthy?"), and is harmed by maternal deprivation . Mary Ainsworth operationalised it with the Strange Situation , a structured lab sequence of separations and reunions. Found: infants sort into secure (uses mother as a base, distressed at separation, comforted at reunion), insecure-avoidant (indifferent, avoids reunion), and insecure-resistant/ambivalent (clingy yet angry, hard to soothe); Main & Solomon later added disorganised . Matters: the bridge from object relations to empirical developmental psychology; attachment styles predict later relationships (the adult four-category model). Trap: Bowlby = the theory (secure base, internal working model, maternal deprivation); Ainsworth = the Strange Situation and the three styles; Main = disorganised. Don't credit the Strange Situation to Bowlby. Recap — studies. Freud's cases (Anna O. = Breuer's, talking cure; Little Hans = Oedipus/phobia; Dora = transference; Rat Man = obsessional) · Bandura Bobo (observational learning; learning ≠ performance) + snake-phobia (mastery is the strongest efficacy source) · Rogers Q-sort (real–ideal cong

chunks.heading: Extended concept bank (the rest of the book, chapter by chapter)
chunks.text: Extended concept bank (the rest of the book, chapter by chapter) The chapters above are the spine. This bank picks up the remaining named terms theorist by theorist — the full defence-mechanism list, every Jungian archetype, Adler's safeguarding tendencies, Horney's ten neurotic needs, Erikson's virtues, Maslow's B-values, Kelly's eleven corollaries, and so on — so each has a home you can slot it into. Every entry is the kind of one-line fact an MCQ distractor is built from.

chunks.heading: Freud — the full defence-mechanism list (catalogued by Anna Freud)
chunks.text: Freud — the full defence-mechanism list (catalogued by Anna Freud) Defence One line Repression The master defence: unconscious blocking of threatening material. (Conscious version = suppression , the only mature/conscious one.) Denial Refuse to accept an external reality. Projection Attribute your own unacceptable impulse to someone else. Displacement Redirect an impulse onto a safer substitute target . Sublimation Channel the impulse into a socially valued activity (the healthiest classical defence). Reaction formation Act as the opposite of the true impulse. Rationalisation Invent a logical-sounding excuse for the real reason. Regression Retreat to an earlier developmental stage under stress. Intellectualisation Strip the emotion out, deal only with abstract facts. Identification Take on the qualities of an admired/feared other (incl. identification with the aggressor). Introjection Absorb another's values/qualities wholesale into the self. Undoing A ritual act to magically "cancel" a bad thought/deed. Isolation of affect Keep the memory, sever the feeling. Splitting See self/others as all-good or all-bad (borderline; Klein/Kernberg). Projective identification Project a part of the self into another and induce them to act it out (Klein). Compensation Make up for a weakness by excelling elsewhere (more Adlerian). Fantasy / daydreaming Gratify frustrated wishes imaginatively (i

chunks.heading: Jung — the full archetype list
chunks.text: Jung — the full archetype list Archetype What it is Persona The public mask, the role we present to society. Shadow The dark, animal, denied side; the source of creativity as well as vice. Anima The feminine side within a man. Animus The masculine side within a woman. Self The unifying, central archetype of wholeness; goal of individuation, symbolised by the mandala . Great Mother Archetype of nurturance and fertility (and devouring). Wise Old Man Archetype of meaning, wisdom, the spirit/sage. Hero The figure who conquers evil; champion of the ego against the unconscious. Trickster / others Plus rebirth, child, maiden, etc. — Jung held archetypes are innumerable. Other Jung terms to own: complexes (emotionally charged clusters in the personal unconscious, e.g. a mother complex), the two attitudes (introversion / extraversion), the four functions (thinking, feeling = rational; sensing, intuiting = irrational), individuation (lifelong integration into the self), and the transcendent function (uniting opposites).

chunks.heading: Adler — birth order & safeguarding tendencies
chunks.text: Adler — birth order & safeguarding tendencies Position Typical Adlerian portrait First-born "Dethroned" by the next child; often conservative, responsible, power-oriented, may feel insecure. Second / middle Competitive, ambitious (runs to catch the pacemaker ahead); often the best-adjusted. Youngest Pampered baby of the family; can be highly motivated to outdo all, or dependent and avoidant. Only child Never dethroned; precocious, may be pampered, rivalrous with adults rather than peers. Safeguarding tendencies (Adler's neurotic protections of self-esteem, a forerunner of defence mechanisms): excuses ("yes, but…" / "if only…"), aggression (depreciation, accusation, self-accusation), and distancing / withdrawal (moving backward, standing still, hesitating, constructing obstacles). Plus the core terms: inferiority feelings → compensation → (if it fails) inferiority complex or over-compensating superiority complex ; style of life ; creative power of the self ; fictional finalism ; social interest (Gemeinschaftsgefühl) ; the three life tasks (work, friendship/society, love).

chunks.heading: Horney — the ten neurotic needs & three trends
chunks.text: Horney — the ten neurotic needs & three trends The three trends (toward / against / away) are distilled from ten neurotic needs : (1) affection & approval, (2) a dominant partner to run one's life, (3) narrow limits to life (undemanding), (4) power, (5) exploitation of others, (6) prestige/social recognition, (7) personal admiration, (8) personal achievement/ambition, (9) self-sufficiency & independence, (10) perfection & unassailability. Trend Needs it groups Type Moving toward people (compliance) Affection, a dominant partner, narrow limits (1–3) Self-effacing / compliant Moving against people (aggression) Power, exploitation, prestige, admiration, achievement (4–8) Expansive / aggressive Moving away from people (detachment) Self-sufficiency, perfection (9–10) Resigned / detached Plus: basic anxiety (isolated and helpless in a hostile world) vs basic hostility ; the idealised (self-)image and the "tyranny of the should" ; real self vs idealised self; rejection of penis envy in favour of cultural power-envy and men's "womb envy" .

chunks.heading: Erikson — the eight stages with virtues (and Marcia's statuses)
chunks.text: Erikson — the eight stages with virtues (and Marcia's statuses) Stage (age) Crisis Basic virtue / strength Maladaptation Infancy (0–1) Trust vs mistrust Hope Withdrawal Early childhood (1–3) Autonomy vs shame/doubt Will Compulsion Play age (3–5) Initiative vs guilt Purpose Inhibition School age (6–11) Industry vs inferiority Competence Inertia Adolescence (12–18) Identity vs role confusion Fidelity Repudiation Young adulthood Intimacy vs isolation Love Exclusivity Middle adulthood Generativity vs stagnation Care Rejectivity Old age Ego integrity vs despair Wisdom Disdain Marcia's four identity statuses (crisis/exploration × commitment): diffusion (neither), foreclosure (commitment, no exploration), moratorium (exploring, no commitment yet), achievement (commitment after exploration). Erikson coined "identity crisis" ; key term epigenetic principle .

chunks.heading: Allport — the trait taxonomy & the proprium
chunks.text: Allport — the trait taxonomy & the proprium Level / term What it is Cardinal trait So dominant it pervades a whole life (rare; a "Scrooge"). Central traits The 5–10 core descriptors of a person (the reference-letter words). Secondary dispositions Situation-specific preferences, shown only sometimes. Common vs individual traits Shared/comparable across people vs unique to the person (he favoured the latter, personal dispositions ). Proprium Allport's word for the self/ego, developing through ~7 aspects (bodily self → self-identity → self-esteem → self-extension → self-image → rational coping → propriate striving ). Functional autonomy A motive becomes independent of its origin (perseverative vs propriate functional autonomy). Idiographic / morphogenic Study of the unique individual (Allport's preferred approach; he rejected factor analysis).

chunks.heading: Maslow — the full hierarchy, B-values & the self-actualiser
chunks.text: Maslow — the full hierarchy, B-values & the self-actualiser Hierarchy (bottom → top): physiological → safety → belongingness/love → esteem → self-actualisation ; later additions split the upper region into cognitive (know/understand) and aesthetic needs below self-actualisation, and self-transcendence above it. Lower four = deficiency (D-)needs ; the top = being (B-)needs / growth needs . Characteristics of self-actualisers: accurate perception of reality; acceptance of self/others/nature; spontaneity & naturalness; problem-centred (not self-centred); need for privacy & autonomy; freshness of appreciation; peak experiences ; Gemeinschaftsgefühl (social interest); deep but few interpersonal relationships; democratic character; ethical discrimination of means/ends; philosophical humour; creativeness; resistance to enculturation. B-values (the "meta-needs" pursued at the top): truth, goodness, beauty, unity/wholeness, aliveness, uniqueness, perfection, justice, order, simplicity, richness, effortlessness, playfulness, self-sufficiency, meaningfulness. The Jonah complex = fear of one's own greatness; metapathology = the malaise from frustrated B-values; measured by the POI (Shostrom) .

chunks.heading: Rogers — the fully functioning person
chunks.text: Rogers — the fully functioning person Core machinery: the actualising tendency (and the organism's organismic valuing process ); the self / self-concept ; real self vs ideal self → congruence vs incongruence ; conditions of worth imposed by conditional positive regard; the cure = unconditional positive regard (UPR) ; the therapist's three core conditions = empathy, congruence/genuineness, UPR. The fully functioning person (Rogers' ideal of growth) shows: (1) openness to experience (no defensiveness), (2) existential living (fully in the present moment), (3) organismic trusting (trusting one's own judgement), (4) experiential freedom (sense of free choice and responsibility), and (5) creativity .

chunks.heading: Kelly — the fundamental postulate & eleven corollaries
chunks.text: Kelly — the fundamental postulate & eleven corollaries Fundamental postulate: "a person's processes are psychologically channelised by the ways in which they anticipate events." The eleven corollaries : Corollary One line Construction We anticipate events by construing their replications (we read recurring themes). Individuality People differ in how they construe the same event. Organisation Each person organises constructs into a hierarchy (some superordinate to others). Dichotomy Constructs are bipolar (kind–cruel). Choice We pick the pole of a construct that promises the most extension/definition of our system. Range Each construct applies only to a limited range of events (its range of convenience). Experience We revise constructs as we successively construe events. Modulation How much a system can change is limited by the permeability of its constructs. Fragmentation We can hold sub-systems that are mutually inconsistent. Commonality People who construe experience similarly are psychologically similar. Sociality To relate to someone you must construe their construction processes (role-taking). Plus Kelly's cognitive re-definitions of emotion: anxiety (events lie outside one's constructs), threat (awareness of imminent comprehensive change), fear (imminent incidental change), guilt (acting against one's core role construct), hostility (forcing reality to validate a failed c

chunks.heading: Skinner & Bandura — the learning machinery
chunks.text: Skinner & Bandura — the learning machinery Term Whose / what Operant vs respondent Skinner: operant (emitted, shaped by consequences) vs respondent/classical (elicited reflex). Positive/negative reinforcement Add pleasant / remove aversive — both increase behaviour. Positive/negative punishment Add aversive / remove pleasant — both decrease behaviour (Skinner thought punishment unreliable). Schedules Fixed/variable × ratio/interval; variable-ratio = highest, most extinction-resistant responding (the slot machine). Shaping Reinforcing successive approximations. Extinction / superstition Stop reinforcing → behaviour fades; accidental reinforcement → "superstitious" pigeon behaviour. Functional analysis (A-B-C) Antecedent → Behaviour → Consequence (Skinner's "assessment"). Observational learning Bandura: attention → retention → production → motivation; vicarious reinforcement . Reciprocal determinism Behaviour ↔ personal/cognitive factors ↔ environment, a three-way loop. Self-efficacy (4 sources) Mastery (strongest) → vicarious → verbal persuasion → physiological/emotional state. Self-regulation / self-system Internal standards + self-judgement; later moral disengagement , collective efficacy .

chunks.heading: Trait, facet & temperament terms
chunks.text: Trait, facet & temperament terms Term Whose / what Surface vs source trait Cattell: visible cluster vs underlying causal factor (16 source traits → 16PF). Erg / sentiment / attitude Cattell's dynamic traits: ergs (innate drives), sentiments (learned), attitudes. Fluid vs crystallised intelligence Cattell: raw reasoning vs accumulated knowledge. PEN Eysenck: Psychoticism, Extraversion, Neuroticism (EPI → EPQ); biological, arousal-based. Big Five / OCEAN Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism (Goldberg coined "Big Five"; NEO-PI-R). HEXACO Ashton & Lee: 6 factors, adds Honesty-Humility (low H = the dark triad). BIS / BAS Gray's Reinforcement Sensitivity: BIS (punishment → anxiety), BAS (reward → impulsivity). Locus of control / I-E Scale Rotter (internal vs external; from expectancy × reinforcement value). Sensation seeking / SSS Zuckerman: thrill-and-adventure, experience, disinhibition, boredom susceptibility. Learned helplessness / optimism Seligman; explanatory style = internal–external × stable–unstable × global–specific. Flow Csikszentmihalyi: challenge matches skill → absorbed engagement. EAS temperament Buss & Plomin: Emotionality, Activity, Sociability. Inhibited / uninhibited Kagan's infant temperament (precursor of introversion). Easy / difficult / slow-to-warm-up Thomas & Chess's temperament types; goodness of fit . Recap — bank. Defences

chunks.heading: Fast glossary (one line each, A–Z)
chunks.text: Fast glossary (one line each, A–Z) Last-mile recall: every nameable personality term/theorist on this page reduced to a single line and its author, alphabetical so you can self-test by covering the right column. If a name fires but the definition doesn't, that is the gap to drill. Term One-line definition (and who) Actualising tendency Innate drive of every organism to maintain and enhance itself (Rogers). Anal stage 1–3 yrs, toilet training; fixation → retentive (orderly/stingy) or expulsive (messy) (Freud). Anima / animus The inner feminine in a man / masculine in a woman (Jung). Archetype Universal inherited image in the collective unconscious (Jung). Attachment / Strange Situation Innate secure-base bond (Bowlby); measured by the Strange Situation (Ainsworth). Basic anxiety Feeling isolated and helpless in a hostile world (Horney). Birth order First-born dethroned, middle competitive, youngest pampered, only precocious (Adler). Bobo doll Children imitate observed aggression; learning ≠ performance (Bandura). Cardinal / central / secondary Allport's three trait levels (dominant / core / situational). Castration anxiety / penis envy Phallic-stage fears of boy / girl in the Oedipus/Electra complex (Freud). Collective unconscious Inherited layer shared by all humanity, holds archetypes (Jung, NOT Freud). Compensation Overcoming felt inferiority by developing strengths (Adler).

chunks.heading: Self-test (active recall, by chapter)
chunks.text: Self-test (active recall, by chapter) Recall beats re-reading. Cover the answers, ask each question aloud, then check. If you miss one, jump back to its chapter. The answer follows in green .

chunks.heading: Freud
chunks.text: Freud Name the three structures and their governing principles. Id (pleasure principle), ego (reality principle), superego (morality, formed in the phallic stage). Which defence is the only conscious /mature one, and how does it differ from its twin? Suppression (deliberate set-aside, mature) vs repression (unconscious, neurotic). Whose patient was Anna O., and what did she illustrate? Breuer's; the "talking cure"/catharsis (Freud reported it with him). Order the psychosexual stages. Oral → anal → phallic → latency → genital.

chunks.heading: Jung, Adler, Horney
chunks.text: Jung, Adler, Horney Collective unconscious belongs to whom, and what does it contain? Jung; archetypes (persona, shadow, anima/animus, self). Match the three "wills": pleasure, power, meaning. Freud (pleasure), Adler (power), Frankl (meaning). What is Adler's mark of mental health, and his term for actively shaping one's own personality? Social interest (Gemeinschaftsgefühl); the creative power of the self. Horney's three neurotic trends? Moving toward / against / away from people. Inferiority complex vs basic anxiety, whose is each? Inferiority complex = Adler; basic anxiety = Horney.

chunks.heading: Erikson
chunks.text: Erikson How do Erikson's stages differ from Freud's in number and type? Eight (lifelong) and psychosocial, vs Freud's five (to puberty) and psychosexual. Give the adolescent crisis and its virtue. Identity vs role confusion → fidelity. Marcia's four identity statuses, and the tricky pair? Diffusion, foreclosure, moratorium, achievement; foreclosure (commit, no exploration) vs moratorium (explore, no commitment yet).

chunks.heading: Allport & the trait approach
chunks.text: Allport & the trait approach Allport's three trait levels, and did he use factor analysis? Cardinal / central / secondary; no, he was idiographic. Match the trait numbers: Cattell, Eysenck, FFM, HEXACO. 16 (16PF), 3 (PEN), 5 (OCEAN), 6 (adds Honesty-Humility). Are introverts over- or under-aroused in Eysenck's theory? Over-aroused (high baseline cortical arousal), so they avoid extra stimulation. What does functional autonomy mean? A motive becomes independent of its childhood origin (Allport).

chunks.heading: Maslow & Rogers
chunks.text: Maslow & Rogers D-needs vs B-needs? Deficiency needs (lower four, felt as lack) vs being/growth needs (self-actualisation, felt as pull). Rogers' three therapeutic core conditions? Empathy, congruence/genuineness, unconditional positive regard. What does the Q-sort measure and how? Self-ideal congruence, via the correlation between real-self and ideal-self card sorts (Rogers; Stephenson's tool). Which test operationalised self-actualisation? The Personal Orientation Inventory, POI (Shostrom).

chunks.heading: Kelly, Skinner, Bandura
chunks.text: Kelly, Skinner, Bandura Kelly's image of the person and his philosophy? Man-the-scientist; constructive alternativism. Which reinforcement schedule is most extinction-resistant? Variable-ratio (the slot machine). In the Bobo doll studies, what did the model's punishment affect? Performance, not learning (children still learned the acts). The four sources of self-efficacy in order of strength? Mastery (strongest) → vicarious → verbal persuasion → physiological/emotional state. Self-efficacy vs locus of control? Self-efficacy = Bandura ("can I do this task?"); locus of control = Rotter ("who controls outcomes?").

chunks.heading: Facets & perspective
chunks.text: Facets & perspective Match the facet owners: locus of control, sensation seeking, learned helplessness, flow. Rotter, Zuckerman, Seligman, Csikszentmihalyi. Seligman's pessimistic explanatory style for bad events? Internal, stable, global. What settles the person–situation debate, and roughly how heritable are traits? Interactionism; ~40–60% (Bouchard's Minnesota twins).

chunks.heading: Supplements (object relations, existential, type, Indian)
chunks.text: Supplements (object relations, existential, type, Indian) Match: good-enough mother, separation-individuation, mirroring/self, borderline organisation/TFP, positions. Winnicott, Mahler, Kohut, Kernberg, Klein. Bowlby vs Ainsworth, who gave the theory and who the Strange Situation? Bowlby = theory (secure base, internal working model); Ainsworth = Strange Situation + the three styles (Main added disorganised). What did Harlow's monkeys prefer, and what does it prove? The cloth (comfort) over the wire (feeding) mother; attachment is about contact comfort, not food. Frankl, May, Yalom, own each by a phrase. Logotherapy/will to meaning; the daimonic/meaning of anxiety; four ultimate concerns (death, freedom, isolation, meaninglessness). Triguna's three gunas and the test that measures them? Sattva (balance), Rajas (activity), Tamas (inertia); the Vedic Personality Inventory (VPI). Sheldon vs Kretschmer? Sheldon = somatotypes (endo/meso/ecto); Kretschmer = body build linked to psychosis type. Recap — self-test. If you can answer these cold, you own the spine, the named layer and the rival-theory discriminations. Re-test the misses, then run "All the MCQ traps" and the A–Z glossary once more the night before. That sequence (recall → trap discrimination → glossary sweep) is the highest-yield last-mile routine for this domain. Companion pages: the compact version is in the general-psyc

chunks.heading: Phenomena — illusions, biases, attention/memory glitches & neuropsych signs
chunks.text: Phenomena — illusions, biases, attention/memory glitches & neuropsych signs Second of the four category sweeps. The bucket is "named phenomena": things the mind/brain does that get a name. Perceptual illusions, attention failures, memory phenomena, group phenomena, cognitive biases and neuropsych signs. The stem usually describes the experience and wants the name (or who described it). Built 2026-05-24. Effects Phenomena Theories Theorists Social Psych Cognitive Lookalikes Effect vs phenomenon — same idea, different label. If the term ends in "effect" it's on the Effects page; if it's described as a phenomenon, bias, illusion or sign, it's here. NIMHANS picks whichever label fits the stem, so scan both. Jump to: 1. Perceptual illusions 2. Gestalt grouping 3. Attention & perception 4. Memory phenomena 5. Group / social 6. Cognitive biases 7. Neuropsych & clinical signs

chunks.heading: 1. Perceptual illusions
chunks.text: 1. Perceptual illusions Illusion Who What you see Müller-Lyer Franz Müller-Lyer Two equal lines look unequal depending on arrow-head direction (inward vs outward fins). Ponzo Mario Ponzo Two equal lines on converging "railway" lines look unequal (depth misread). Ebbinghaus (Titchener) circles Ebbinghaus A circle ringed by big circles looks smaller than the same circle ringed by small ones. Zöllner Zöllner Parallel lines look slanted because of crossing hatch marks. Kanizsa triangle Gaetano Kanizsa You "see" a white triangle edge that isn't drawn (illusory/subjective contours). Necker cube Louis Necker A wire cube flips between two 3-D orientations (bistable perception). Rubin's vase Edgar Rubin Faces-or-vase: figure–ground reversal. Ames room Adelbert Ames A distorted room makes equal-size people look giant vs tiny. Moon illusion — The moon looks larger near the horizon than overhead. Hermann grid — Ghostly grey blobs appear at the white intersections of a black grid. Café wall Gregory & Heard Straight mortar lines look wedge-shaped between offset tiles. Phi phenomenon Max Wertheimer Lights flashing in sequence look like one moving light (the founding Gestalt demo of apparent motion). Autokinetic phenomenon used by Sherif A still point of light in the dark seems to drift; Sherif used it to study norm formation. Two "size of equal lines" illusions: Müller-Lyer = arrow fins; Ponz

chunks.heading: 2. Gestalt grouping principles
chunks.text: 2. Gestalt grouping principles Wertheimer, Koffka & Köhler. "The whole is other than the sum of its parts." Master law = Prägnanz (we see the simplest, most stable form). Principle What groups together Proximity Things close together are seen as a group. Similarity Things that look alike are grouped. Continuity (good continuation) We follow smooth, continuous lines over abrupt changes. Closure We fill gaps to see a complete figure. Figure–ground We split a scene into an object and its background. Common fate Things moving together are grouped. Prägnanz (good form) The overarching law: perceive the simplest, most regular organisation.

chunks.heading: 3. Attention & perception phenomena
chunks.text: 3. Attention & perception phenomena Phenomenon Who What it is Inattentional blindness Mack & Rock; Simons & Chabris (gorilla) You miss an obvious unexpected object while attending elsewhere. Change blindness Simons & Levin You fail to notice a large change across a visual interruption. Attentional blink Raymond, Shapiro & Arnell Brief inability to detect a 2nd target ~200–500 ms after the 1st. Cocktail-party phenomenon Colin Cherry Tracking one voice in noise, yet still catching your own name. Weber's law / JND Ernst Weber The just-noticeable difference is a constant proportion of the stimulus. Fechner's law Gustav Fechner Sensation grows with the log of stimulus intensity (founded psychophysics). Sensory adaptation — Constant stimulation → declining response (you stop feeling your clothes). Pareidolia — Seeing meaningful patterns (faces) in random stimuli (clouds, toast). Synaesthesia — One sense automatically triggers another (hearing colours, tasting words). Blindsight Weiskrantz Responding to visual stimuli without conscious sight (V1 damage). Perceptual constancy — Objects seen as stable in size/shape/colour despite changing retinal image.

chunks.heading: 4. Memory phenomena
chunks.text: 4. Memory phenomena Phenomenon Who What it is Tip-of-the-tongue (TOT) Brown & McNeill Knowing a word is there but not retrieving it (you often get its first letter/length). Flashbulb memory Brown & Kulik Vivid, confident memory of where you were during a shocking event (often inaccurate). Déjà vu / jamais vu — Novel scene feels familiar / familiar scene feels alien. Reminiscence bump — Older adults recall disproportionately many memories from ages ~10–30. Childhood (infantile) amnesia — Few/no episodic memories before ~age 3–4. Proactive interference — Old learning blocks new (old password keeps coming up). Retroactive interference — New learning blocks old (new password erases the old one). Forgetting curve Hermann Ebbinghaus Retention drops sharply then levels off; relearning is faster (savings). Misattribution / source monitoring error Schacter Right memory, wrong source (cryptomnesia: feeling you invented something you read).

chunks.heading: 5. Group & social phenomena
chunks.text: 5. Group & social phenomena Phenomenon Who What it is Social facilitation Triplett; Zajonc Presence of others boosts easy tasks, harms hard ones. Social loafing Latané; Ringelmann roots Individuals slack in groups when effort isn't identifiable. Diffusion of responsibility Darley & Latané The mechanism behind the bystander effect: "someone else will." Group polarisation Moscovici; Stoner (risky shift) Group discussion pushes members to a more extreme version of their leaning. Groupthink Irving Janis Cohesive group suppresses dissent for consensus → bad decisions. Deindividuation Festinger; Zimbardo Loss of self-awareness/restraint in a crowd or anonymity. Conformity Solomon Asch Going along with a group's wrong judgement (line task). Obedience Stanley Milgram Following authority's orders against your own conscience (shock study). Bystander apathy Latané & Darley The umbrella phenomenon: less help as the crowd grows. Risky shift Stoner Groups make riskier decisions than individuals (early name for polarisation).

chunks.heading: 6. Cognitive biases & heuristics
chunks.text: 6. Cognitive biases & heuristics Heuristics = mental shortcuts (Tversky & Kahneman). Biases = the systematic errors they cause. Bias / heuristic Who What it is Availability heuristic Tversky & Kahneman Judge frequency by how easily examples come to mind. Representativeness heuristic Tversky & Kahneman Judge by resemblance to a prototype (ignores base rates → conjunction fallacy). Anchoring & adjustment Tversky & Kahneman Cling to an initial value when estimating. Confirmation bias Wason Seeking/weighting evidence that fits your belief. Hindsight bias Fischhoff "I knew it all along" after the outcome is known. Fundamental attribution error coined by Lee Ross Over-attributing others' behaviour to character, under-weighting situation. Self-serving bias — Credit success to self, blame failure on circumstance. Sunk-cost fallacy — Continuing because of past investment that can't be recovered. Gambler's fallacy — Believing past random outcomes change future odds. Loss aversion / framing Kahneman & Tversky (prospect theory) Losses hurt more than equivalent gains feel good. Tells: "judged by ease of recall" = availability; "judged by stereotype/prototype" = representativeness; "blamed the person not the situation" = FAE (Ross). Don't swap the two heuristics.

chunks.heading: 7. Neuropsych & clinical phenomena
chunks.text: 7. Neuropsych & clinical phenomena Phenomenon / sign Who What it is Phantom limb Mitchell; Ramachandran Sensation/pain in an amputated limb (cortical remapping). Capgras delusion Joseph Capgras Belief that a loved one has been replaced by an identical impostor. Fregoli delusion — Belief that different people are one person in disguise. Cotard delusion Jules Cotard Belief that one is dead, doesn't exist, or is rotting (nihilistic delusion). Folie à deux Lasègue & Falret A shared delusion transmitted between two close people. Anosognosia Babinski Unawareness/denial of one's own deficit (e.g. paralysis after stroke). Confabulation — Filling memory gaps with fabricated events without intent to lie (Korsakoff). Hemispatial neglect — Ignoring one side of space after (usually right) parietal damage. Sundowning — Worsening confusion/agitation in the late afternoon/evening (dementia). Pseudobulbar affect — Uncontrollable laughing/crying out of proportion to feeling. La belle indifférence — Surprising lack of concern about a disabling symptom (conversion disorder). Delusional misidentification trio: Capgras = loved one is an impostor; Fregoli = strangers are one disguised person; Cotard = "I am dead." These three are a classic NIMHANS distractor set. That's the phenomena bucket. Cover the right column and name it from the description; that's how it's asked. Other sweeps: Effects , Theori

chunks.heading: Personality & Projective Tests, Deep Reference
chunks.text: Personality & Projective Tests, Deep Reference Built 2026-05-19 after you flagged that the test entries on the assessment cheatsheet were too thin. This page does one job: for every personality + projective + Beck/Bell inventory in the MET/NIMHANS pool, give you item count, scales/subscales, scoring, author + year, and use case in one screen. Memorize the numbers in bold, the rest is texture. Cross-link with the read-first primer for reliability/validity and the revision pack for the one-page table. How MCQ-writers attack this section. Almost every question is one of four moves: (1) swap the item count between two tests, (2) swap the author or year, (3) ask which scale belongs to which test, (4) ask which test is projective vs objective. So your job here is to lock the quadruple (test → items → scales → author/year) cold. Get those four right and you bank the marks.

chunks.heading: 1. MMPI Family (Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory)
chunks.text: 1. MMPI Family (Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory)

chunks.heading: MMPI (original, 1943)
chunks.text: MMPI (original, 1943) Authors: Starke R. Hathaway (psychologist) & J. Charnley McKinley (psychiatrist), University of Minnesota. Year: 1943. Items: 566 true/false statements (often reported as 550 unique + 16 repeats; the canonical number you quote is 566 ). Method of construction: empirical criterion-keyed. Items were retained only if they discriminated a diagnostic group from normals — not based on face validity. This was the breakthrough method versus older content-based inventories. Original norming sample: "Minnesota normals" (724 visitors to the Univ. of Minnesota Hospitals) — later criticised as a narrow, mostly white rural Midwest base, which drove the MMPI-2 restandardisation.

chunks.heading: MMPI-2 (the version exam-writers mean by default)
chunks.text: MMPI-2 (the version exam-writers mean by default) Year: 1989 (restandardisation), revised manual 2001. Items: 567 true/false items. Memorize this exact number. Age range: 18+ years. Reading level: 6th grade. Administration time: 60–90 minutes. Scoring: scores converted to T-scores (mean 50, SD 10). Clinically significant elevation: T ≥ 65 on MMPI-2 (was T ≥ 70 on original MMPI). 10 clinical scales (memorize the order, scale 5 and 0 are the supplementary ones): # Code Name What it picks up 1 Hs Hypochondriasis Bodily preoccupation, somatic complaints 2 D Depression Sadness, hopelessness, low morale 3 Hy Hysteria Conversion features, somatic + denial 4 Pd Psychopathic Deviate Authority conflict, antisocial features 5 Mf Masculinity-Femininity Gender-role interest pattern 6 Pa Paranoia Suspiciousness, ideas of reference 7 Pt Psychasthenia Anxiety, obsessional rumination, doubt 8 Sc Schizophrenia Bizarre thought, alienation 9 Ma Hypomania Elevated mood, overactivity, grandiosity 0 Si Social Introversion Social withdrawal vs sociability Validity scales (the L/F/K triad is the high-yield bit): ? (Cannot Say): number of unanswered items. > 30 omissions invalidates profile. L (Lie): 15 items detecting naive "faking good" — claiming impossibly virtuous behaviour ("I have never told a lie"). High L = unsophisticated impression management. F (Infrequency): 60 items rarely endorsed by norm

chunks.heading: MMPI-2-RF (Restructured Form, 2008)
chunks.text: MMPI-2-RF (Restructured Form, 2008) Items: 338. Scales: 9 Restructured Clinical (RC) scales + a demoralization scale (RCd) + higher-order scales. The "common variance" of demoralization is pulled out so each RC scale measures something more specific. Use: shorter, psychometrically tighter version. Increasingly the research default but MET still tests the classic MMPI-2 numbers.

chunks.heading: MMPI-3 (2020)
chunks.text: MMPI-3 (2020) Items: 335. New norms. Scales: 52 total — H-O scales, RC scales, Specific Problem (SP) scales, PSY-5 scales.

chunks.heading: MMPI-A (Adolescent)
chunks.text: MMPI-A (Adolescent) Items: 478. Ages 14–18. Released 1992. There is also an MMPI-A-RF (2016, 241 items).

chunks.heading: 2. 16PF (Sixteen Personality Factor Questionnaire)
chunks.text: 2. 16PF (Sixteen Personality Factor Questionnaire) Author: Raymond B. Cattell (with Tatsuoka & Eber on later editions). Year: first edition 1949. Current edition is the 16PF Fifth Edition (1993) . Items: 185 items (5th edition). Each item is 3-choice: agree / ? / disagree, except the reasoning subtest which is forced-choice. Age range: 16+ years. Administration time: 35–50 minutes. Method of construction: factor analysis of the lexicon. Cattell started with Allport & Odbert's list of ~4500 trait words, reduced to ~160 surface traits, then factor-analysed to 16 source traits . Scoring: raw scores → Sten scores (Standard Ten: mean 5.5, SD 2, range 1–10). Sten 1–3 = low pole, 4–7 = average, 8–10 = high pole. The 16 primary factors (Cattell letter codes; you do not have to memorize every letter but the names of the high/low poles get tested): Code Low pole ←→ High pole A Reserved ↔ Warm B Concrete reasoning ↔ Abstract reasoning C Reactive (emotional) ↔ Emotionally stable E Deferential ↔ Dominant F Serious ↔ Lively G Expedient ↔ Rule-conscious H Shy ↔ Socially bold I Utilitarian ↔ Sensitive L Trusting ↔ Vigilant M Grounded ↔ Abstracted N Forthright ↔ Private O Self-assured ↔ Apprehensive Q1 Traditional ↔ Open to change Q2 Group-oriented ↔ Self-reliant Q3 Tolerates disorder ↔ Perfectionistic Q4 Relaxed ↔ Tense 5 global factors (second-order, conceptually close to the Big Five): Extra

chunks.heading: 3. NEO Personality Inventory (Five-Factor Model)
chunks.text: 3. NEO Personality Inventory (Five-Factor Model) Authors: Paul T. Costa Jr. & Robert R. McCrae (NIH/National Institute on Aging). Year: NEO-PI 1985 → NEO-PI-R 1992 → NEO-PI-3 2010. Items: 240 items (NEO-PI-R and NEO-PI-3). 5-point Likert (Strongly disagree → Strongly agree). 8 items per facet × 30 facets. NEO-FFI / NEO-FFI-3: short form, 60 items , gives the 5 domain scores only (no facets). Useful when time is tight. Age range: 17+ (NEO-PI-3 extended down to age 12). Forms S (self-report) and R (observer rating). 5 domains × 6 facets (memorize the mnemonic OCEAN , plus at least two facets per domain): Domain Facets O — Openness to Experience Fantasy, Aesthetics, Feelings, Actions, Ideas, Values C — Conscientiousness Competence, Order, Dutifulness, Achievement Striving, Self-Discipline, Deliberation E — Extraversion Warmth, Gregariousness, Assertiveness, Activity, Excitement-Seeking, Positive Emotions A — Agreeableness Trust, Straightforwardness, Altruism, Compliance, Modesty, Tender-Mindedness N — Neuroticism Anxiety, Angry Hostility, Depression, Self-Consciousness, Impulsiveness, Vulnerability Scoring: raw → T-scores. No validity scales in the classical sense (NEO assumes honest responding), though item-position consistency checks exist. Use case: non-clinical research, occupational selection, characterising personality structure for therapy planning. The dominant trait model

chunks.heading: 4. EPQ / EPQ-R (Eysenck Personality Questionnaire)
chunks.text: 4. EPQ / EPQ-R (Eysenck Personality Questionnaire) Authors: Hans J. Eysenck & Sybil B. G. Eysenck. Lineage: Maudsley Medical Questionnaire (1952) → Maudsley Personality Inventory (MPI, 1959) → Eysenck Personality Inventory (EPI, 1964) → EPQ (1975) → EPQ-R (1985) → EPQ-R Short (1992). Items: EPQ 90 items ; EPQ-R 100 items ; EPQ-R Short 48 items. Yes/No format. Age range: adult. Junior EPQ for ages 7–15. Three (later four) PEN dimensions: P — Psychoticism: tough-mindedness, aggression, low empathy. Added in 1975 (the move from EPI to EPQ). E — Extraversion: sociability, impulsivity, sensation-seeking. N — Neuroticism: emotional reactivity, anxiety. L — Lie scale: social desirability. Theoretical anchor: Eysenck linked each dimension to biology — Extraversion to cortical arousal (introverts have higher baseline arousal), Neuroticism to limbic/ANS reactivity, Psychoticism to dopaminergic function. This is what makes EPQ a "biologically grounded" trait theory and is a common MCQ pairing (Eysenck = biology of personality). Use case: personality research, especially anything testing the arousal theory of extraversion. Clinical screening is secondary.

chunks.heading: 5. MBTI (Myers-Briggs Type Indicator)
chunks.text: 5. MBTI (Myers-Briggs Type Indicator) Authors: Katharine Cook Briggs & her daughter Isabel Briggs Myers. Built on Carl Jung's Psychological Types (1921). Year: first version 1944; commercial release 1962 (Educational Testing Service); current MBTI Form M (1998) . Items: Form M = 93 forced-choice items , Form Q = 144 items (adds 20 facets). Form G (older) had 126 items. Age range: 14+. Four dichotomies → 16 types: E vs I — Extraversion / Introversion (energy direction). S vs N — Sensing / iNtuition (information style). T vs F — Thinking / Feeling (decision style). J vs P — Judging / Perceiving (lifestyle / outer-world orientation). Scoring: forced-choice → preference score on each dichotomy → categorical type (e.g., INTJ, ESFP). Critically, scores are not dimensional; the test claims discrete types. This is the main psychometric criticism of MBTI : traits are normally distributed, dichotomisation throws away information, and test-retest reliability for type assignment is mediocre (~50% of takers get a different type on retest within weeks). Use case: career counselling, team building, coaching. Not recommended for clinical diagnosis or selection. Often invoked in MET as a contrast case: "Which test claims discrete types instead of continuous traits?" → MBTI.

chunks.heading: 6. CPI (California Psychological Inventory)
chunks.text: 6. CPI (California Psychological Inventory) Author: Harrison Gough. Year: 1957 → CPI-434 (1996) → CPI-260 short form. Items: 434 (full) / 260 (short). True-false. Scales: 20 "folk-concept" scales (Dominance, Sociability, Empathy, Independence, etc.) grouped under 4 broad themes: Interpersonal, Self-management, Achievement, Personal Style. Also 3 vector scales. Use case: normal populations — explicitly the non-clinical complement to MMPI. Used in selection, counselling, leadership development.

chunks.heading: 7. TAT (Thematic Apperception Test)
chunks.text: 7. TAT (Thematic Apperception Test) Authors: Henry A. Murray & Christiana D. Morgan, Harvard Psychological Clinic. Year: 1935. Manual published 1943. Stimuli: 31 picture cards total — 30 black-and-white ambiguous scenes + 1 blank card. 20 cards are administered per subject , selected by age (adult / child) and sex (M / F). Cards are labelled with these codes (e.g., 3BM = card 3 for Boys + Men). Procedure: subject is asked to make up a story for each picture — what led up to the scene, what is happening now, what the characters are thinking and feeling, and how it will end. Stories are recorded verbatim. Theoretical basis: projective hypothesis — when stimulus is ambiguous, the subject "projects" their dominant needs (achievement, affiliation, power, etc.) and the environmental press they perceive. Built directly on Murray's needs-press theory of personality (Explorations in Personality, 1938). Scoring systems: Murray's original system: code needs and press in each story. SCORS (Social Cognition and Object Relations Scale): Westen, 1985 — 8 dimensions of object relations. Defense Mechanism Manual (DMM): Cramer. McClelland's nAch scoring: used in achievement-motivation research. Indian adaptation: Indian TAT by Uma Choudhury (1960) — culture-adapted scenes with Indian figures. Use case: uncovering unconscious motives, conflicts, defenses, and interpersonal schemata. Common in cli

chunks.heading: 8. Rorschach Inkblot Test
chunks.text: 8. Rorschach Inkblot Test Author: Hermann Rorschach (Swiss psychiatrist). Year: published Psychodiagnostik in 1921. Rorschach died in 1922 at 37, before he could refine the system. Stimuli: 10 inkblot cards. 5 are achromatic (black + grey: cards I, IV, V, VI, VII), 2 are black + red (cards II, III), and 3 are fully chromatic (cards VIII, IX, X). Often summarised as "5 black/grey, 2 red-and-black, 3 colour" or simply "5 chromatic + 5 achromatic" in shorthand. Administration: two phases. (1) Free Association / Response phase : "What might this be?" (2) Inquiry phase : clinician asks where on the blot the subject saw it and what features (form, colour, shading, movement) made it look that way. Scoring — Exner Comprehensive System (1974), the dominant system till 2011: Location: W (whole blot), D (common detail), Dd (unusual detail), S (white space). Determinants — what made it look like that: F = form / shape. M = human movement; FM = animal movement; m = inanimate movement. C = pure colour; FC = form-dominated colour; CF = colour-dominated form. (Form-colour ratio is a classic Rorschach inference about emotional control.) C' = achromatic colour. T = texture (shading). V = vista (shading-depth). Y = diffuse shading. FD = form-dimension. (2) = pair. r = reflection. Content: H (human), Hd (human detail), A (animal), Ad (animal detail), An (anatomy), Bl (blood), Sx (sex), Xy (X-ray),

chunks.heading: 9. Bell's Adjustment Inventory
chunks.text: 9. Bell's Adjustment Inventory Author: Hugh M. Bell. Year: Student form 1934; Adult form 1938; Indian adaptations by R. K. Ojha (Hindi) and others. Items: 140 items (Student form). Adult form has 160 items. Yes/No/? format. Age range: Student form for high school + college students; Adult form for general adult population. Areas of adjustment scored (Student form measures 4; Adult form adds Occupational): Home adjustment — relationships with family. Health adjustment — somatic preoccupation, physical wellbeing. Social adjustment — submissiveness vs aggressiveness in social situations. Emotional adjustment — stability vs instability of mood. Occupational adjustment (Adult form only) — satisfaction and adjustment to work. Scoring: higher score = poorer adjustment in that area. Total adjustment score is the sum across areas. Score brackets are labelled excellent / good / average / unsatisfactory / very unsatisfactory. Use case: screening for adjustment problems in school counselling, college counselling centres, and Indian educational/research settings (very commonly used in Indian masters dissertations — that is why it shows up on MET despite being old).

chunks.heading: 10. Beck Inventories
chunks.text: 10. Beck Inventories All authored or co-authored by Aaron T. Beck (often with colleagues at the University of Pennsylvania Centre for Cognitive Therapy). Memorize each one's item count and 0–3 Likert scoring; they all share the same response-scale skeleton.

chunks.heading: BDI / BDI-II — Beck Depression Inventory
chunks.text: BDI / BDI-II — Beck Depression Inventory BDI: 1961 (Beck, Ward, Mendelson, Mock, Erbaugh). 21 items, 0–3 each. BDI-II: 1996. 21 items , self-report, each rated 0–3. Total 0–63. Items revised to match DSM-IV depressive criteria (added agitation, worthlessness, concentration difficulty; removed body image, work difficulty, weight loss, somatic preoccupation). Time frame: past 2 weeks. Cutoffs: 0–13 minimal, 14–19 mild, 20–28 moderate, 29–63 severe. Reading level: 5th–6th grade. Use: screening, severity tracking. Not diagnostic on its own.

chunks.heading: BAI — Beck Anxiety Inventory
chunks.text: BAI — Beck Anxiety Inventory Year: 1988 (Beck, Epstein, Brown, Steer). Items: 21 items , 0–3, total 0–63. Time frame: past week. Cutoffs: 0–7 minimal, 8–15 mild, 16–25 moderate, 26–63 severe. Design intent: measure anxiety symptoms with minimal overlap with depression . BAI deliberately loads on somatic anxiety items (sweating, dizziness, racing heart) rather than mood items.

chunks.heading: BHS — Beck Hopelessness Scale
chunks.text: BHS — Beck Hopelessness Scale Year: 1974. Items: 20 true/false items. Use: measures pessimism about the future. Strongly predictive of eventual suicide (more predictive than depression severity alone). Cutoff ≥ 9 flags elevated risk.

chunks.heading: BSS / BSI — Beck Scale for Suicide Ideation
chunks.text: BSS / BSI — Beck Scale for Suicide Ideation Year: 1979 (clinician version), 1991 (self-report version). Items: 21 items , 0–2 each. First 5 screen for desire to live/die and active/passive ideation; if any are positive, complete the remaining 14 detail items. Use: assessment of suicidal ideation, intent, and planning over the past week.

chunks.heading: BYI — Beck Youth Inventories
chunks.text: BYI — Beck Youth Inventories Year: 2001, second edition 2005. Ages 7–18. Items: 5 scales × 20 items each = 100 items: Depression, Anxiety, Anger, Disruptive Behavior, Self-Concept.

chunks.heading: Other Beck instruments worth recognising
chunks.text: Other Beck instruments worth recognising BSSI (Beck Scale for Suicide Ideation) — see above. Clark-Beck Obsessive-Compulsive Inventory (CBOCI): 25 items. Beck Self-Concept Test.

chunks.heading: 11. Other Personality + Adjustment Inventories on the MET Radar
chunks.text: 11. Other Personality + Adjustment Inventories on the MET Radar Test Items Author / Year What it does PAI (Personality Assessment Inventory) 344 items, 4-point Leslie Morey, 1991 22 non-overlapping scales (4 validity, 11 clinical, 5 treatment, 2 interpersonal). MMPI's main rival. HPI (Hogan Personality Inventory) 206 items Robert Hogan, 1986 7 primary scales mapped to Big Five for workplace use. MCMI-IV (Millon Clinical Multiaxial Inventory) 195 items, T/F Theodore Millon, current ed. 2015 14 personality-disorder scales + 10 clinical-syndrome scales. Aligned to DSM personality patterns. HEXACO-PI-R 200 items (60-item brief) Ashton & Lee, 2004 6 factors: Honesty-Humility, Emotionality, eXtraversion, Agreeableness, Conscientiousness, Openness. Mooney Problem Check List 288 items (adult), 330 (college) Mooney & Gordon, 1950 Checklist of 11 problem areas (Health, Finances, Social, etc.) — popular in Indian school counselling research. Sinha's Anxiety Scale (SAS) / Sinha's Comprehensive Anxiety Test (SCAT) 90 items A. K. P. Sinha & L. N. K. Sinha Indian-normed adult anxiety scale, common in Indian dissertations. Saxena's Adjustment Inventory varies (~60) D. N. Saxena Indian school-counselling adjustment scale, sometimes paired with Bell's in MET questions.

chunks.heading: 12. Projective Tests Beyond Rorschach + TAT
chunks.text: 12. Projective Tests Beyond Rorschach + TAT Test Stimulus Author / Year What it scores CAT (Children's Apperception Test) 10 animal cards (CAT-A) or 10 human cards (CAT-H) Leopold & Sonya Bellak, 1949 TAT for children 3–10. Animal figures used because young children identify more easily with animals. SAT (Senior Apperception Test) 16 cards Bellak & Bellak, 1973 TAT for older adults — themes of loneliness, dependency, illness. Rosenzweig Picture-Frustration Study (P-F Study) 24 cartoon frustration scenes Saul Rosenzweig, 1944 Scores direction of aggression (extra-, intro-, im-punitive) × type (obstacle-dominance, ego-defense, need-persistence). Holtzman Inkblot Technique (HIT) 45 inkblot cards, 1 response per card Wayne Holtzman, 1961 Psychometrically tighter alternative to Rorschach (better reliability, parallel forms A and B). Rotter Incomplete Sentences Blank (RISB) 40 sentence stems Julian Rotter, 1950 "I wish…", "My mother…" — scored for adjustment on a 0–6 scale. Draw-A-Person (DAP / Machover) Draw a person, then another of opposite sex Karen Machover, 1949 Body image, self-concept. Goodenough-Harris DAP scores for cognitive maturity. House-Tree-Person (HTP) Draw house, tree, person John Buck, 1948 Combined personality + cognitive screen; symbolic interpretation. Kinetic Family Drawing (KFD) "Draw your family doing something" Burns & Kaufman, 1970 Family dynamics, interact

chunks.heading: 14. Top MCQ Traps (do not lose these marks)
chunks.text: 14. Top MCQ Traps (do not lose these marks) MMPI-2 = 567 items, 10 clinical scales, 3+ validity scales (L, F, K). Don't confuse with 16PF's 16 factors. MMPI-2 uses T-scores (mean 50, SD 10). Clinical cutoff T ≥ 65 (was 70 on original MMPI). Sten is 16PF, not MMPI. L scale = naive faking-good; F scale = exaggeration / random / severe pathology; K scale = subtle defensiveness. Don't swap them. 16PF = 185 items, 16 primary factors, 5 globals, Sten scores, Cattell. Big Five (OCEAN) ≠ 16PF — Big Five is Costa & McCrae. NEO-PI-R / NEO-PI-3 = 240 items. NEO-FFI = 60. Don't confuse the long and short forms. NEO has 5 domains × 6 facets = 30 facets. 16PF has 16 factors × 0 facets but 5 globals. EPQ-R = 100 items. PEN model: Psychoticism, Extraversion, Neuroticism + Lie. Psychoticism was the addition that made EPI → EPQ in 1975. MBTI = forced-choice, type-based (16 types), 4 dichotomies (E/I, S/N, T/F, J/P). Jung-derived. Common criticism: dichotomisation, poor retest reliability. TAT = 31 cards total, 20 administered. Murray & Morgan, 1935. Theory: needs-press. Rorschach = 10 inkblots. Hermann Rorschach, 1921. Not 20, not 12. Scored by Exner system → R-PAS (2011). CAT = Bellak, 1949, 10 cards. Animal version for kids; human version exists too. Bell's Adjustment Inventory: Student form = 140 items, 4 areas (Home, Health, Social, Emotional). Adult form = 160 items, adds Occupational. BDI-

chunks.heading: 15. Author + Year Speed Drill
chunks.text: 15. Author + Year Speed Drill Starke Hathaway & Charnley McKinley → MMPI (1943). Raymond Cattell → 16PF (1949). Paul Costa & Robert McCrae → NEO-PI / NEO-PI-R / NEO-PI-3. Hans & Sybil Eysenck → EPI (1964), EPQ (1975), EPQ-R (1985). Katharine Briggs & Isabel Briggs Myers → MBTI (1944, commercial 1962). Harrison Gough → CPI (1957). Henry Murray & Christiana Morgan → TAT (1935). Hermann Rorschach → Rorschach (1921). Leopold Bellak → CAT (1949). Wayne Holtzman → HIT (1961). Julian Rotter → RISB (1950). Saul Rosenzweig → P-F Study (1944). Karen Machover → DAP (1949). John Buck → HTP (1948). Lauretta Bender → Bender-Gestalt (1938). Hugh Bell → Bell's Adjustment Inventory (1934/1938). Aaron Beck → BDI (1961), BHS (1974), BSS (1979), BAI (1988), BDI-II (1996). Leslie Morey → PAI (1991). Theodore Millon → MCMI (1977, current MCMI-IV 2015). Uma Choudhury → Indian TAT (1960).
