chunks.heading: Psychotherapy, Full Section Cheatsheet
chunks.text: Psychotherapy, Full Section Cheatsheet Section 5 of MET. 15 questions (MET) / 10 (NIMHANS). Built 2026-05-17 to close the cheatsheet gap noted on the notes index. School-by-school. Founders, mechanism, technique, indication, MCQ trap. Cross-link with the Learning & Conditioning page for behaviour-therapy terms and the consolidated revision pack for Ellis vs Beck, defenses, and CBT triggers.

chunks.heading: 1. Psychoanalytic / Psychodynamic
chunks.text: 1. Psychoanalytic / Psychodynamic

chunks.heading: Freud, the scaffolding
chunks.text: Freud, the scaffolding Topographic model: conscious, preconscious, unconscious. Structural model: id (pleasure principle, primary process), ego (reality principle, secondary process), superego (conscience + ego ideal). Psychosexual stages: oral (0-1.5), anal (1.5-3), phallic (3-6) — Oedipus / Electra, latency (6-puberty), genital (puberty-adulthood). Fixation → adult character traits. Defenses: Vaillant hierarchy: psychotic (denial, distortion) → immature (projection, acting out, regression, somatization) → neurotic (intellectualisation, displacement, reaction formation, repression, isolation of affect) → mature (humour, sublimation, suppression, altruism, anticipation).

chunks.heading: Classical technique
chunks.text: Classical technique Free association — the fundamental rule. Interpretation of resistances and transference. Dream analysis — manifest vs latent content. Working through — repeated re-examination across contexts until insight becomes integrated and behavioural change emerges. Distinguishes intellectual from emotional/behavioural insight. Frequency: classical psychoanalysis 3-5×/week, couch, years. Psychoanalytic / psychodynamic therapy: 1-2×/week, face-to-face, months-years.

chunks.heading: Post-Freudians, the canon
chunks.text: Post-Freudians, the canon Theorist Core contribution Alfred Adler Individual Psychology. Inferiority feelings → striving for superiority. Social interest. Birth order. Style of life. Early recollections in assessment. Carl Jung Analytical Psychology. Collective unconscious. Archetypes (persona, shadow, anima/animus, self). Individuation. Introversion/extraversion. Word association test. Anna Freud Ego psychology. Defense mechanisms systematised. Child analysis through play. Melanie Klein Object relations. Paranoid-schizoid → depressive position. Splitting, projective identification. Internal objects. Play therapy. Donald Winnicott Object relations. "Good-enough mother," holding environment, true vs false self, transitional object. Heinz Kohut Self psychology. Narcissistic injury, mirroring, idealising, twinship selfobjects. Empathic immersion. Karen Horney Basic anxiety. Neurotic needs. "Tyranny of the should." Feminine psychology critique of Freud. Erik Erikson 8 psychosocial stages (Trust v Mistrust → Integrity v Despair). Identity crisis. Ego psychology bridge to lifespan dev. Harry Stack Sullivan Interpersonal psychiatry. "Self-system." Anxiety as interpersonal. Influenced IPT. Otto Kernberg Transference-Focused Psychotherapy (TFP) for BPD. Borderline personality organisation. Splitting + identity diffusion. MCQ trap: Working through is NOT free association nor a single int

chunks.heading: 2. Behaviour Therapy
chunks.text: 2. Behaviour Therapy Founders: Joseph Wolpe , Hans Eysenck , B. F. Skinner , Albert Bandura . Mechanism: directly manipulate antecedents, behaviours, consequences via classical + operant conditioning + social learning.

chunks.heading: Core techniques
chunks.text: Core techniques Technique Mechanism Indication Systematic desensitisation (Wolpe) Reciprocal inhibition: relaxation paired with graded imagined exposure up a fear hierarchy Phobias (classic) In-vivo exposure Real-world graded exposure without relaxation; habituation + extinction Specific phobia, agoraphobia, OCD, PTSD Flooding / implosion Full-intensity exposure without escape until anxiety extinguishes Phobias (less used due to dropout) Exposure & Response Prevention (ERP) (Foa, Kozak) Exposure to obsessional trigger + prevention of compulsive response OCD — first-line behavioural Tx Aversion therapy Pairing unwanted behaviour with aversive UCS (covert sensitisation as imaginal version) Paraphilias, substance use (limited evidence + ethical issues) Token economy Operant: secondary reinforcers (tokens) exchanged for primary reinforcers Inpatient / institutional settings, ID, ADHD classrooms Contingency management Operant: rewards contingent on target behaviour SUDs (esp. stimulant) Behavioural activation (Lewinsohn, Jacobson) Scheduled engagement in rewarding/mastery activities; reverses depressive withdrawal-rumination cycle Depression — comparable to CBT Modeling (Bandura) Observational learning, vicarious reinforcement; participant modeling Phobias, social skills Shaping Reinforce successive approximations of target behaviour Skill acquisition, autism intervention Chaining L

chunks.heading: 3. Cognitive and Cognitive-Behavioural Therapy
chunks.text: 3. Cognitive and Cognitive-Behavioural Therapy

chunks.heading: Beck's Cognitive Therapy
chunks.text: Beck's Cognitive Therapy Cognitive triad of depression: negative views of (1) self, (2) world/experience, (3) future. Schemas → automatic thoughts → emotion/behaviour. Common cognitive distortions: all-or-nothing thinking, overgeneralisation, mental filter, disqualifying the positive, jumping to conclusions (mind reading / fortune telling), magnification or minimisation, emotional reasoning, "should" statements, labelling, personalisation. Techniques: Socratic questioning (guided discovery), thought records, downward arrow, behavioural experiments, activity scheduling, graded task assignment. Indications: depression (originator), anxiety, OCD, PTSD, eating disorders, psychosis (CBTp).

chunks.heading: Ellis's REBT (Rational Emotive Behaviour Therapy)
chunks.text: Ellis's REBT (Rational Emotive Behaviour Therapy) ABC model: A activating event → B beliefs (rational or irrational) → C consequences (emotional + behavioural). Then D dispute, E new effect. Three core irrational demands: I must do well; others must treat me well; the world must be easy/fair. Distinct from Beck: Ellis confronts irrational beliefs more directly; Beck uses Socratic discovery. Both target cognition-emotion-behaviour loop.

chunks.heading: Trigger words to distinguish in MCQs
chunks.text: Trigger words to distinguish in MCQs Cue Best answer "Cognitive triad," "automatic thought," "schema," "guided discovery" Beck "ABC model," "irrational belief," "dispute," "musturbation" Ellis (REBT) "Reciprocal inhibition," "hierarchy," "relaxation pairing" Wolpe (systematic desensitisation) "Free association," "transference," "working through" Freudian / psychodynamic "Empathy, congruence, UPR" Rogers (person-centred) "Hexaflex, cognitive defusion, values" ACT (Hayes) "Mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation, interpersonal effectiveness" DBT (Linehan) "OARS, change talk, evocation" Motivational Interviewing (Miller & Rollnick) "Empty chair, top-dog / underdog" Gestalt (Perls) "Family map, joining, enmeshment, disengagement" Structural family therapy (Minuchin) "Paradoxical intention, restraining" Strategic family therapy (Haley, Watzlawick) "Solution-focused, miracle question" SFBT (de Shazer, Berg) "Externalising the problem" Narrative therapy (White, Epston)

chunks.heading: 4. Humanistic / Existential
chunks.text: 4. Humanistic / Existential

chunks.heading: Rogers — person-centred therapy (PCT)
chunks.text: Rogers — person-centred therapy (PCT) Three core conditions (1957, necessary + sufficient): empathy, unconditional positive regard (UPR), congruence (genuineness). Actualising tendency as the engine. Therapist's job: provide the conditions; the client does the work. Non-directive. Reflection of feeling. No interpretation. Self vs ideal-self congruence as outcome marker (Q-sort).

chunks.heading: Gestalt — Fritz Perls
chunks.text: Gestalt — Fritz Perls Focus on the here-and-now, awareness of present experience, "figure-ground" of attention. Techniques: empty chair (dialogue with absent person / disowned part of self), top-dog / underdog dialogue, exaggeration, "I" statements, attention to non-verbals, integration of polarities. Goal: integrate disowned parts → wholeness.

chunks.heading: Existential — Frankl, May, Yalom
chunks.text: Existential — Frankl, May, Yalom Viktor Frankl — Logotherapy. Search for meaning. Three sources of meaning: creative (work / contribution), experiential (love / beauty), attitudinal (response to unavoidable suffering). Techniques: paradoxical intention, dereflection. Rollo May. Existential anxiety vs neurotic anxiety. Daimonic. Freedom and destiny. Irvin Yalom — 4 "ultimate concerns": death, freedom (responsibility), isolation, meaninglessness. Group therapy specialist (next section).

chunks.heading: Glasser — Reality / Choice Theory
chunks.text: Glasser — Reality / Choice Theory WDEP framework: Wants, Doing, Evaluation, Planning. Focus on present, responsibility, total behaviour. Used in school + corrections settings.

chunks.heading: 5. Group Therapy — Yalom
chunks.text: 5. Group Therapy — Yalom The group is a social microcosm ; relationship patterns from outside life replay in the group. Therapist's job is to surface the here-and-now process.

chunks.heading: Yalom's 11 therapeutic factors
chunks.text: Yalom's 11 therapeutic factors Instillation of hope Universality ("I'm not the only one") Imparting information Altruism (helping others is itself therapeutic) Corrective recapitulation of the primary family group Development of socialising techniques Imitative behaviour Interpersonal learning (the engine, paired with here-and-now) Group cohesiveness (the group analogue of the therapeutic alliance) Catharsis Existential factors (responsibility, isolation, meaning, mortality) Process group format: 6-10 members + therapist(s). Bion's group dynamics (basic assumption groups: dependency, fight-flight, pairing) influential. MCQ: "social microcosm" + "here-and-now" + "interpersonal learning" → Yalom.

chunks.heading: 6. Family / Systemic
chunks.text: 6. Family / Systemic School Founder(s) Key concepts / technique Structural Minuchin Family map, subsystems, boundaries (clear / rigid-disengaged / diffuse-enmeshed), joining, enactment, restructuring. Strategic Haley, Madanes, Watzlawick (MRI) Brief, problem-focused. Symptom serves a function. Directives, paradoxical interventions, ordeal therapy. Bowenian (multigenerational) Murray Bowen Differentiation of self. Triangles. Family projection process. Genogram. Emotional cutoff. Experiential / symbolic Virginia Satir, Carl Whitaker Communication stances (placater, blamer, computer, distractor, leveller). Family sculpting, family reconstruction. Milan systemic Selvini Palazzoli, Boscolo, Cecchin, Prata Circular questioning, hypothesising, neutrality. Reflecting team. Narrative White, Epston Externalising the problem ("the OCD," not "you"). Re-authoring. Unique outcomes. Solution-focused brief (SFBT) de Shazer, Insoo Kim Berg Miracle question, scaling, exception-seeking. Future + competence focused. 4-8 sessions typical.

chunks.heading: 7. Third-Wave / Integrative
chunks.text: 7. Third-Wave / Integrative

chunks.heading: DBT — Dialectical Behaviour Therapy (Linehan, 1993)
chunks.text: DBT — Dialectical Behaviour Therapy (Linehan, 1993) Synthesis of behavioural change + Zen acceptance ("dialectics"). Primary target: BPD with chronic suicidality. 4 skill modules: mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation, interpersonal effectiveness. Standard programme: weekly individual therapy + weekly group skills training + phone coaching + therapist consultation team. ~1 year. Hierarchy of targets: life-threatening behaviours → therapy-interfering behaviours → quality-of-life-interfering behaviours.

chunks.heading: ACT — Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (Hayes)
chunks.text: ACT — Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (Hayes) Goal: psychological flexibility, not symptom reduction. Hexaflex (6 processes): Acceptance, Cognitive Defusion, Self-as-Context, Present-Moment Contact, Values, Committed Action. Each opposed by an inflexibility process (experiential avoidance, fusion, attachment to conceptualised self, etc.). Underpinned by Relational Frame Theory (RFT). Techniques: defusion ("I'm having the thought that…"), values clarification, metaphors (passengers on the bus, tug-of-war with a monster).

chunks.heading: MBCT — Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy (Segal, Williams, Teasdale)
chunks.text: MBCT — Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy (Segal, Williams, Teasdale) 8-week group programme combining MBSR (Kabat-Zinn) + cognitive therapy. Indication: relapse prevention in recurrent depression (≥3 episodes).

chunks.heading: MBSR — Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (Kabat-Zinn 1979)
chunks.text: MBSR — Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (Kabat-Zinn 1979) 8-week group programme. Body scan, sitting meditation, mindful movement (yoga). Chronic pain, stress, anxiety.

chunks.heading: IPT — Interpersonal Therapy (Klerman & Weissman, 1984)
chunks.text: IPT — Interpersonal Therapy (Klerman & Weissman, 1984) Time-limited (12-16 sessions). Originally for MDD. Four problem areas: grief, role disputes, role transitions, interpersonal deficits. Choose one as the focus. Evidence base extends to bulimia, postpartum depression, adolescent depression.

chunks.heading: MI — Motivational Interviewing (Miller & Rollnick, 1991, 3rd ed. 2013)
chunks.text: MI — Motivational Interviewing (Miller & Rollnick, 1991, 3rd ed. 2013) Spirit (PACE): Partnership, Acceptance, Compassion, Evocation. Processes: Engaging → Focusing → Evoking → Planning. Core skills (OARS): Open questions, Affirmations, Reflections, Summaries. Listen for and amplify change talk (DARN-CAT: Desire, Ability, Reason, Need → Commitment, Activation, Taking steps). Indication: ambivalence, especially in SUDs; also weight loss, medication adherence, HIV risk.

chunks.heading: EMDR (Francine Shapiro, 1987)
chunks.text: EMDR (Francine Shapiro, 1987) 8-phase protocol pairing brief recall of trauma memory with bilateral stimulation (eye movements / taps / tones). Indication: PTSD (APA, NICE, WHO endorsed). Mechanism debated (working-memory taxation, REM-like processing, dual attention). Comparable to trauma-focused CBT in head-to-head trials.

chunks.heading: CPT — Cognitive Processing Therapy (Resick & Schnicke)
chunks.text: CPT — Cognitive Processing Therapy (Resick & Schnicke) 12-session manualised trauma-focused CBT for PTSD. Stuck points → impact statement → Socratic dialogue + worksheets.

chunks.heading: Prolonged Exposure (Foa)
chunks.text: Prolonged Exposure (Foa) Imaginal + in-vivo exposure to trauma memories and avoided stimuli. Manualised. Equally evidence-based for PTSD.

chunks.heading: TFP / MBT for BPD
chunks.text: TFP / MBT for BPD TFP — Transference-Focused Psychotherapy (Kernberg): twice-weekly psychodynamic, here-and-now transference interpretation, "object relations dyads." MBT — Mentalization-Based Treatment (Bateman & Fonagy): builds capacity to understand own and others' mental states. Day-hospital and outpatient versions.

chunks.heading: 8. Trauma Therapist Lineage (high-yield)
chunks.text: 8. Trauma Therapist Lineage (high-yield) Therapist Contribution Pierre Janet Dissociation, traumatic memory (late 1800s, predates Freud) Judith Herman Complex PTSD; 3-stage trauma recovery (safety → remembrance/mourning → reconnection) Bessel van der Kolk "The body keeps the score." Trauma + somatics. Polyvagal influences. Edna Foa Prolonged Exposure protocol; ERP for OCD; emotional processing theory Patricia Resick Cognitive Processing Therapy Francine Shapiro EMDR Peter Levine Somatic Experiencing (body-based) Marsha Linehan DBT (BPD + chronic suicidality, often trauma-rooted)

chunks.heading: 9. Common-Factors Framework
chunks.text: 9. Common-Factors Framework Research (Lambert, Wampold) finds outcome variance roughly: ~40% client + extra-therapeutic factors, ~30% relationship (alliance), ~15% expectancy / placebo, ~15% specific technique. Implication: most schools work, mostly via common factors (therapeutic alliance, empathy, expectancy, mobilisation of client resources). Specific techniques matter most for specific disorders with strong protocols (ERP for OCD, exposure for PTSD, behavioural activation for depression). Bordin's working alliance: goals + tasks + bond.

chunks.heading: 10. Indications Quick-Map (what to recommend, MCQ-grade)
chunks.text: 10. Indications Quick-Map (what to recommend, MCQ-grade) Condition First-line psychotherapy MDD (mild–moderate) CBT, behavioural activation, IPT OCD ERP (CBT family); add SSRI if needed Specific phobia In-vivo exposure / systematic desensitisation Social anxiety CBT (Clark & Wells / Heimberg) Panic disorder CBT with interoceptive exposure (Barlow) GAD CBT, applied relaxation, MBCT PTSD Trauma-focused CBT (PE, CPT), EMDR BPD DBT, MBT, TFP, schema therapy (Young) Bulimia / BED CBT-E (Fairburn) Anorexia nervosa (adolescent) FBT (Maudsley) Substance use MI, CBT relapse-prevention (Marlatt), contingency management, 12-step facilitation Schizophrenia (adjunct) CBTp, family interventions (psychoeducation, expressed-emotion work), social skills training Couples Emotionally Focused Therapy (Johnson), Gottman Method, integrative behavioural couple therapy (Christensen, Jacobson) Adolescents — depression IPT-A, CBT Children — anxiety CBT (Coping Cat / Kendall), parent-focused (PCIT) Recurrent depression — relapse prevention MBCT

chunks.heading: 11. Ethics + Frame (MET-style MCQ traps)
chunks.text: 11. Ethics + Frame (MET-style MCQ traps) Boundaries: dual relationships generally avoided; rural and minority-community practice acknowledged exceptions. Confidentiality limits: imminent harm to self / others (Tarasoff duty to warn / protect), child abuse, court order. Informed consent: nature of therapy, alternatives, risks, fees, limits of confidentiality. Multicultural competence: awareness, knowledge, skills (Sue & Sue). Termination: planned, gradual, address relapse-prevention, leave the door open.

chunks.heading: 12. 12 MCQ Traps to Lock
chunks.text: 12. 12 MCQ Traps to Lock Working through ≠ free association. It is repeated re-encounter with the conflict/interpretation across contexts. ERP is for OCD; systematic desensitisation is for phobias. Beck = cognitive triad + Socratic; Ellis = ABC + dispute. Don't swap. Rogers' three core conditions are empathy, UPR, congruence. No "interpretation." Empty chair = Gestalt, not psychoanalysis. DBT was developed for BPD (Linehan), not for depression. 4 modules: mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation, interpersonal effectiveness. ACT hexaflex: 6 processes (acceptance, defusion, self-as-context, present moment, values, committed action). Not 4, not 8. IPT 4 problem areas: grief, role disputes, role transitions, interpersonal deficits. Not "thoughts / feelings / behaviours / body." Motivational Interviewing spirit = PACE (Partnership, Acceptance, Compassion, Evocation); skills = OARS. Yalom's "here-and-now" + "social microcosm" are group-therapy markers. Minuchin = structural family therapy ; enmeshed vs disengaged boundaries; joining + restructuring. EMDR = Shapiro, 1987, 8 phases, for PTSD. Mechanism debated; efficacy comparable to TF-CBT. Cross-references: Learning & Conditioning terms · Consolidated revision pack · Abnormal cheatsheet (DSM categories pair with treatments above) · Drill in MET Mock 4 (14 therapy Qs) · Adjacent: Biopsych + Testing paper .

chunks.heading: Research Methodology + Biostatistics, Full Primer
chunks.text: Research Methodology + Biostatistics, Full Primer Built 2026-05-02. Covers everything MET might ask in section 6 (Biostatistics & Research Methodology). Read top-to-bottom. Memorize the tables and the MCQ traps at the end.

chunks.heading: 1. Types of Data (Levels of Measurement)
chunks.text: 1. Types of Data (Levels of Measurement) Stevens (1946) gave us the four levels. Knowing the level dictates which statistical test you can use. Level Properties Example Allowed stats Nominal Categories only, no order Sex, blood group, religion, diagnosis (yes/no) Mode, frequency, chi-square Ordinal Order, but unequal intervals Pain scale 0-10, Likert (agree/disagree), socio-economic class Median, percentile, Spearman's rho, Mann-Whitney U Interval Equal intervals, no true zero Temperature in °C, IQ, calendar years Mean, SD, t-test, ANOVA, Pearson's r Ratio Equal intervals + true zero Height, weight, reaction time, age All of the above + geometric mean, ratios meaningful Memory hook: NOIR = Nominal, Ordinal, Interval, Ratio (in increasing order of information).

chunks.heading: 2. Descriptive Statistics
chunks.text: 2. Descriptive Statistics

chunks.heading: Central Tendency (where the middle is)
chunks.text: Central Tendency (where the middle is) Mean — arithmetic average. Sensitive to outliers. Use for symmetric/normal data. Median — 50th percentile. Robust to outliers. Use for skewed data or ordinal data. Mode — most frequent value. Only measure for nominal data. A distribution can be bimodal/multimodal.

chunks.heading: Dispersion (how spread out the data is)
chunks.text: Dispersion (how spread out the data is) Range = max − min. Crude, sensitive to outliers. IQR (Interquartile Range) = Q3 − Q1. Robust. Used in box plots. Variance = mean of squared deviations from the mean. Units are squared. Standard Deviation (SD) = √variance. Same units as the data. The default dispersion measure. Standard Error of the Mean (SEM) = SD / √n. Dispersion of the sample mean , not of individuals. Always smaller than SD. Coefficient of Variation (CV) = SD/mean × 100%. Compares variability across different scales.

chunks.heading: Shape
chunks.text: Shape Skewness — asymmetry. Positive skew = long right tail (mean > median > mode). Negative skew = long left tail (mean < median < mode). Kurtosis — peakedness. Leptokurtic = tall, narrow peak (high kurtosis, fat tails). Platykurtic = flat. Mesokurtic = normal.

chunks.heading: 3. Distributions
chunks.text: 3. Distributions

chunks.heading: Normal (Gaussian) Distribution
chunks.text: Normal (Gaussian) Distribution Bell-shaped, symmetric, mean = median = mode at center. Defined by μ and σ. 68-95-99.7 rule: 68% within ±1 SD, 95% within ±2 SD (more precisely 1.96), 99.7% within ±3 SD. z-score = (x − μ) / σ. Standardizes any value to the standard normal (μ=0, σ=1). Central Limit Theorem (CLT): the sampling distribution of the mean approaches normal as n increases, regardless of the shape of the underlying population. Foundation of inferential statistics. Rule of thumb: n ≥ 30.

chunks.heading: Other distributions you should recognize
chunks.text: Other distributions you should recognize t distribution — like normal but with fatter tails, shaped by degrees of freedom (df). Approaches normal as df → ∞. Chi-square (χ²) — right-skewed, only positive values. Used for categorical data. F distribution — ratio of two variances. Used in ANOVA and regression. Binomial — discrete, two outcomes (success/failure) over n trials. Poisson — count of rare events in fixed time/space (e.g., suicides per year, ER admissions per hour).

chunks.heading: 4. Inferential Statistics
chunks.text: 4. Inferential Statistics

chunks.heading: Hypothesis Testing Framework
chunks.text: Hypothesis Testing Framework State H₀ (null) : no effect / no difference. State H₁ (alternative) : there is an effect. Choose α (significance level), usually 0.05. Compute the test statistic and p-value. If p < α, reject H₀. If p ≥ α, fail to reject H₀. Important: we never accept H₀, we only fail to reject it. Absence of evidence ≠ evidence of absence.

chunks.heading: Errors
chunks.text: Errors H₀ true H₀ false Reject H₀ Type I error (α) — false positive Correct (power, 1−β) Fail to reject H₀ Correct (1−α) Type II error (β) — false negative Type I (α) = saying there's an effect when there isn't. Standard cap at 0.05. Type II (β) = missing a real effect. Standard target ≤ 0.20. Power = 1 − β. Probability of correctly detecting a real effect. Convention: aim for 0.80. Power increases when: n ↑, effect size ↑, α ↑ (more lenient), variability ↓, one-tailed test.

chunks.heading: One-tailed vs Two-tailed
chunks.text: One-tailed vs Two-tailed Two-tailed (default): tests whether the difference is non-zero in either direction. α split, 0.025 in each tail. One-tailed: tests for difference in a specific direction. More power, but only if you have a strong a priori reason. Considered conservative practice to use two-tailed by default.

chunks.heading: p-values
chunks.text: p-values Probability of observing the data (or more extreme) if H₀ is true. NOT the probability that H₀ is true. Common MCQ trap. p < 0.05 = "statistically significant" (by convention, not by nature). Statistical significance ≠ clinical/practical significance.

chunks.heading: Confidence Intervals (CI)
chunks.text: Confidence Intervals (CI) Range of plausible values for the true population parameter. 95% CI means: if we repeated the study many times, 95% of constructed CIs would contain the true value. If 95% CI for a difference excludes 0, p < 0.05. If 95% CI for a ratio (OR/RR) excludes 1, p < 0.05. Wider CI = less precise estimate (small n or high variability).

chunks.heading: Effect Size
chunks.text: Effect Size Magnitude of the effect, independent of sample size. Cohen's d for mean differences: 0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large. Pearson's r for correlation: 0.10 small, 0.30 medium, 0.50 large. Eta squared (η²) / partial η² for ANOVA: 0.01 small, 0.06 medium, 0.14 large. Odds Ratio (OR) / Relative Risk (RR) for case-control / cohort.

chunks.heading: 5. Parametric Tests
chunks.text: 5. Parametric Tests Assume normal distribution (or large n via CLT) and interval/ratio data. Question Test Notes Mean of one sample vs known value One-sample t-test df = n − 1 Two related (paired) means (pre/post, twins) Paired t-test df = n − 1 (n = pairs) Two independent group means Independent samples t-test df = n₁ + n₂ − 2. Assumes equal variance (use Welch's if not). Three or more independent group means One-way ANOVA F-test. If significant, follow with post-hoc (Tukey HSD, Bonferroni, Scheffé). Three or more related group means (within-subjects) Repeated-measures ANOVA Each subject in all conditions. Sphericity assumption. Two factors at once (e.g., drug × dose) Two-way / Factorial ANOVA Tests main effects + interaction. Linear association between two continuous variables Pearson's r Range −1 to +1. r² = variance explained. Predict Y from X (linear) Linear regression Y = a + bX + ε. Multiple regression for several predictors. Predict binary outcome Logistic regression Output = log odds, gives Odds Ratios.

chunks.heading: Parametric assumptions (always 4)
chunks.text: Parametric assumptions (always 4) Normality of the dependent variable / residuals Homogeneity of variance (Levene's test) Independence of observations Interval/ratio measurement

chunks.heading: 6. Non-parametric Tests
chunks.text: 6. Non-parametric Tests Use when assumptions are violated, sample is small, or data is ordinal. Parametric equivalent Non-parametric test One-sample t-test Wilcoxon signed-rank (or sign test) Paired t-test Wilcoxon signed-rank Independent t-test Mann-Whitney U (also called Wilcoxon rank-sum) One-way ANOVA Kruskal-Wallis H Repeated-measures ANOVA Friedman test Pearson's r Spearman's rho (or Kendall's tau) Comparing categorical proportions Chi-square (χ²) for independence/goodness of fit; Fisher's exact for small n Paired categorical (pre/post yes/no) McNemar's test

chunks.heading: 7. Sampling
chunks.text: 7. Sampling

chunks.heading: Probability sampling (random, generalizable)
chunks.text: Probability sampling (random, generalizable) Simple random — every individual has equal chance. Lottery method. Stratified random — divide population into strata (sex, age groups, etc.), then sample randomly within each. Ensures representation. Cluster — divide into clusters (schools, villages), randomly select clusters, study everyone within. Cheaper for large geographic areas. Systematic — every kth person from a list. k = N/n. Risk: periodicity in the list. Multistage — combination (e.g., random districts → random schools → random students).

chunks.heading: Non-probability sampling (less rigorous, often used in qualitative research)
chunks.text: Non-probability sampling (less rigorous, often used in qualitative research) Convenience — whoever is available. Most biased. Purposive (judgmental) — researcher chooses based on expertise/criteria. Quota — fill quotas (e.g., 50 men, 50 women) but not randomly. Snowball — participants recruit other participants. Used for hidden/stigmatized populations.

chunks.heading: Sample size — drivers
chunks.text: Sample size — drivers Larger when: smaller expected effect size, higher variability, lower α (e.g., 0.01), higher power required, multiple comparisons. Pilot study or prior literature gives the variance estimate. Common formulas use Cohen's tables, G*Power software.

chunks.heading: 8. Research Designs
chunks.text: 8. Research Designs

chunks.heading: Quantitative — by control over variables
chunks.text: Quantitative — by control over variables Design Manipulation Random assignment Strength True experimental (RCT) Yes Yes Highest internal validity. Gold standard for causation. Quasi-experimental Yes No Used when randomization is impossible (school classes, hospitals) Pre-experimental Yes (loosely) No One-group pretest-posttest, very weak. Many threats to validity. Non-experimental / Observational No No Just observe. Cohort, case-control, cross-sectional.

chunks.heading: Observational / Epidemiological
chunks.text: Observational / Epidemiological Design Direction Measure Use when Cohort Forward (exposure → outcome) Relative Risk (RR) Rare exposure, common outcome. Prospective stronger than retrospective. Case-control Backward (outcome → exposure) Odds Ratio (OR) Rare outcome (e.g., suicide). Cheaper, faster. Cross-sectional Single time point Prevalence Snapshots. Cannot establish temporality. Ecological Group-level data Correlation Risk: ecological fallacy (group → individual). Case study / case series Descriptive — Generates hypotheses, not tests them.

chunks.heading: By time
chunks.text: By time Cross-sectional — one time point. Cheap, no causation. Longitudinal — same subjects over time. Causation possible. Risk: attrition (drop-out). Cohort sequential — combines cross-sectional and longitudinal. Distinguishes age vs cohort effects.

chunks.heading: 9. Clinical Trial Phases & Design Features
chunks.text: 9. Clinical Trial Phases & Design Features Phase Purpose Sample size Phase 0 Microdosing, exploratory pharmacokinetics ~10-15 Phase I Safety, dose-finding, healthy volunteers (or patients for cancer drugs) 20-100 Phase II Efficacy + safety in target population 100-300 Phase III Confirmatory efficacy, comparison vs standard. Required for licensing. 1,000-3,000 Phase IV Post-marketing surveillance. Long-term effects, rare adverse events. Thousands+

chunks.heading: Blinding
chunks.text: Blinding Single-blind — subject doesn't know group allocation. Double-blind — subject AND researcher (assessor) don't know. Triple-blind — also data analyst is blinded. Open-label — no blinding. Used when blinding is impossible (surgery vs no surgery).

chunks.heading: Other RCT design features
chunks.text: Other RCT design features Placebo control — inert intervention to control for expectancy effects. Active control — comparison vs current standard treatment (more ethical when one exists). Crossover design — each subject receives both treatments in random order, separated by washout. Each subject is their own control. Cannot use for chronic/cure conditions. Intention-to-treat (ITT) analysis — analyze subjects in their originally assigned group, even if they dropped out or switched. Preserves randomization, more conservative. Per-protocol analysis — only analyze subjects who completed protocol. Inflates effect sizes.

chunks.heading: 10. Variables
chunks.text: 10. Variables Independent variable (IV) — manipulated or grouping variable. Cause. Dependent variable (DV) — measured outcome. Effect. Confounding variable — third variable associated with BOTH IV and DV; creates spurious associations. Control by randomization, matching, stratification, or statistical adjustment. Mediator (intervening) — explains how IV affects DV. IV → Mediator → DV. (Stress → cortisol → immune suppression.) Moderator — affects the strength or direction of the IV-DV relationship. (Therapy works better for women than men: sex moderates therapy → outcome.) Extraneous variable — any variable other than IV that could affect DV. Becomes a confound if associated with IV.

chunks.heading: 11. Validity in Research
chunks.text: 11. Validity in Research Different from validity of a test (which is in section 4 assessment). Here we mean validity of a study's conclusions . Type Question Threats Internal validity Did the IV cause the DV? History, maturation, testing, instrumentation, regression to mean, selection, attrition (Cook & Campbell) External validity Can we generalize to other people, settings, times? Sampling bias, artificial setting, novelty effects Construct validity Are we measuring the construct we claim? Mono-operation bias, mono-method bias, demand characteristics Statistical conclusion validity Is the statistical inference correct? Low power, Type I/II errors, violated assumptions, unreliable measures

chunks.heading: 12. Qualitative Methods
chunks.text: 12. Qualitative Methods Method Aim Hallmark Phenomenology (Husserl, Giorgi) Lived experience of a phenomenon "Bracketing" personal assumptions; rich description Grounded theory (Glaser & Strauss, 1967) Build theory from data Constant comparison, theoretical sampling, open/axial/selective coding Ethnography Understand a culture from within Long-term immersion, participant observation Narrative analysis How people story their lives Life history interviews Thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke, 2006) Identify recurring themes 6 phases: familiarize → coding → themes → review → define → write up Case study In-depth look at one case Multiple data sources triangulated Discourse analysis How language constructs meaning Examines power, ideology in talk/text

chunks.heading: Trustworthiness criteria (Lincoln & Guba, 1985)
chunks.text: Trustworthiness criteria (Lincoln & Guba, 1985) Credibility ≈ internal validity. Achieved by triangulation, member checking, prolonged engagement. Transferability ≈ external validity. Thick description of context. Dependability ≈ reliability. Audit trail. Confirmability ≈ objectivity. Reflexivity, audit.

chunks.heading: 13. Mixed Methods
chunks.text: 13. Mixed Methods Combines qualitative + quantitative for a fuller picture. Sequential explanatory: quant first, then qual to explain results. Sequential exploratory: qual first to develop hypotheses, then quant to test. Convergent (parallel): both done together, results compared. Embedded: one supplements the other (e.g., qual interviews within an RCT).

chunks.heading: 14. Research Ethics
chunks.text: 14. Research Ethics

chunks.heading: Foundational documents (memorize the order)
chunks.text: Foundational documents (memorize the order) Nuremberg Code (1947) — after Nazi medical experiments. First major ethics code. Voluntary consent absolute. Declaration of Helsinki (1964, last revised 2013) — World Medical Association. Ethics for medical research. Belmont Report (1979) — US, after Tuskegee syphilis study. Three principles below. CIOMS Guidelines — international ethics for biomedical research. ICMR Guidelines (India) — Indian Council of Medical Research, 2017 revision.

chunks.heading: Belmont Principles (memorize these three)
chunks.text: Belmont Principles (memorize these three) Respect for persons — autonomy, informed consent. Special protection for vulnerable groups. Beneficence — maximize benefits, minimize harm. Justice — fair distribution of risks and benefits. No exploiting vulnerable populations.

chunks.heading: Informed consent — required elements
chunks.text: Informed consent — required elements Purpose, procedures, expected duration Risks and benefits Alternative procedures Confidentiality Voluntary participation; right to withdraw without penalty Contact info for questions

chunks.heading: IRB / Ethics Committee
chunks.text: IRB / Ethics Committee Reviews proposals before data collection. Multidisciplinary: scientists + non-scientists + community member + lay person. Categories of review: exempt (low risk, anonymous data), expedited (minimal risk), full board (greater than minimal risk).

chunks.heading: Key ethical violations to know
chunks.text: Key ethical violations to know Tuskegee syphilis study (1932-1972) — Black men denied treatment to study natural progression of syphilis. Led directly to the Belmont Report. Milgram obedience experiment (1961) — deception, severe psychological distress. Stanford Prison Experiment (1971, Zimbardo) — inadequate safeguards, role conflict (Zimbardo as researcher AND superintendent). Little Albert (1920, Watson) — fear conditioning of an infant, no debriefing. Willowbrook hepatitis study (1956-1970) — children with intellectual disabilities deliberately infected with hepatitis.

chunks.heading: 15. Critical Appraisal & Evidence Hierarchy
chunks.text: 15. Critical Appraisal & Evidence Hierarchy

chunks.heading: Evidence hierarchy (top = strongest)
chunks.text: Evidence hierarchy (top = strongest) Systematic reviews / meta-analyses of RCTs Single well-designed RCT Cohort study Case-control study Cross-sectional / case series Case report Expert opinion / editorials

chunks.heading: Tools (good to recognize)
chunks.text: Tools (good to recognize) CONSORT — reporting standard for RCTs PRISMA — reporting standard for systematic reviews/meta-analyses STROBE — reporting for observational studies SPIRIT — reporting for trial protocols COREQ — reporting for qualitative research

chunks.heading: Diagnostic test stats (high-yield)
chunks.text: Diagnostic test stats (high-yield) Sensitivity = TP / (TP + FN). True positive rate. Sensitive test rules OUT (SnNout). Specificity = TN / (TN + FP). True negative rate. Specific test rules IN (SpPin). PPV = TP / (TP + FP). Positive predictive value. Depends on prevalence. NPV = TN / (TN + FN). Negative predictive value. Depends on prevalence. Likelihood ratios are prevalence-independent. LR+ = sensitivity / (1 − specificity). ROC curve — plots sensitivity vs (1 − specificity) across thresholds. AUC = 0.5 useless, 1.0 perfect.

chunks.heading: 16. Common MCQ Traps
chunks.text: 16. Common MCQ Traps "p < 0.05 means H₀ is false" — WRONG. p is conditional on H₀ being true. It does not give the probability of H₀. "Statistical significance = clinical importance" — WRONG. Tiny effects can be significant with huge n. "Cohort = retrospective; case-control = prospective" — REVERSED in many textbooks. Cohort can be either; case-control is always retrospective (start with the outcome and look back). Confusing OR and RR — OR ≈ RR only when outcome is rare (< 10%). For common outcomes, OR overstates RR. Sensitivity vs Specificity confusion — Sensitivity uses people who HAVE disease (column with disease); Specificity uses people who DON'T. SD vs SEM — SD describes data spread; SEM describes precision of the mean. SEM is always smaller. Researchers sometimes use SEM to make data look prettier — be skeptical. Type I vs Type II — α = false positive (reject true H₀). β = false negative (miss real effect). "Sigh, I missed it" = II. "Random sampling = random assignment" — DIFFERENT. Random sampling is about who gets in the study (external validity). Random assignment is about which group they go in (internal validity). "r = 0 means no relationship" — only for linear relationship. A perfect U-shaped curve has r ≈ 0. "ANOVA tells you which group differs" — NO. ANOVA only tells you at least one differs. Use post-hoc (Tukey, Bonferroni) for pairwise. Cross-sectional and caus

chunks.heading: Memorization Hooks
chunks.text: Memorization Hooks NOIR levels of measurement: Nominal, Ordinal, Interval, Ratio. "Sigh, I missed it" = Type II error. Cohort = "future" , Case-control = "past". SnNout, SpPin — Sensitive test, Negative result rules OUT; Specific test, Positive result rules IN. Mediator = how ; Moderator = for whom / when . 0.2 / 0.5 / 0.8 — Cohen's d small / medium / large. 0.10 / 0.30 / 0.50 — Pearson r small / medium / large. Belmont 3: Respect, Beneficence, Justice. RCT phases I→II→III→IV : safety → efficacy → confirmation → surveillance. Power = 1 − β. Aim for 0.80 (β = 0.20). Sihan MET 2026 + NIMHANS Prep — Section 6: Biostatistics & Research Methodology

chunks.heading: Biopsych — the disaster zone
chunks.text: Biopsych — the disaster zone Six wrongs out of 15 on the mock. Three of them sit on the same axis: pituitary ↔ hypothalamus ↔ metabolic neurochemistry . Lock these four blocks first. priority your-note n1_bio01 (PKU)

chunks.heading: Amino-acid → neurotransmitter pathway (PKU sits at step 1)
chunks.text: Amino-acid → neurotransmitter pathway (PKU sits at step 1) Your note: "DOnt know this. need to learn" Phenylalanine → Tyrosine via phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH) . PKU = PAH broken . Phenylalanine piles up (brain-toxic), tyrosine drops, melanin drops (fair hair/skin), classic musty odour. Autosomal recessive. Treat: low-Phe diet for life. Tyrosine → L-DOPA → Dopamine → Norepinephrine → Epinephrine. Whole catecholamine chain. Parkinson's loses DA at step 3 → treat with L-DOPA (DA itself doesn't cross BBB). Tryptophan → 5-HTP → Serotonin → Melatonin. Indolamine chain. SSRIs raise synaptic 5-HT. Tryptophan also → niacin (B3); pellagra = niacin deficiency. Histidine → Histamine. CNS arousal. Antihistamines that cross BBB sedate. Glutamate → GABA via GAD (B6 cofactor). Glutamate is the main excitatory NT; GABA is the main inhibitory NT. Benzos + alcohol potentiate GABA-A. priority your-note n1_bio03, n1_bio04

chunks.heading: Pituitary + hypothalamus (NIMHANS retests this axis every year)
chunks.text: Pituitary + hypothalamus (NIMHANS retests this axis every year)

chunks.heading: Anterior pituitary — FLAT PiG
chunks.text: Anterior pituitary — FLAT PiG F SH, L H, A CTH, T SH, P rolactin, G H. Six hormones, all tropic except prolactin + GH . Posterior pituitary : ADH + Oxytocin. Made in supraoptic + paraventricular hypothalamic nuclei, stored + released by posterior pituitary. Melatonin = pineal , not pituitary. Calcitonin = thyroid C cells. PTH = parathyroid. Insulin + glucagon + somatostatin = pancreatic islets .

chunks.heading: Hypothalamic nuclei lock-list
chunks.text: Hypothalamic nuclei lock-list Nucleus Function Lesion sign VMH (ventromedial) Satiety Hyperphagia + obesity (Hetherington-Ranson rat) LH (lateral) Hunger / arousal Aphagia + lethargy Anterior Cooling Hyperthermia Posterior Heating Poikilothermia SCN (suprachiasmatic) Circadian master clock Loss of circadian rhythm Supraoptic + paraventricular ADH + oxytocin synthesis Diabetes insipidus (ADH ↓) Mammillary bodies Memory (Papez circuit) Korsakoff's, anterograde amnesia + confabulation Arcuate DA to anterior pituitary; appetite (NPY/AgRP, POMC) Prolactin dysregulation Hierarchy trick. Thalamus = sensory relay (everything except smell). Hypothalamus = autonomic + endocrine integration. Brainstem (medulla) = autonomic reflex control (HR, BP, breathing). If the stem says "integrates endocrine, visceral, autonomic," the answer is hypothalamus, not brainstem. priority your-note n1_bio07, n1_bio15

chunks.heading: Wernicke-Korsakoff — one disease, two phases
chunks.text: Wernicke-Korsakoff — one disease, two phases Your note: "What is korsakoff, need to learn this" Cause: thiamine (vit B1) deficiency . Classic context: chronic alcoholism (poor diet + reduced absorption + thiamine demand). Wernicke encephalopathy (acute): triad of confusion + ophthalmoplegia + ataxia . Reversible if treated. Critical rule: IV thiamine BEFORE glucose. Giving glucose first burns the last thiamine and precipitates Wernicke. Korsakoff psychosis (chronic): anterograde amnesia + confabulation . Largely irreversible. Lesion = mammillary bodies + dorsomedial thalamus . Memory aid: WAR + KAR. Wernicke = (W)hite-eyes + (A)taxia + confusion (R)eversible. Korsakoff = (K)onfabulation + (A)nterograde + (R)etrograde, ir(R)eversible. Confabulation = false memories without intent to deceive. Distinguishes Korsakoff from malingering. Also in frontal lobe + ACoA aneurysm rupture. priority n1_bio13

chunks.heading: Extrapyramidal side effects (EPSEs), in time order
chunks.text: Extrapyramidal side effects (EPSEs), in time order You missed this on the mock by picking acute dystonia for an orofacial chronic case — flip the time-course around in your head and these stop tripping you. EPSE Onset Picture Treat Acute dystonia Hours to days Oculogyric crisis, torticollis, tongue protrusion (spasm) IM anticholinergic (procyclidine), benzos Akathisia Days to weeks Subjective restlessness, pacing, can't sit still Propranolol, lower dose, benzos Parkinsonism Weeks to months Bradykinesia, rigidity, pill-rolling tremor, mask face Anticholinergic, switch to atypical Tardive dyskinesia Months to years Orofacial choreoathetosis , lip-smacking, often irreversible Reduce/switch; VMAT2 inhibitor (tetrabenazine, valbenazine) Trigger word. If stem says "long-term antipsychotics" + "lip-smacking / tongue movements," it's tardive dyskinesia , no matter how plausible the other options sound. Monitor with AIMS (Abnormal Involuntary Movement Scale). NMS = idiosyncratic, hyperthermia + rigidity + autonomic instability + raised CK → stop drug, dantrolene/bromocriptine. lock-in your-note n1_bio02

chunks.heading: Adrenaline vs noradrenaline + adrenal anatomy
chunks.text: Adrenaline vs noradrenaline + adrenal anatomy Your note: "What about norepinephrine?" Adrenal cortex (GFR = salt, sugar, sex). Outside → in: Zona Glomerulosa = aldosterone (mineralocorticoid); Zona Fasciculata = cortisol (glucocorticoid); Zona Reticularis = androgens (DHEA). Adrenal medulla. Chromaffin cells = epinephrine (~80%) + norepinephrine (~20%). Directly innervated by sympathetic preganglionic fibres (skips the postganglionic step). NE/Noradrenaline is also the postganglionic sympathetic NT at most target organs (heart, vessels, sweat except palms). E is the hormonal systemic arm of the same response. HPA axis: hypothalamus CRH → anterior pituitary ACTH → adrenal cortex cortisol. Cortisol feeds back negatively to both. Dexamethasone suppression test = exogenous steroid that should shut down ACTH; non-suppression suggests Cushing's or pituitary tumour. lock-in n1_bio11

chunks.heading: Assessment — IQ history + WAIS structure
chunks.text: Assessment — IQ history + WAIS structure Two wrongs on the mock, both pure trivia. You flagged "don't know shit about the scoring" and "need to revise binet, terman, and all those people." priority your-note n1_ass08

chunks.heading: IQ history timeline — one row per name
chunks.text: IQ history timeline — one row per name Your note: "Need to revise what binet, terman, and all those people introduced one by one" Year Person What they introduced 1905 Binet + Simon (France) First practical intelligence test. Age-graded items. Concept of mental age . 1912 William Stern Coined IQ = (MA / CA) × 100 . The "ratio IQ." 1916 Lewis Terman (Stanford) American adaptation = Stanford-Binet . Used ratio IQ. 1939 David Wechsler Wechsler-Bellevue. Introduced Deviation IQ (M=100, SD=15) . Solved the adult problem (ratio IQ flattens with age). 1955+ Wechsler WAIS series. Verbal + Performance split. 1986 Stanford-Binet 4th Switched from ratio to deviation IQ. 2003 Stanford-Binet 5th Current US version, 5 factors aligned with CHC theory.

chunks.heading: Theorists of intelligence (not test-builders)
chunks.text: Theorists of intelligence (not test-builders) Spearman (1904): factor analysis → g (general) + s (specific). Thurstone (1938): 7 Primary Mental Abilities (verbal, word fluency, number, spatial, memory, perceptual speed, reasoning). Rejected g. Cattell (1963): fluid (Gf) vs crystallised (Gc) . Carroll (1993) + Cattell-Horn → CHC model (current dominant 3-stratum framework). Gardner (1983): multiple intelligences (9). Influential, weak empirical support. Sternberg (1985): triarchic (analytical / creative / practical) → later WICS model. Goleman (1995): popularised EQ (built on Salovey & Mayer 1990). priority your-note n1_ass04, n1_ass05

chunks.heading: WAIS-IV structure + scoring
chunks.text: WAIS-IV structure + scoring Your note: "Dont know shit about the scoring on this" / "Dont know anything about this" (subtest count) Index Core subtests (3+3+2+2 = 10) Supplemental VCI (Verbal Comprehension) Similarities, Vocabulary, Information Comprehension PRI (Perceptual Reasoning) Block Design, Matrix Reasoning, Visual Puzzles Picture Completion, Figure Weights WMI (Working Memory) Digit Span, Arithmetic Letter-Number Sequencing PSI (Processing Speed) Symbol Search, Coding Cancellation

chunks.heading: The two parallel scoring scales
chunks.text: The two parallel scoring scales Subtest scaled score: Mean = 10 , SD = 3 . Range typically 1-19. Scaled 10 = 50th percentile. 13 = +1 SD = 84th. 7 = -1 SD = 16th. Index / composite (VCI, PRI, WMI, PSI, FSIQ): Mean = 100 , SD = 15 . Same conversion logic.

chunks.heading: IQ classification (WAIS-IV)
chunks.text: IQ classification (WAIS-IV) ≥130 Very Superior · 120-129 Superior · 110-119 High Average · 90-109 Average · 80-89 Low Average · 70-79 Borderline · <70 ID range. DSM-5 ID severity is now based on adaptive functioning , not IQ alone.

chunks.heading: Wechsler family
chunks.text: Wechsler family WAIS-IV : 16-90. WISC-V : 6-16 (added Fluid Reasoning index). WPPSI-IV : 2;6 - 7;7. India: MISIC (Malin's WISC), BKT (Binet-Kamat-Telugu), VSMS (Vineland Social Maturity Scale, Doll/Malin), Seguin Form Board. standard scores

chunks.heading: Standard-score family (memorise this one table)
chunks.text: Standard-score family (memorise this one table) Score Mean SD Use Z-score 0 1 Generic; how many SDs from mean T-score 50 10 MMPI, CBCL, BDI IQ / Deviation IQ 100 15 WAIS, Stanford-Binet SAT / GRE 500 100 Standardised tests Stanine 5 2 9-point school testing Wechsler subtest scaled 10 3 WAIS-IV subtests Z ↔ percentile shortcuts. Z=0 → 50th. Z=±1 → 16th / 84th. Z=±2 → 2.5th / 97.5th. Z=±3 → 0.1st / 99.9th. SE (standard error) ≠ SD. SE = SD / √n — the SD of the sampling distribution of the mean. CV = (SD/mean) × 100 = unitless relative variability.

chunks.heading: Therapy — who founded what
chunks.text: Therapy — who founded what Three wrongs on the mock, all "school-attribution" failures — nothing conceptually hard, pure pairing. Plus two of your most explicit notes are here. priority your-note n1_thr09

chunks.heading: Splitting + BPD defenses + Vaillant hierarchy
chunks.text: Splitting + BPD defenses + Vaillant hierarchy Your note: "What is splitting?" Splitting = inability to hold opposing qualities (good + bad) about the same person at the same time. Person experienced as all-good (idealised) one moment, all-bad (devalued) the next. Targets flip rapidly, often mid-session. Kernberg identified it as core defense in BPD; Klein first described it in early infancy (paranoid-schizoid position).

chunks.heading: Vaillant's hierarchy of defenses
chunks.text: Vaillant's hierarchy of defenses Level Defenses Seen in Pathological / Psychotic Denial (psychotic), Distortion, Delusional projection Psychosis, severe states Immature Acting out, Passive aggression, Projection, Splitting , Somatisation, Fantasy, Dissociation PDs (esp. cluster B), adolescence Neurotic Repression, Reaction formation, Displacement, Intellectualisation, Rationalisation , Isolation of affect, Undoing Anxiety / OCD / neurotic functioning Mature Altruism, Anticipation, Humour, Sublimation, Suppression Healthy adult

chunks.heading: BPD-specific defenses (Kernberg) + treatments
chunks.text: BPD-specific defenses (Kernberg) + treatments Defenses: splitting, projective identification, primitive idealisation, devaluation, omnipotent control, denial. Klein's positions: paranoid-schizoid (splitting, projection, idealisation/devaluation, <6 months) → depressive (integration of good + bad object, ~6 months). BPD = stuck in paranoid-schizoid. Treatments: DBT (Linehan), MBT (Bateman & Fonagy, mentalisation-based), TFP (Clarkin & Kernberg, transference-focused), Schema Therapy (Young). priority n1_thr04

chunks.heading: Ellis vs Beck — the dividing line
chunks.text: Ellis vs Beck — the dividing line You picked Beck on a "musterbation" question on the mock. The two are easy to swap. Trigger-words: Ellis — REBT (1955). ABC model (Activating event → Belief → Consequence) + D ispute + E ffective new philosophy. Targets irrational beliefs , especially "musts / shoulds / oughts" (musterbation) , awfulizing, catastrophising, low-frustration-tolerance, global self-rating. Confrontational style. Beck — Cognitive Therapy (1960s). Cognitive triad in depression: negative view of self / world / future . Targets automatic thoughts, cognitive distortions, schemas . Collaborative empiricism , Socratic. Beck's distortions: all-or-nothing, overgeneralisation, mental filter, disqualifying the positive, jumping to conclusions (mind-reading + fortune-telling), magnification / minimisation, emotional reasoning, "should" statements, labelling, personalisation. Trigger words. "Musterbation / ABC / irrational belief / disputation" → Ellis . "Cognitive triad / schema / automatic thought / cognitive distortion" → Beck . CBT waves. 1st-wave = behaviour therapy (Wolpe, Skinner). 2nd-wave = cognitive (Ellis, Beck, Meichenbaum). 3rd-wave = DBT (Linehan, Zen-rooted), ACT (Hayes), MBCT (Segal/Williams/Teasdale), MBSR (Kabat-Zinn). priority n1_thr01

chunks.heading: Group-modality founders
chunks.text: Group-modality founders You picked "group analysis" for Maxwell Jones. Maxwell Jones = therapeutic community, not group analysis. Modality Founder Key idea Therapeutic community Maxwell Jones (Henderson Hospital, 1953) Democratic ward; communalism + reality confrontation (Rapoport's 4) Milieu therapy Bettelheim; Stanton & Schwartz Total environment as treatment. Broader than TC Group analysis S.H. Foulkes Psychoanalytic group work, group-as-a-whole, "matrix" T-groups / sensitivity training Kurt Lewin (NTL, 1947) Here-and-now feedback, organisational application Encounter groups Carl Rogers (1960s) Humanistic, personal growth Psychodrama J.L. Moreno Acting out conflicts, role reversal, doubling Self-help (AA) Bill W. & Dr. Bob (1935) 12 steps, peer support Yalom's group therapy Irvin Yalom 11 therapeutic factors (universality, altruism, etc.) your-note n1_thr03

chunks.heading: Logotherapy + existential family
chunks.text: Logotherapy + existential family Your note: "Need more info on this" Viktor Frankl (1905-1997). Austrian psychiatrist + Holocaust survivor. Built Logotherapy = "third Viennese school" (after Freud + Adler). Book: Man's Search for Meaning (1946). Core premise: primary human motivation = will to meaning (vs Freud's will to pleasure, Adler's will to power). Three paths to meaning: (1) creative work / deed; (2) experience / love; (3) attitude toward unavoidable suffering. Techniques: paradoxical intention (deliberately try the feared thing — predates ERP), dereflection (shift attention from symptom), Socratic dialogue. "Existential vacuum" = meaninglessness, boredom, conformism, "Sunday neurosis."

chunks.heading: Existential / humanistic family tree
chunks.text: Existential / humanistic family tree Existential therapy: Rollo May, Yalom (4 ultimate concerns: death, freedom, isolation, meaninglessness) , Binswanger (Daseinsanalysis). Person-centred: Rogers — UPR + empathy + congruence (three "necessary and sufficient conditions"). Gestalt: Perls — empty chair, here-and-now, awareness, I-thou. Self-actualisation: Maslow — hierarchy (physiological / safety / love / esteem / self-actualisation [+ self-transcendence late]). lock-in n1_thr08

chunks.heading: DBT structure (NIMHANS asks this every paper)
chunks.text: DBT structure (NIMHANS asks this every paper) Marsha Linehan (1993), originally for chronically suicidal BPD. Mindfulness component drawn from her Zen Buddhism practice. Dialectic: simultaneous truth of acceptance + change . The synthesis is the therapy. 4 modules: Mindfulness (core) · Distress Tolerance · Emotion Regulation · Interpersonal Effectiveness . Delivery: individual therapy + skills group + phone coaching + therapist consultation team. "Wise mind" = integration of emotion mind + reasonable mind.

chunks.heading: Family therapy four-by-four (recap)
chunks.text: Family therapy four-by-four (recap) School Founder Core idea Structural Minuchin Subsystems, boundaries, hierarchies. Restructure enmeshment / disengagement. Strategic Haley , Madanes (MRI: Watzlawick) Symptoms maintain power balance. Directives, paradox, reframing. Bowenian / intergenerational Bowen Differentiation of self, triangulation, genograms. Experiential Satir , Whitaker Communication patterns (placater, blamer, computer, distractor, leveler), affect. Milan systemic Selvini-Palazzoli et al. Circular questioning, hypothesising, neutrality, paradox.

chunks.text: ICD vs DSM duration cheat — NIMHANS is ICD-leaning Your note: "Need more of these things related to ICD, never read ICD" Disorder ICD-10 / 11 DSM-5 Schizophrenia ≥1 month ≥6 months total (≥1 month active) Brief psychotic disorder <1 month (acute polymorphic) ≥1 day to <1 month Schizophreniform (not a separate category) 1-6 months Major depressive episode ≥2 weeks ≥2 weeks Mania ≥1 week (or any if hospitalised) ≥1 week (or any if hospitalised) Hypomania ≥4 days ≥4 days Dysthymia / Persistent depressive ≥2 years ≥2 years adults / 1 year children Cyclothymia ≥2 years ≥2 years adults / 1 year children GAD ≥6 months ≥6 months Panic disorder recurrent unexpected attacks recurrent + ≥1 month worry / change PTSD >1 month after event >1 month after event Acute stress reaction (ICD) / disorder (DSM) up to 1 month 3 days to 1 month Adjustment disorder within 1 month, lasts <6 months within 3 months, <6 months after stressor ends Anorexia nervosa BMI <17.5 no specific BMI, "significantly low" Rule. Always check which classification the stem names. NIMHANS leans ICD (Indian), MET often DSM. If unspecified, NIMHANS papers usually accept ICD answers. priority n1_abn11

chunks.heading: Ego-dystonic vs ego-syntonic
chunks.text: Ego-dystonic vs ego-syntonic Ego-dystonic = experienced as alien / unwanted / not me . Ego-syntonic = experienced as consistent with self / "this is who I am" . OCD obsessions are ego-dystonic → insight preserved, patient fights the thought, distressed. Not the same as "poor insight" (DSM-5 specifier). Personality disorders are typically ego-syntonic → patient doesn't see traits as a problem → poor insight + poor treatment-seeking.

chunks.heading: OCD high-yield (NIMHANS recurring)
chunks.text: OCD high-yield (NIMHANS recurring) DSM-5: OCD moved out of anxiety into own chapter "Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders" (with BDD, hoarding, trichotillomania, excoriation). Treatment: SSRIs (high dose, 10-12 wks trial), clomipramine (TCA, serotonergic), ERP (Exposure and Response Prevention) = gold standard psychotherapy. Neurobiology: CSTC loop (cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical), hyperactive OFC + caudate. Insight specifiers: good/fair, poor, absent/delusional. priority n1_abn02

chunks.heading: Delusional misidentification four-pack + extras
chunks.text: Delusional misidentification four-pack + extras Othello syndrome: delusion that spouse is unfaithful . Strong link to alcohol-use disorder + IPV. Capgras syndrome: familiar person has been replaced by an identical impostor . Recognition without familiarity. Ventral-visual / limbic disconnection. Fregoli syndrome: multiple strangers are the same persecutor in disguise . Familiarity without recognition. Opposite of Capgras. De Clérambault (erotomania): belief a high-status person is in love with the patient. Cotard delusion: belief one is dead / non-existent / decomposing. Severe psychotic depression. Folie à deux: delusion transmitted from a "dominant" inducer to a closely related recipient. Dropped from DSM-5 as separate diagnosis, still used clinically. lock-in n1_abn12

chunks.heading: Schizophrenia theorists (this is a 2023 + 2024 NIMHANS repeat)
chunks.text: Schizophrenia theorists (this is a 2023 + 2024 NIMHANS repeat) Kraepelin (1893): "dementia praecox" = early-onset deteriorating psychosis. Distinguished from "manic-depressive insanity" (now bipolar). The Kraepelinian dichotomy = foundation of modern nosology. Bleuler (1908): renamed it schizophrenia ("splitting of mind"). 4 As: Association (loose), Affect (flat), Ambivalence, Autism (withdrawal). "Fundamental" vs "accessory" symptoms. Schneider (1959): first-rank symptoms : thought insertion / withdrawal / broadcasting, audible thoughts, voices commenting / arguing, somatic passivity, delusional perception. Used in ICD-10; ICD-11 dropped emphasis. Crow: Type I (positive sx, drug-responsive) vs Type II (negative sx, treatment-resistant). Outdated. Andreasen + Carpenter: positive / negative / disorganised dimensions.

chunks.heading: Social Psych — named effects + ABCD personalities
chunks.text: Social Psych — named effects + ABCD personalities Three wrongs on the mock, all "named concept" trivia (Genovese, Type D, anomie). Each is one paragraph of reading. priority your-note n1_soc06

chunks.heading: The ABCD personality family
chunks.text: The ABCD personality family Your note: "What is type D. I know type a and b" Type Profile Risk for Type A (Friedman & Rosenman, 1959) Hostility, time-urgency, competitiveness, achievement-driven, impatient CHD — hostility is the active ingredient; "TABP" alone is a weaker predictor Type B Relaxed, easy-going, low urgency, non-competitive Lower CHD risk Type C (Temoshok) Emotionally inhibited, appeasing, suppresses anger, pleasing Cancer progression (controversial) Type D (Denollet, 1996) Negative affectivity + Social inhibition Cardiac mortality + depression + poor MI outcomes. Measured with DS14 priority your-note n1_soc10

chunks.heading: Anomie + the sociologists
chunks.text: Anomie + the sociologists Your note: "Never heard of this" Durkheim (1893, 1897): anomie = breakdown / unclear / conflicting social norms during periods of rapid change (industrialisation, economic shock). Individual loses moral guidance → deviance + despair. Per Suicide (1897): anomic suicide , one of four types (egoistic, altruistic, anomic, fatalistic). Also: mechanical vs organic solidarity, collective consciousness. Merton (1938): extended anomie to strain theory . Mismatch between cultural goals (wealth) and legitimate means → 5 adaptations: conformity, innovation (crime), ritualism, retreatism, rebellion . Weber: bureaucracy, "iron cage," Protestant work ethic, rationalisation. Marx: alienation (from product, process, species-being, others). Mead: symbolic interactionism, "I" vs "Me," generalised other. Cooley: looking-glass self, primary vs secondary groups. Goffman: dramaturgy, front-stage / back-stage, stigma. your-note n1_soc01

chunks.heading: Named social-psych effects (you asked for the bigger list)
chunks.text: Named social-psych effects (you asked for the bigger list) Your note: "Need more topics like this to study" Bystander effect (Latané + Darley, Kitty Genovese 1964) = diffusion of responsibility + pluralistic ignorance . Latané's 5 steps: notice → interpret as emergency → assume responsibility → know how to help → decide to help. Any step can break. Cognitive dissonance (Festinger 1957) = inconsistency between attitudes / behaviour produces drive to reduce. Foot-in-the-door (Freedman & Fraser): small request first, larger later. Door-in-the-face (Cialdini): large refused first, smaller after. Low-balling (Cialdini): initial offer changed after commitment. Cialdini's 6 weapons of influence: reciprocity, scarcity, social proof, liking, authority, commitment + consistency. Self-fulfilling prophecy (Merton). Pygmalion effect (Rosenthal & Jacobson teacher-expectancy). Stereotype threat (Steele & Aronson): awareness of stereotype impairs performance. Group polarisation (Stoner): groups become more extreme than individual averages. Groupthink (Janis): 8 symptoms (illusion of invulnerability, etc.). Bay of Pigs example. Social loafing (Ringelmann / Latané): individual effort drops in groups. Social facilitation (Triplett / Zajonc): easy tasks ↑, hard tasks ↓ in presence of others. Deindividuation (Zimbardo): loss of self in groups. Stanford prison. Conformity / obedience: Asch (lines),

chunks.heading: Biostats — risk ratios, sampling, reliability
chunks.text: Biostats — risk ratios, sampling, reliability priority your-note n1_bst01

chunks.heading: RR / OR / HR / NNT — the four-row table that owns biostats MCQs
chunks.text: RR / OR / HR / NNT — the four-row table that owns biostats MCQs Your note: "wtf is risk ratio?" Measure What it is When used RR (risk ratio / relative risk) incidence in exposed / incidence in unexposed Cohort, RCT OR (odds ratio) odds of exposure in cases / odds in controls Case-control (you can't compute incidence) HR (hazard ratio) instantaneous risk ratio over time Survival analysis, Cox regression ARR (absolute risk reduction) risk-unexposed − risk-exposed RCTs NNT 1 / ARR How many to treat to prevent 1 outcome RR = 1 → no association. RR > 1 → exposure raises risk. RR < 1 → exposure protects. OR ≈ RR when outcome is rare (<10%). OR exaggerates effect when outcome is common. priority your-note n1_bst01b

chunks.heading: Plug-in formulae (you asked for standard error etc.)
chunks.text: Plug-in formulae (you asked for standard error etc.) Quantity Formula Note SEM (standard error of the mean) SD / √n SD of the sampling distribution of the mean. Bigger n → smaller. Always < SD. SEm (standard error of measurement) SD × √(1 − r) r = reliability. The trap pair with SEM. Stem says "reliability" → this one. SD √[Σ(x − x̄)² / (n − 1)] Variance = SD². z-score (x − mean) / SD For a sample mean: (x̄ − μ) / SEM. 95% CI mean ± 1.96 × SEM 1.96 (95%), 2.58 (99%). Cohen's d (M₁ − M₂) / pooled SD 0.2 / 0.5 / 0.8. CV (coefficient of variation) (SD / mean) × 100 Unitless relative variability. r² (Pearson r)² Variance explained. NNT 1 / ARR Round up. Lower = better drug. OR from 2×2 (a×d) / (b×c) ad over bc. Odds ↔ probability odds = p / (1 − p) p = odds / (1 + odds). The one trap: SEM (SD/√n, precision of a mean) vs SEm (SD√(1−r), error band on one score) sound identical. "reliability" in the stem → SEm. priority n1_bst05

chunks.heading: Sampling: probability vs non-probability
chunks.text: Sampling: probability vs non-probability Method Probability? One-liner Simple random Yes Pure random from frame Systematic Yes Every kth person from frame Stratified Yes Random within every stratum . Lowest sampling error. Cluster Yes Random whole clusters , all units within. Cheap, higher error. Multi-stage cluster Yes Cluster → subcluster → individual Quota No Researcher fills predetermined quotas. Can't compute SE. Purposive / judgmental No Hand-picked by researcher for a reason Convenience No Whoever is around Snowball No Chain referral. Hidden populations. Lock-in. "Can I compute SE?" → probability. "Did the researcher hand-pick?" → non-probability. Stem says " does NOT allow calculation of sampling error " → non-probability (usually quota). Stratified vs cluster (often swapped): Stratified = split into strata then sample from each . Cluster = pick whole clusters then sample everyone within. Stratified guarantees representation; cluster saves cost. priority n1_bst08

chunks.heading: Reliability vs validity — statistic by concept
chunks.text: Reliability vs validity — statistic by concept Concept Statistic Question asked Test-retest reliability Pearson r over time Same person, two occasions, same result? Inter-rater reliability Cohen's κ (categorical), ICC (continuous), Fleiss' κ (>2 raters) Two raters, same person, same score? Internal consistency Cronbach's α , KR-20 (dichotomous), split-half Do items measure the same thing? Parallel forms Pearson r between forms Two versions, same score? Face validity Subjective Looks like it measures the thing? Content validity Expert review / CVI Covers the domain? Criterion validity r with criterion Concurrent (same time) or predictive (future) Construct validity Factor analysis, MTMM Measures the latent construct? Convergent + discriminant. Lock-in. "Agreement between raters" → κ . "Items hang together / scale consistency" → α . Landis-Koch for κ: >0.81 almost perfect; 0.61-0.80 substantial; 0.41-0.60 moderate; <0.40 weak. your-note n1_bst06

chunks.heading: Factor analysis basics (you flagged this completely)
chunks.text: Factor analysis basics (you flagged this completely) Your note: "Dont know anything about this" Kaiser-Guttman rule: retain factors with eigenvalue > 1.0. Eigenvalue = variance explained by a factor in standardised units. >1 means the factor explains more variance than a single observed variable would. Scree plot (Cattell): plot eigenvalues against factor number. Find the "elbow" where the line flattens. Keep factors above the elbow. EFA (exploratory): no a-priori structure, let data tell you. Common in scale development. CFA (confirmatory): you have a model, test it. Uses SEM. Rotation: orthogonal (varimax) = factors stay uncorrelated. Oblique (promax, oblimin) = factors allowed to correlate. Psych constructs usually correlate. Loading: correlation of an item with a factor. ≥0.30 = weak, ≥0.40 = moderate, ≥0.50 = strong. PCA vs FA: PCA = data reduction, total variance. FA = latent structure, common variance. lock-in

chunks.heading: Parametric ↔ non-parametric pairing + reporting guidelines
chunks.text: Parametric ↔ non-parametric pairing + reporting guidelines Parametric Non-parametric Use Independent t-test Mann-Whitney U (Wilcoxon rank-sum) Compare 2 independent groups Paired t-test Wilcoxon signed-rank Compare 2 related/paired scores (pre-post) One-way ANOVA Kruskal-Wallis H 3+ independent groups Repeated-measures ANOVA Friedman test 3+ related conditions Pearson r Spearman ρ (or Kendall τ) Correlation (none, categorical) Chi-square / Fisher's exact 2 categorical variables

chunks.heading: Reporting guidelines
chunks.text: Reporting guidelines CONSORT = RCTs. PRISMA = systematic reviews / meta-analyses. STARD = diagnostic accuracy. STROBE = observational. COREQ / SRQR = qualitative. SPIRIT = trial protocols. CARE = case reports. TRIPOD = prediction models. Evidence pyramid: 1a SR of RCTs > 1b RCT > 2a Cohort > 2b Case-control > 3 Case series > 4 Expert opinion. Type I (α) = false positive. Type II (β) = false negative. Power = 1 − β .

chunks.heading: General / Cognitive — Baddeley + Wallas + Weber
chunks.text: General / Cognitive — Baddeley + Wallas + Weber priority n1_gen01

chunks.heading: Baddeley working-memory model
chunks.text: Baddeley working-memory model Component Role Capacity / type Central executive Attentional controller , task-switching (NOT a store) Modality-free, limited Phonological loop Verbal + acoustic info ~2 seconds; phonological store + articulatory rehearsal Visuospatial sketchpad Visual + spatial info "Inner eye"; visual cache + inner scribe Episodic buffer (2000) Binds slave systems + LTM into coherent episode Limited multimodal store Trap. Central executive is the controller , episodic buffer is the store that binds across modalities . If the stem says "integrates phonological + visuospatial + LTM," the answer is the episodic buffer .

chunks.heading: Memory taxonomy (Squire's model)
chunks.text: Memory taxonomy (Squire's model) Long-term memory = Declarative / Explicit (conscious; Episodic + Semantic; hippocampus + MTL) plus Non-declarative / Implicit (unconscious; Procedural + Priming + Classical conditioning + Non-associative). Short-term / working memory = Baddeley's model. Sensory memory: iconic (visual, ~250ms, Sperling), echoic (auditory, ~2-4s). Procedural = basal ganglia + cerebellum + motor cortex (none touched in H.M.). your-note n1_gen02

chunks.heading: Wallas creativity stages + theorists
chunks.text: Wallas creativity stages + theorists Your note: "DOnt know this theory" Preparation — gather info, define problem, attempt direct solutions. Incubation — set aside, unconscious processing. Illumination — the "aha" moment. Verification — test and refine. (Some add "intimation" between incubation and illumination as a 5th stage.)

chunks.heading: Creativity bundle
chunks.text: Creativity bundle Guilford: convergent vs divergent thinking . Divergent = many possible solutions, marker of creativity. Alternate Uses Test . Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking (TTCT): fluency, flexibility, originality, elaboration. Mednick: Remote Associates Test (RAT) — find 4th word linking three remote ones. Csikszentmihalyi: flow (skill = challenge). Systems model (person + domain + field). Amabile: componential model = domain skills + creativity-relevant processes + task motivation. Sternberg: investment theory ("buy low, sell high"). lock-in n1_gen10

chunks.heading: Weber / Fechner / Stevens + signal detection
chunks.text: Weber / Fechner / Stevens + signal detection Weber's Law (1834): ΔI / I = k . JND is a constant fraction of original intensity. In a room with 1 candle, adding 1 is obvious; in a room with 100, you need ~10. Fechner's Law (1860): Sensation = k × log(intensity). Subjective magnitude grows as the log of physical intensity. Stevens' Power Law (1957): Sensation = k × (intensity) a . Different exponents per modality (brightness ~0.33, length ~1.0, electric shock ~3.5). Psychophysics methods (Fechner): method of limits, method of constant stimuli, method of adjustment. Signal detection theory (Green & Swets): d' = sensitivity (separates signal from noise). β / c = response criterion (bias). 4 outcomes: hit, miss, false alarm, correct rejection. lock-in your-note n1_gen03

chunks.heading: Bandura observational learning — ARRM
chunks.text: Bandura observational learning — ARRM Your note: "Accidentally marked this wrong" The careless miss. You knew this. Bandura's 4 processes: Attention → Retention → Reproduction → Motivation (ARRM). Reinforcement is not required — vicarious reinforcement (watching someone else get rewarded) is enough. Bobo Doll study (1961) proved kids imitate aggression they only observed . Reciprocal determinism: behaviour, person, environment all influence each other. Self-efficacy = belief in one's ability to execute the behaviours needed for an outcome. Four sources: mastery experience, vicarious experience, social persuasion, physiological / affective state. Modelling: live, symbolic (media), verbal-instructional.

chunks.heading: Self-concept bundle (you asked for "more concepts like looking-glass self")
chunks.text: Self-concept bundle (you asked for "more concepts like looking-glass self") your-note n1_soc08 Your note: "Need more concepts like this" Looking-glass self (Cooley, 1902): 3 steps → I imagine how I appear, I imagine the other's judgement, I feel a self-feeling. Self is built from imagined reflections, not actual ones. Mead's "I" and "Me": I = spontaneous, subjective. Me = internalised social self. Generalised other = internalised perspective of "society." Self-perception theory (Bem): we infer our attitudes from our behaviour. Self-schema (Markus): cognitive generalisations about the self. Possible selves (Markus & Nurius): future-oriented self-representations. Self-discrepancy theory (Higgins): actual / ideal / ought selves. Ideal − actual → depression; ought − actual → anxiety. Social identity theory (Tajfel & Turner): personal vs group identity; in-group favouritism. Self-determination theory (Deci & Ryan): autonomy + competence + relatedness.

chunks.heading: Developmental (you got 10/10, but you flagged 2)
chunks.text: Developmental (you got 10/10, but you flagged 2) your-note n1_dev01

chunks.heading: Thomas & Chess temperament + adjacent
chunks.text: Thomas & Chess temperament + adjacent Your note: "Dont know this model" Thomas & Chess (NYLS, 1956+): 9 dimensions clustered into 3 types + mixed . Easy (~40%): regular rhythms, positive approach, adapts fast, positive mood. Difficult (~10%): irregular rhythms, withdraws, slow adapt, negative + intense. Slow-to-warm-up (~15%): low activity, mild reactions, slow but eventual adapt. Mixed (~35%): no clean fit. Goodness of fit: developmental outcome depends on the match between temperament + parenting demands. Kagan: behavioural inhibition (shy / fearful infants, 15-20% of toddlers). Linked to amygdala reactivity. Rothbart: reactivity + self-regulation; adds an effortful-control dimension. Buss & Plomin (EAS): Emotionality, Activity, Sociability. your-note n1_dev02

chunks.heading: Marshmallow Test + Mischel hot/cool
chunks.text: Marshmallow Test + Mischel hot/cool Your note: "Briefly explain this to me" Mischel (Stanford, 1960s-70s): 3-5 year olds offered 1 marshmallow now or 2 if they waited ~15 min. Outcome = wait time . Follow-ups (Mischel & Shoda): waiting predicted SAT, BMI, social competence, self-regulation in adolescence + adulthood. Mechanism: waiters used cognitive strategies (look away, distract, reframe marshmallow as "cloud not food"). Basis of hot/cool system : hot = limbic, impulsive; cool = prefrontal, regulatory. Replication caveat: Watts, Duncan & Quan (2018) found effects shrink substantially when family SES is controlled. Paradigm is real, deterministic narrative is overstated. Connects to: executive function (Diamond), self-regulation (Rothbart), delay aversion in ADHD (Sonuga-Barke).

chunks.heading: Exam-day execution rules
chunks.text: Exam-day execution rules Underline NOT / EXCEPT / LEAST / ALL in the stem before reading options. Half your "knew it but got it wrong" misses are negation-blindness. Cost the same as not knowing the answer. If 3 options agree and 1 disagrees on an antonym / "NOT" question, the outlier is usually the answer. Read the relationship in the stem (synonym? antonym? part-whole? cause-effect?) before scanning options. Eliminate options with extreme words on RC main-idea questions: "every, always, never, all, none, only, must." Pick the most general statement the passage actually supports. Hedging language ("can," "may," "in some cases," "a range of") → tone is "supportive but qualified," not absolute. If the stem names ICD, give ICD durations. If DSM, give DSM. If unspecified on NIMHANS, default to ICD. For trigger-word school attribution: "musterbation / ABC / irrational" → Ellis. "Cognitive triad / schema / automatic thought" → Beck. "Empty chair / here-and-now" → Perls / Gestalt. "Therapeutic community" → Maxwell Jones. "Logotherapy / will to meaning" → Frankl. "Zen + mindfulness for BPD" → Linehan / DBT. Don't guess on biostats unless the four-row table (RR/OR/HR/NNT) is firm. Your mock-1 numbers had you guessing 4-5 of 10 biostats Qs — that's a coin flip for ~20% of NIMHANS marks. Marathon pacing: 100 Qs / 90 min = 54 sec/Q. If a question takes >90 sec, mark + skip. Come back if t
