chunks.heading: 1. Macro View: Sleep is Two Modes
chunks.text: 1. Macro View: Sleep is Two Modes Sleep splits into NREM (Non-REM) and REM (Rapid Eye Movement) . NREM has 3 stages. Total = 4 stages of sleep. NREM REM Brain activity Slows progressively Fast, almost like awake Muscle tone Normal, relaxed Atonia (paralyzed) Eye movements Slow or absent Rapid bursts Dreaming Rare, thought-like Vivid, narrative Heart rate / BP Low, stable Variable, elevated Breathing Slow, regular Irregular Thermoregulation Works Fails (we do not shiver/sweat normally) Memory role Declarative consolidation (esp. NREM 3) Procedural + emotional consolidation

chunks.heading: 2. The Four Stages
chunks.text: 2. The Four Stages

chunks.heading: NREM Stage 1 — Transition (about 5% of night)
chunks.text: NREM Stage 1 — Transition (about 5% of night) EEG: theta waves (4–8 Hz) . Very light sleep, easily woken. People often say they were not asleep. Hypnagogic images, muscle twitches (hypnic jerks). Duration: 5–10 minutes at start of night.

chunks.heading: NREM Stage 2 — Light Sleep (about 45–55% of night)
chunks.text: NREM Stage 2 — Light Sleep (about 45–55% of night) EEG: theta + sleep spindles (12–14 Hz bursts) + K-complexes (large single waves). Core sign of being “truly asleep.” Body temperature drops, heart rate slows. Most of the night spent here. Increases as night progresses. Spindles come from the thalamus, gate sensory input so you stay asleep.

chunks.heading: NREM Stage 3 — Slow-Wave Sleep / Deep Sleep / Delta (about 15–20%)
chunks.text: NREM Stage 3 — Slow-Wave Sleep / Deep Sleep / Delta (about 15–20%) EEG: delta waves (0.5–4 Hz), high amplitude . Deepest sleep. Hard to rouse. If woken, groggy (sleep inertia). Growth hormone released here. Immune repair, glycogen restoration. Parasomnias (sleepwalking, sleep terrors, bedwetting) come OUT of NREM 3, not REM. Common in children because children have more delta sleep. Dominates the FIRST HALF of the night.

chunks.heading: REM — Paradoxical Sleep (about 20–25%)
chunks.text: REM — Paradoxical Sleep (about 20–25%) EEG: mixed frequency, low amplitude , looks almost like awake. “Paradoxical” because brain is active but body is paralyzed. Muscle atonia (pons actively suppresses motor output via medial medulla → spinal cord). Only eye muscles and diaphragm keep moving. Vivid narrative dreams. Emotional, story-like. Eye bursts (the “RE” in REM). Autonomic instability: irregular HR, BP, breathing. Penile/clitoral tumescence. REM episodes GET LONGER across the night. First REM is short (10 min), last REM can be 45+ min. Dominates the SECOND HALF of the night.

chunks.heading: 3. Sleep Cycle Architecture
chunks.text: 3. Sleep Cycle Architecture One full cycle = ~90 minutes . Sequence through the night, typical young adult: Night start: Wake → N1 → N2 → N3 → N2 → REM → (first cycle, ~90 min, mostly N3, short REM) → N2 → N3 → N2 → REM → (second cycle, less N3, longer REM) → N2 → REM → (third cycle, minimal N3, long REM) → N2 → REM → (fourth / fifth cycles: REM-dominated, minimal N3) 4–6 cycles per 8 hours. First half of night = deep sleep heavy (N3 for body repair). Second half = REM heavy (for memory consolidation and dreams). If sleep is cut short, you lose REM disproportionately.

chunks.heading: 4. Neural Control
chunks.text: 4. Neural Control

chunks.heading: Sleep onset
chunks.text: Sleep onset Promoted by adenosine accumulating through the day (caffeine blocks adenosine receptors, which is why coffee keeps you awake). VLPO (Ventrolateral preoptic nucleus) of the hypothalamus = “sleep switch.” GABAergic, inhibits wake-promoting regions. Melatonin from pineal gland, released in darkness.

chunks.heading: Wake
chunks.text: Wake Ascending Reticular Activating System (ARAS) of the brainstem. Neurotransmitters: histamine (tuberomammillary nucleus), orexin/hypocretin (lateral hypothalamus), norepinephrine (locus coeruleus), serotonin (raphe), acetylcholine (PPT/LDT). Loss of orexin neurons = narcolepsy .

chunks.heading: REM vs NREM switching
chunks.text: REM vs NREM switching Driven by a flip-flop between: REM-ON cells: cholinergic neurons in PPT/LDT (acetylcholine surge during REM). REM-OFF cells: aminergic neurons (NE in locus coeruleus, 5-HT in raphe) — silent during REM. Atonia mechanism: during REM, pontine REM-on neurons activate medial medulla (magnocellular nucleus) → hyperpolarizes spinal motor neurons → full-body paralysis except diaphragm and eyes.

chunks.heading: Circadian
chunks.text: Circadian SCN (Suprachiasmatic nucleus) of the hypothalamus = master clock, ~24.2 hr intrinsic period. Entrained by light via the retinohypothalamic tract (non-visual, from intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells). SCN → pineal gland → melatonin release in darkness. Core body temperature dips at night (~2 AM), rises in morning.

chunks.heading: 5. Sleep Across the Lifespan
chunks.text: 5. Sleep Across the Lifespan Age Total sleep % REM Notes Newborn 16–18 hrs ~50% Enters sleep via REM (adults enter via N1) Infant (1 yr) 14 hrs ~30% — Child (5 yr) 11–12 hrs ~25% Most parasomnias occur now Adolescent 9 hrs ~20% Delayed sleep phase is developmentally normal Adult 7–8 hrs ~20–25% Standard baseline Elderly (65+) 6–7 hrs ~15–20% Less N3, more awakenings, phase advance

chunks.heading: 6. Sleep Disorders (DSM-5, MCQ High Yield)
chunks.text: 6. Sleep Disorders (DSM-5, MCQ High Yield)

chunks.heading: Dyssomnias (difficulty with amount/timing/quality)
chunks.text: Dyssomnias (difficulty with amount/timing/quality) Disorder Core feature Treatment Insomnia Difficulty falling/staying asleep, 3 nights/wk × 3 months CBT-I first line, then hypnotics short-term Narcolepsy Excessive daytime sleepiness, cataplexy (sudden muscle tone loss triggered by emotion), sleep paralysis , hypnagogic/hypnopompic hallucinations . Cause: orexin/hypocretin deficiency . REM intrudes into wake. Modafinil, stimulants; sodium oxybate for cataplexy Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA) Airway collapses during sleep, repeated apneas/hypopneas, snoring, daytime sleepiness CPAP Central Sleep Apnea Brainstem fails to signal breathing CPAP/BiPAP Restless Legs Syndrome Urge to move legs, worse at rest/night, relieved by movement. Dopamine deficit, low iron Dopamine agonists (pramipexole), iron Circadian Rhythm Disorders Delayed sleep phase, advanced sleep phase, shift work, jet lag Light therapy, melatonin Kleine-Levin Syndrome Recurrent episodes of hypersomnia + hyperphagia + hypersexuality. Young males Rare

chunks.heading: Parasomnias (abnormal events during sleep)
chunks.text: Parasomnias (abnormal events during sleep) Disorder Stage Core feature Sleepwalking (somnambulism) NREM 3 Complex motor activity, eyes open, no memory. Children. Sleep terrors (night terrors) NREM 3 Sudden arousal with scream, autonomic storm, no memory. Children. Nightmares REM Vivid scary dream, full recall on waking. Any age. REM Sleep Behavior Disorder (RBD) REM Loss of atonia . Patient acts out dreams (punching, yelling). Associated with α-synucleinopathies (Parkinson, Lewy body dementia). Older males. Sleep paralysis REM onset/offset Brief atonia while awake, terrifying. Can occur in narcolepsy or isolated. Bruxism Any stage Teeth grinding Enuresis (bedwetting) NREM 3 Children. Usually resolves with age.

chunks.heading: 7. Sleep and Memory
chunks.text: 7. Sleep and Memory Declarative / explicit memory (facts, events) consolidated during NREM (especially slow-wave sleep). Hippocampus replays during delta. Procedural / implicit memory (motor skills) consolidated during REM and Stage 2 (spindles) . Emotional memory consolidated during REM (amygdala active, prefrontal cortex quiet → emotional tagging without rational evaluation). Sleep deprivation hurts consolidation disproportionately.

chunks.heading: 8. Sleep and Deprivation
chunks.text: 8. Sleep and Deprivation Total sleep deprivation (24 hr): impaired vigilance, slowed reaction time, mood lability, microsleeps. Chronic partial sleep restriction is as bad as acute total deprivation over time, but people feel less impaired (adaptation perception). REM rebound after REM deprivation: next night’s sleep has more REM to “catch up.” Delta rebound similarly. Sleep deprivation paradoxically treats depression short-term (via increased BDNF, reduced REM intrusion), though benefit resolves after sleep.

chunks.heading: 9. MCQ Trap Cluster (memorize cold)
chunks.text: 9. MCQ Trap Cluster (memorize cold) Muscle atonia → REM. Always. Not delta, not stage 2. Sleep spindles + K-complexes → NREM 2. Signature feature. Delta waves + slow-wave sleep + “deep sleep” → NREM 3. Paradoxical sleep = REM. Brain awake, body asleep. Parasomnias (sleepwalking, night terrors, enuresis) → NREM 3 , not REM. RBD (REM sleep behavior disorder) = loss of atonia in REM. Elderly men, α-synucleinopathy warning sign. Narcolepsy = orexin/hypocretin deficiency. Cataplexy is pathognomonic. SCN = master circadian clock , entrained by light via retinohypothalamic tract . Melatonin from pineal gland , released in darkness . Adenosine drives sleep pressure; caffeine blocks adenosine receptors. REM-ON neurons = cholinergic (PPT/LDT). REM-OFF = aminergic (NE, 5-HT). Newborns enter sleep via REM (active sleep), adults enter via NREM 1. N3 dominates first half of night; REM dominates second half. Declarative memory → NREM (delta). Procedural → REM + spindles. Sleep cycle = ~90 minutes. 4–6 cycles per night. Growth hormone released in NREM 3. Pons + medial medulla → atonia during REM (hyperpolarize spinal motor neurons). Temperature regulation fails during REM (poikilothermic). Kleine-Levin = hypersomnia + hyperphagia + hypersexuality (the three H’s). Insomnia DSM-5 threshold: 3 nights/week for 3 months.

chunks.heading: 10. Quick Recall Facts
chunks.text: 10. Quick Recall Facts If a question says … → answer is … - “Paralysis during sleep” → REM - “Sleep spindles” → NREM 2 - “K-complexes” → NREM 2 - “Delta waves” → NREM 3 - “Slow-wave sleep” → NREM 3 - “Paradoxical sleep” → REM - “Growth hormone secreted in” → NREM 3 - “Acetylcholine peaks in” → REM - “Orexin deficiency” → Narcolepsy - “Cataplexy” → Narcolepsy - “Sudden screaming with autonomic arousal in a 7-year-old, no memory” → Sleep terrors (NREM 3) - “Acting out dreams in a 68-year-old male” → RBD (REM) - “Urge to move legs worse at rest” → RLS - “Cortex looks asleep, body is moving” → sleepwalking (NREM 3) - “Cortex looks awake, body is paralyzed” → REM - “Master circadian clock” → SCN - “Melatonin secreted by” → Pineal gland - “Sleep onset driven by” → Adenosine + VLPO - “Caffeine mechanism” → Adenosine receptor blocker - “Sleep cycle length” → ~90 minutes Sihan MET 2026 Prep · Generated 2026-04-22

chunks.heading: Social Psychology: the full chapter, from scratch
chunks.text: Social Psychology: the full chapter, from scratch Read this like a textbook, not a cheatsheet. Every chapter explained from first principles, then the named effects, the theorists and the traps. Anchored to your Baron & Branscombe, Social Psychology (13th ed.) , walked through in book order: the science & its methods · social cognition · perception & attribution · the self · attitudes & persuasion · prejudice · attraction & love · social influence · prosocial behaviour · aggression · groups. NIMHANS weights this domain heavily (heavier than MET), and the dominant question type is which name goes with which effect , so the attribution-style pairs are flagged throughout. Effects Phenomena Theories Theorists Social Psych Cognitive Lookalikes How to use this page. It is built to learn from , not just revise. Each topic has: (1) the problem it was trying to solve, (2) the core idea in plain language with an everyday example, (3) the named concepts unpacked one by one in tables, and (4) coloured boxes recapping the exam-testable fact and the trap. Amber boxes = the intuition / why it matt

chunks.heading: 0. Social psychology as a science
chunks.text: 0. Social psychology as a science What the field actually claims. Social psychology is the scientific study of how the thoughts, feelings and behaviour of individuals are influenced by the actual, imagined or implied presence of others (Allport's classic definition). The key word is scientific : it does not settle questions by intuition or anecdote, it runs studies. And the key insight, repeated throughout Baron, is the power of the situation : ordinary people do extraordinary things (help, conform, obey, aggress) far more because of where they are and who is around than because of fixed traits. That theme, situation over disposition, returns in obedience (Milgram), bystander apathy (Latané & Darley) and the attribution chapter (the FAE is precisely our failure to see it). The role of theory. A theory is an integrated set of principles that explains and predicts observed events. Good social psychology runs a loop: a theory generates a specific, falsifiable hypothesis ; a study tests it; results refine or refute the theory. A theory is never "proven", only supported or disconfirmed, and it earns its keep by making predictions that could have failed but did not.

chunks.heading: The three core research methods
chunks.text: The three core research methods Baron's methods chapter contrasts three ways to gather evidence, each with a trade-off between control and realism. Method What you do Strength / limit Experimental Manipulate one factor (the independent variable, IV ), hold everything else constant, measure the effect on the dependent variable, DV . Use random assignment to conditions. The only method that establishes cause and effect . Limit: artificiality, low external validity if over-controlled. Correlational Measure two or more variables as they naturally occur and see if they covary (correlation coefficient, −1 to +1). Good for real-world variables you cannot ethically manipulate. Limit: correlation ≠ causation (direction problem + third-variable problem). Survey Ask a representative sample questions to describe a population's attitudes/behaviour. Cheap, broad. Limit: sampling bias, wording effects, social-desirability responding. The IV/DV intuition. The IV is the cause you dial (the dose), the DV is the effect you read off (the symptom). Picture the experimenter's hand on a knob (IV) and an eye on a dial (DV). Random assignment is what lets you claim the knob, not some pre-existing difference between people, moved the dial. Correlational work has no knob, you only watch two dials move together, which is why it cannot tell you which one is driving.

chunks.heading: Mediators, moderators and meta-analysis
chunks.text: Mediators, moderators and meta-analysis A mediator is the mechanism , the variable that comes between cause and effect and explains why the IV affects the DV (frustration → anger → aggression: anger mediates). A moderator is a variable that changes the strength or direction of the relationship, telling you when or for whom it holds (heat increases aggression more for provoked people). A meta-analysis statistically combines many studies to estimate the true overall effect size, the gold standard for asking "does this effect really hold?"

chunks.heading: Deception, ethics and replication
chunks.text: Deception, ethics and replication Because telling participants the true purpose would change their behaviour, social psychology often uses deception (a cover story). This is allowed only under strict ethical safeguards: informed consent , the right to withdraw, minimising harm, and a thorough debriefing afterwards that reveals the true purpose and removes any deception's after-effects. An Institutional Review Board / ethics committee must approve the study first. The discipline has also taken its replication crisis seriously: a finding is trusted only when independent labs replicate it, which is why classic single studies (Milgram, the marshmallow studies) are now discussed alongside their replications and failures. NIMHANS angle. NIMHANS, being a clinical and research institute, asks methods crisply: define IV vs DV, name the only method that proves causation (experimental), state why correlation cannot (third-variable + directionality), and distinguish mediator (the why , the mechanism in between) from moderator (the when/for whom , changes the strength). Also expect: the purpose of debriefing after deception, and what an ethics board protects.

chunks.heading: A fourth method, and the four lenses Baron uses
chunks.text: A fourth method, and the four lenses Baron uses Alongside the big three there is systematic / naturalistic observation (watching and recording behaviour as it occurs, without intervening, e.g. counting jaywalkers). Baron's opening chapter also frames the whole book through four perspectives that recur in every later chapter, and NIMHANS likes to name them: Perspective The core claim Cognitive To explain social behaviour, study how people think : notice, store, recall, interpret. The dominant modern lens (schemas, heuristics, attribution all live here). Evolutionary Some social tendencies (mate choice, helping kin, fear of strangers) were shaped by natural selection because they aided survival/reproduction. Social neuroscience Links social behaviour to brain activity and biology (fMRI, hormones), e.g. the amygdala in out-group fear, oxytocin in trust. Cultural / multicultural Many "findings" hold differently across cultures; social psych must test whether an effect is universal or culture-bound (individualist vs collectivist). The hidden bias to name. Baron stresses that the social psychologist is also a thinker prone to the very biases the field studies, so methods (random assignment, double-blind procedures, pre-registration, replication) exist precisely to keep the researcher's expectations from manufacturing the result. This is why "expectancy effects / experimenter bias" is

chunks.heading: 1. Social cognition (how we think about the social world)
chunks.text: 1. Social cognition (how we think about the social world) The problem. The social world throws more information at us than we could ever fully process. So the mind takes shortcuts. Social cognition is the study of how we notice, store, recall and use information about people and situations , and especially of the predictable errors those shortcuts produce. The governing idea is that we are "cognitive misers" : we spend mental effort sparingly, defaulting to fast, cheap strategies that are usually good enough but sometimes badly wrong.

chunks.heading: Dual-process thinking: automatic vs controlled
chunks.text: Dual-process thinking: automatic vs controlled Underlying everything here is the dual-process view (popularised as System 1 vs System 2). Automatic processing is fast, effortless, unconscious and emotional; controlled processing is slow, effortful, deliberate and logical. Most social judgement runs on autopilot (System 1), and the biases below are largely automatic processing's blind spots. This same automatic/controlled split reappears in persuasion (peripheral vs central route, §4) and prejudice (implicit vs explicit attitudes, §5).

chunks.heading: Heuristics: the mental shortcuts
chunks.text: Heuristics: the mental shortcuts A heuristic is a rule of thumb that gives a quick answer without full analysis. Three dominate the syllabus. Term Who What it is Heuristics (availability, representativeness, anchoring) Tversky & Kahneman Mental shortcuts: judge by ease of recall (availability) / by resemblance to a prototype (representativeness) / by clinging to a first value then adjusting too little (anchoring & adjustment). Fuller list on the Phenomena page. Schema Bartlett (social use: Fiske & Taylor) Mental framework that guides what we notice, encode and recall about people/situations. Priming — A recently activated schema shapes the next interpretation, even unconsciously. Feel each heuristic. Availability : you fear plane crashes more than car crashes because crashes make the news and spring to mind easily, even though driving is deadlier. Representativeness : told someone is quiet and loves poetry, you guess "librarian" over "salesperson" because they fit the prototype , ignoring that salespeople vastly outnumber librarians (base-rate neglect). Anchoring : the first price you hear drags your estimate toward it. A schema is the bigger structure these run on, a packaged expectation ("restaurant" schema tells you to wait for a menu); priming is switching a schema on so it colours what comes next.

chunks.heading: The biases of social thought
chunks.text: The biases of social thought When heuristics misfire systematically, we get biases , errors that lean reliably in one direction. Baron groups several together. Term Who What it is Self-fulfilling prophecy Robert Merton An expectation makes itself come true by changing behaviour (basis of the Pygmalion effect). Counterfactual thinking Kahneman & Tversky Imagining "what might have been"; near-misses sting most (the bronze medallist is happier than the silver). Optimistic / unrealistic-optimism bias Neil Weinstein We think bad things are less likely to happen to us than to others. Negativity bias — Negative info weighs more heavily than equally strong positive info. Planning fallacy Kahneman & Tversky We chronically underestimate how long our own tasks will take. Magical thinking — Assumptions that defy causality (law of contagion / similarity; won't eat fudge shaped like dog faeces).

chunks.heading: What schemas actually do, and why they stick
chunks.text: What schemas actually do, and why they stick Baron is precise about a schema's three effects, a favourite "schemas influence ___" item: they shape attention (what info we notice), encoding (what gets stored, usually schema-consistent info, though wildly inconsistent info also grabs attention), and retrieval (what we later recall, biased toward the schema). Two further effects matter: Term What it is Perseverance effect Beliefs and schemas survive even after the evidence that created them is totally discredited. First impressions are sticky. Self-fulfilling effect of schemas A schema can make the social world confirm it (we treat people per the schema, they respond in kind), tying back to Merton's self-fulfilling prophecy.

chunks.heading: Two more "errors of social thought"
chunks.text: Two more "errors of social thought" Term Who What it is Thought suppression & the rebound effect Daniel Wegner Trying not to think of something (the "white bear") makes it intrude more once you relax control; the monitoring process keeps the unwanted thought primed. Overconfidence barrier — We have more confidence in our judgements and predictions than their accuracy warrants; a recurring obstacle to accurate social thought. NIMHANS angle. Wegner's rebound effect is the cognitive model behind why "just stop thinking about it" fails in OCD, PTSD intrusions and insomnia, and why acceptance -based therapies (ACT, mindfulness) outperform suppression. Pair it with the perseverance effect, which explains why a discredited self-belief ("I'm a failure") persists in depression. Affect and cognition cut both ways. Mood shapes thought (positive mood broadens thinking and increases heuristic use; we recall mood-congruent material), and thought shapes mood (how you appraise an event determines how you feel about it). This two-way street is why a good mood makes you a lazier, more shortcut-prone thinker. Two near-twins: availability = judged by how easily examples come to mind (recent, vivid, emotional). Representativeness = judged by how well it matches a prototype (and so neglects base rates). If the stem stresses "easy to recall / vivid", it's availability; if it stresses "fits the stereo

chunks.heading: 2. Social perception & attribution
chunks.text: 2. Social perception & attribution The problem. To navigate other people we must answer two questions about them: what are they feeling right now (read from nonverbal cues) and why did they do that (attribution). Social perception is how we form impressions and infer causes from limited information.

chunks.heading: Nonverbal communication
chunks.text: Nonverbal communication Before a word is spoken we read nonverbal channels : facial expressions (Ekman's six basic emotions are largely universal), eye contact (gaze), body language and posture, touch , and paralanguage (tone, pace, pauses). These leak information the person may not mean to send, which is why we often trust the nonverbal over the verbal. Baron adds the cues to deception : microexpressions (fleeting true feelings that flash before they are masked), interchannel discrepancies (the face says one thing, the hands or voice another), and changes in eye contact and linguistic style . Despite all this, people detect lies barely above chance, because liars control the easy channels and we over-trust the face.

chunks.heading: Attribution: explaining behaviour
chunks.text: Attribution: explaining behaviour Attribution theory asks how we decide whether an action springs from the person (an internal/dispositional cause) or the circumstance (an external/situational cause). Three classic models built the field. Theory / term Who What it is Attribution theory Fritz Heider We explain behaviour as internal (disposition) or external (situation); the person as "naïve psychologist." Correspondent inference theory Jones & Davis We infer a trait from acts that are freely chosen, unexpected and low in social desirability. Covariation model Harold Kelley Attribution uses consensus, consistency & distinctiveness (high all three → situation/stimulus; low consensus + low distinctiveness + high consistency → the person). Walk Kelley's three Cs. Your friend laughs at a comedian. Consensus : does everyone laugh? Distinctiveness : does she laugh only at this comedian? Consistency : does she laugh every time? High on all three (everyone laughs, only at him, every time) → it's the comedian (external). Low consensus + low distinctiveness (no one else laughs, she laughs at everything) + high consistency → it's her (internal). Heider gave the basic internal/external split; Jones & Davis asked when an act reveals a true trait; Kelley added the data-driven rule.

chunks.heading: The attributional biases
chunks.text: The attributional biases Theory / term Who What it is Fundamental attribution error (correspondence bias) coined by Lee Ross Over-blaming others' character, under-weighting their situation. Actor–observer effect Jones & Nisbett My acts = situation; your acts = your character. Self-serving bias — My success = me; my failure = bad luck/situation. Just-world hypothesis Melvin Lerner Belief that people get what they deserve → blaming the victim. Facial-feedback hypothesis Tomkins; Ekman Your facial expression feeds back to intensify/trigger the felt emotion. Thin slices Ambady & Rosenthal Surprisingly accurate judgements from very brief (seconds) exposure to behaviour.

chunks.heading: Impression formation & management
chunks.text: Impression formation & management Solomon Asch showed first impressions form fast and that some traits are central (swapping "warm" for "cold" in a trait list transforms the whole impression, while "polite/blunt" barely moves it). The primacy effect means early information weighs most. Baron contrasts Asch's configural / gestalt view (traits fuse into a whole) with Norman Anderson's information-integration / averaging model (we mentally average the weighted values of each trait to form an overall impression). We also lean on an implicit personality theory , a lay assumption about which traits go together ("warm people are also generous"), which is how one central trait drags the rest. On the flip side, impression management (self-presentation) is our effort to control the impression others form of us, a theme Goffman framed dramaturgically (life as theatre, front-stage vs back-stage); its tactics include self-promotion (look competent), ingratiation (flattery, agreement, to look likeable) and self-deprecation . Asch vs Anderson, and Kelley's two extra rules. Asch (configural): an impression is more than the sum of traits, a central trait reorganises the whole. Anderson (averaging): we weight and average traits like a mental calculator, so adding a mildly positive trait to a strongly positive set can lower the average. Separately, when judging why someone acted, Kelley added two

chunks.heading: 3. The self
chunks.text: 3. The self The problem. The self is both the thinker and the thing thought about. Social psychology asks: how do we build a self-concept (the content, "who am I"), how do we set our self-esteem (the evaluation, "how do I feel about who I am"), and what lengths do we go to to protect that esteem? The recurring finding is that the self is fundamentally social : we know ourselves largely by comparison to, and reflection in, other people. Theory / term Who What it is Social comparison theory Leon Festinger We evaluate ourselves by comparison to others (upward comparison to better-off = motivating but deflating; downward to worse-off = self-enhancing). Self-perception theory Daryl Bem When attitudes are weak or ambiguous, we infer them by observing our own behaviour ("I'm eating salad, I guess I like salad"). Self-discrepancy theory E. Tory Higgins Actual vs ideal self → dejection (sadness, disappointment); actual vs ought self → agitation (anxiety, guilt). Self-monitoring Mark Snyder High self-monitors tailor behaviour to the situation; low ones act from inner attitudes. Self-efficacy Albert Bandura Belief in your capacity to carry out the actions a specific task needs. Self-handicapping Berglas & Jones Setting up an excuse in advance (not studying, drinking before a test) to protect self-esteem from possible failure. Self-verification William Swann We seek feedback that confirms

chunks.heading: Building the self-concept (the content side Baron opens with)
chunks.text: Building the self-concept (the content side Baron opens with) Before the esteem defences, Baron lays out how the self-concept is built and stored: Term Who What it is Self-reference effect Rogers et al. Information processed in relation to the self is remembered better; the self is a powerful memory organiser. Possible selves Markus & Nurius Images of what we might become (hoped-for, feared, expected selves) that motivate and guide behaviour. Self-complexity Patricia Linville Having many distinct self-aspects buffers mood swings; a simple self lets one bad domain flood the whole self. Sociometer theory Mark Leary Self-esteem is an internal gauge of social acceptance/belonging; it drops when we feel rejected.

chunks.heading: The self across cultures (high-yield NIMHANS contrast)
chunks.text: The self across cultures (high-yield NIMHANS contrast) Hazel Markus & Shinobu Kitayama drew the field's biggest cultural distinction: the independent self-construal (typical of individualist/Western cultures, the self defined by internal traits, separate, self-promoting) versus the interdependent self-construal (typical of collectivist cultures including India, the self defined by relationships, roles and group harmony). This single distinction explains cultural differences in the FAE (weaker in collectivist cultures), self-serving bias, self-enhancement (lower in East Asian samples) and conformity. India is the textbook collectivist/interdependent case. The thread. Notice how many of these are defences of self-esteem, not neutral descriptions: self-handicapping pre-loads an excuse, self-affirmation patches a wound in one domain by celebrating another, BIRGing borrows glory, terror management props up the whole worldview against death anxiety. The self is not a calm observer, it is a press secretary working to keep esteem intact. The exceptions are the cooler cognitive ones: social comparison (Festinger, how we measure ourselves) and self-perception (Bem, how we infer attitudes from behaviour). Two self-discrepancy directions (Higgins): falling short of your ideal self (hopes, what you want to be) → dejection (sad, depressed). Falling short of your ought self (duties, what you

chunks.heading: 4. Attitudes & persuasion
chunks.text: 4. Attitudes & persuasion The problem. An attitude is an evaluation of an object (person, issue, thing) along a like–dislike dimension. The classic ABC structure has three components: A ffective (feelings), B ehavioural (action tendencies) and C ognitive (beliefs). Attitudes serve functions (knowledge, ego-defence, value-expression, utilitarian). The two big questions in this chapter are: do attitudes actually predict behaviour? and how do you change them (persuasion)?

chunks.heading: Where attitudes come from, and the implicit/explicit split
chunks.text: Where attitudes come from, and the implicit/explicit split Baron lists the routes by which attitudes form, mostly low-level learning: classical conditioning (an object repeatedly paired with positive/negative stimuli, including subliminal conditioning and mere exposure ), instrumental conditioning (attitudes that earn approval are reinforced), and observational learning / social comparison (we adopt the attitudes of models and reference groups). Twin studies show attitudes even have a partly heritable component. Crucially, Baron splits: Term What it is Explicit attitudes Conscious, reportable, controllable evaluations. Implicit attitudes Automatic, often unconscious evaluations, measured by the Implicit Association Test (IAT) via reaction times; can diverge from what we say, and predict spontaneous behaviour.

chunks.heading: The attitude–behaviour link
chunks.text: The attitude–behaviour link For decades the embarrassing answer was "barely". The famous demonstration is the LaPiere study : a researcher toured 1930s America with a Chinese couple and was served almost everywhere, yet when later asked by mail, most of those same establishments said they would refuse Chinese guests. Stated attitude did not match actual behaviour. The resolution came from Fishbein & Ajzen : attitudes predict behaviour best through intentions , and intentions are shaped by attitudes plus subjective norms plus (in the planned-behaviour update) perceived behavioural control. Attitudes also predict better when they are strong, specific, accessible, and based on direct experience.

chunks.heading: Persuasion: how attitudes change
chunks.text: Persuasion: how attitudes change Theory / term Who What it is Yale attitude-change approach Carl Hovland Who says what to whom: source (credibility, attractiveness), message, and audience factors in persuasion. Elaboration Likelihood Model (ELM) Petty & Cacioppo Persuasion via the central route (thoughtful scrutiny of arguments, when motivated & able) vs the peripheral route (surface cues: attractiveness, length, expert badge). Heuristic-Systematic Model (HSM) Shelly Chaiken Same dual-route idea: systematic (effortful argument analysis) vs heuristic (rules of thumb, "experts are right"). Theory of reasoned action / planned behaviour Fishbein & Ajzen Intention (from attitudes + subjective norms + perceived behavioural control) predicts behaviour. Inoculation theory William McGuire A weak counter-argument first "vaccinates" an attitude against later strong attacks. Psychological reactance Jack Brehm Threaten a freedom → people want the forbidden thing more (boomerang effect). LaPiere study Richard LaPiere The classic attitude–behaviour gap: stated prejudice did not match actual service to a Chinese couple. The dual route, intuitively. When you care and can concentrate (buying a house), you take the central route, weighing real arguments, and the resulting attitude is durable. When you do not care or are distracted (a soft-drink jingle), you take the peripheral route, swayed by wh

chunks.heading: Cognitive dissonance & consistency theories
chunks.text: Cognitive dissonance & consistency theories The most-tested idea in the whole chapter. When two cognitions clash, or behaviour contradicts an attitude, we feel an unpleasant tension ( dissonance ) and are driven to reduce it, usually by changing the attitude to fit the behaviour . Theory / term Who What it is Cognitive dissonance Leon Festinger Tension from clashing cognitions drives attitude change to reduce it. Insufficient justification / induced compliance Festinger & Carlsmith The $1 group changed their attitude more than the $20 group (less external reward = more dissonance = more internal attitude change). Effort justification Aronson & Mills The harder/more embarrassing the initiation, the more we value the group we joined. Balance theory Fritz Heider We seek consistency among our liking relationships (P-O-X triangles; an imbalanced triangle pressures change). Hypocrisy paradigm Aronson et al. Make people publicly advocate a behaviour (e.g. condom use), then remind them of their own past failures to do it → dissonance drives them to actually change behaviour. Free-choice dissonance Jack Brehm After a hard choice between close options, we boost the chosen and derogate the rejected option ("spreading of alternatives") to quiet post-decision dissonance. Why $1 beat $20. Participants did a boring task then were paid to tell the next person it was fun. Those paid $20 had a b

chunks.heading: 5. Stereotyping, prejudice & discrimination
chunks.text: 5. Stereotyping, prejudice & discrimination The problem, and the three words kept straight. A stereotype is the cognitive component (a belief about a group's traits). Prejudice is the affective component (a negative feeling toward a group). Discrimination is the behavioural component (unequal treatment). They are the ABC of intergroup bias. The chapter asks where this bias comes from (identity, competition, personality, cognition) and what reduces it (contact).

chunks.heading: Sources of prejudice
chunks.text: Sources of prejudice Theory / term Who What it is Social identity theory Tajfel & Turner Part of our self-esteem comes from group membership → we favour the in-group and derogate the out-group to feel good. Minimal group paradigm Henri Tajfel Even arbitrary, meaningless group splits (coin toss, dot-estimation) produce in-group favouritism. Realistic conflict theory Muzafer Sherif Competition over scarce resources breeds intergroup hostility (Robbers Cave study); superordinate (shared) goals reduce it. Authoritarian personality Theodor Adorno A rigid, conventional, submissive-to-authority personality (measured by the F-scale) prone to prejudice. Scapegoat theory (frustration–aggression roots) Frustration is displaced onto a weaker out-group blamed for problems. Identity vs competition vs personality. Three different engines. Social identity (Tajfel & Turner) : bias arises just from categorising people into us/them, no real conflict needed, the minimal group studies prove arbitrary groups suffice. Realistic conflict (Sherif) : bias arises from real competition over resources, and Robbers Cave showed shared goals (a broken-down truck both camps must pull) dissolve it. Authoritarian personality (Adorno) : bias sits inside a particular personality type . NIMHANS loves to swap these three.

chunks.heading: The modern, subtle forms (and the cost to targets)
chunks.text: The modern, subtle forms (and the cost to targets) Baron stresses that open bigotry has gone underground into subtler forms, which NIMHANS can name: Term Who What it is Modern / subtle (aversive) racism — People who endorse equality still hold automatic negative reactions and discriminate when they can attribute it to something else; bias is implicit, not openly avowed. Hostile vs benevolent sexism Glick & Fiske Two-part "ambivalent sexism": hostile (women seeking power are a threat) plus benevolent (women are wonderful but fragile and need protection). Benevolent sounds positive but still keeps women subordinate. Tokenism — A trivial positive act toward an out-group member used as an excuse to then discriminate; also the strain on a lone "token" group member. Glass ceiling — An invisible barrier keeping qualified members of devalued groups out of top positions. Hostile vs benevolent sexism (Glick & Fiske): hostile = openly negative/antagonistic toward women who challenge the status quo. Benevolent = subjectively positive ("cherish and protect them") but patronising and still keeps women in restricted roles. Both are prejudice; the "nice"-sounding one is benevolent.

chunks.heading: The cognitive machinery of stereotypes
chunks.text: The cognitive machinery of stereotypes Theory / term Who What it is Illusory correlation Hamilton & Gifford Perceiving a link between minority-group membership and rare (negative) behaviour that is not really there (two distinctive things co-occur and stick). Out-group homogeneity effect — "They're all alike"; we see less variability in out-groups than in our own group. Stereotype threat Steele & Aronson Fear of confirming a negative stereotype about your group depresses your performance on the stereotyped task. Stereotype content model Susan Fiske Groups are judged on two dimensions, warmth × competence → four emotions: admiration (warm+competent), envy (cold+competent), pity (warm+incompetent), contempt (cold+incompetent).

chunks.heading: Reducing prejudice
chunks.text: Reducing prejudice Theory / term Who What it is Contact hypothesis Gordon Allport Contact reduces prejudice only if four conditions hold: equal status, common goals, intergroup cooperation, and institutional support. Jigsaw classroom Elliot Aronson Cooperative learning where each pupil holds one essential piece of the lesson → forces interdependence, cuts prejudice. A practical application of the contact hypothesis. Common in-group identity model (recategorisation) Gaertner & Dovidio Get rival groups to recategorise "us vs them" into a single inclusive "we" (one superordinate group) → former out-group members now get in-group warmth. Learning not to hate / breaking the cycle — Because prejudice is partly learned, modelling tolerance, perspective-taking and reducing stereotype activation can interrupt its transmission. Stereotype threat vs self-fulfilling prophecy: stereotype threat (Steele & Aronson) = the target's own anxiety about confirming the stereotype hurts their performance. Self-fulfilling prophecy (Merton, §1) = the perceiver's expectation changes how they treat the target, eliciting the expected behaviour. One is driven from inside the target, the other from the outside perceiver. NIMHANS angle. Indian-context applications are fair game: caste, religion and language as in-group/out-group lines fit social identity and realistic conflict; the contact hypothesis (Allpor

chunks.heading: 6. Interpersonal attraction, relationships & love
chunks.text: 6. Interpersonal attraction, relationships & love The problem. Why do we like and love some people and not others, and what holds relationships together? Baron moves from the cold, almost mechanical predictors of initial attraction (who do you even end up near and noticing) to theories of love and finally to the economic models of why relationships last or end .

chunks.heading: Predictors of initial attraction
chunks.text: Predictors of initial attraction Theory / term Who What it is Propinquity (proximity) effect Festinger, Schachter & Back The closer people live or sit, the more likely they form friendships (the Westgate housing study). Mere-exposure effect Robert Zajonc Repeated exposure to a stimulus, by itself, increases liking for it. Similarity–attraction Donn Byrne We like those with similar attitudes (not "opposites attract"); the "law of attraction". Matching hypothesis Walster & Berscheid We tend to pair with partners of roughly our own level of physical attractiveness. "What is beautiful is good" Dion, Berscheid & Walster The physical-attractiveness stereotype: we assume good-looking people also have better personalities. Evolutionary mate preferences David Buss Across cultures, men weight youth and physical attractiveness (fertility cues), women weight status and resources (provisioning); explained as evolved reproductive strategies (parental investment). Reciprocity of liking — We like those who like us; learning someone likes you boosts your liking for them. Critique to keep. The evolutionary mate-preference account (Buss) is heavily tested but also heavily criticised: social-role theory (Eagly & Wood) argues the same sex differences fall out of women's restricted access to resources and power, not genes. Know both sides, NIMHANS likes "which explanation." Why proximity and exposur

chunks.heading: Theories of love
chunks.text: Theories of love Theory / term Who What it is Triangular theory of love Robert Sternberg Intimacy + passion + commitment combine into 7 love types (all three = consummate love). Passionate vs companionate love Hatfield & Berscheid Intense arousal and longing (passionate) vs deep affection, trust and care that lasts (companionate). Two-factor theory of love (misattribution of arousal) Dutton & Aron Arousal from a scary suspension bridge gets relabelled as romantic attraction to the person you meet there. Adult attachment styles Hazan & Shaver Secure / anxious-ambivalent / avoidant styles carried from infant attachment into romantic love.

chunks.heading: Why relationships last or end
chunks.text: Why relationships last or end Theory / term Who What it is Social exchange theory Thibaut & Kelley Relationships are weighed as rewards minus costs, compared against a comparison level (CL) and the comparison level for alternatives (CL-alt). Equity theory Walster / Adams We are happiest when our ratio of inputs to outcomes matches the partner's (over- and under-benefit both cause distress). Investment model Caryl Rusbult Commitment = satisfaction + investment size − quality of alternatives. Social penetration / self-disclosure Altman & Taylor Relationships deepen as self-disclosure grows in breadth and depth ; reciprocal disclosure builds intimacy. Phases of dissolution Steve Duck Break-ups move through stages: intrapsychic (private dissatisfaction) → dyadic (confrontation) → social (telling the network) → grave-dressing (constructing the break-up story). The dark side Baron covers too. Beyond attraction, the chapter treats loneliness (the painful gap between desired and actual relationships, a health risk), jealousy (sex differences: evolutionary view says men fear sexual infidelity, women emotional infidelity), and social allergens (a partner's small repeated annoyances that accumulate into disgust). These are easy "name the term" items. The two-factor love trick. Dutton & Aron's bridge study is misattribution of arousal in action: men who crossed a high, swaying bridge (phys

chunks.heading: 7. Social influence (conformity, compliance, obedience)
chunks.text: 7. Social influence (conformity, compliance, obedience) The problem, and the three levels. Social influence is changing because of others, and it comes in three intensities. Conformity = changing to match a group with no direct request (you just go along). Compliance = changing in response to a direct request (the sales techniques). Obedience = changing in response to a direct order from an authority. The levels rise from implicit group pressure to explicit command.

chunks.heading: Conformity & obedience
chunks.text: Conformity & obedience Term Who What it is Conformity Solomon Asch Going along with a unanimous group's obviously wrong answer (the line-judging task); ~33% conformity rate. Norm formation Muzafer Sherif Used the autokinetic illusion (a still dot of light appears to move) to show groups converge on a shared norm. Informational vs normative influence Deutsch & Gerard We conform to be right (informational, especially when uncertain) vs to be liked/accepted (normative). Obedience to authority Stanley Milgram 65% of ordinary people delivered "lethal" 450V shocks when an authority calmly ordered them to continue. Minority influence Serge Moscovici A consistent minority can shift the majority, via genuine private conversion rather than mere public compliance. What raises or lowers Asch conformity, and the kinds of norms. Conformity rises with group size (up to ~3–4, then plateaus) and unanimity , and collapses the moment one ally / dissenter breaks ranks. Baron also separates two kinds of social norm, a Cialdini distinction NIMHANS likes: Term Who What it is Descriptive norms Cialdini et al. What most people actually do ("everyone litters here"). Tell people what is, and they copy it. Injunctive norms Cialdini et al. What most people approve/disapprove of ("littering is wrong"). More durable for changing behaviour. Mindlessness / the "because" effect Ellen Langer A request with any r

chunks.heading: Compliance techniques
chunks.text: Compliance techniques Term Who What it is Six principles of influence Robert Cialdini Reciprocity, commitment/consistency, social proof, authority, liking, scarcity. Foot-in-the-door Freedman & Fraser Get agreement to a small request first → a bigger one later gets agreed to (works via commitment/consistency). Door-in-the-face Robert Cialdini Make a big request that is refused first → the smaller real request now looks reasonable (reciprocal concession). Lowballing Robert Cialdini Get a commitment at a good price, then raise the cost; people stick to the deal anyway. That's-not-all technique Jerry Burger Add a bonus or drop the price before the person decides → boosts compliance. Norm of reciprocity Alvin Gouldner We feel obliged to return favours (the engine behind door-in-the-face and free samples). Foot-in-the-door vs door-in-the-face: FITD = small → big (Freedman & Fraser, via consistency). DITF = big → small (Cialdini, via reciprocal concession). Lowballing = get the yes, then change the deal. That's-not-all = sweeten the offer before the yes. Examiners love swapping the direction (small-then-big vs big-then-small). NIMHANS angle. Milgram and Asch are perennial favourites: lock the headline numbers (Milgram ~65% to maximum voltage; Asch ~33% conformity) and the situational factors that reduce obedience (authority less close/legitimate, peers who rebel, victim more present)

chunks.heading: 8. Prosocial behaviour (helping)
chunks.text: 8. Prosocial behaviour (helping) The problem. Why do we help, when do we fail to, and is helping ever truly selfless? The chapter splits into situational work (the bystander effect: why help fails) and motivational work (the egoism vs altruism debate: why we help at all).

chunks.heading: When help fails: the bystander effect
chunks.text: When help fails: the bystander effect Term Who What it is Bystander effect & 5-step decision model Latané & Darley More witnesses → less help. The five steps: notice the event → interpret it as an emergency → take responsibility → know how to help → decide to act. (Sparked by the Kitty Genovese case.) Diffusion of responsibility Darley & Latané "Someone else will do it"; responsibility spreads thin in a crowd (fails step 3). Pluralistic ignorance — Everyone stays calm because no one else looks worried, so no one reads it as an emergency (fails step 2). Why a crowd freezes you. Latané & Darley's five-step model is a chain, and the crowd snaps it at two links. At step 2 (interpret) , you look around, see other calm faces, and conclude it must not be an emergency, that is pluralistic ignorance . At step 3 (take responsibility) , with many present, each person assumes someone else will act, that is diffusion of responsibility . More witnesses make both failures more likely, so paradoxically you are less likely to be helped in a big crowd.

chunks.heading: Why we help: egoism vs altruism
chunks.text: Why we help: egoism vs altruism Term Who What it is Empathy–altruism hypothesis C. Daniel Batson Feeling empathy for the victim produces genuinely selfless helping, aimed at their welfare, not our own relief. Negative-state relief model Robert Cialdini We help to relieve our own bad mood; helping is ultimately egoistic. Arousal: cost–reward model Piliavin et al. A bystander's unpleasant arousal at seeing distress motivates help, and we help when the costs of helping are low and costs of not helping are high. Kin selection / reciprocal altruism Hamilton; Trivers Evolutionary: help relatives (shared genes, kin selection) or those likely to return the favour (reciprocal altruism). Norm of social responsibility — A social norm that we should help those who depend on us, regardless of any return.

chunks.heading: What makes helping more or less likely
chunks.text: What makes helping more or less likely Beyond the crowd, Baron lists the factors that boost helping: similarity to the victim, seeing a helpful model , feeling gratitude , being in a good mood (the "feel-good, do-good" effect ), and the victim being not responsible for their plight. Helping drops with a hurry (the Good Samaritan study, Darley & Batson: seminary students late for a talk stepped over a slumped man), diffuse responsibility, and ambiguity. Two more named ideas: Term Who What it is Empathic joy hypothesis Smith et al. We help partly to feel the pleasure of having a positive impact; we want feedback that our help worked. Threat-to-self-esteem / reactions to receiving help Nadler & Fisher Receiving aid can feel demeaning and imply inferiority, so recipients sometimes refuse help or resent the helper, especially from a similar other. Why we help, the egoism vs altruism split: Batson (empathy–altruism) = there is true altruism, born of empathy and aimed at the other's welfare. Cialdini (negative-state relief) and Piliavin (arousal:cost-reward) = we ultimately help to fix our own discomfort, so helping is egoistic. That contrast (selfless vs self-serving motive) is the question. NIMHANS angle. The bystander 5-step model and its two crowd failures (pluralistic ignorance at "interpret", diffusion of responsibility at "take responsibility") are textbook MCQ material, expect

chunks.heading: 9. Aggression
chunks.text: 9. Aggression The problem, and the first distinction. Aggression is behaviour intended to harm another who does not want to be harmed. Baron first splits its types: hostile aggression (driven by anger, the goal is to hurt, often impulsive) vs instrumental aggression (a cold means to some other end, money, status), with a related relational aggression (harming through gossip, exclusion, reputation). The chapter then traces a historical arc: from a simple drive theory (frustration always causes aggression), through its cognitive reformulation (frustration only readies aggression, cues pull the trigger), to social learning (aggression is imitated) and integrative models. Theory / term Who What it is Frustration–aggression hypothesis Dollard, Doob, Miller et al. Original strong form: frustration (a blocked goal) always breeds aggression, and aggression always traces back to frustration. Reformulated frustration–aggression Leonard Berkowitz Frustration creates only a readiness (negative affect); aggression follows when aggressive cues are present. Weapons effect Berkowitz & LePage The mere presence of a weapon increases aggression, because the weapon is an aggressive cue. Social learning of aggression Albert Bandura Aggression is learned by observing and imitating models (the Bobo doll studies). General Aggression Model (GAM) Anderson & Bushman Integrative: person + situation inputs

chunks.heading: Social & cultural causes, and how to reduce it
chunks.text: Social & cultural causes, and how to reduce it Term Who What it is Media violence & desensitisation Anderson, Bushman Repeated exposure to violent media raises aggressive thoughts, affect and behaviour and blunts emotional response to real violence (desensitisation); also primes aggressive scripts. Culture of honour Nisbett & Cohen In cultures (e.g. the US South) where reputation must be defended, insults trigger far more aggression; shows aggression is culturally shaped, not just biological. Hostile attribution bias Kenneth Dodge Aggressive individuals over-read others' ambiguous acts as hostile in intent, then retaliate; central to aggressive children and conduct problems. Bullying Dan Olweus Repeated aggression against a less powerful target; involves bullies, victims and bystanders. Reducing aggression (Baron's toolkit). Catharsis does not work. What does: punishment only under strict conditions (prompt, certain, proportionate, or it backfires); incompatible responses (humour, empathy, mild non-aggressive feelings that can't co-exist with anger); apology and mitigating information ; cognitive interventions and exposure to non-aggressive models ; and self-regulation training. NIMHANS angle. Determinants of aggression are testable as a list: biological (low serotonin, high testosterone, amygdala/prefrontal function, the role of alcohol disinhibition) and situational/social (h

chunks.heading: 10. Groups & individuals
chunks.text: 10. Groups & individuals The problem. What does the mere presence of, or membership in, a group do to the individual, to effort, to self-restraint, and to the quality of decisions? The chapter pairs opposing effects (presence can boost or sap effort; groups can decide better or worse) and the deciding variable is usually whether you are individually identifiable.

chunks.heading: What actually makes a "group"
chunks.text: What actually makes a "group" Baron opens by defining a group's structure: roles (expected behaviours for a position), status (rank within the group), norms (shared rules), and cohesiveness (the forces binding members together). These are the four ingredients that turn a mere collection of people into a group, and they set up everything that follows.

chunks.heading: Presence of others: facilitation vs loafing
chunks.text: Presence of others: facilitation vs loafing Term Who What it is Social facilitation Triplett; Zajonc An audience or co-actor boosts performance on easy/well-learned tasks but hurts hard/novel ones (Zajonc: arousal strengthens the dominant response). Evaluation apprehension Nickolas Cottrell It is the fear of being judged , not mere physical presence, that creates the facilitation arousal. Social loafing Latané, Williams & Harkins People exert less effort in a group when their individual output cannot be identified (the Ringelmann rope-pull roots). Deindividuation Festinger; Zimbardo Anonymity and arousal in a crowd → loss of self-awareness and personal restraint (the Stanford prison study). The first historical experiment. Triplett (1898) noticed cyclists rode faster racing others than alone, arguably social psychology's first experiment. Zajonc explained it: an audience raises arousal, and arousal strengthens whatever response is dominant , the right one on an easy task (so you do better) but the wrong one on a hard task (so you do worse). Cottrell refined it: the arousal comes from evaluation apprehension , fear of being judged, not bare presence.

chunks.heading: Group decision-making & conflict
chunks.text: Group decision-making & conflict Term Who What it is Group polarisation Moscovici & Zavalloni Group discussion pushes members toward a more extreme version of their initial average leaning. Risky shift James Stoner The earlier-discovered special case: groups often reach riskier decisions than the individuals would alone. Groupthink Irving Janis A highly cohesive group suppresses dissent to preserve consensus → defective decisions (Bay of Pigs). Tragedy of the commons / social dilemma Garrett Hardin Individually rational self-interest collectively depletes a shared resource everyone needs. GRIT Charles Osgood Graduated and Reciprocated Initiatives in Tension-reduction: small, announced, unilateral concessions invite reciprocation and de-escalate conflict. Perceived fairness: distributive vs procedural justice Adams; Thibaut & Walker; Tyler Distributive justice = fairness of outcomes (the split itself). Procedural justice = fairness of the process used to decide; people accept even bad outcomes if the process felt fair (voice, neutrality). Transactional justice = fairness of interpersonal treatment.

chunks.heading: Leadership
chunks.text: Leadership Term Who What it is Great-person / trait theory — Leaders are born with distinguishing traits; weakly supported on its own. Transactional vs transformational leadership Bass; Burns Transactional leaders exchange rewards for performance (manage the status quo); transformational leaders inspire and remake followers' values and vision (charisma, intellectual stimulation). Risky shift was the clue to polarisation. Stoner first found groups decide riskier than individuals. Later work showed that was only half the story: groups can also shift more cautious if members started cautious. The general law is group polarisation (Moscovici & Zavalloni), discussion amplifies the pre-existing tilt in either direction. Groupthink (Janis) is the pathological extreme of cohesion, where the drive for agreement crushes realistic appraisal, with classic symptoms (illusion of invulnerability, self-censorship, mindguards, illusion of unanimity). Facilitation vs loafing: social facilitation = others present make you try harder (you are watched and evaluated individually ). Social loafing = others present make you try less (your effort is pooled and your individual output is hidden ). The deciding variable is whether your individual output is identifiable. Bonus: risky shift is the special case, group polarisation is the general rule. NIMHANS angle. Watch the deindividuation attribution: Fes

chunks.heading: 11. The landmark studies, walked through
chunks.text: 11. The landmark studies, walked through Baron teaches social psychology through its classic experiments, and NIMHANS/MET stems often describe a study and ask you to name it, its author, or its conclusion. Here each landmark is walked through in the same shape: the question , what they did , what they found , why it matters , and the trap . Learn the design, not just the headline number, because examiners test the procedure ("participants judged the length of lines" vs "a dot of light that appeared to move") as the giveaway.

chunks.heading: Triplett (1898) — the first social-psychology experiment
chunks.text: Triplett (1898) — the first social-psychology experiment Question: does the presence of others change performance? What: Norman Triplett noticed cyclists posted faster times racing against others than against the clock alone, then had children wind fishing reels alone vs alongside a co-actor. Found: children wound faster in the presence of a co-actor. Matters: widely cited as the first published social-psychology experiment and the seed of social facilitation . Trap: Triplett observed facilitation; Zajonc later explained it (arousal strengthens the dominant response); Cottrell refined the cause to evaluation apprehension .

chunks.heading: Sherif (1936) — autokinetic norm formation
chunks.text: Sherif (1936) — autokinetic norm formation Question: how do group norms form when reality is ambiguous? What: in a dark room a stationary pinpoint of light appears to move (the autokinetic effect , an optical illusion). Alone, people gave wildly different estimates of how far it "moved"; in groups, their estimates converged on a shared figure, and each person kept using that group figure even when later tested alone. Found: a private, internalised norm forms and persists. Matters: the model case of informational social influence (we use others as evidence when uncertain). Trap: Sherif = ambiguous stimulus, real internal conversion (informational); Asch = unambiguous stimulus, public compliance (normative). The "dot of light" is the tell for Sherif.

chunks.heading: Asch (1951) — conformity on the line task
chunks.text: Asch (1951) — conformity on the line task Question: will people conform to a group that is clearly wrong? What: a single real participant judged which of three comparison lines matched a standard, seated among confederates who unanimously gave the same wrong answer on critical trials. The correct answer was obvious. Found: about 75% of participants conformed on at least one trial; the conformity rate per critical trial was about 33–37% . Conformity rose with group size (up to 3–4, then plateaued) and unanimity , and collapsed the moment a single ally also dissented (it dropped to roughly a quarter of its level). Matters: normative pressure can override the plain evidence of one's senses. Trap: lock the two numbers separately (≈75% conformed at least once; ≈33% per trial) and remember one dissenting ally is what frees the participant, not the size of the majority.

chunks.heading: Milgram (1963) — obedience to authority
chunks.text: Milgram (1963) — obedience to authority Question: how far will ordinary people go in harming another when ordered by an authority? What: the participant ("teacher") was told to deliver escalating shocks (15V up to 450V , labelled "XXX") to a "learner" (a confederate, who was never actually shocked) for wrong answers, while a calm experimenter in a lab coat issued four scripted prods ("the experiment requires that you continue"). Found: 65% went all the way to 450V; almost all went past the point the learner screamed and fell silent. Matters: situational pressure, not sadism, produced the obedience, ordinary people did it. The factors that REDUCED obedience (a favourite list): the authority was physically absent or gave orders by phone; the authority's legitimacy was undercut (ordinary office vs Yale); the victim was more present (same room, then touch-proximity); and crucially peers who rebelled (disobedient models) cut obedience sharply. Obedience rose when responsibility could be diffused (the teacher only read words while another "pressed the switch"). Trap: the headline is ~65% ; know at least two factors that lower it (proximity of victim, rebellious peers, reduced authority legitimacy). Milgram's concept of the agentic state (seeing oneself as the authority's instrument, not the author of the act) is the explanatory mechanism.

chunks.heading: Zimbardo (1971) — the Stanford Prison Experiment
chunks.text: Zimbardo (1971) — the Stanford Prison Experiment Question: do situations and roles, not dispositions, drive cruelty? What: college men were randomly assigned to be "guards" or "prisoners" in a mock basement prison; the study was meant to run two weeks. Found: guards rapidly became abusive and prisoners passive/distressed; it was halted after six days . Matters: headline demonstration of deindividuation and the power of assigned roles over individual character. Trap: Festinger coined "deindividuation"; Zimbardo gave the dramatic demonstration. Modern critique (demand characteristics, guards coached, low replicability) is now part of the discussion, so a stem may ask what the study is criticised for.

chunks.heading: Festinger & Carlsmith (1959) — $1 vs $20
chunks.text: Festinger & Carlsmith (1959) — $1 vs $20 Question: when does doing something for too little reward change your attitude? What: participants did an excruciatingly boring task, then were paid either $1 or $20 to tell a waiting participant it was enjoyable, then privately rated how much they had actually enjoyed it. Found: the $1 group rated the task as more enjoyable. Matters: classic cognitive dissonance via insufficient justification , with too little external reason to lie, the only way to resolve the tension is to believe the lie. Trap: the counter-intuitive direction ( less reward → more attitude change) is the whole point; $20 gave an external justification, so no dissonance.

chunks.heading: Latané & Darley (1968–70) — the bystander effect
chunks.text: Latané & Darley (1968–70) — the bystander effect Question: why do witnesses fail to help? What: two famous variants. In the smoke-filled room study, participants filling out a questionnaire saw smoke seep in; alone, most reported it quickly, but in a group of passive confederates most sat in the haze and said nothing ( pluralistic ignorance ). In the seizure study, the more bystanders a participant believed were on an intercom, the slower and less likely they were to help a person apparently having a fit ( diffusion of responsibility ). Found: more witnesses → less helping. Matters: formalised as the five-step decision model (notice → interpret as emergency → assume responsibility → know how → decide/act). Trap: match the failure to the step, pluralistic ignorance breaks step 2 (interpret), diffusion of responsibility breaks step 3 (assume responsibility). The Kitty Genovese case was the journalistic spark, though its "38 witnesses" detail was later shown to be exaggerated.

chunks.heading: Darley & Batson (1973) — the Good Samaritan study
chunks.text: Darley & Batson (1973) — the Good Samaritan study Question: does being in a hurry suppress helping? What: seminary students walked to give a talk (some on the parable of the Good Samaritan) and passed a man slumped, coughing, in a doorway; the experimenters varied how rushed the student was. Found: being in a hurry was the strongest predictor of not helping; the talk topic barely mattered. Matters: shows the power of the situation over personal values/personality even in the most prosocially primed people. Trap: the lesson is "hurry > piety," situational time pressure beats disposition.

chunks.heading: Bandura (1961–63) — the Bobo doll
chunks.text: Bandura (1961–63) — the Bobo doll Question: is aggression learned by imitation? What: children watched an adult model either attack or ignore an inflatable Bobo doll, then were mildly frustrated and left alone with it. Found: children who saw aggression imitated it (including novel acts and verbal aggression); seeing the model rewarded increased imitation, seeing the model punished decreased performance but not learning (they could still reproduce the acts when later incentivised). Matters: founded social learning theory and the learning/performance distinction; a bridge to the personality and learning chapters. Trap: children learned the aggression by observation regardless of the model's consequences; consequences only changed whether they performed it.

chunks.heading: Tajfel (1971) — the minimal group paradigm
chunks.text: Tajfel (1971) — the minimal group paradigm Question: how little does it take to produce in-group bias? What: strangers were split into groups on a trivial, meaningless basis (e.g. supposed preference for Klee vs Kandinsky paintings, or a coin toss), then allocated points/money to anonymous in-group and out-group members. Found: people favoured their own group even though groups were arbitrary, there was no prior contact, no self-interest, and no conflict, and they would even sacrifice absolute in-group gain to maximise the difference over the out-group. Matters: the empirical bedrock of social identity theory (Tajfel & Turner), categorisation alone breeds favouritism. Trap: minimal group = bias with no real competition; contrast with Sherif's realistic conflict, where bias needs competition over resources.

chunks.heading: Sherif (1954) — the Robbers Cave study
chunks.text: Sherif (1954) — the Robbers Cave study Question: what creates and what cures intergroup hostility? What: at a boys' summer camp, two groups (Eagles, Rattlers) were formed, then put into competition for prizes, breeding real hostility (name-calling, raids). The experimenters then introduced superordinate goals , problems both groups had to solve together (a broken water supply, a stuck truck needing every boy to pull). Found: competition manufactured prejudice; shared goals requiring cooperation dissolved it, mere contact alone did not . Matters: the field demonstration of realistic conflict theory and the reason the contact hypothesis requires cooperation toward common goals , not just proximity. Trap: it was the superordinate (shared) goal , not contact by itself, that reduced hostility.

chunks.heading: Dutton & Aron (1974) — the shaky-bridge study
chunks.text: Dutton & Aron (1974) — the shaky-bridge study Question: can arousal from one source be mislabelled as attraction? What: men crossed either a high, swaying suspension bridge (fear arousal) or a low, stable bridge, where an attractive female interviewer gave them her number. Found: men from the scary bridge were far more likely to call her and rated her as more attractive. Matters: misattribution of arousal , an application of Schachter & Singer's two-factor theory of emotion (arousal + a cognitive label = the felt emotion) to romantic attraction. Trap: the arousal was really fear; participants relabelled it as attraction.

chunks.heading: LaPiere (1934) — attitudes vs behaviour
chunks.text: LaPiere (1934) — attitudes vs behaviour Question: do stated attitudes predict actual behaviour? What: LaPiere toured the US with a young Chinese couple and recorded their treatment at ~250 hotels/restaurants; they were refused only once. Months later he wrote to the same establishments asking whether they would serve Chinese guests; over 90% said no . Found: a glaring gap between expressed prejudice and real behaviour. Matters: set off decades of work resolved by Fishbein & Ajzen (attitudes predict behaviour through intentions , and best when specific, strong, accessible). Trap: LaPiere = the attitude–behaviour gap ; the resolution (intentions, specificity) is the theory-of-reasoned-action/planned-behaviour line. Recap §11. Triplett (facilitation, first experiment) · Sherif autokinetic (informational, ambiguous, internalised norm) · Asch lines (normative, ≈33%/trial, one ally frees you) · Milgram (~65% to 450V; proximity/legitimacy/rebel-peers reduce it; agentic state) · Zimbardo SPE (roles/deindividuation, stopped at 6 days) · Festinger & Carlsmith ($1>$20, insufficient justification) · Latané & Darley (bystander, pluralistic ignorance + diffusion) · Darley & Batson (Good Samaritan, hurry beats values) · Bandura Bobo (observational learning; learning vs performance) · Tajfel minimal group (bias with no conflict) · Sherif Robbers Cave (competition makes it, superordinate goals

chunks.heading: 12. Extended concept bank (the rest of Baron, chapter by chapter)
chunks.text: 12. Extended concept bank (the rest of Baron, chapter by chapter) Everything above is the spine. This bank picks up the remaining named terms Baron uses that examiners can still pull, organised in the same chapter order so you can slot each into its home section. Treat it as the "long tail" of nameable concepts, every entry is the kind of one-line definition an MCQ distractor is built from.

chunks.heading: More on social cognition (§1)
chunks.text: More on social cognition (§1) Term Who What it is Base-rate fallacy Kahneman & Tversky Ignoring the underlying frequency of a category in favour of vivid case information (the engine behind representativeness errors). Conjunction fallacy (the "Linda" problem) Tversky & Kahneman Judging a specific conjunction ("feminist bank teller") as more likely than its broader component ("bank teller"), which is logically impossible. False consensus effect Ross et al. Overestimating how many others share our opinions, traits and choices ("everyone thinks like me"). False uniqueness effect — Underestimating how common our desirable abilities are ("hardly anyone is as honest as me"). Hindsight bias Baruch Fischhoff "I knew it all along", once an outcome is known we see it as having been inevitable/predictable. Framing effect Tversky & Kahneman The same option chosen or rejected depending on whether it is described as a gain ("90% survive") or a loss ("10% die"). Confirmation bias — Seeking and weighting evidence that fits an existing belief, ignoring disconfirming evidence (keeps schemas alive). Illusion of control Ellen Langer Overestimating our personal control over chance outcomes (blowing on dice, picking your own lottery numbers). Gambler's fallacy / hot-hand — Misreading independent random events as due to "even out" (gambler's) or as streaky (hot-hand). Bias blind spot Emily Pronin See

chunks.heading: More on perception & attribution (§2)
chunks.text: More on perception & attribution (§2) Term Who What it is Ultimate attribution error Thomas Pettigrew The FAE applied to groups : an out-group member's bad act is blamed on their disposition/group ("typical of them"), their good act is explained away as luck or an exception. The cognitive cement of prejudice. Defensive attribution — Blaming a victim more as the consequences grow worse and as we resemble the victim less, to feel safe ("it couldn't happen to me"). Two-step attribution model Gilbert & others We first automatically make a dispositional inference, then effortfully correct for the situation, and the correction often fails when we are busy or tired (why the FAE is so robust). Belief in a just world Melvin Lerner (Cross-ref §2.) The need to believe the world is fair, so good things happen to good people, drives victim-blaming. Negativity / trait negativity bias in impressions — One clearly negative trait taints an overall impression more than an equally strong positive trait improves it. Halo effect Edward Thorndike One positive global impression (usually attractiveness or likeability) bleeds into ratings of unrelated specific traits. Nonverbal "leakage" Ekman & Friesen True feelings escape through the channels we control least (legs, feet, voice pitch) while we manage the face.

chunks.heading: More on the self (§3)
chunks.text: More on the self (§3) Term Who What it is Looking-glass self Charles Cooley We build our self-concept from how we imagine we appear to others, the self as a social reflection. The "I" and the "me" William James / G.H. Mead The self as both knower/actor ("I") and the object known/evaluated ("me"). Objective self-awareness theory Duval & Wicklund Focusing attention on the self (a mirror, a camera) makes us compare to standards and feel the gap, increasing conformity to our own ideals or escape from self-focus. Self-regulation & ego depletion Roy Baumeister Self-control draws on a limited resource that fatigues with use, so willpower fails after prior exertion (the "strength model"; note replication debate). Self-serving cognitions / better-than-average effect — Most people rate themselves as above average on desirable traits (a statistical impossibility en masse). Self-schema Hazel Markus Cognitive generalisations about the self that organise and guide processing of self-relevant information. Self-concept clarity Jennifer Campbell The degree to which self-beliefs are clearly and confidently defined and internally consistent; low clarity links to low self-esteem. Independent vs interdependent self Markus & Kitayama (Cross-ref §3.) Western/individualist self defined by inner traits vs collectivist/Indian self defined by relationships and roles.

chunks.heading: More on attitudes & persuasion (§4)
chunks.text: More on attitudes & persuasion (§4) Term Who What it is Functions of attitudes Daniel Katz Attitudes serve four jobs: knowledge (organise the world), utilitarian/instrumental (gain reward, avoid punishment), ego-defensive (protect self-esteem), and value-expressive (state who we are). Changing an attitude requires addressing its function. Sleeper effect Carl Hovland A message from a low-credibility source has little impact at first but gains persuasive force over time as the source is forgotten but the content remembered. Fear appeals — Fear persuades best at moderate levels and only when paired with a clear, doable way to avoid the threat; too much fear triggers denial. Forewarning — Warning people that a persuasion attempt is coming lets them marshal counter-arguments and resist it.
