Need for cognition Cacioppo & Petty A trait, the enjoyment of effortful thinking; high-NFC people are persuaded via the central route, low-NFC via the peripheral route. Mere-thought / attitude polarisation Abraham Tesser Merely thinking about an attitude object, without new information, makes the attitude more extreme. Bogus pipeline Jones & Sigall A fake lie-detector that makes people report their true (often less socially desirable) attitudes; a methods trick for measuring real prejudice. Ego-defensive vs value-expressive change — Same surface attitude, different root, so the same counter-messag

chunks.heading: More on prejudice (§5)
chunks.text: More on prejudice (§5) Term Who What it is Right-wing authoritarianism (RWA) Bob Altemeyer The modern, better-validated successor to Adorno's authoritarian personality: submission to authority + conventionalism + aggression toward sanctioned targets. Social dominance orientation (SDO) Sidanius & Pratto A preference for group-based hierarchy and inequality; predicts prejudice independently of RWA. System justification theory John Jost People are motivated to defend and rationalise the existing social order, even when it disadvantages their own group. Subtyping — Filing stereotype-disconfirming individuals into a special "exception" subtype, which protects the overall stereotype from change. Shifting standards Monica Biernat Judging members of different groups against different, group-based yardsticks ("good... for a woman"). Self-image threat & prejudice Fein & Spencer People derogate out-group members more after their own self-esteem is threatened, and doing so restores it. Kernel-of-truth / outgroup attribution — (Cross-ref ultimate attribution error.) Stereotypes feel justified because biased attribution manufactures confirming "evidence". Realistic vs symbolic threat Stephan & Stephan (Integrated Threat Theory) Prejudice is fed by perceived realistic threats (to resources, safety) and symbolic threats (to values, worldview), plus intergroup anxiety and negative stereotypes.

chunks.heading: More on attraction & relationships (§6)
chunks.text: More on attraction & relationships (§6) Term Who What it is Reward / reinforcement-affect model Byrne & Clore We like people associated with rewards (good feelings), even when they merely happened to be present when something good occurred. Gain–loss theory of attraction Aronson & Linder We are most attracted to someone whose liking for us increases over time (a gain) and most stung when it decreases (a loss), more than by steady constant liking. Need to belong Baumeister & Leary A fundamental human motive to form and maintain lasting positive relationships; its frustration harms health and well-being. Sternberg's seven love types Robert Sternberg From the three components: liking (intimacy only), infatuation (passion only), empty (commitment only), romantic (intimacy+passion), companionate (intimacy+commitment), fatuous (passion+commitment), and consummate (all three). Communal vs exchange relationships Margaret Clark & Mills Communal partners give based on the other's needs without scorekeeping (close relationships); exchange partners track reciprocity (acquaintances, business). Accommodation & the investment of "we" Rusbult In committed relationships people inhibit the urge to retaliate to a partner's bad behaviour, responding constructively instead. Excitation / Coolidge & novelty effects — Shared novel and arousing activities re-energise long-term relationships (an applied

chunks.heading: More on social influence (§7)
chunks.text: More on social influence (§7) Term Who What it is Idiosyncrasy credits Edwin Hollander Conforming early earns "credits" a group member can later spend on dissent or innovation without rejection. Conversion theory of minority influence Serge Moscovici A consistent minority causes private conversion (genuine, often delayed, internalised change) rather than the public compliance a majority gets. Pique technique — An unusual request ("can you spare 37 cents?") disrupts automatic refusal and raises compliance by making people think. Disrupt-then-reframe Davis & Knowles A confusing twist in the pitch followed by a reframe ("it's 300 pennies... that's a bargain!") boosts compliance. Playing hard to get / scarcity Cialdini Things that seem rare or hard to obtain are valued and pursued more (links to reactance). Social impact theory Bibb Latané Influence on a target = a function of the strength , immediacy and number of the sources present. Obedience: agentic vs autonomous state Stanley Milgram People shift from the autonomous state (acting on their own values) to the agentic state (seeing themselves as an authority's tool, not responsible).

chunks.heading: More on prosocial behaviour (§8)
chunks.text: More on prosocial behaviour (§8) Term Who What it is Prosocial / altruistic personality — A cluster (empathy, belief in a just world, social responsibility, internal locus, low egocentrism) predicting consistent helping across situations. Bystander calculus / cost–reward Piliavin et al. (Cross-ref §8.) Bystanders weigh costs of helping vs costs of not helping; we help most when helping is cheap and not-helping is costly. Just-world belief & helping Lerner Believing the world is fair can reduce helping (the victim "deserved" it) or motivate it (to restore fairness). Volunteerism & the functional approach Clary & Snyder Sustained long-term helping (volunteering) is driven by the personal functions it serves (values, understanding, career, social, esteem, protective). Overjustification & helping — Paying or over-rewarding people for helping can undermine the intrinsic motive to help later. "Feel-good, do-good" effect — (Cross-ref §8.) Positive mood reliably raises helping; guilt also raises it. Defensive helping — Helping an out-group in a condescending way that actually maintains the in-group's higher status.

chunks.heading: More on aggression (§9)
chunks.text: More on aggression (§9) Term Who What it is Heat hypothesis Anderson Higher temperatures reliably increase aggression and violent crime rates (a situational/environmental cause). Alcohol myopia Steele & Josephs Alcohol narrows attention to immediate provoking cues and impairs inhibition, disinhibiting aggression. Displaced & triggered displaced aggression — Aggression aimed at a safer target than the real provoker (displaced); a minor provocation from that target then triggers an outsized response (triggered displaced). Type A behaviour pattern & aggression — Time-urgent, competitive, hostile individuals show more interpersonal aggression than easygoing Type B. Narcissism / threatened egotism Baumeister & Bushman It is inflated, unstable high self-esteem (narcissism), not low self-esteem, that predicts aggression when the ego is threatened. Sexual aggression & the confluence model Malamuth Sexual coercion arises from the confluence of hostile masculinity and impersonal-sex orientation; violent pornography raises acceptance of aggression toward women. Deindividuation & aggression Zimbardo (Cross-ref §10.) Anonymity lowers restraint and raises aggressive, antinormative behaviour in crowds/online.

chunks.heading: More on groups (§10)
chunks.text: More on groups (§10) Term Who What it is Ringelmann effect Max Ringelmann The historical root of social loafing: per-person pull on a rope falls as the group grows, from coordination loss + reduced effort. Process loss vs process gain Ivan Steiner Group output usually falls short of the sum of members' potential because of coordination and motivation losses (process loss). Brainstorming productivity loss — Real interacting groups generate fewer ideas than the same number working alone (nominal groups win), due to production blocking and evaluation apprehension. Transactive memory Daniel Wegner Groups develop a shared system for who-knows-what, so members offload knowledge to one another and recall more together. Groupthink symptoms & remedies Irving Janis Symptoms: illusion of invulnerability, collective rationalisation, belief in the group's morality, stereotyping out-groups, self-censorship, illusion of unanimity, direct pressure on dissenters, mindguards . Remedies: a devil's advocate, outside experts, leader withholds opinion, second-chance meetings. Social dilemmas: prisoner's dilemma & commons — Mixed-motive situations where individually rational defection produces a collectively worse outcome; cooperation needs trust, communication and sanctions. Fiedler's contingency model of leadership Fred Fiedler Effective leadership depends on the match between leader style (task- v

chunks.heading: 13. The MCQ traps, collected
chunks.text: 13. The MCQ traps, collected Method core: experiment = the only design proving causation (manipulate IV, measure DV, random assignment). Correlation ≠ causation (third-variable + directionality). Mediator = the why (mechanism in between); moderator = the when/for whom (changes strength). Availability = ease of recall · representativeness = fit to a prototype (neglects base rates) · anchoring = stuck on a first value. All three = Tversky & Kahneman. The attribution swap: FAE (Ross) = over-blame others' character · actor–observer (Jones & Nisbett) = my acts = situation, your acts = character · self-serving = my success = me, my failure = the situation. Attribution models in order: Heider (naïve psychologist, internal/external) → Jones & Davis (correspondent inference) → Kelley (covariation: consensus, consistency, distinctiveness). Self-discrepancy (Higgins): ideal-self gap → dejection (sad) ; ought-self gap → agitation (anxious) . Self cluster: social comparison = Festinger · self-perception = Bem · self-monitoring = Snyder · self-efficacy = Bandura · self-handicapping = Berglas & Jones · self-verification = Swann · self-affirmation = Steele · spotlight = Gilovich · BIRGing = Cialdini · TMT = Greenberg, Pyszczynski & Solomon. Dissonance vs self-perception: Festinger = arousal/discomfort , applies when the attitude was strong; Bem = no arousal, just inference , applies when the a

chunks.heading: 14. Fast glossary (one line each, A–Z)
chunks.text: 14. Fast glossary (one line each, A–Z) Last-mile recall: every nameable term on this page reduced to a single line and its author, alphabetical so you can self-test by covering the right column. If a name fires but the definition doesn't, that is the gap to drill. Term One-line definition (and who) Actor–observer effect My acts → situation, your acts → your character (Jones & Nisbett). Agentic state Seeing oneself as an authority's instrument, not the author of the act (Milgram). Anchoring & adjustment Cling to a first value, adjust too little (Tversky & Kahneman). Authoritarian personality Rigid, submissive-to-authority, prejudice-prone; F-scale (Adorno). Availability heuristic Judge likelihood by ease of recall (Tversky & Kahneman). Balance theory We seek consistency in liking-relationships, P-O-X triads (Heider). Base-rate fallacy Ignore underlying frequencies for vivid cases (Kahneman & Tversky). BIRGing Basking in reflected glory, "we won" (Cialdini). Bystander effect More witnesses → less help; 5-step model (Latané & Darley). Catharsis (myth) Venting drains aggression, largely unsupported; it raises it. Cognitive dissonance Tension from clashing cognitions drives attitude change (Festinger). Companionate love Deep affection, trust, care that lasts (Hatfield & Berscheid). Conjunction fallacy Specific conjunction judged likelier than its component, "Linda" (Tversky & Kahnem

chunks.heading: 15. Self-test (active recall, by chapter)
chunks.text: 15. Self-test (active recall, by chapter) Recall beats re-reading. Cover the answers, ask yourself each question aloud, then check. If you miss one, jump back to its section. The answer follows in green .

chunks.heading: §0 Science & methods
chunks.text: §0 Science & methods Which is the only method that establishes cause and effect, and what two features make it work? Experimental; manipulating the IV + random assignment. Distinguish a mediator from a moderator. Mediator = the mechanism in between (the why ); moderator = changes the strength/direction (the when/for whom ). Name Baron's four perspectives. Cognitive, evolutionary, social neuroscience, cultural.

chunks.heading: §1 Social cognition
chunks.text: §1 Social cognition Availability vs representativeness, what is each judged by? Availability = ease of recall; representativeness = fit to a prototype (neglects base rates). What three processes do schemas bias? Attention, encoding, retrieval, plus they persevere after disconfirmation. Who showed thought suppression backfires, and what is it called? Wegner; the rebound (white-bear) effect.

chunks.heading: §2 Perception & attribution
chunks.text: §2 Perception & attribution Put the three attribution theorists in order with their contribution. Heider (internal/external, naïve psychologist) → Jones & Davis (correspondent inference) → Kelley (covariation: consensus, consistency, distinctiveness). FAE vs actor–observer vs self-serving, whose behaviour/outcome does each concern? FAE = others' acts (blame character); actor–observer = my acts (situation) vs yours (character); self-serving = my outcomes (credit success, dodge failure). Asch's configural view vs Anderson's model? Asch = central traits reorganise the whole; Anderson = we average weighted trait values.

chunks.heading: §3 The self
chunks.text: §3 The self Higgins: ideal-self gap leads to ___, ought-self gap leads to ___. Dejection (sad); agitation (anxious). Independent vs interdependent self-construal, and where does India sit? Markus & Kitayama; India = interdependent/collectivist. Match: Bem, Festinger, Snyder, Swann, Steele. Self-perception; social comparison; self-monitoring; self-verification; self-affirmation.

chunks.heading: §4 Attitudes & persuasion
chunks.text: §4 Attitudes & persuasion What did LaPiere demonstrate, and who resolved it? The attitude–behaviour gap; Fishbein & Ajzen (via intentions). Why did the $1 group change attitudes more than the $20 group? Insufficient justification, no external reason to lie, so they had to believe it (Festinger & Carlsmith). Dissonance vs self-perception, what is the deciding clue? Arousal/discomfort + strong prior attitude (Festinger) vs no arousal, weak attitude, mere inference (Bem).

chunks.heading: §5 Prejudice
chunks.text: §5 Prejudice Social identity vs realistic conflict vs authoritarian personality, the engine of each? Categorisation alone (Tajfel & Turner) vs resource competition (Sherif) vs a personality type (Adorno). Allport's four conditions for contact to reduce prejudice? Equal status, common goals, intergroup cooperation, institutional support. Hostile vs benevolent sexism, which sounds "nice"? Benevolent (cherish/protect), still subordinating (Glick & Fiske).

chunks.heading: §6 Attraction & love
chunks.text: §6 Attraction & love Order the early predictors of attraction. Propinquity (Festinger et al.) → mere exposure (Zajonc) → similarity (Byrne) → matching/beauty stereotype. What does the investment model add to social exchange, and its clinical use? Commitment = satisfaction + investment − alternatives (Rusbult); explains staying in unsatisfying/abusive relationships. Name Duck's break-up phases. Intrapsychic → dyadic → social → grave-dressing.

chunks.heading: §7 Social influence
chunks.text: §7 Social influence Sherif vs Asch, ambiguous or unambiguous, informational or normative? Sherif = ambiguous, informational, internalised; Asch = unambiguous, normative, public compliance. Milgram's headline figure and two factors that reduce obedience? ~65% to 450V; victim more present / rebellious peers / less legitimate or absent authority. FITD vs DITF direction and mechanism? FITD = small→big (consistency); DITF = big→small (reciprocal concession).

chunks.heading: §8 Prosocial
chunks.text: §8 Prosocial The five steps of the bystander model, and which step each crowd-failure breaks? Notice → interpret → take responsibility → know how → act; pluralistic ignorance breaks step 2, diffusion of responsibility breaks step 3. Batson vs Cialdini/Piliavin on why we help? Batson = true altruism from empathy; Cialdini (negative-state relief) & Piliavin (arousal:cost-reward) = egoistic.

chunks.heading: §9 Aggression
chunks.text: §9 Aggression How did Berkowitz reformulate frustration–aggression, and what's the weapons effect? Frustration creates only readiness (negative affect); aggressive cues fire it; a weapon's mere presence is such a cue (Berkowitz & LePage). True or false: catharsis reduces aggression. False, venting tends to raise later aggression. Low or inflated self-esteem predicts aggression? Inflated, unstable (narcissism), when ego is threatened (Baumeister & Bushman).

chunks.heading: §10 Groups
chunks.text: §10 Groups Facilitation vs loafing, what is the deciding variable? Whether your individual output is identifiable (identifiable → try harder; hidden → loaf). Who coined deindividuation vs who gave the famous demonstration? Festinger coined it; Zimbardo (Stanford prison) demonstrated it. Distributive vs procedural justice, and which can matter more? Fair outcome vs fair process; people accept bad outcomes if the process felt fair. Recap §15. If you can answer these cold, you have the spine, the named layer and the discriminations. Re-test the ones you missed, then run the §13 traps and §14 glossary once more the night before. That sequence (recall → trap discrimination → glossary sweep) is the highest-yield last-mile routine for this domain. Companion pages: the four type sweeps (one named thing per row) are the chips at the top: Effects , Phenomena , Theories , Theorists . The one-line testable list is in the textbook's Rapid Recall . For the cognitive-psychology side of heuristics and dual-process thinking see the Cognitive sweep. Sihan NIMHANS + MET 2026 prep · /notes/social-psych/ · teaching chapter

chunks.heading: Gap 1, Sleep Architecture (Diagnostic Q3 and set-01 Q7 both missed)
chunks.text: Gap 1, Sleep Architecture (Diagnostic Q3 and set-01 Q7 both missed) Sihan has consistently confused REM and Stage 3 NREM (delta) . The discriminating feature is muscle atonia — it happens in REM, not in delta. Memory hook, “PARADOX”: REM is called “paradoxical sleep” because the brain looks almost awake (fast, mixed-frequency EEG) but the body is paralyzed (atonia). Delta is the opposite — slow brain, normal muscle tone, deep restoration. Stage EEG Muscles Dreams Notes Wake Beta (13-30 Hz) Active — — NREM 1 Theta (4-8 Hz) Relaxed Hypnagogic images Drowsy, hard to tell asleep NREM 2 Theta + spindles + K-complexes Relaxed Rare Most of the night is in NREM 2 NREM 3 (delta / slow-wave) Delta (0.5-4 Hz) Normal tone Rare, thought-like Deepest, growth hormone released REM Mixed freq, like awake Atonia (paralysis) Vivid narrative Pons suppresses motor output. Eye movements only MCQ trigger words: - “muscle paralysis” / “atonia” / “body paralysis” → REM - “slow-wave” / “delta” / “deep sleep” → NREM 3 - “sleep spindles” / “K-complexes” → NREM 2 - “paradoxical sleep” → REM - “night terrors” / “sleepwalking” / “bedwetting” → NREM 3 (not REM; these are parasomnias out of deep sleep)

chunks.heading: Gap 2, Neuroendocrine — Cortisol Source (Diagnostic Q4 missed)
chunks.text: Gap 2, Neuroendocrine — Cortisol Source (Diagnostic Q4 missed) Sihan picked adrenal medulla for cortisol. Correct is adrenal cortex . These two layers of the adrenal gland do completely different things. Adrenal anatomy from outside in: - Cortex (outer layer), three zones: - Zona Glomerulosa → Aldosterone (salt/water, mineralocorticoid) - Zona Fasciculata → Cortisol (glucose/stress, glucocorticoid) ★ - Zona Reticularis → Sex steroids (androgens, small amounts) - Medulla (inner layer): - Epinephrine (~80%) and Norepinephrine (~20%) - Modified sympathetic post-ganglionic neurons (chromaffin cells) - Fast response catecholamines, fight-or-flight Memory hook, “GFR, salt sugar sex”: - G lomerulosa → salt (aldosterone) - F asciculata → sugar (cortisol, raises blood glucose) - R eticularis → sex (androgens) - Medulla = adrenaline (fast, not a steroid) HPA axis sequence (re-memorize): Stressor → Hypothalamus secretes CRH → Anterior pituitary secretes ACTH → Adrenal cortex (zona fasciculata) secretes cortisol → Negative feedback to hypothalamus + pituitary.

chunks.heading: Gap 3, Dopamine Pathways (Diagnostic Q5 missed)
chunks.text: Gap 3, Dopamine Pathways (Diagnostic Q5 missed) Sihan picked hippocampus for substantia nigra projection. Correct is striatum. The four major dopamine pathways are a classic MCQ cluster. Pathway From To Function Disease Nigrostriatal ★ Substantia nigra pars compacta Striatum (caudate + putamen) Motor control, habit Parkinson’s disease (degeneration here) Mesolimbic Ventral tegmental area (VTA) Nucleus accumbens, amygdala, hippocampus Reward, motivation Addiction, positive symptoms of schizophrenia Mesocortical VTA Prefrontal cortex Cognition, executive Negative symptoms of schizophrenia Tuberoinfundibular Arcuate nucleus (hypothalamus) Median eminence → pituitary Inhibits prolactin Blocked by antipsychotics → hyperprolactinemia, gynecomastia Memory hook, “NI-MESO2-TUBE”: - N igrostriatal → Parkinson’s (motor) - Meso limbic → positive symptoms + addiction (reward) - Meso cortical → negative symptoms (cognition) - Tube roinfundibular → prolactin (endocrine)

chunks.heading: Gap 1, Predictive vs Concurrent Validity (Q2 missed)
chunks.text: Gap 1, Predictive vs Concurrent Validity (Q2 missed) Predictive: criterion measured LATER , in the future. - Example: GRE score today → graduate GPA 2 years from now. - Example: Job aptitude test → job performance 6 months after hire. - Example: Admission test → first-year medical school grades. Concurrent: criterion measured at the SAME TIME . - Example: New depression scale today vs HAM-D today (comparing to an established gold standard). - Example: IQ test vs teacher rating of intelligence, both this week. Memory hook: Predictive = Postponed. Concurrent = Current.

chunks.heading: Gap 2, MMPI-2 Clinical Scales (Q3 missed, said 8)
chunks.text: Gap 2, MMPI-2 Clinical Scales (Q3 missed, said 8) MMPI-2 has 10 clinical scales , not 8. Memorize them cold. # Scale Abbreviation Measures 1 Hypochondriasis Hs Somatic concerns 2 Depression D Sadness, hopelessness 3 Hysteria Hy Physical complaints under stress 4 Psychopathic Deviate Pd Antisocial, authority conflicts 5 Masculinity-Femininity Mf Gender role interests 6 Paranoia Pa Suspiciousness 7 Psychasthenia Pt Anxiety, obsessive 8 Schizophrenia Sc Bizarre thoughts 9 Hypomania Ma Elevated mood, hyperactivity 0 Social Introversion Si Social withdrawal Mnemonic, “His Deep Hysterical Past Makes Paul Panic Secretly Most Mornings, Silently”: Hs, D, Hy, Pd, Mf, Pa, Pt, Sc, Ma, Si. Plus validity scales: L (Lie), F (Infrequency), K (Correction), ? (Cannot Say), VRIN (Variable Response Inconsistency), TRIN (True Response Inconsistency). Total items: 567 true/false. Do not confuse with: 16PF (Cattell, 16 primary factors, different test entirely).

chunks.heading: Gap 3, TAT Cards (Q4 missed, said 10)
chunks.text: Gap 3, TAT Cards (Q4 missed, said 10) TAT (Thematic Apperception Test): - Creator: Henry Murray with Christiana Morgan, 1935. - Total cards: 31 cards . - Per administration: 20 cards , chosen by age (adult vs child) and sex of subject. - Stimulus: ambiguous black-and-white scenes of people. - Theory: subject projects unconscious needs (Murray’s needs-press theory) onto the ambiguous scene. Do not confuse with: - Rorschach = 10 inkblots (5 chromatic, 5 achromatic). Herman Rorschach, 1921. - CAT (Children’s Apperception Test) = Bellak, 1949. Animal figures for children. Memory hook: T AT = T hirty-one, Rorschach = Ten.

chunks.heading: Gap 4, KR-20 vs Cohen Kappa (Q5 missed, said kappa)
chunks.text: Gap 4, KR-20 vs Cohen Kappa (Q5 missed, said kappa) These are completely different reliability methods. Kappa is NOT internal consistency. Method What it measures When to use KR-20 Internal consistency for dichotomous items (right/wrong, true/false) 1 administration, 0/1 scoring. Special case of Cronbach’s α. Cronbach’s α Internal consistency for Likert/multi-point items 1 administration, multi-point scoring. Split-half + Spearman-Brown Internal consistency (quick approximation) 1 administration, splits test in half, corrects. Test-retest Stability across time 2 administrations, 2+ weeks apart. Alternate forms Equivalence of two versions 2 versions of the test. Cohen’s kappa Inter-rater agreement on categorical data 2+ raters scoring the same protocols, correcting for chance agreement. ICC Inter-rater agreement on continuous data 2+ raters, numeric scores. Kappa asks: “How much do two raters agree on category assignments, beyond chance?” Does not care about items or internal structure. KR-20 asks: “How consistent are right/wrong items on this one test, with each other?” If a question says: - “30-item right/wrong exam, one administration, reliability” → KR-20 - “Two clinicians diagnosing the same patients” → Kappa - “21-item Beck Depression Inventory, Likert 0-3, internal consistency” → Cronbach’s α

chunks.heading: 1.1 The neuron and glia
chunks.text: 1.1 The neuron and glia Dendrites receive input (spines multiply surface area). Soma integrates input. Axon hillock = trigger zone, decides if threshold is reached. Axon conducts the AP. Axon terminals release neurotransmitter. Neuron types: Sensory (afferent, periphery → CNS, pseudounipolar); Motor (efferent, CNS → muscle/gland, multipolar); Interneurons (local CNS processing, most common). Glial cell Location Function Oligodendrocyte CNS Myelinates many axons (one cell, many segments) Schwann cell PNS Myelinates one axon segment per cell Astrocyte CNS Blood-brain barrier, K+ buffering, NT recycling Microglia CNS Immune defence, phagocytosis Ependymal cell Ventricles Produces and circulates CSF Satellite cell PNS ganglia Supports cell bodies in PNS TRAP: CNS myelination = oligodendrocyte. PNS myelination = Schwann cell.

chunks.heading: 1.2 The action potential (the single most testable neurophysiology topic)
chunks.text: 1.2 The action potential (the single most testable neurophysiology topic) An AP is a ~1 ms electrical pulse travelling down the axon. The whole story is " Na+ in, K+ out ": Na+ rushing in depolarises; K+ leaving repolarises. Resting membrane potential ~ −70 mV. Set by K+ leak channels (membrane ~50× more permeable to K+), NOT by the Na/K pump. Threshold ~ −55 mV. Na/K pump: 3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in per ATP. Electrogenic. Maintains the gradient but does not set RMP. Phase 1 Depolarisation: voltage-gated Na+ channels open → Na+ in → spike to ~ +30 mV. Phase 2 Repolarisation: Na+ channels inactivate, voltage-gated K+ channels open (slower) → K+ out. Phase 3 Hyperpolarisation: K+ channels stay open briefly → undershoot below −70 mV. Phase 4 Return: K+ channels close, Na/K pump restores ions. Ion concentrations: "K is in, Na is out, Cl is out, Ca is way out." Equilibrium potentials: K+ −90 mV, Na+ +60 mV, Cl− −65 mV, Ca²⁺ +120 mV. All-or-none law: once threshold is reached the AP fires at constant amplitude; stimulus intensity is coded by frequency , not amplitude. Refractory periods: Absolute = Na+ channels inactivated, no stimulus however strong can fire another AP (ensures one-way propagation). Relative = membrane hyperpolarised (K+ still open), a stronger stimulus can fire one. TRAP: Inactivated ≠ closed. The Na+ channel has 3 states: closed (resting), open (during AP), inactivated (a

chunks.heading: 1.3 Neurotransmitters (the 7 families)
chunks.text: 1.3 Neurotransmitters (the 7 families) NT Class / made from Cleared by Clinical link Acetylcholine (ACh) Choline + acetyl-CoA Acetylcholinesterase Low in Alzheimer's; myasthenia gravis (anti-AChR); NMJ Dopamine Catecholamine (Tyrosine → DOPA → DA) Reuptake, MAO, COMT ↑ mesolimbic = +ve schizophrenia. Low nigrostriatal = Parkinson's. Reward/addiction. Norepinephrine Catecholamine (DA + β-hydroxylase) Reuptake, MAO Arousal, sympathetic. Locus coeruleus. Low in depression. Serotonin (5-HT) Indolamine (Tryptophan) Reuptake (SERT), MAO Mood, sleep, appetite. Low → depression, OCD. Raphe nuclei. Glutamate Amino acid (Glutamine) Astrocyte reuptake Main excitatory NT. NMDA/AMPA/kainate. LTP, learning. Excess = excitotoxicity. GABA Amino acid (from Glutamate via GAD) Reuptake Main inhibitory NT. GABA-A ionotropic = target of benzos, alcohol, barbiturates. Endorphins Peptide (POMC) Peptidases Pain modulation, runner's high. μ, κ, δ receptors. TRAP: Hippocampal LTP depends on the NMDA receptor (coincidence detector — needs glutamate AND postsynaptic depolarisation to displace the Mg²⁺ block; Ca²⁺ entry triggers LTP). AMPA carries the fast EPSP. Hebb: "neurons that fire together wire together."

chunks.heading: 1.4 Nervous system organisation
chunks.text: 1.4 Nervous system organisation Nervous System ├── CNS (brain + spinal cord) └── PNS ├── Somatic NS (voluntary, skeletal muscle) └── Autonomic NS ├── Sympathetic ("fight/flight") — thoracolumbar T1–L2, NE ├── Parasympathetic ("rest/digest") — craniosacral (CN III,VII,IX,X + S2–S4), ACh └── Enteric ("gut brain") ANS contrasts: Sympathetic ↑ heart rate, dilates pupil, ↓ GI; pre/post-ganglionic NT = ACh/NE (sweat glands are the ACh exception). Parasympathetic ↓ heart rate (vagus), constricts pupil, ↑ GI; ACh/ACh.

chunks.heading: 1.5 Brain anatomy & lobes
chunks.text: 1.5 Brain anatomy & lobes Region Structures Function Forebrain Cortex, basal ganglia, limbic system, thalamus, hypothalamus Higher cognition, emotion, motor planning, autonomic control Midbrain Tectum (sup/inf colliculi), tegmentum, substantia nigra, red nucleus, PAG Visual/auditory reflexes, motor control, pain modulation Hindbrain Pons, medulla, cerebellum Vital functions, balance, fine motor coordination Lobe Key areas Lesion produces Frontal Motor cortex (precentral), prefrontal, Broca's (L) Paralysis, executive deficits, Broca's aphasia, personality change (Phineas Gage) Parietal Somatosensory (postcentral), association cortex Left hemispatial neglect if right lesion; Gerstmann's if left; agnosia Temporal Primary auditory, Wernicke's (L), hippocampus, amygdala Wernicke's aphasia, anterograde amnesia, Klüver-Bucy Occipital Primary visual (V1), visual association Cortical blindness, visual agnosia, prosopagnosia (fusiform) Thalamus — sensory relay for all senses except smell. LGN (vision), MGN (hearing), VPL (touch), VPM (face). Hypothalamus — homeostasis, hormones, the 4 Fs. VMH lesion = hyperphagia + obesity ; LH lesion = aphagia . SCN = circadian. Supraoptic → ADH. Paraventricular → oxytocin + CRH. Basal ganglia — caudate, putamen, globus pallidus, subthalamic nucleus, substantia nigra. Red nucleus is NOT basal ganglia (it's midbrain tegmentum). Lesions: Parkinson's (SN),

chunks.heading: 1.5b Limbic system: function by structure
chunks.text: 1.5b Limbic system: function by structure Structure Function Lesion / clinical hook Hippocampus Forms and consolidates new declarative (explicit) memories; spatial navigation (place cells) Bilateral damage = anterograde amnesia (patient H.M.) Amygdala Fear conditioning, threat detection, attaches emotional weight to memory Damage = Klüver-Bucy (placidity, hyperorality, hypersexuality), blunted fear Hypothalamus Homeostasis and the 4 Fs; the bridge from limbic system to endocrine (via pituitary) and autonomic systems VMH lesion = overeating; LH lesion = no eating Cingulate gyrus (anterior) Emotion regulation, conflict/error monitoring, attention, the affective (suffering) component of pain Cingulotomy historically used for severe OCD/chronic pain Fornix Output cable carrying hippocampal signals to the mammillary bodies and hypothalamus Section disrupts memory recall Mammillary bodies Memory relay station in the Papez circuit Degenerate in Wernicke-Korsakoff (thiamine/B1 deficiency): confabulation, anterograde amnesia Septal nuclei Reward and pleasure; dampen aggression Olds and Milner self-stimulation studies (the "pleasure centre") Olfactory bulb Smell, the only sense that reaches cortex without a thalamic relay Explains the strong smell-to-memory and smell-to-emotion link Papez circuit (emotion + memory loop): hippocampus → fornix → mammillary bodies → anterior thalamus → cing

chunks.heading: 1.5c Basal ganglia: function by structure
chunks.text: 1.5c Basal ganglia: function by structure Overall job: initiate and scale voluntary movement, suppress unwanted movement, and drive procedural (habit) learning. It works as a loop: cortex → striatum → pallidum → thalamus → back to cortex. Structure Function Lesion / disorder Striatum = caudate + putamen Main input zone, receives signals from the cortex Degenerates in Huntington's (chorea) Caudate Cognition, goal-directed action, part of OCD circuitry Overactive caudate loops in OCD and Tourette's Putamen Habit learning and motor execution Loss of movement automaticity Globus pallidus (GPi / GPe) Output zone; GPi is the main inhibitory output to the thalamus Pallidotomy / deep-brain-stimulation target in Parkinson's Subthalamic nucleus Brake within the indirect pathway Lesion = hemiballismus (wild flinging of one side) Substantia nigra (pars compacta) Supplies dopamine to the striatum Degenerates in Parkinson's (resting tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia) Direct vs indirect pathway: the direct pathway (dopamine on D1, the "go" route) facilitates movement; the indirect pathway (dopamine on D2, the "no-go" route) suppresses it. Dopamine from the substantia nigra tips the balance toward movement, so losing it (Parkinson's) makes movement hard to start. TRAP: Parkinson's is hypokinetic (too little movement, dopamine loss in the substantia nigra). Huntington's and hemiballismus are hyper

chunks.heading: 1.6 Cranial nerves I–XII
chunks.text: 1.6 Cranial nerves I–XII # Name Type Function I Olfactory S Smell. Only CN that does NOT relay through thalamus. II Optic S Vision. Decussates at optic chiasm. III Oculomotor M Most extraocular muscles, levator palpebrae, pupillary constriction. IV Trochlear M Superior oblique only. Smallest CN. V Trigeminal B Face sensation, mastication. VI Abducens M Lateral rectus only. VII Facial B Facial expression, taste (anterior 2/3), salivation, lacrimation. VIII Vestibulocochlear S Hearing + balance. IX Glossopharyngeal B Taste (posterior 1/3), pharynx, parotid. X Vagus B Parasympathetic to thorax/abdomen, larynx, pharynx. XI Spinal accessory M SCM and trapezius. XII Hypoglossal M Tongue movement. Mnemonics: names — " On Old Olympus' Towering Tops A Finn And German Viewed Some Hops ." Type — " Some Say Marry Money But My Brother Says Big Brains Matter Most " (S=sensory, M=motor, B=both, I→XII). Parasympathetic carriers: III, VII, IX, X.

chunks.heading: 1.7 Sensory systems
chunks.text: 1.7 Sensory systems Vision: rods (peripheral, low light, no colour) + cones (foveal, colour, acuity). Cones densest at the fovea centralis. Optic disc = blind spot. Pathway: retina → optic nerve → chiasm (nasal fibres cross) → optic tract → LGN → V1. Theories: trichromatic (Young-Helmholtz, retinal) + opponent-process (Hering, post-retinal). Dorsal stream "where/how" (parietal); ventral stream "what" (temporal). Audition: outer → middle (malleus, incus, stapes) → cochlea → hair cells on basilar membrane → CN VIII → cochlear nuclei → MGN → Heschl's gyrus. Place theory (Békésy): base = high frequencies, apex = low; best for high. Frequency theory: firing rate = frequency, works <500 Hz. Volley principle bridges mid-range. Somatosensation: dorsal column-medial lemniscus (touch, vibration, proprioception, decussates at medulla) vs spinothalamic (pain, temp, decussates at spinal level of entry). Taste: sweet, salty, sour, bitter, umami. CN VII / IX / X. Insula = primary gustatory cortex. Smell: olfactory epithelium → bulb → piriform cortex (no thalamus relay), closest to limbic system.

chunks.heading: 1.8 Motor systems
chunks.text: 1.8 Motor systems Pyramidal (corticospinal): M1 (Brodmann 4) → internal capsule → peduncle → pons → medullary pyramids. Decussates at the pyramids of the medulla (~85–90% → lateral corticospinal tract). Extrapyramidal: rubrospinal (flexor bias), vestibulospinal (postural extensor), reticulospinal (locomotion), tectospinal (head/neck orienting). UMN lesion LMN lesion Tone Spasticity (↑) Flaccidity (↓) Reflexes Hyperreflexia, clonus, +Babinski Hyporeflexia/areflexia Atrophy Mild, late Severe, early Fasciculations Absent Present

chunks.heading: 1.9 The "A" deficits, aphasias & lesion syndromes
chunks.text: 1.9 The "A" deficits, aphasias & lesion syndromes Term Deficit Apraxia Can't sequence learned, purposeful movements despite intact motor/sensory function (can't mime brushing hair) Ataxia Loss of coordination and balance (cerebellar) — clumsy, unsteady gait, dysmetria. A motor-control problem, not planning Agnosia Can't recognise objects/faces/sounds despite intact senses (e.g. prosopagnosia) Aphasia Language deficit — Broca's (non-fluent, comprehension intact), Wernicke's (fluent, poor comprehension) Alexia / Agraphia / Anomia Can't read / can't write / can't name (word-finding) Lesion Syndrome Broca's area (L inferior frontal) Non-fluent aphasia, comprehension intact Wernicke's area (L superior temporal) Fluent but meaningless speech, poor comprehension Arcuate fasciculus Conduction aphasia (poor repetition) Bilateral hippocampus Anterograde amnesia (case HM) Mammillary bodies + thalamus (thiamine) Korsakoff's, confabulation Right inferior parietal Left hemispatial neglect Left parietal (angular gyrus) Gerstmann's: agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia, L-R disorientation Bilateral amygdala Klüver-Bucy: hyperoral, hypersexual, placid, visual agnosia Substantia nigra Parkinson's: bradykinesia, rigidity, resting tremor Subthalamic nucleus Hemiballismus Fusiform face area Prosopagnosia (face blindness)

chunks.heading: 1.10 Endocrine & the HPA axis
chunks.text: 1.10 Endocrine & the HPA axis Gland Hormone Action Hypothalamus CRH, TRH, GHRH, GnRH, somatostatin, dopamine Releasing/inhibiting factors to anterior pituitary Anterior pituitary ACTH, TSH, GH, FSH/LH, prolactin Trophic hormones Posterior pituitary ADH (vasopressin), oxytocin Made in hypothalamus, stored here. ADH → water reabsorption. Oxytocin → labour, milk ejection, bonding. Adrenal cortex Cortisol, aldosterone, DHEA (GFR: glomerulosa/fasciculata/reticularis) Stress, salt/water, sex precursor Adrenal medulla Epinephrine, NE Sympathetic surge Thyroid / Pineal / Pancreas T3/T4/calcitonin · Melatonin · Insulin/glucagon Metabolism · circadian · glucose HPA axis: stress → hypothalamus releases CRH → anterior pituitary releases ACTH → adrenal cortex (zona fasciculata) releases cortisol . Negative feedback to hypothalamus + pituitary. Cortisol awakening response peaks ~30 min after waking; trough ~midnight. Condition HPA pattern MDD Hyper -cortisol, blunted rhythm, DST non-suppression PTSD Hypo -cortisol, exaggerated negative feedback (the paradox) Cushing's ↑ cortisol, central obesity, striae, depression in 50–80% Addison's ↓ cortisol, hyperpigmentation (MSH from POMC), apathy Stress theory: Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome = A larm → R esistance → E xhaustion (he coined "stress"). Cannon coined "fight or flight" and "homeostasis." McEwen — allostatic load (wear and tear of chr

chunks.heading: 1.11 Sleep (full primer)
chunks.text: 1.11 Sleep (full primer) Sleep = NREM (3 stages) + REM. One cycle ~ 90 min ; 4–6 cycles/night. N3 dominates the first half; REM dominates the second half and lengthens through the night. Stage EEG / signature Notes NREM 1 (~5%) Theta (4–8 Hz) Light, hypnic jerks, hypnagogic images NREM 2 (~45–55%) Sleep spindles + K-complexes Most of the night; spindles gate sensory input NREM 3 (~15–20%) Delta (0.5–4 Hz, high amplitude) Deep/slow-wave. Growth hormone. Parasomnias (sleepwalking, night terrors, enuresis) come OUT of N3 REM (~20–25%) Mixed, low-voltage (looks awake) Paradoxical : brain active, body in atonia . Vivid dreams, eye bursts, autonomic instability, thermoregulation fails. NOT delta-dominant. Neural control: sleep pressure from adenosine (caffeine blocks adenosine receptors); VLPO = GABAergic "sleep switch"; wake driven by the ARAS (histamine, orexin, NE, 5-HT, ACh). SCN = master circadian clock, entrained by light via the retinohypothalamic tract → pineal → melatonin in darkness. REM-ON = cholinergic (PPT/LDT); REM-OFF = aminergic (NE, 5-HT). Memory: declarative consolidated in NREM (delta replay); procedural in REM + spindles; emotional in REM. Disorders: Narcolepsy = orexin/hypocretin deficiency; cataplexy is pathognomonic. RBD = loss of atonia in REM, older men, α-synucleinopathy warning (Parkinson/Lewy body). RLS = urge to move legs at rest (dopamine/iron). Kleine-L

chunks.heading: 1.12 Emotion, arousal, learning & LTP
chunks.text: 1.12 Emotion, arousal, learning & LTP Theories of emotion: James-Lange (body first, "we feel sad because we cry"); Cannon-Bard (body + emotion simultaneously, thalamic); Schachter-Singer (two-factor: arousal + cognitive label); Lazarus (appraisal precedes emotion). Yerkes-Dodson law: inverted-U of arousal vs performance. Optimum is lower for complex tasks, higher for simple/well-learned tasks. Memory substrates: hippocampus (declarative consolidation), amygdala (emotional/fear), striatum (procedural/habit), cerebellum (motor conditioning). LTP strengthens synapses (NMDA receptor critical, Ca²⁺ entry, AMPA insertion); LTD weakens them. Papez circuit: hippocampus → fornix → mammillary → anterior thalamus → cingulate → entorhinal → hippocampus.

chunks.heading: 1.13 Mania first-line drugs & psychopharmacology
chunks.text: 1.13 Mania first-line drugs & psychopharmacology First-line for acute mania: Lithium · Valproate (Divalproex) · atypical antipsychotics (Olanzapine, Risperidone, Quetiapine, Aripiprazole). Carbamazepine is second-line. NOT first-line (your mock miss): Fluoxetine and any SSRI/antidepressant — they can trigger a manic switch . Antidepressants are avoided in acute mania. Drug class Mechanism Used in SSRI (fluoxetine, sertraline) Block 5-HT reuptake Depression, OCD, anxiety SNRI (venlafaxine, duloxetine) Block 5-HT + NE reuptake Depression, GAD, neuropathic pain TCA Block 5-HT + NE reuptake; many side effects Depression (older), pain MAOI Block monoamine breakdown; tyramine diet Atypical/refractory depression Typical antipsychotic (haloperidol) D2 antagonist +ve schizophrenia. SE: EPS, tardive dyskinesia Atypical (clozapine, risperidone, olanzapine) D2 + 5-HT2A antagonist Schizophrenia (+ some −ve). Clozapine = agranulocytosis risk Benzodiazepines GABA-A positive modulator Anxiety, insomnia, status epilepticus Lithium Unclear (inositol depletion) Bipolar mania prophylaxis Stimulants (methylphenidate) ↑ DA + NE ADHD, narcolepsy

chunks.heading: 1.14 Genetic, chromosomal & metabolic disorders
chunks.text: 1.14 Genetic, chromosomal & metabolic disorders Three things per disorder: (1) genetic mechanism, (2) one physical/biochemical sign, (3) one behavioural/cognitive sign. Disorder Mechanism One-line ID + behaviour Down Trisomy 21 (95% non-disjunction/maternal age; 5% translocation = inheritable) Flat face, single palmar crease; IQ 30–70, sociable; early Alzheimer's after 40 (extra APP). Most common chromosomal cause of ID. Edwards / Patau Trisomy 18 / Trisomy 13 Clenched fists, rocker-bottom feet / cleft lip, polydactyly. Severe ID, <10% survive 1 yr Klinefelter 47,XXY Tall, gynecomastia, small testes, infertile; verbal IQ < performance Turner 45,X0 (only viable monosomy) Short, webbed neck, amenorrhoea; normal verbal, poor visuospatial Fragile X CGG repeat on FMR1, X-linked Long face, large ears, macroorchidism; most common inherited cause of ID , hand-flapping, ASD overlap Williams 7q11.23 microdeletion (elastin) Elfin face, supravalvular aortic stenosis; hypersocial "cocktail party" speech, musical Prader-Willi Paternal 15q11-13 deletion Hypotonic infant → hyperphagia, obesity; skin-picking, food obsessions Angelman Maternal 15q11-13 deletion Ataxic gait, seizures; severe ID, no speech, inappropriate laughter "happy puppet" Cri-du-chat 5p deletion Cat-like cry , microcephaly; severe ID DiGeorge / VCFS 22q11.2 deletion (CATCH-22) Cardiac, cleft palate, hypocalcaemia; highest si

chunks.heading: 2.1 Foundational principles
chunks.text: 2.1 Foundational principles Cephalocaudal (head → toe) · Proximodistal (centre → periphery). Critical period = rigid biological window, lost if missed (Lorenz imprinting). Sensitive period = optimal but flexible (language acquisition). Continuity vs discontinuity; nature vs nurture (interactionist consensus); active vs passive child (bidirectionality). Prenatal stages: Germinal (0–2 wk), Embryonic (2–8 wk, most vulnerable to teratogens, organogenesis) , Fetal (8 wk–birth, growth). Teratogens: alcohol (FAS, most common preventable ID), tobacco, thalidomide (limbs), rubella (1st trimester), lead/mercury, Zika (microcephaly).

chunks.heading: 2.2 Piaget — cognitive development
chunks.text: 2.2 Piaget — cognitive development Stage Age Achievements / limits Sensorimotor 0–2 Object permanence (~8 mo), goal-directed action, A-not-B error Preoperational 2–7 Symbolic thought, language, pretend play; egocentrism, animism, centration, no conservation Concrete Operational 7–11 Conservation, reversibility, classification, seriation, decentration Formal Operational 11+ Abstract, hypothetico-deductive logic; adolescent egocentrism (imaginary audience, personal fable) Key concepts: Schema; Assimilation (fit new info into schema); Accommodation (modify schema); Equilibration (the engine of change). Sensorimotor 6 substages: reflexes → primary CR (on body) → secondary CR (on objects) → coordination (8–12 mo, object permanence) → tertiary CR (experimentation) → mental representation (deferred imitation). TRAP: Object permanence (sensorimotor, ~8 mo) ≠ Conservation (concrete operational, ~7 yr). And Piagetian "egocentrism" = a cognitive limit, NOT narcissism.

chunks.heading: 2.3 Vygotsky — sociocultural
chunks.text: 2.3 Vygotsky — sociocultural ZPD = gap between what a child can do alone vs with help from a more knowledgeable other (MKO). Scaffolding = temporary tailored support, withdrawn as competence grows. Private speech → inner speech, guides cognition. Language is the master tool, internalised from social interaction. TRAP: "Scaffolding" is Bruner's term, applied to Vygotsky's ZPD. Vygotsky's own terms are ZPD and MKO. One line: Piaget = child as lone scientist (development → learning). Vygotsky = child as apprentice (learning → development, mediated by culture).

chunks.heading: 2.4 Bronfenbrenner — ecological / bioecological systems
chunks.text: 2.4 Bronfenbrenner — ecological / bioecological systems System What it is Examples Microsystem Direct, face-to-face settings; bidirectional Family, school, peers, daycare Mesosystem Interactions between microsystems (a system of microsystems, not a setting) Parent-teacher meeting, home-school link Exosystem Settings the child is not in but which still affect them Parent's workplace, school board, mass media Macrosystem Cultural blueprint Ideology, customs, laws, religion, SES Chronosystem Time dimension. Added later (originally 4 systems) Divorce, pandemic, sociohistorical era PPCT (1994 Bioecological refinement): P rocess = proximal processes, the engine (regular reciprocal interactions over time). P erson = Demand (visible: age/gender), Resource (skills, intelligence), Force (temperament, motivation). C ontext = the 5 systems. T ime = micro/meso/macro time. TRAPS: Exosystem ≠ no influence (acts via the microsystem, e.g. dad loses job). Mesosystem is NOT a setting, it's the link between two. Mass media = exosystem, not macrosystem. Chronosystem was added later (originally 4 systems). If the stem mentions: nested environments, cultural context, parent's workplace, indirect influence → answer is Bronfenbrenner . He co-founded Head Start (1965).

chunks.heading: 2.5 Erikson — 8 psychosocial stages
chunks.text: 2.5 Erikson — 8 psychosocial stages Age Conflict Virtue 0–1.5 Trust vs Mistrust Hope 1.5–3 Autonomy vs Shame/Doubt Will 3–6 Initiative vs Guilt Purpose 6–12 Industry vs Inferiority Competence 12–18 Identity vs Role Confusion Fidelity 18–40 Intimacy vs Isolation Love 40–65 Generativity vs Stagnation Care 65+ Integrity vs Despair Wisdom Marcia's identity statuses (expansion of stage 5, by crisis × commitment): Diffusion (no/no), Foreclosure (no/yes, handed down), Moratorium (yes-in-progress/no), Achievement (yes/yes).

chunks.heading: 2.6 Freud — psychosexual stages
chunks.text: 2.6 Freud — psychosexual stages Age Stage Theme / fixation 0–1 Oral Mouth; smoking, overeating, dependency 1–3 Anal Bowel control; anal-retentive (orderly) or expulsive (messy) 3–6 Phallic Genitals; Oedipus/Electra; superego forms 6–12 Latency Urges dormant, same-sex friends 12+ Genital Mature sexuality

chunks.heading: 2.7 Kohlberg — moral development
chunks.text: 2.7 Kohlberg — moral development Level Stages Driver Preconventional 1. Punishment-obedience · 2. Instrumental exchange Self-interest Conventional 3. Good boy/girl · 4. Law and order Approval, social order Postconventional 5. Social contract · 6. Universal ethical principles Abstract principles Method = Heinz dilemma (steal drug to save wife?); the stage is the reasoning , not the choice. TRAP: Gilligan's critique = Kohlberg's stages reflect a male "justice" orientation; women often reason via an "ethics of care." She added a parallel orientation, did not replace him.

chunks.heading: 2.8 Attachment — Bowlby, Ainsworth, Main
chunks.text: 2.8 Attachment — Bowlby, Ainsworth, Main Bowlby's 4 phases: Pre-attachment (0–6 wk) → Attachment-in-the-making (6 wk–8 mo) → Clear-cut attachment (8–18 mo, separation + stranger anxiety peak ) → Reciprocal relationships (18–24 mo+, internal working model). Style Separation Reunion Caregiver Secure (B, ~60%) Distressed Easily comforted, returns to play Sensitive, responsive Avoidant (A, ~20%) Little distress Avoids/ignores caregiver Rejecting Resistant/Ambivalent (C, ~10%) Very distressed Seeks + resists, can't be soothed Inconsistent Disorganized (D) Confused, freezing Approach + avoid, dazed Frightening / trauma TRAP: Disorganized (D) was added by Main & Solomon , not Ainsworth (her original 3 = A/B/C). Adult AAI: Secure-Autonomous (B), Dismissing (A), Preoccupied (C), Unresolved (D). Foundational experiments: Harlow (wire vs cloth mother, contact comfort > food); Lorenz (imprinting, critical period); Bowlby's WHO report (1951, maternal deprivation).

chunks.heading: 2.9 Parenting (Baumrind) & temperament (Thomas & Chess)
chunks.text: 2.9 Parenting (Baumrind) & temperament (Thomas & Chess) High demand Low demand High warmth Authoritative (best outcomes) Permissive / Indulgent Low warmth Authoritarian Neglectful (Maccoby & Martin's 4th, worst) TRAP: Authoritative (warm + firm, good) ≠ Authoritarian (cold + harsh, bad). Thomas & Chess temperament: Easy (~40%), Difficult (~10%), Slow-to-warm-up (~15%). Goodness of fit = match between temperament and environmental demands predicts adjustment.

chunks.heading: 2.10 Language development & milestones
chunks.text: 2.10 Language development & milestones Age Milestone 0–2 mo Crying, reflexive sounds 2–4 mo Cooing (vowels) 6 mo Babbling (consonants + vowels) 10–14 mo First word; holophrastic (one word = whole thought) 18–24 mo Two-word / telegraphic ("more milk") 2–3 yr Vocab burst, overregularization ("goed", "foots") 3–5 yr Complex grammar, ~2000 words by 5 Theories: Skinner (behaviourist, operant/imitation); Chomsky (nativist, LAD + Universal Grammar + poverty of stimulus); Vygotsky/Bruner (social-interactionist, LASS); Piaget (cognitive, thought before language). TRAP: Overregularization ("goed", "mouses") is a sign of rule learning , not regression. Aging: crystallized intelligence (vocab, knowledge) preserved/rises; fluid intelligence (processing speed, novel problems) declines. Socioemotional selectivity (Carstensen). Kübler-Ross 5 stages of dying: denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance (not claimed to be universal/linear). 3. Abnormal Psychology MET 15 Q · NIMHANS 15 Q · DSM-heavy

chunks.heading: 3.1 Defining abnormality & classification
chunks.text: 3.1 Defining abnormality & classification The 4 Ds: Deviance, Distress, Dysfunction, Danger (some add Duration). Deviance alone ≠ abnormal (a genius IQ is deviant, not pathological). DSM-5 (2013) / DSM-5-TR (2022) ICD-11 (2019) Publisher APA, US-centric WHO, global Axes No axes (dropped from DSM-IV) Chapter 6 = mental/behavioural/neurodev OCD / PTSD Own chapters (out of anxiety) Own chapters; ICD-11 adds Complex PTSD Schizophrenia subtypes Removed Removed Asperger's Folded into ASD Folded into ASD Bereavement exclusion (MDD) Removed More cautious New in DSM-5 Hoarding, Excoriation Also recognized TRAP: Multi-axial system = DSM-IV. DSM-5 dropped it. "Axis I disorder" is pre-DSM-5 vocabulary. MSE order (ABS-MTPCIJ): Appearance, Behaviour, Speech, Mood/affect, Thought (form + content), Perception, Cognition, Insight, Judgment. Mood = subjective; affect = observed. Insight = awareness of illness; judgment = real-world decisions. Approaches: Biological · Psychodynamic · Behavioural · Cognitive (Beck/Ellis) · Humanistic (Rogers/Perls) · Sociocultural · Biopsychosocial (Engel 1977) · Diathesis-stress. Historical: Hippocrates (humors), Pinel/Tuke (moral treatment), Kraepelin (dementia praecox), Bleuler (renamed schizophrenia).

chunks.heading: 3.2 Anxiety, OCD & trauma
chunks.text: 3.2 Anxiety, OCD & trauma Disorder Core feature Duration GAD Excessive worry, multiple domains, hard to control ≥ 6 months Panic Disorder Recurrent unexpected attacks + worry/behaviour change Attack peaks ≤ 10 min Specific Phobia / Social Anxiety / Agoraphobia Single object / scrutiny / escape-is-hard (≥2 of 5 situations) ≥ 6 months Separation Anxiety Fear of separation from attachment figure ≥ 4 wk kids / 6 mo adults TRAP: OCD is NOT in the anxiety chapter in DSM-5 (own chapter), and neither is PTSD (Trauma- and stressor-related chapter). OCD & related: OCD (obsessions + compulsions, ego-dystonic), BDD, Hoarding (new) , Trichotillomania, Excoriation (new) . Trauma: PTSD (> 1 month: intrusion + avoidance + negative cognition/mood + arousal), Acute Stress Disorder (3 days–1 month), Adjustment Disorders, Reactive Attachment, Disinhibited Social Engagement. ICD-11 adds Complex PTSD (PTSD + disturbances in self-organization). TRAP: OCPD ≠ OCD. OCPD = ego-syntonic perfectionist personality style (Cluster C). OCD = ego-dystonic obsessions/compulsions (own chapter).

chunks.heading: 3.3 Mood disorders
chunks.text: 3.3 Mood disorders Disorder Required Duration MDD ≥ 5 of 9 SIG-E-CAPS, must include depressed mood OR anhedonia ≥ 2 weeks Persistent Depressive (Dysthymia) Chronic low-grade depression ≥ 2 yrs (1 yr kids) Bipolar I ≥ 1 manic episode (depression not required) Mania ≥ 1 week (or any if hospitalised) Bipolar II Hypomania + ≥1 MDE; never full mania Hypomania ≥ 4 days Cyclothymia Hypomanic + depressive symptoms, never full episode ≥ 2 yrs PMDD / DMDD Premenstrual mood / severe temper outbursts in kids Most cycles / onset before 10 SIG-E-CAPS (MDD): Sleep, Interest, Guilt, Energy, Concentration, Appetite, Psychomotor, Suicidal ideation + depressed mood = 9. DIG-FAST (mania): Distractibility, Indiscretion, Grandiosity, Flight of ideas, Activity, Sleep ↓, Talkativeness. TRAP: Bipolar I needs mania ≥ 1 week . Bipolar II = hypomania + MDE, never full mania. Suicide: strongest single predictor = previous attempt ; highest-risk dx = MDD + substance use. SAD PERSONS scale.

chunks.heading: 3.4 Schizophrenia & psychotic disorders
chunks.text: 3.4 Schizophrenia & psychotic disorders Kraepelin coined dementia praecox ; Bleuler renamed it schizophrenia ("split mind" = fragmented thought, NOT split personality). Bleuler's 4 As : Associations (loose), Affect (flat), Ambivalence, Autism (withdrawal). Schneider's First-Rank Symptoms (thought insertion/withdrawal/broadcasting, audible thoughts, voices commenting, made impulses, somatic passivity, delusional perception): suggestive, NOT diagnostic alone in DSM-5. Positive (added): hallucinations, delusions, disorganized speech/behaviour. Negative (taken away): flat affect, alogia, avolition, anhedonia, asociality. DSM-5: ≥ 2 of 5 symptoms (at least one from delusions/hallucinations/disorganized speech), active ≥ 1 month, total disturbance ≥ 6 months . Disorder Duration Brief Psychotic Disorder 1 day to < 1 month Schizophreniform 1 to < 6 months Schizophrenia ≥ 6 months Schizoaffective Mood episode + psychosis, but ≥ 2 wks psychosis without mood symptoms Delusional Disorder ≥ 1 month delusions only TRAP: Schizophrenia ≠ DID (split mind ≠ split personality). DSM-5 removed schizophrenia subtypes (paranoid/catatonic).

chunks.heading: 3.5 Dissociative & somatic symptom disorders
chunks.text: 3.5 Dissociative & somatic symptom disorders Dissociative: Amnesia (± fugue), DID (≥ 2 identities, severe early trauma), Depersonalization/Derealization ( reality testing intact ). Somatic Symptom Disorder (distress + excessive thoughts about symptoms); Illness Anxiety (replaces hypochondriasis); Conversion (neuro symptoms, no medical cause, la belle indifférence ); Factitious (intentional, sick-role gain — Munchausen self, by-proxy on another); Malingering (conscious, external gain; a V-code, not a disorder). TRAP: Conversion = unconscious, no gain. Factitious = conscious, internal (sick role). Malingering = conscious, external (money, court).

chunks.heading: 3.6 Eating, sleep, SUD & neurodevelopmental
chunks.text: 3.6 Eating, sleep, SUD & neurodevelopmental Anorexia (requires significantly low weight) · Bulimia (binge + compensation, normal/above weight) · BED (binge, no compensation) · ARFID · Pica · Rumination. Substance Use Disorder: DSM-5 merged abuse + dependence; ≥ 2 of 11 criteria/12 mo; 2–3 mild, 4–5 moderate, ≥ 6 severe. Tolerance/withdrawal from prescribed meds taken as directed don't count. Neurodevelopmental: IDD (severity by adaptive function, not just IQ); ASD (DSM-5 merged Asperger's/PDD-NOS); ADHD onset before 12 (was 7 in DSM-IV), ≥ 2 settings; Specific Learning Disorder (dyslexia/dysgraphia/dyscalculia); Tourette's (motor + vocal tics ≥ 1 yr, onset < 18).

chunks.heading: 3.7 Personality disorders (incl. BPD vs NPD, Type A–D)
chunks.text: 3.7 Personality disorders (incl. BPD vs NPD, Type A–D) Cluster Theme Disorders A Odd / eccentric Paranoid, Schizoid, Schizotypal B Dramatic / emotional / erratic Antisocial, Borderline, Histrionic, Narcissistic C Anxious / fearful Avoidant, Dependent, Obsessive-Compulsive PD Borderline (BPD) Narcissistic (NPD) Pervasive instability of relationships, self-image, affect; fear of abandonment; impulsivity; self-harm; chronic emptiness. Higher in females. Grandiosity; need for excessive admiration ; lack of empathy; sense of being special/entitled. The discriminator (your mock miss): pervasive instability of relationships and self-image is the BPD feature NOT defining of NPD. Both can show emptiness, but instability + abandonment terror = BPD. (Antisocial: disregard for rights, age ≥18 + Conduct Disorder before 15.) TRAP: Schizoid (detached, no odd beliefs) ≠ Schizotypal (detached + magical thinking/perceptual oddities, on the schizophrenia spectrum). Type A–D: Type A = hostility/competitiveness/time-urgency (CHD risk). Type B = relaxed. Type C = suppressed emotion (cancer-linked, weaker evidence). Type D ("distressed") = negative affectivity + social inhibition; predicts poor cardiac prognosis (your mock miss).

chunks.heading: 3.8 Treatment quick-map
chunks.text: 3.8 Treatment quick-map Disorder First-line psychotherapy Common pharmacology MDD CBT, IPT, behavioural activation SSRIs OCD ERP SSRIs (high dose), clomipramine PTSD TF-CBT, EMDR, Prolonged Exposure SSRIs (sertraline, paroxetine FDA-approved) Schizophrenia CBTp, family psychoeducation Atypical antipsychotics Bipolar Psychoeducation, IPSRT Lithium, valproate, lamotrigine, atypicals BPD DBT (Linehan), MBT, schema therapy Symptom-targeted Anorexia / Bulimia FBT (Maudsley) for teens; CBT-E Fluoxetine (only SSRI FDA-approved for bulimia) 4. Psychological Assessment & Tests MET 15 Q · NIMHANS 10 Q The whole map: a psychological test is a measuring instrument that must be (a) consistent = reliability and (b) accurate = validity . Everything else is a way to estimate one of those, interpret scores against norms, or an example of a real test.

chunks.heading: 4.1 Item analysis
chunks.text: 4.1 Item analysis Difficulty index p = proportion who got the item right (0–1). Sweet spot 0.50 for free-response, ~0.625 for a 4-option MCQ (halfway between guessing 0.25 and ceiling). p > 0.80 too easy, < 0.20 too hard. Discrimination index D = p(top 27%) − p(bottom 27%), range −1 to +1. D > 0.40 good. Negative D = mis-keyed/ambiguous item, discard immediately.

chunks.heading: 4.2 Reliability (consistency)
chunks.text: 4.2 Reliability (consistency) Classical test theory: Observed = True + Error. Reliability = proportion of variance that is true. Test-retest (across time; standard window 2–4 wks). Parallel forms (across forms). Split-half + Spearman-Brown correction (r_full = 2·r_half / (1 + r_half)); Cronbach α (≥0.7 acceptable, ≥0.8 good) = mean of all possible split-halves; KR-20 for dichotomous (0/1) items. Inter-rater: Cohen κ (categorical, Landis & Koch: 0.61–0.80 substantial, 0.81+ almost perfect), ICC (continuous). SEM = SD·√(1 − r_xx). Higher reliability → smaller SEM → tighter confidence band around a score. TRAP: Cronbach α is NOT a measure of unidimensionality — a test can have high α and still measure two constructs. And κ is NOT internal consistency.

chunks.heading: 4.3 Validity (accuracy)
chunks.text: 4.3 Validity (accuracy) Content: covers the domain (expert panels, Lawshe's CVR). Face validity = looks valid to a layperson, the weakest form. Criterion: Concurrent (criterion now) vs Predictive = Postponed (criterion later). Construct: convergent (correlates with similar) + discriminant (not with unrelated) + nomological network. Campbell & Fiske's multitrait-multimethod matrix (MTMM, 1959). Validity ceiling: max validity = √(reliability). Unreliable tests cannot be strongly valid. Reliability is necessary but not sufficient for validity.

chunks.heading: 4.4 Test classification
chunks.text: 4.4 Test classification Type Means Maximum performance (ability/aptitude/achievement, e.g. IQ) Do your best . There is a right answer Typical performance (personality, interest, attitude) What you usually do. No right answer Power test Hard items, generous time — measures ceiling of ability Speed test Easy items, tight time — measures how fast The exact trap you missed: an IQ test is an ability test (maximum performance), not a power or speed test. Achievement = what you learned (past, WIAT). Aptitude = what you can learn (future, DAT/SAT). Intelligence = general capacity. Norm-referenced (vs peers) vs criterion-referenced (vs absolute standard). Formative (during) vs summative (end).

chunks.heading: 4.5 Standard scores & norms
chunks.text: 4.5 Standard scores & norms Standard score = M + (SD × z). Percentile rank = % of norm group at or below the score (ordinal, gaps unequal). Scale Mean SD Use z 0 1 Universal T (MMPI, neuropsych) 50 10 Clinical cutoff T ≥ 65 Wechsler FSIQ / Index 100 15 WAIS, WISC, WPPSI; "average" 90–109 Old Stanford-Binet (1960–86) 100 16 Classic Wechsler-vs-Binet trap Wechsler subtest scaled 10 3 Range 1–19. Scaled 10 = 50th percentile (your mock miss) Stanine 5 2 Range 1–9 Sten (16PF) 5.5 2 Range 1–10 Normal curve / 68-95-99.7: ±1 SD = 68% (so +1 SD ≈ 84th pct, −1 SD ≈ 16th); ±2 SD = 95% (+2 SD ≈ 98th); ±3 SD = 99.7%. Mean = 50th percentile. Memorise 68-95-99.7 .

chunks.heading: 4.6 Intelligence tests
chunks.text: 4.6 Intelligence tests IQ formula history: Mental Age (Binet 1908) → Ratio IQ = (MA/CA)×100 (Stern 1912, applied by Terman in Stanford-Binet 1916) → Deviation IQ (Wechsler 1939); SB switched to deviation IQ in 1960 (SD 16); SB-5 (2003) dropped to SD 15. Binet rejected a single global IQ score himself. Index WAIS-IV (16–90, 4 indices) WISC-V (6–16, 5 indices) Verbal Comprehension Similarities, Vocabulary, Information Similarities, Vocabulary Perceptual / Visual-Spatial Block Design, Matrix Reasoning, Visual Puzzles (PRI) Block Design, Visual Puzzles (VSI) Fluid Reasoning (folded into PRI) Matrix Reasoning, Figure Weights (FRI) Working Memory Digit Span, Arithmetic, Letter-Number Sequencing Digit Span, Picture Span Processing Speed Symbol Search, Coding Coding, Symbol Search The exact trap you missed: Letter-Number Sequencing is WAIS-IV core but NOT a WISC-V core subtest (WISC-V uses Picture Span). The WISC-IV→V change: old PRI split into VSI + FRI → 5 indices, not 4. WAIS-IV = 15 subtests total (10 core); WISC-V = 21 total (10 primary). Raven's Progressive Matrices (Raven): nonverbal, culture-reduced g. SPM = 60 items (5 sets), CPM = 36 (children/elderly/ID), APM scored = 36 (+ 12 practice). Lock CPM = APM = 36. Bhatia's Battery (C.M. Bhatia, 1955): performance IQ for Indian/low-literacy, ages 11–16. 5 subtests: Koh's Block Design, Alexander's Pass-Along, Pattern Drawing, Immedi

chunks.heading: 4.7 Personality tests — objective & projective
chunks.text: 4.7 Personality tests — objective & projective Test What it is MMPI-2 (Hathaway & McKinley) 567 items , empirical criterion-keyed. 10 clinical scales (Hs, D, Hy, Pd, Mf, Pa, Pt, Sc, Ma, Si) + validity scales (L = Lie, F = Infrequency, K = Correction, + VRIN/TRIN). T-scores; clinical ≥ 65. Read code types, not single scales. 16PF (Cattell) 16 source traits + 5 globals, Sten scores. NOT Big Five . NEO-PI-R/3 (Costa & McCrae) Big Five (OCEAN), 5 domains × 6 facets, 240 items. EPQ (Eysenck) PEN — Psychoticism, Extraversion, Neuroticism + Lie. Rorschach Projective. 10 inkblots (5 chromatic, 5 achromatic), 1921. Exner / R-PAS scoring. TAT (Murray & Morgan) Projective, needs-press. 31 cards total , 20 administered. CAT (Bellak) = animal cards for children. SCT (RISB) Projective, semi-structured sentence completion (Rotter). Draw-A-Person (Goodenough-Harris) Visual-motor integration + rough cognitive estimate; usable when verbal testing fails; also a projective screen. Bender-Gestalt Visual-motor integration; screen for organicity. Vineland (VABS) Adaptive behaviour (ID assessment). WCST / Stroop Executive function/set-shifting (frontal) / selective attention + response inhibition. Card-count traps: Rorschach = 10 inkblots. TAT = 31 total cards. MMPI-2 = 10 clinical scales (not 8) and 567 items. Attitude scales: Thurstone (equal-appearing intervals), Likert (summated 5-point), Guttman

chunks.heading: 5.1 Psychoanalytic / psychodynamic
chunks.text: 5.1 Psychoanalytic / psychodynamic Freud structure: id (pleasure principle), ego (reality principle), superego (conscience + ego ideal). Topographic: conscious/preconscious/unconscious. Technique: free association (the fundamental rule), interpretation of resistance + transference, dream analysis (manifest vs latent), working through . Defenses (Vaillant): psychotic (denial) → immature (projection, acting out, regression) → neurotic (intellectualisation, displacement, reaction formation, repression) → mature (humour, sublimation, suppression, altruism). Theorist Core contribution Adler Individual Psychology; inferiority → striving for superiority; social interest; birth order Jung Analytical Psychology; collective unconscious; archetypes; individuation Klein / Winnicott Object relations; splitting, projective identification / "good-enough mother," transitional object Kohut Self psychology; mirroring, idealizing, twinship selfobjects Kernberg TFP for BPD; borderline personality organisation; splitting + identity diffusion Kohut's self psychology (your flagged gap): the self develops through 3 selfobject needs — Mirroring (being admired → healthy ambition), Idealizing (merging with a calm strong other → ideals), Twinship (feeling alike). Failure of mirroring → grandiosity + craving admiration (narcissistic pathology). Failure of mirroring + idealizing → a fragmented, empty self .

chunks.heading: 5.2 Behaviour therapy
chunks.text: 5.2 Behaviour therapy Technique Mechanism / indication Systematic desensitisation (Wolpe) Reciprocal inhibition: relaxation + graded imagined exposure up a fear hierarchy. Phobias In-vivo exposure / Flooding Real-world graded / full-intensity exposure; habituation + extinction ERP (Foa) Exposure + response prevention. First-line behavioural Tx for OCD Token economy / Contingency management Operant secondary reinforcers; institutional, SUD Behavioural activation (Lewinsohn/Jacobson) Scheduled rewarding activity; depression Modeling (Bandura) / Shaping / Chaining Observational learning / new behaviour / linking existing behaviours Biofeedback Physiological readouts shape autonomic control; tension headache, anxiety

chunks.heading: 5.3 Cognitive & CBT
chunks.text: 5.3 Cognitive & CBT Beck's Cognitive Therapy: cognitive triad (negative self/world/future), schemas → automatic thoughts, distortions (all-or-nothing, overgeneralisation, catastrophising). Techniques: Socratic questioning/guided discovery, thought records, behavioural experiments. Ellis's REBT: ABC model (Activating event → Belief → Consequence, then D dispute, E new effect); 3 irrational demands ("musturbation"). More directly confrontational than Beck.

chunks.heading: 5.4 Humanistic / existential
chunks.text: 5.4 Humanistic / existential Rogers (person-centred): 3 core conditions — empathy, unconditional positive regard, congruence (necessary + sufficient). Non-directive; engine = actualizing tendency. Gestalt (Perls): here-and-now, empty chair , top-dog/underdog, figure-ground. Frankl (Logotherapy): search for meaning; paradoxical intention, dereflection. Yalom: 4 ultimate concerns (death, freedom, isolation, meaninglessness). Glasser (Reality): WDEP. Your mock miss: the approach that prefers "real relationship" + UPR over the term "therapeutic alliance" is Person-centred (Rogers) . The "alliance" (bond/goals/tasks) is Bordin's construct.

chunks.heading: 5.5 Third-wave, group & family
chunks.text: 5.5 Third-wave, group & family DBT (Linehan, for BPD): 4 modules — mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation, interpersonal effectiveness. ACT (Hayes): hexaflex 6 processes — acceptance, defusion, self-as-context, present moment, values, committed action. MBCT = relapse prevention in recurrent depression. MI (Miller & Rollnick): spirit PACE, skills OARS. IPT : 4 problem areas — grief, role disputes, role transitions, interpersonal deficits. EMDR (Shapiro): 8 phases, bilateral stimulation, for PTSD. Yalom's group factors (11): universality, interpersonal learning (the engine), group cohesiveness, catharsis, instillation of hope, altruism, existential factors… "social microcosm + here-and-now" = Yalom. Family: Structural (Minuchin: family map, enmeshed/disengaged, joining); Strategic (Haley/Watzlawick: directives, paradox); Bowenian (differentiation, genogram); Satir (communication stances); Milan (circular questioning); Narrative (White/Epston: externalising); SFBT (de Shazer/Berg: miracle question, scaling).
