chunks.heading: 5.6b "Which of these is a component of ___?" — what belongs vs the trap that doesn't
chunks.text: 5.6b "Which of these is a component of ___?" — what belongs vs the trap that doesn't MET/NIMHANS love the recognition item: four options, pick the one that genuinely belongs to a named therapy. The wrong options are always real concepts from a different therapy. So learn both sides. Green = belongs. Red = distractor + where it actually comes from. Therapy Components that BELONG Distractors that do NOT (and their real home) DBT (Linehan, for BPD + chronic suicidality) 4 skill modules : Mindfulness · Distress Tolerance · Emotion Regulation · Interpersonal Effectiveness (" My Dog Eats Iguanas "). 4 treatment modes : individual therapy · group skills training · phone coaching · therapist consultation team. Built on dialectics (acceptance + change). "cognitive restructuring / cognitive triad" → Beck · "free association" → Freud · "hexaflex / cognitive defusion" → ACT · "unconditional positive regard" → Rogers ACT (Hayes) Hexaflex , 6 processes: Acceptance · Cognitive Defusion · Self-as-Context · Present-Moment Contact · Values · Committed Action. Goal = psychological flexibility , not symptom reduction. the 4 DBT modules · "ABC model" → Ellis · "miracle question" → SFBT . Tags: "hexaflex," "defusion," "I'm having the thought that…" = ACT CBT (Beck's cognitive therapy) Cognitive triad (self/world/future) · schemas → automatic thoughts · cognitive distortions · Socratic questioning (g

chunks.heading: 5.7 Learning & conditioning
chunks.text: 5.7 Learning & conditioning Family Terms Classical (Pavlovian) Extinction, spontaneous recovery, generalization, discrimination Operant shaping tools Shaping, chaining, fading, prompting Operant schedules FR, VR, FI, VI Cognitive / social Latent (Tolman), insight (Köhler), observational (Bandura) Non-associative Habituation, sensitization Shaping = reinforce successive approximations of a new behaviour. Chaining = link existing behaviours (each is the S D for the next; backward chaining preferred clinically). Fading = remove the prompt (extinction removes the reinforcer ). Prompting hierarchy: physical → modelling → gestural → verbal → visual. Extinction: watch for the extinction burst ; extinction suppresses, doesn't erase. Spontaneous recovery proves the memory is intact. Generalization is the default; discrimination is trained by differential reinforcement. Schedules: VR = highest, steadiest rate, most resistant to extinction (gambling). VI = steady moderate (checking phone). FR = post-reinforcement pause then burst (piece-work). FI = scallop (studying before a weekly quiz). Resistance: VR > VI > FR > FI > continuous. Latent learning (Tolman, cognitive map — learning without reinforcement, shown later). Insight learning (Köhler's Sultan, sudden "aha"). Observational learning (Bandura Bobo doll; 4 processes ARRM: Attention → Retention → Reproduction → Motivation; vicarious re

chunks.heading: 5.8 Ethics in practice
chunks.text: 5.8 Ethics in practice Principle (Beauchamp & Childress) One line / in practice Autonomy Respect the client's right to decide — informed consent, right to refuse Beneficence Act for the client's good — choose the treatment most likely to help Non-maleficence "First, do no harm" — withhold harmful/unproven methods, stay within competence Justice Fairness — no discrimination, equitable access Informed consent = disclosure + capacity + voluntariness. Assent = a minor's agreement alongside a parent's consent. Paternalism = overriding a competent person's choice (violates autonomy). Confidentiality = your duty; privacy = the client's right; privileged communication = legal protection in court. Other terms: Fidelity (loyalty), Veracity (truth-telling), Competence, Dual/multiple relationship (boundary violation), Negligence (below standard of care). Confidentiality is NOT absolute — it breaks for risk of serious harm to self/others, suspected child/elder abuse (mandatory reporting), or court order. Tarasoff duty to warn/protect: a credible threat against an identifiable person obliges the therapist to act — non-maleficence/beneficence to a third party overrides confidentiality. The classic swap: beneficence = do good vs non-maleficence = avoid harm . 6. Research Methods & Biostatistics MET 10 Q · NIMHANS 15 Q · biggest NIMHANS gap

chunks.heading: 6.1 Levels of measurement & descriptive stats
chunks.text: 6.1 Levels of measurement & descriptive stats Level (NOIR) Property Allowed stats Nominal Categories, no order Mode, frequency, chi-square Ordinal Ordered, unequal intervals (Likert, ranks) Median, percentile, Spearman, Mann-Whitney Interval Equal intervals, no true zero (°C, IQ) Mean, SD, t-test, ANOVA, Pearson r Ratio Equal intervals + true zero (weight, RT) All of the above + ratios Central tendency: mean (pulled by outliers), median (robust, best for skew), mode (only nominal). Dispersion: range, IQR, variance, SD; SEM = SD/√n (precision of the mean, always smaller than SD). Skew: positive = right tail (mean > median > mode). Kurtosis: leptokurtic (peaked), platykurtic (flat).

chunks.heading: 6.2 Standard scores, percentiles & the normal curve
chunks.text: 6.2 Standard scores, percentiles & the normal curve Scale Mean SD "Average" range Wechsler subtest scaled 10 3 8–12. Scaled 10 = 50th percentile Wechsler FSIQ / Index 100 15 90–109 z-score 0 1 −1 to +1 T-score (MMPI) 50 10 40–60; clinical ≥ 65 Sten (16PF) 5.5 2 4–7 Stanine 5 2 4–6 68-95-99.7: ±1 SD = 68% (+1 SD ≈ 84th pct, −1 SD ≈ 16th), ±2 SD = 95% (+2 SD ≈ 98th), ±3 SD = 99.7%. Mean = 50th. Central Limit Theorem: the sampling distribution of the mean → normal as n grows (rule of thumb n ≥ 30).

chunks.heading: 6.3 Hypothesis testing, errors & p-values
chunks.text: 6.3 Hypothesis testing, errors & p-values H0 true H0 false Reject H0 Type I (α, false +) Correct (power) Retain H0 Correct Type II (β, false −) — "Sigh, I missed it" α = type I rate (false positive, conventionally 0.05). β = type II rate (false negative). Power = 1 − β (aim ≥ 0.80; rises with larger n, larger effect, larger α, lower variability, one-tailed). p-value = probability of the observed result or more extreme if H0 were true. NOT the probability that H0 is true. p < α → reject H0. 95% CI: if repeated, 95% of intervals would contain the true parameter. Excludes 0 (difference) or 1 (OR/RR) → significant at p < 0.05.

chunks.heading: 6.4 Effect size & stats one-liners
chunks.text: 6.4 Effect size & stats one-liners Statistic Benchmarks / lock this Cohen's d 0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large Pearson r 0.10 / 0.30 / 0.50. r² = variance explained (r=0.90 → r²=0.81 = 81%). Correlation ≠ causation Odds ratio (OR) / Relative Risk (RR) = 1 No association. >1 increased risk, <1 protective (your mock miss) NNT (Number Needed to Treat) 1 / ARR (Absolute Risk Reduction). Lower NNT = better drug (your mock miss) "Data" Plural ("data are…"); datum is singular TRAP: OR ≈ RR only when the outcome is rare (< 10%); for common outcomes OR overstates RR.

chunks.heading: 6.5 Choosing the test
chunks.text: 6.5 Choosing the test Parametric Non-parametric equivalent One-sample / paired t-test Wilcoxon signed-rank Independent t-test Mann-Whitney U One-way ANOVA Kruskal-Wallis Repeated-measures ANOVA Friedman Pearson r Spearman ρ Categorical proportions Chi-square (Fisher's exact if expected cell < 5); McNemar (paired) Parametric assumptions (4): normality, homogeneity of variance, independence, interval/ratio data. Post-hoc after significant ANOVA: Tukey HSD (equal n), Bonferroni (α/k, conservative), Scheffé (most conservative). Regression: linear (Y=a+bX), logistic (binary → odds ratios), mediation (X→M→Y, "how"), moderation (X×M interaction, "for whom").

chunks.heading: 6.6 Research designs & diagnostic stats
chunks.text: 6.6 Research designs & diagnostic stats Design Direction / measure True experiment (RCT) Random assignment + control; highest internal validity Cohort Forward (exposure → outcome); Relative Risk Case-control Backward (outcome → exposure); Odds Ratio ; rare outcomes Cross-sectional Single time point; prevalence; no causation Solomon four-group Detects + separates pretest sensitisation from the treatment effect Diagnostic stats: Sensitivity = TP/(TP+FN), high-sensitivity test rules a condition OUT when negative ( SnNout ). Specificity = TN/(TN+FP), rules a condition IN when positive ( SpPin ). PPV/NPV depend on prevalence; likelihood ratios don't. ROC plots sensitivity vs (1−specificity). Threats to internal validity: history, maturation, testing, instrumentation, regression to the mean, selection, attrition, Hawthorne effect, demand characteristics, experimenter (Rosenthal) effect. RCT phases: I (safety, 20–100) → II (efficacy, 100–300) → III (confirmatory, 1000+) → IV (surveillance). Blinding: single/double/triple. ITT vs per-protocol. Reporting: CONSORT (RCTs), PRISMA (systematic reviews/meta), STROBE (observational), COREQ (qualitative). Ethics: Belmont 3 (respect, beneficence, justice), Nuremberg Code, Declaration of Helsinki. TRAPS: Cohort can be prospective or retrospective; case-control is always retrospective. Random sampling (external validity) ≠ random assignment (inte

chunks.heading: 6.7 Formulae you can be asked to plug into
chunks.text: 6.7 Formulae you can be asked to plug into Quantity Formula Note / trap Standard error of the mean (SEM) SEM = SD / √n Precision of the mean . Bigger n → smaller SEM. Always < SD. Standard error of measurement (SEm) SEm = SD × √(1 − r) r = reliability. The trap pair with SEM above. High reliability → small SEm → tight score band. Standard deviation SD = √[Σ(x − x̄)² / (n − 1)] Variance = SD². Sample uses n − 1 (Bessel). z-score z = (x − mean) / SD For a sample mean use SEM: z = (x̄ − μ) / SEM. 95% confidence interval CI = mean ± 1.96 × SEM 1.96 for 95%, 2.58 for 99%. Excludes 0 → significant. Cohen's d d = (M₁ − M₂) / pooled SD 0.2 / 0.5 / 0.8 = small / medium / large. Coefficient of determination r² = (Pearson r)² = proportion of variance explained. r = 0.9 → 81%. Relative Risk (RR) RR = EER / CER Risk in exposed ÷ risk in unexposed. Cohort studies. Odds Ratio (OR) OR = (a×d) / (b×c) From the 2×2 table. Case-control studies. Absolute Risk Reduction (ARR) ARR = CER − EER Plain difference in event rates. Relative Risk Reduction (RRR) RRR = ARR / CER Proportion of baseline risk removed. Number Needed to Treat (NNT) NNT = 1 / ARR Round up. Lower = better drug. (Your mock miss.) Sensitivity / Specificity Sn = TP/(TP+FN); Sp = TN/(TN+FP) SnNout / SpPin. PPV / NPV PPV = TP/(TP+FP); NPV = TN/(TN+FN) Both shift with prevalence; LRs don't. Odds ↔ probability odds = p / (1 − p) p = odds

chunks.heading: 7.1 Subject-verb agreement
chunks.text: 7.1 Subject-verb agreement The verb agrees with the subject in number, not the nearest noun. Each, every, either, neither, one, anyone, everyone, nobody → singular ("Each of the participants was given…"). Either/or, neither/nor → verb agrees with the nearer subject ("Neither the patient nor the family members were informed"). "A number of" = plural; "the number of" = singular. None defaults singular in formal writing. "Data are" — data is technically plural (datum singular); treat as plural in exam contexts. Singular-looking: news, mathematics, physics, politics, statistics. Plural-only: scissors, trousers, glasses.

chunks.heading: 7.2 Voice & conditionals
chunks.text: 7.2 Voice & conditionals Active → passive: object becomes subject; verb → "be" + past participle. "The committee will announce the results" → "The results will be announced by the committee." Conditional If-clause Main clause Zero (general truths) present present First (real future) present will + base Second (hypothetical) past would + base Third (counterfactual past) past perfect ("Had she taken") would have + past participle Mixed past perfect would + base " Had she taken the medication, she would have recovered sooner" = third conditional (inversion is formal).

chunks.heading: 7.3 Punctuation & prepositions
chunks.text: 7.3 Punctuation & prepositions Restrictive vs non-restrictive clauses: non-restrictive (extra info, removable) → commas + "who"; restrictive (defines which) → no commas, "that". "The patient, who was anxious, refused" (one patient) vs "The patient who was anxious refused" (picks out one of several). Semicolon joins two independent clauses; colon introduces a list/explanation. It's = it is; its = possessive. Prepositions: insist on , depend on, comply with, consist of, refer to, suffer from, object to, accuse of, married to (not with), prefer X to Y, superior/inferior to (not than), discuss (no preposition). "Between you and me ."

chunks.heading: 7.4 Modifiers, parallelism & common corrections
chunks.text: 7.4 Modifiers, parallelism & common corrections Dangling modifier: "Walking down the street, the building looked tall" (the building isn't walking). Parallelism: "reading, writing, and swimming" (not "to swim"). Like (before a noun) vs as (before a clause). Who (subject) vs whom (object). Less (uncountable) vs fewer (countable). Between (two) vs among (3+). "The reason is that " (not "because"). Predicate adjective follows a linking verb ("The data were inconclusive ").

chunks.heading: 7.5 Vocabulary, one-word substitutions & idioms
chunks.text: 7.5 Vocabulary, one-word substitutions & idioms Word Meaning / pairing Gregarious Sociable (antonym: reclusive) Ephemeral Lasting briefly (synonym: transient) Ambivalent Mixed feelings (NOT indifferent = no feeling) Garrulous / loquacious / verbose Talkative / wordy Laconic / taciturn / reticent Few words / reserved Sagacious / cogent / pragmatic Wise / convincing / practical Frugal / abstemious Sparing with money / with food & drink Capricious / whimsical / vacillate Unpredictable / playful / waver Egregious / belligerent / obstinate Outstandingly bad / hostile / stubborn Definition Word Fluent in many languages Polyglot Fear of confined / open spaces Claustrophobia / Agoraphobia Hates / loves humanity Misanthrope / Philanthropist Walker in sleep Somnambulist Cure-all medicine Panacea Speech without preparation Extempore Never drinks alcohol Teetotaller Idioms: bury the hatchet (make peace), hit the nail on the head (be right), beat around the bush (avoid the point), bite the bullet (endure), a blessing in disguise, cut corners, burn the midnight oil. Spelling confusables: affect (verb) / effect (noun); principal / principle; stationary (still) / stationery (paper); discreet / discrete; complement / compliment; conscientious. Doubling rule: double the consonant in stressed CVC verbs (refer → referring) but not unstressed (open → opening).

chunks.heading: 7.6 Reading comprehension strategy
chunks.text: 7.6 Reading comprehension strategy Main idea: re-read first/last sentences; eliminate options that are too narrow or too broad (overreach). RC tone: read qualifiers/hedges ("a range of", "can alleviate") → often "supportive but qualified." Inference = implied, stay close to the text. Vocab in context = substitute and check meaning. Specific detail = go back and find it. 8. Social Psychology, Memory, The Acts & Founders

chunks.heading: 8.1 Social psychology
chunks.text: 8.1 Social psychology Concept What it is Bystander effect Presence of others inhibits helping . Two drivers: diffusion of responsibility + pluralistic ignorance . (Latané & Darley, after Kitty Genovese , 1964) Diffusion of responsibility "Someone else will do it" — responsibility splits across the group Pluralistic ignorance Everyone privately unsure, reads others' calm as "no emergency" Social loafing Less effort in a group than alone (Ringelmann) Social facilitation Others improve easy/well-learned tasks, impair hard ones Deindividuation Loss of self-awareness/restraint in a group/anonymity (mobs) Groupthink / Group polarization Harmony → bad decisions (Janis) / discussion amplifies initial leanings Conformity / Obedience Group pressure (Asch) / authority (Milgram). Normative vs informational influence Cognitive dissonance Discomfort from conflicting attitudes/behaviour → attitude change (Festinger) Attribution theory (Heider) How we explain behaviour: internal/dispositional ("he's like that") vs external/situational ("the traffic made him late"). Kelley's covariation = we weigh consensus, consistency, distinctiveness. Weiner = locus + stability + controllability. Fundamental attribution error Over-attribute others' behaviour to disposition, under-weigh situation Actor–observer bias My behaviour = situation; your same behaviour = your character Self-serving bias / Just-world

chunks.heading: 8.2 Memory & cognitive
chunks.text: 8.2 Memory & cognitive System What it holds Sensory memory <1 sec raw input. Iconic (visual), echoic (auditory) Short-term / Working memory ~15–30 sec, 7±2 items. Baddeley: central executive + phonological loop + visuospatial sketchpad + episodic buffer LTM — Explicit (declarative) Conscious recall. Splits into ↓ • Episodic Events with what / where / when context (your first day of college) • Semantic Facts, general knowledge, meanings (capital of France) LTM — Implicit (non-declarative) No conscious recall. Includes ↓ • Procedural / Priming / Conditioning Skills "how to" / exposure speeds processing / classically conditioned Prospective memory Remembering to do something later Quick map: Explicit = episodic + semantic (conscious). Implicit = procedural + priming (unconscious). "What/where/when of an event" → episodic (your mock miss).

chunks.text: 8.3 The Acts & laws Act Year The one thing they test Mental Healthcare Act (MHCA) 2017 Decriminalised suicide; Advance Directive + Nominated Representative ; Mental Health Review Boards; capacity-based consent. Minors can appoint a nominated representative; views considered age-appropriately. RPwD Act 2016 Replaced 1995 Act; recognises 21 disabilities ; ≥40% = "benchmark disability" Mental Health Act 1987 The old act MHCA 2017 replaced (admission/licensing focused) National Trust Act 1999 Welfare of autism, CP, ID, multiple disabilities; legal guardianship RCI Act 1992 Regulates training/registration of rehab professionals incl. clinical psychologists; the RCI licence (CRR) POCSO / POSH 2012 / 2013 Children from sexual offences (mandatory reporting) / sexual harassment of women at workplace Juvenile Justice Act 2015 Care & protection of children; children in conflict with law

chunks.heading: 9.1 Theorist → concept
chunks.text: 9.1 Theorist → concept Person What they are known for History / schools Wundt First psychology lab (1879), introspection, structuralism Titchener Structuralism (brought it to the US) William James Functionalism, "Principles of Psychology" Wertheimer Founded Gestalt psychology, phi phenomenon (apparent motion) Koffka / Kohler Gestalt psychology; Kohler = insight learning (chimps) Neisser "Father of cognitive psychology", coined the term (1967) Galton Individual differences, first mental tests, eugenics, correlation Learning Pavlov Classical conditioning Watson Behaviourism, Little Albert Thorndike Law of effect, puzzle box Skinner Operant conditioning, schedules of reinforcement Tolman Cognitive maps, latent learning Bandura Social learning, Bobo doll, self-efficacy Perception / attention / cognition Weber JND is a constant proportion of the stimulus (Weber's law) Fechner Psychophysics; sensation grows with the log of intensity Broadbent Early-selection filter model of attention Treisman Attenuation model; feature integration theory Chomsky Language acquisition device, universal grammar Sapir-Whorf Linguistic relativity (language shapes thought) Memory Ebbinghaus Forgetting curve, nonsense syllables Sperling Iconic (visual sensory) memory Miller Magic number 7 plus or minus 2 (STM capacity) Atkinson & Shiffrin Multi-store model (sensory / STM / LTM) Baddeley Working memory model

chunks.heading: 9.1a Theorist detail — the big ones explained
chunks.text: 9.1a Theorist detail — the big ones explained Not just the name → the setup, the finding, the number, the trap. Social psych first since that is where the named-experiment questions cluster. Theorist What they actually did · the trap Social psychology Asch Conformity. Line-judgement task: pick which of 3 lines matches a standard. Confederates deliberately gave a wrong answer; about 75% of real subjects conformed at least once, ~33% on average. Conformity is normative (fit in / avoid disapproval), not informational. Trap: Asch = group peer pressure; Milgram = authority . Conformity dropped sharply with one dissenting ally. Milgram Obedience. "Teacher" told by experimenter to shock a "learner" for wrong answers, up to 450V. 65% went to the maximum shock. Showed ordinary people obey a legitimate authority. Trap: obedience = following an authority's order ; conformity (Asch) = matching peers . Zimbardo Stanford Prison Experiment. Students randomly assigned guard/prisoner roles; "guards" turned abusive fast, study stopped after 6 days. Power of the situation/assigned role over personality (deindividuation). Trap: situational, not dispositional. Sherif Robbers Cave / realistic conflict theory. Two boys' camp groups; competition bred hostility, and superordinate goals (shared tasks neither group could solve alone) reduced it. Contact alone was not enough. Tajfel Social identity theory

chunks.heading: 9.2 Durations & numbers
chunks.text: 9.2 Durations & numbers Item Lock this Major depressive episode at least 2 weeks Persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) at least 2 years (1 year in children) Manic episode at least 1 week (or any length if hospitalised) Hypomanic episode at least 4 days Generalised anxiety disorder at least 6 months PTSD symptoms longer than 1 month Acute stress disorder 3 days to 1 month Schizophrenia 6 months total, at least 1 month active phase Schizophreniform 1 to 6 months Brief psychotic disorder 1 day to 1 month Insomnia disorder 3 nights per week for at least 3 months Iconic memory (visual sensory) about 0.25 to 1 second (Sperling) Echoic memory (auditory sensory) about 2 to 4 seconds Short-term memory 15 to 30 seconds, capacity 7 plus or minus 2 (Miller) IQ standard deviation Wechsler 15, Stanford-Binet 16 (SB-5 uses 15)

chunks.heading: 9.3 Components & "how many"
chunks.text: 9.3 Components & "how many" Model The parts DBT (4 skill modules) mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation, interpersonal effectiveness ACT hexaflex (6) acceptance, defusion, present moment, self-as-context, values, committed action Rogers' core conditions (3) congruence/genuineness, unconditional positive regard, empathy Beck's cognitive triad (3) negative view of self, world, future Ellis ABC Activating event, Belief, Consequence Big Five (OCEAN) Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism Baddeley working memory (4) central executive, phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad, episodic buffer Kubler-Ross (5) denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance Yalom therapeutic factors 11 (e.g. universality, instillation of hope, catharsis, group cohesiveness) Piaget stages (4) sensorimotor, preoperational, concrete operational, formal operational Kohlberg 3 levels (pre-conventional, conventional, post-conventional), 6 stages

chunks.heading: 9.4 General psychology nuggets
chunks.text: 9.4 General psychology nuggets Area Lock this Perception: psychophysics Weber's law (JND is a constant proportion of the stimulus); Fechner's law (sensation grows with the log of intensity) Perception: signal detection hit / miss / false alarm / correct rejection; d-prime = sensitivity, beta = response criterion Perception: feature integration (Treisman) preattentive feature detection, then attention binds features into objects Gestalt laws proximity, similarity, closure, continuity, common fate, figure-ground Attention models Broadbent early-selection filter; Treisman attenuation; Deutsch-Norman late selection; Stroop = automatic reading interferes Memory model Atkinson-Shiffrin: sensory then short-term then long-term; serial position = primacy + recency Emotion theories James-Lange (arousal then emotion), Cannon-Bard (simultaneous), Schachter-Singer two-factor (arousal + label), Lazarus (appraisal first) Arousal Yerkes-Dodson: performance is best at moderate arousal (inverted U) Reinforcement schedules variable ratio gives the highest steady rate and is most resistant to extinction

chunks.heading: 9.5 Landmark experiments
chunks.text: 9.5 Landmark experiments Study Showed Milgram Obedience to authority (65 percent went to the maximum shock) Asch Conformity to a wrong majority Zimbardo (Stanford Prison) Power of assigned roles / situation Darley & Latane Bystander effect, diffusion of responsibility (Kitty Genovese) Festinger & Carlsmith Cognitive dissonance (the 1 dollar group changed attitude more than the 20 dollar group) Sherif (Robbers Cave) Realistic conflict; superordinate goals reduce it Tajfel (minimal group) Social identity, in-group favouritism from arbitrary grouping Bandura (Bobo doll) Observational learning / modelling of aggression Seligman Learned helplessness TRAP: James-Lange = body first ("I tremble, therefore I am afraid"). Cannon-Bard = body and feeling at once. Schachter-Singer = body plus a cognitive label. Mixing these up is a classic exam trap.

chunks.heading: 9.6 Schools / perspectives of psychology
chunks.text: 9.6 Schools / perspectives of psychology Perspective Core idea · key name Structuralism Break consciousness into elements via introspection · Wundt, Titchener Functionalism What is the purpose of behaviour (adaptation) · William James Behaviourism Only observable behaviour; stimulus–response · Watson, Skinner, Pavlov Gestalt "The whole is more than the sum of parts" · Wertheimer, Koffka, Köhler Psychoanalytic Unconscious drives, early childhood · Freud Humanistic ("3rd force") Free will, self-actualisation, growth · Rogers, Maslow Cognitive Mind as information processor; memory, thinking · Neisser Biological / Evolutionary Behaviour from brain, genes, neurochemistry / shaped by natural selection Trigger: "lab + introspection" → Wundt/structuralism. "purpose/adaptation" → James/functionalism. "whole > parts" → Gestalt. "free will/self-actualisation" → humanistic.

chunks.heading: 9.7 Motivation & drive
chunks.text: 9.7 Motivation & drive Theory Says Maslow's hierarchy Physiological → safety → love/belonging → esteem → self-actualisation . Lower needs first Drive-reduction (Hull) Need → drive → behaviour to restore homeostasis Arousal / Yerkes-Dodson Seek optimal arousal; moderate arousal = best performance (inverted-U); hard tasks need lower arousal Incentive theory Pulled by external rewards (vs pushed by internal drives) Intrinsic vs extrinsic For its own sake vs for a reward. Overjustification effect : paying for an enjoyed task kills intrinsic motivation Self-determination (Deci & Ryan) Three needs: autonomy, competence, relatedness McClelland Need for achievement, affiliation, power

chunks.heading: 9.8 States of consciousness (sleep one-glance)
chunks.text: 9.8 States of consciousness (sleep one-glance) Item Recall Sleep stages NREM 1→2→3 (deep / slow-wave / delta), then REM (dreaming, paralysis, EEG looks awake) Cycle length ~90 min; REM lengthens toward morning Circadian rhythm ~24 hr clock; suprachiasmatic nucleus + melatonin (pineal) Sleep spindles / K-complexes Hallmark of Stage 2 NREM Delta waves Stage 3 deep sleep; sleepwalking / night terrors arise here

chunks.heading: 9.9 Personality — theories & types
chunks.text: 9.9 Personality — theories & types Approach One thing to remember Big Five (OCEAN) Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism — the dominant trait model Eysenck Three dimensions: Extraversion, Neuroticism, Psychoticism (PEN); biologically based Cattell 16 PF ; source vs surface traits; factor analysis Allport Cardinal, central, secondary traits Freud (structural) Id (pleasure) – Ego (reality) – Superego (morality) Bandura Reciprocal determinism : person ↔ behaviour ↔ environment; self-efficacy Rogers Self-concept; congruence between real and ideal self; conditions of worth Locus of control (Rotter) Internal ("I control outcomes") vs external ("luck/fate does")

chunks.heading: 9.10 Intelligence — theories
chunks.text: 9.10 Intelligence — theories Theorist Model Spearman Two-factor: general g + specific s ; factor analysis Thurstone 7 primary mental abilities (no single g) Cattell-Horn Fluid (novel reasoning, declines with age) vs crystallised (knowledge, stable/rises) Gardner Multiple intelligences (linguistic, logical, musical, spatial, bodily, inter/intra-personal, naturalist) Sternberg Triarchic : analytical, creative, practical Goleman / Salovey-Mayer Emotional intelligence (perceive, use, understand, manage emotion) Cross-link: IQ scoring, deviation IQ, WAIS/WISC subtests live in §4 Assessment ; "scaled score 10 = 50th percentile" is your mock miss.

chunks.heading: 9.11 Freudian defense mechanisms
chunks.text: 9.11 Freudian defense mechanisms Defense Quick example Repression Push a threatening thought out of awareness (the master defense) Denial Refuse to accept reality ("I'm not sick") Projection Attribute your own impulse to someone else ("you hate me") Displacement Redirect a feeling to a safer target (yell at the dog, not the boss) Sublimation Channel an impulse into a useful act (aggression → surgery/sport) — the "mature" one Reaction formation Act the opposite of the true feeling (hate disguised as overcare) Rationalisation Logical-sounding excuse for the real motive ("I didn't want it anyway") Regression Revert to an earlier developmental stage under stress Intellectualisation / Undoing Use abstract thinking to avoid the feeling / ritually cancel an act

chunks.heading: 9.12 Heuristics & cognitive biases
chunks.text: 9.12 Heuristics & cognitive biases Bias / heuristic What it is Availability heuristic Judge likelihood by how easily examples come to mind (plane crashes feel common) Representativeness Judge by resemblance to a prototype; ignores base rates Anchoring Over-rely on the first number/info given Confirmation bias Seek info that confirms what you already believe Framing effect Same info, different wording → different choice (90% survive vs 10% die) Hindsight bias "I knew it all along" after the outcome is known Functional fixedness / Mental set Can't see a novel use for an object / stuck on a strategy that worked before

chunks.heading: 9.13 Learning — fast contrasts
chunks.text: 9.13 Learning — fast contrasts Pair Difference Classical vs operant Pavlov: involuntary, stimulus pairing. Skinner: voluntary, consequences shape behaviour Positive vs negative Positive = add a stimulus; Negative = remove one. Reinforcement ↑ behaviour, punishment ↓ it Escape vs avoidance Escape ends an aversive stimulus already on; avoidance prevents its onset (your mock miss) Shaping / spontaneous recovery Reward successive approximations / an extinguished response briefly returns after a pause Conditioning detail (escape/avoidance, alliance, object relations) is in §5 ; emotion-theory and psychophysics rows are in 9.4 above.

chunks.text: 9.14 Biostatistics rapid recall NIMHANS's biggest gap Cue Lock this Choosing the test — 2 groups, parametric independent t-test (paired data → paired t-test) 3+ groups, parametric ANOVA (one-way); repeated measures if same subjects 2 groups, non-parametric Mann-Whitney U (paired → Wilcoxon signed-rank) 3+ groups, non-parametric Kruskal-Wallis Two categorical variables Chi-square (Fisher's exact if cells small) Strength of a linear relationship Pearson r (parametric) / Spearman rho (ranks) Odds ratio / relative risk = 1 no association ; >1 = risk, <1 = protective (your mock miss) NNT = 1 / ARR ; ARR = control event rate − treatment event rate Type I error (alpha) false positive — reject a true null Type II error (beta) false negative — keep a false null; power = 1 − beta p-value P(data this extreme if null true). And p < 0.05 only means st

chunks.heading: 9.15 Assessment — reliability, validity & score conversions
chunks.text: 9.15 Assessment — reliability, validity & score conversions Item Lock this Reliability types test-retest (stability), inter-rater (between scorers), internal consistency ( Cronbach's alpha / split-half), parallel forms Validity types content, criterion ( concurrent + predictive ), construct ( convergent + discriminant ), face Reliability vs validity Reliability is necessary but not sufficient for validity; a test can be reliable but not valid, never valid without being reliable z-score mean 0 , SD 1 T-score mean 50 , SD 10 Deviation IQ (Wechsler) mean 100 , SD 15 (Stanford-Binet old = 16) Wechsler scaled subtest score mean 10 , SD 3 — so scaled score 10 = 50th percentile (your mock miss) Sten / Stanine sten mean 5.5 (SD 2); stanine mean 5 (SD 2) Normal curve 68 / 95 / 99.7 within 1 / 2 / 3 SD; percentile = % scoring at or below you

chunks.heading: 9.16 Abnormal — disorder → hallmark & first-line
chunks.text: 9.16 Abnormal — disorder → hallmark & first-line Disorder Hallmark · first-line Major depression 2+ weeks low mood/anhedonia · SSRI (+ CBT) Bipolar I (mania) 1+ week elevated mood · lithium / valproate (mood stabiliser); antidepressant alone can trigger mania Schizophrenia positive + negative symptoms, 6 months · antipsychotic; clozapine for treatment-resistant OCD obsessions + compulsions · SSRI (high dose) + ERP (exposure & response prevention) Panic disorder recurrent unexpected attacks · SSRI + CBT Specific phobia marked fear of object/situation · exposure therapy (systematic desensitisation) PTSD symptoms >1 month after trauma · trauma-focused CBT / EMDR; SSRI GAD 6 months excessive worry · CBT; SSRI/SNRI (buspirone) Borderline PD instability of mood/relationships/self, fear of abandonment · DBT ADHD inattention/hyperactivity · stimulants (methylphenidate) Trigger: "compulsions/rituals" → OCD & ERP. "fear of abandonment + DBT" → BPD. "treatment-resistant schizophrenia" → clozapine.

chunks.heading: 9.17 Neuro one-glance — cranial nerves, localisation, aphasia
chunks.text: 9.17 Neuro one-glance — cranial nerves, localisation, aphasia Item Recall 12 cranial nerves (order) O lfactory, O ptic, O culomotor, T rochlear, T rigeminal, A bducens, F acial, V estibulocochlear, G lossopharyngeal, V agus, A ccessory, H ypoglossal Sensory / motor / both " Some Say Marry Money But My Brother Says Big Brains Matter Most " (S/M/B per nerve) Broca's aphasia non-fluent, effortful, comprehension intact · frontal (Broca's area) Wernicke's aphasia fluent but meaningless, poor comprehension · temporal (Wernicke's area) Conduction aphasia can't repeat · arcuate fasciculus Frontal lobe executive function, planning, personality (Phineas Gage) Hippocampus forming new long-term memories (H.M. → anterograde amnesia) Amygdala fear, emotional salience Cerebellum balance, coordination, motor learning Hypothalamus homeostasis, 4 F's, drives the pituitary

chunks.heading: 9.17a Motor control — who does what classic NIMHANS swap-trap
chunks.text: 9.17a Motor control — who does what classic NIMHANS swap-trap Structure Job Lock the trap Premotor cortex plans externally / sensory-cued movement (see it, reach for it); preps posture before M1 fires premotor = external / cue-driven SMA (supplementary motor area) plans internally generated, self-initiated movement; sequencing from memory + bimanual coordination SMA = internal / from within (premotor vs SMA = external vs internal) Basal ganglia initiate / select / gate movement; set vigour , scale force & amplitude "scales force / amplitude" → basal ganglia · resting tremor (Parkinson's) · chorea = Huntington's Cerebellum timing, coordination, balance, error correction; compares intended vs actual and smooths on the fly "timing / smoothing / coordination" → cerebellum · intention tremor, ataxia, dysmetria Two traps: resting tremor = basal ganglia, intention tremor = cerebellum. "Force/amplitude" = basal ganglia, "timing/smoothing" = cerebellum. Full version on the biopsych cheatsheet §8 .

chunks.heading: 9.18 The Acts, founders & "X is to Y"
chunks.text: 9.18 The Acts, founders & "X is to Y" Pairing Lock this Mental Healthcare Act 2017 (India) — decriminalised suicide, right to treatment, advance directive RPwD Act (Rights of Persons with Disabilities) 2016 — 21 disabilities, replaced the 1995 Act RCI Act (Rehabilitation Council of India) 1992 — regulates training of psychologists/therapists POCSO 2012 — Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Wundt : ___ first psychology lab (1879) Binet : ___ first practical intelligence test (mental age) Aaron Beck : ___ cognitive therapy / cognitive triad Carl Rogers : ___ client-centred therapy Joseph Wolpe : ___ systematic desensitisation Beck vs Ellis cognitive triad / collaborative empiricism vs REBT / ABC, more confrontational

chunks.heading: 9.19 Language — grammar traps & one-word substitutions
chunks.text: 9.19 Language — grammar traps & one-word substitutions Trap The fix Subject-verb agreement "Each / every / neither / one of" takes a singular verb; "a number of" = plural, "the number of" = singular Either/neither ... or/nor verb agrees with the nearer subject Fewer vs less fewer = countable, less = uncountable Between vs among between = two, among = three or more Lie vs lay lie (recline, no object) vs lay (put down, takes an object) One-word: fear of enclosed spaces claustrophobia (open/public spaces = agoraphobia) One-word: study of populations demography One-word: one who knows many languages polyglot One-word: incapable of being corrected incorrigible One-word: bitter attack in speech/writing diatribe (vs panegyric/eulogy = praise) Highest fast-marks section — grammar and vocab are pure recall, no reasoning. Deeper drills in §7 . Exam-day rules Longest option is often correct on these papers, but only as a tiebreaker, never over knowledge. "NOT" / "EXCEPT" questions — circle the NOT, you're hunting the odd one out. This is where tired people lose marks. Negative marking −0.25: answer if you can eliminate 2 options; skip a pure blind guess. Don't change a first instinct unless you find a concrete reason to. That's the whole syllabus on one page. chunks.heading: Theories — every named theory/model, its author, the one-line hook
chunks.text: Theories — every named theory/model, its author, the one-line hook Third of the four category sweeps. The bucket is "named theories/models." Grouped by domain so you see the rival theories side by side (that's how they're tested: "which theory says X?" or "who proposed it?"). Built 2026-05-24. Effects Phenomena Theories Theorists Social Psych Cognitive Lookalikes Two question shapes. (1) "Who gave [theory]?" → name the author. (2) "Which theory holds that [claim]?" → name the theory. Rival theories in one domain are each other's distractors (James-Lange vs Cannon-Bard, Piaget vs Vygotsky), so always learn the contrast , not the theory alone. Jump to: 1. Learning 2. Motivation 3. Emotion 4. Personality 5. Development 6. Social 7. Intelligence 8. Memory & cognition 9. Language 10. Stress & abnormal 11. Perception 12. Career & counselling

chunks.heading: 1. Learning theories
chunks.text: 1. Learning theories Theory Author Core claim Classical conditioning Ivan Pavlov Neutral stimulus paired with a reflex-evoking one comes to evoke the reflex. Connectionism / Law of Effect Edward Thorndike Responses followed by satisfaction are stamped in (trial-and-error, puzzle box). Operant conditioning B. F. Skinner Behaviour is shaped by its consequences (reinforcement/punishment). Contiguity theory Edwin Guthrie One-trial learning by sheer stimulus–response pairing in time. Insight learning Wolfgang Köhler Sudden restructuring of a problem ("aha"), shown in chimps (Sultan). Latent learning / cognitive maps Edward Tolman Learning happens without reinforcement and shows up later (maze rats). Social / observational learning Albert Bandura We learn by watching and modelling others (Bobo doll). Rescorla–Wagner model Rescorla & Wagner Conditioning depends on surprise / prediction error, not mere pairing. Premack principle David Premack A high-frequency activity can reinforce a low-frequency one ("grandma's rule"). Conditions / hierarchy of learning Robert Gagné Eight learning types from signal learning up to problem-solving; later five learned capabilities + nine instructional events. Meaningful learning / advance organizers David Ausubel New material is learned by anchoring it to existing knowledge; pre-teach an advance organizer first. Reception, not discovery. Discovery learn

chunks.heading: 2. Motivation theories
chunks.text: 2. Motivation theories Theory Author Core claim Hierarchy of needs Abraham Maslow Needs climb from physiological → safety → love → esteem → self-actualisation. ERG theory Clayton Alderfer Existence, Relatedness, Growth (Maslow condensed; allows regression). Two-factor (motivation-hygiene) Frederick Herzberg Hygiene factors prevent dissatisfaction; motivators create satisfaction. Drive-reduction Clark Hull Behaviour reduces physiological drives to restore homeostasis. Arousal theory / Yerkes–Dodson law Yerkes & Dodson Performance peaks at moderate arousal (inverted-U). Self-determination theory Deci & Ryan Intrinsic motivation needs autonomy, competence, relatedness. Expectancy theory Victor Vroom Effort = expectancy × instrumentality × valence. Goal-setting theory Edwin Locke Specific, hard, accepted goals drive higher performance. Need for achievement (nAch) McClelland; Atkinson Achievement/affiliation/power needs; measured via TAT. Flow Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi Total absorption when challenge matches skill. Opponent-process theory Richard Solomon Every emotional state triggers an opposing after-reaction (addiction, thrill). Theory X / Theory Y Douglas McGregor Managers either assume workers dislike work and need control (X) or seek responsibility and self-direction (Y). Incentive theory (behaviourist tradition) Behaviour is pulled by external rewards/goals, not just pushed by

chunks.heading: 3. Emotion theories (order of events is the trap)
chunks.text: 3. Emotion theories (order of events is the trap) Theory Author Sequence James–Lange James & Lange Stimulus → bodily arousal → emotion ("we're afraid because we tremble"). Cannon–Bard Cannon & Bard Stimulus → arousal and emotion simultaneously (thalamic). Schachter–Singer two-factor Schachter & Singer Arousal + cognitive label → emotion. Cognitive appraisal Richard Lazarus Appraisal of the event comes first; cognition precedes emotion. Affective primacy Robert Zajonc Emotion can occur before and without cognition ("preferences need no inferences"). Facial-feedback hypothesis Tomkins; Ekman Facial expressions feed back to intensify/trigger the felt emotion. Basic emotions Paul Ekman Six universal, cross-cultural facial emotions. Wheel of emotions Robert Plutchik Eight primary emotions in opposing pairs, combining into others. The classic swap: James-Lange = body first ; Cannon-Bard = both at once ; Schachter-Singer = arousal + label ; Lazarus = appraisal first ; Zajonc = feeling before thinking . Lazarus vs Zajonc is the famous "primacy of cognition vs affect" debate.

chunks.heading: 4. Personality theories
chunks.text: 4. Personality theories Theory Author Core idea Psychoanalytic Sigmund Freud Id/ego/superego; psychosexual stages; unconscious conflict & defences. Analytical psychology Carl Jung Collective unconscious, archetypes, introversion/extraversion. Individual psychology Alfred Adler Inferiority/superiority, striving for superiority, style of life, birth order. Trait (idiographic) Gordon Allport Cardinal/central/secondary traits; functional autonomy. 16PF / factor trait Raymond Cattell 16 source traits via factor analysis; fluid vs crystallised intelligence. PEN model Hans Eysenck Psychoticism, Extraversion, Neuroticism (biological arousal basis). Big Five / Five-Factor (OCEAN) Costa & McCrae Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism. Need-press / personology Henry Murray Needs interact with environmental "press"; gave the TAT. Personal construct theory George Kelly "Man as scientist"; we build bipolar constructs to predict events. Social-cognitive Albert Bandura Reciprocal determinism; self-efficacy. Locus of control / social learning Julian Rotter Behaviour = expectancy × reinforcement value; internal vs external control. Person–situation / CAPS Walter Mischel Behaviour is situation-specific; cognitive-affective system; delay of gratification. Self theory (humanistic) Carl Rogers Self-concept, congruence, unconditional positive regard, fully-functioning p

chunks.heading: 5. Developmental theories
chunks.text: 5. Developmental theories Theory Author Core idea Cognitive development Jean Piaget 4 stages: sensorimotor, preoperational, concrete & formal operational. Sociocultural Lev Vygotsky Learning is social; ZPD & scaffolding; language drives thought. Psychosocial development Erik Erikson 8 lifespan stages, each a crisis (trust vs mistrust … integrity vs despair). Psychosexual development Sigmund Freud Oral, anal, phallic, latency, genital stages. Moral development Lawrence Kohlberg Pre-conventional → conventional → post-conventional reasoning. Ethic of care Carol Gilligan Critiqued Kohlberg; women reason via care/relationships, not just justice. Ecological systems Urie Bronfenbrenner Micro/meso/exo/macro/chrono systems; later PPCT model. Attachment theory John Bowlby Innate bonding system; secure base; internal working models. Strange Situation / styles Mary Ainsworth Secure, anxious-ambivalent, avoidant (Main later: disorganised). Identity statuses James Marcia Diffusion, foreclosure, moratorium, achievement (crisis × commitment). Temperament types Thomas & Chess Easy, difficult, slow-to-warm-up; goodness-of-fit. Maturation theory Arnold Gesell Development unfolds on a biological timetable (norms). Piaget vs Vygotsky: Piaget = development drives learning, individual discovery, fixed stages. Vygotsky = learning drives development, social/cultural, ZPD. Erikson's stages (psychosocial

chunks.heading: 6. Social-psychology theories
chunks.text: 6. Social-psychology theories Theory Author Core idea Cognitive dissonance Leon Festinger Tension from clashing cognitions drives attitude change. Social comparison Leon Festinger We evaluate ourselves by comparing to others. Attribution theory Fritz Heider We explain behaviour as internal (dispositional) or external (situational). Covariation model Harold Kelley Attribution uses consensus, consistency, distinctiveness. Correspondent inference Jones & Davis We infer disposition from freely chosen, low-social-desirability acts. Attribution of motivation Bernard Weiner Locus × stability × controllability shapes emotion & expectancy. Balance theory Fritz Heider We seek consistency among our liking/relationships (P-O-X triangles). Social identity theory Tajfel & Turner Group membership shapes self-concept; in-group favouritism. Realistic conflict theory Muzafer Sherif Competition over scarce resources breeds intergroup hostility (Robbers Cave). Elaboration Likelihood Model Petty & Cacioppo Persuasion via central (thoughtful) vs peripheral (cues) route. Self-perception theory Daryl Bem We infer our own attitudes by observing our behaviour. Psychological reactance Jack Brehm Threatened freedom → wanting the forbidden thing more. Social exchange theory Thibaut & Kelley Relationships weighed by rewards minus costs (comparison level). Equity theory J. S. Adams We want a fair ratio of in

chunks.heading: 7. Intelligence theories
chunks.text: 7. Intelligence theories Theory Author Core idea Two-factor (g + s) Charles Spearman A general factor g plus task-specific factors; factor analysis. Primary mental abilities Louis Thurstone 7 independent abilities, no single g . Fluid vs crystallised (Gf-Gc) Cattell & Horn (→ CHC) Fluid = reasoning power; crystallised = accumulated knowledge. Structure of intellect J. P. Guilford 180 abilities (operations × content × products); divergent thinking. Multiple intelligences Howard Gardner 8+ independent intelligences (linguistic, musical, bodily-kinesthetic…). Triarchic theory Robert Sternberg Analytical, creative, practical intelligence. Hierarchical model Philip Vernon g at top → verbal-educational & spatial-mechanical → specifics. Emotional intelligence Salovey & Mayer (popularised by Goleman) Perceiving, using, understanding, managing emotion. PASS theory Das, Naglieri & Kirby Intelligence = Planning, Attention, Simultaneous & Successive processing (built on Luria's brain functions). Three-stratum theory (CHC) John Carroll g at the top, 8 broad abilities below, ~70 narrow ones; merged with Cattell-Horn into the CHC model behind modern IQ tests.

chunks.heading: 8. Memory & cognition models
chunks.text: 8. Memory & cognition models Model Author Core idea Multi-store model Atkinson & Shiffrin Sensory → short-term → long-term, linked by attention & rehearsal. Working memory model Baddeley & Hitch Central executive + phonological loop + visuospatial sketchpad (+ episodic buffer). Levels of processing Craik & Lockhart Memory depends on depth of encoding, not a fixed store. Episodic vs semantic memory Endel Tulving Memory for events vs general knowledge (later: procedural, encoding specificity). Dual-coding theory Allan Paivio Verbal + visual codes; images are remembered better. Spreading activation Collins & Loftus Semantic network where activating one concept primes related ones. Reconstructive memory / schema theory Frederic Bartlett Memory isn't a recording; we rebuild it to fit our schemas (the "War of the Ghosts" study). Basis of eyewitness error.

chunks.heading: 9. Language-development theories
chunks.text: 9. Language-development theories Theory Author Core idea Behaviourist (learning) B. F. Skinner Language is learned via imitation + reinforcement. Nativist / LAD / Universal Grammar Noam Chomsky Innate language-acquisition device; grammar is hard-wired (rebutted Skinner). Critical period hypothesis Eric Lenneberg Language must be acquired within an early window. Interactionist / LASS Jerome Bruner Social interaction (language acquisition support system) scaffolds language. Linguistic relativity (Sapir–Whorf) Sapir & Whorf Language shapes/constrains thought. Cognitive Jean Piaget Language follows cognitive development (thought before language). The famous clash: Skinner (learned via reinforcement) vs Chomsky (innate LAD/UG). Chomsky's review of Skinner's Verbal Behavior launched the cognitive revolution.

chunks.heading: 10. Stress & abnormal-psychology models
chunks.text: 10. Stress & abnormal-psychology models Model Author Core idea General Adaptation Syndrome Hans Selye Alarm → resistance → exhaustion response to chronic stress. Transactional model of stress Lazarus & Folkman Stress = primary + secondary appraisal; problem- vs emotion-focused coping. Diathesis–stress model — Disorder arises when a predisposition (diathesis) meets enough stress. Biopsychosocial model George Engel Illness from interacting biological, psychological & social factors. Learned helplessness Seligman & Maier Uncontrollable aversive events → giving up; model of depression. Cognitive triad Aaron Beck Depression = negative views of self, world & future; schemas. ABC model Albert Ellis Activating event → Belief → Consequence; irrational beliefs drive distress (REBT). Hopelessness theory Abramson, Metalsky & Alloy Reformulated helplessness: a depressive attributional style.

chunks.heading: 11. Perception theories
chunks.text: 11. Perception theories Theory Author Core idea Gestalt Wertheimer, Koffka, Köhler The whole is organised by grouping laws (Prägnanz). Direct / ecological perception James Gibson Bottom-up: the optic array provides enough info directly (affordances). Constructivist perception Richard Gregory Top-down: perception is hypothesis-testing from prior knowledge. Feature-integration theory Anne Treisman Features detected in parallel; attention binds them into objects. Signal detection theory Green & Swets Detection = sensitivity (d′) + response criterion (bias), not a fixed threshold.

chunks.heading: 12. Career & counselling theories
chunks.text: 12. Career & counselling theories Theory Author Core idea RIASEC / vocational types John Holland Match person type to work environment (Realistic, Investigative, Artistic, Social, Enterprising, Conventional). Life-span, life-space Donald Super Career develops across life stages; self-concept implemented in work. Developmental career choice Eli Ginzberg Occupational choice as a developmental process (fantasy → tentative → realistic). Social learning / happenstance John Krumboltz Career shaped by learning experiences and planned chance. Needs theory of career Anne Roe Early parent-child climate shapes whether you pick person-oriented vs non-person-oriented careers. Circumscription & compromise Linda Gottfredson Children narrow career options by gender, then prestige, then interests; compromise when reality bites. That's the theories bucket. For each domain, learn the rival theories as a contrast set, then pin each to its author. Other sweeps: Effects , Phenomena , Theorists . chunks.heading: Theorists — who's who, what each one owns, the one-line tell
chunks.text: Theorists — who's who, what each one owns, the one-line tell Last of the four category sweeps. This is the reverse drill: name → what they're famous for . When a stem gives you a person and four contributions (or a contribution and four people), this is the page. Grouped by field. The neighbouring sweeps go the other way (concept → person): Theories , Effects . Built 2026-05-24. Effects Phenomena Theories Theorists Social Psych Cognitive Lookalikes How it's asked. "Who proposed X?", "X is associated with whom?", or "Match the theorist to the concept." The distractor is always a same-field contemporary (Freud's circle, the trait theorists, the attachment crew). Learn each person as a bundle so a single concept pulls the whole name up. Jump to: 1. Psychoanalytic & neo-Freudian 2. Humanistic & trait 3. Behaviourist & learning 4. Cognitive & developmental 5. Social psychologists 6. Intelligence & testing 7. Statistics & psychometrics 8. Therapy founders

chunks.heading: 1. Psychoanalytic & neo-Freudian
chunks.text: 1. Psychoanalytic & neo-Freudian Theorist What they own Sigmund Freud Psychoanalysis; id/ego/superego; psychosexual stages; defence mechanisms; the unconscious; dream interpretation. Carl Jung Analytical psychology; collective unconscious; archetypes; introversion/extraversion; coined the Electra complex; word-association. Alfred Adler Individual psychology; inferiority/superiority complex; striving for superiority; style of life; birth order; social interest. Karen Horney Basic anxiety; moving toward/against/away from people; womb envy (reply to penis envy); neurotic needs. Erik Erikson 8 psychosocial stages; identity crisis; ego psychology. Erich Fromm Escape from Freedom; character orientations; humanistic psychoanalysis. Harry Stack Sullivan Interpersonal theory; the self-system; good-me/bad-me/not-me. Melanie Klein Object relations; play therapy; paranoid-schizoid & depressive positions. Anna Freud Child psychoanalysis; systematised the defence mechanisms. D. W. Winnicott Good-enough mother; transitional object; holding environment; true/false self. Heinz Kohut Self psychology; narcissism; empathic mirroring. Complex ownership: inferiority/superiority = Adler ; womb envy = Horney ; Electra = Jung (named it), Oedipus = Freud. Don't default everything to Freud.

chunks.heading: 2. Humanistic & trait theorists
chunks.text: 2. Humanistic & trait theorists Theorist What they own Abraham Maslow Hierarchy of needs; self-actualisation; peak experiences; Jonah complex. Carl Rogers Person-centred therapy; self-concept; congruence; unconditional positive regard; fully-functioning person. Gordon Allport Cardinal/central/secondary traits; functional autonomy; idiographic approach; contact hypothesis. Raymond Cattell 16PF; source vs surface traits; fluid vs crystallised intelligence. Hans Eysenck PEN model (Psychoticism, Extraversion, Neuroticism); biological basis of personality. Costa & McCrae Big Five / NEO-PI (OCEAN). Henry Murray Personology; needs & press; the TAT; Icarus complex; nAch roots. George Kelly Personal construct theory; rep grid; "man as scientist." Rollo May / Victor Frankl Existential psychology; May (anxiety/the daimonic); Frankl (logotherapy, meaning). William Sheldon Somatotypes (endo/meso/ectomorph).

chunks.heading: 3. Behaviourist & learning theorists
chunks.text: 3. Behaviourist & learning theorists Theorist What they own Ivan Pavlov Classical conditioning; the salivating dogs. John B. Watson Founded behaviourism; Little Albert; "give me a dozen healthy infants…". B. F. Skinner Operant conditioning; reinforcement schedules; Skinner box; verbal behaviour; radical behaviourism. Edward Thorndike Law of Effect; connectionism; puzzle box; the halo effect. Edward Tolman Latent learning; cognitive maps; purposive behaviourism. Wolfgang Köhler Insight learning (chimps); Gestalt; the bouba/kiki demo. Albert Bandura Social learning; Bobo doll; self-efficacy; reciprocal determinism. Edwin Guthrie Contiguity theory (one-trial learning). Clark Hull Drive-reduction theory; mathematico-deductive behaviourism. Joseph Wolpe Systematic desensitisation; reciprocal inhibition.

chunks.heading: 4. Cognitive & developmental theorists
chunks.text: 4. Cognitive & developmental theorists Theorist What they own Jean Piaget Cognitive-development stages; schemas; assimilation/accommodation; object permanence; conservation. Lev Vygotsky Sociocultural theory; ZPD; scaffolding; private speech. Jerome Bruner Discovery learning; spiral curriculum; enactive/iconic/symbolic; LASS. Lawrence Kohlberg Stages of moral development. Urie Bronfenbrenner Ecological systems; PPCT model. John Bowlby Attachment theory; maternal deprivation; internal working models. Mary Ainsworth Strange Situation; secure/anxious/avoidant attachment. Harry Harlow Rhesus monkeys; contact comfort over food (wire vs cloth mother). Noam Chomsky Universal grammar; LAD; rebutted Skinner; cognitive revolution. Ulric Neisser "Cognitive Psychology" (named the field); ecological memory. Endel Tulving Episodic vs semantic memory; encoding specificity. Baddeley & Hitch Working-memory model. Elizabeth Loftus Misinformation effect; eyewitness memory; false memories. The animal-study set: dogs = Pavlov ; cats/puzzle box = Thorndike ; chimps/insight = Köhler ; monkeys/contact comfort = Harlow ; rats/cognitive maps = Tolman ; Bobo doll = Bandura ; Little Albert = Watson .

chunks.heading: 5. Social psychologists
chunks.text: 5. Social psychologists Theorist What they own Leon Festinger Cognitive dissonance; social comparison; deindividuation roots. Kurt Lewin Father of social psych; field theory; B = f(P,E); action research; group dynamics. Solomon Asch Conformity (line task); impression formation (central traits). Stanley Milgram Obedience to authority; small-world / six degrees. Philip Zimbardo Stanford prison experiment; deindividuation; the Lucifer effect. Muzafer Sherif Realistic conflict; Robbers Cave; autokinetic norm formation. Fritz Heider Attribution theory; balance theory. Lee Ross Coined the fundamental attribution error; false-consensus effect. Tajfel & Turner Social identity theory; minimal group paradigm. Irving Janis Groupthink. Latané & Darley Bystander effect; diffusion of responsibility. Robert Cialdini Six principles of influence. Jack Brehm Psychological reactance. Norman Triplett First social-psych experiment → social facilitation.

chunks.heading: 6. Intelligence & testing
chunks.text: 6. Intelligence & testing Theorist What they own Alfred Binet First practical intelligence test (with Simon); mental age. Lewis Terman Stanford-Binet; longitudinal study of gifted children ("Termites"). David Wechsler WAIS/WISC; deviation IQ (mean 100, SD 15). Charles Spearman Two-factor theory; g ; factor analysis. Louis Thurstone Primary mental abilities; attitude scaling. J. P. Guilford Structure of intellect; divergent thinking. Howard Gardner Multiple intelligences. Robert Sternberg Triarchic theory; love triangle. Raymond Cattell Fluid vs crystallised intelligence. Salovey & Mayer Emotional intelligence (Goleman popularised). Hermann Rorschach The inkblot test. Henry Murray The TAT (with Morgan).

chunks.heading: 7. Statistics & psychometrics
chunks.text: 7. Statistics & psychometrics Theorist What they own Francis Galton Correlation concept; regression to the mean; eugenics; first mental tests. Karl Pearson Product-moment correlation (r); chi-square; standard deviation term. Charles Spearman Rank correlation (rho); Spearman-Brown formula. Ronald Fisher ANOVA; F-distribution; null hypothesis; p < .05; experimental design. W. S. Gosset ("Student") The t-test / t-distribution (pen name; Guinness brewery, 1908). Jacob Cohen Effect size (Cohen's d); kappa; statistical power. Lee Cronbach Cronbach's alpha; construct validity (with Meehl); generalisability theory. William McCall T-score (mean 50, SD 10). Rensis Likert The summative agree–disagree scale. Louis Guttman Scalogram (cumulative scaling). Charles Osgood Semantic differential. Georg Rasch Rasch model / item response theory. The high-frequency stats pairings: r & chi-square = Pearson ; ANOVA/F = Fisher ; t-test = Gosset ; alpha = Cronbach ; effect size d = Cohen ; correlation idea = Galton . These recur every year.

chunks.heading: 8. Therapy founders
chunks.text: 8. Therapy founders Founder Therapy Sigmund Freud Psychoanalysis (free association, transference). Aaron Beck Cognitive therapy / CBT; cognitive triad. Albert Ellis REBT; ABC model; irrational beliefs. Carl Rogers Person-centred / client-centred therapy. Fritz Perls Gestalt therapy; empty chair; here-and-now. Joseph Wolpe Systematic desensitisation; behaviour therapy. Viktor Frankl Logotherapy (meaning); paradoxical intention. William Glasser Reality therapy; choice theory. Marsha Linehan Dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT). Steven Hayes Acceptance & commitment therapy (ACT). Eric Berne Transactional analysis (Parent-Adult-Child). Salvador Minuchin Structural family therapy. Jacob Moreno Psychodrama; group psychotherapy; the term "group therapy." Irvin Yalom Existential & group therapy; 11 therapeutic factors. Francine Shapiro EMDR. CBT family swap: cognitive triad & cognitive therapy = Beck ; REBT & ABC = Ellis ; DBT = Linehan ; ACT = Hayes . Beck and Ellis are the constant distractor pair. That's the theorists bucket. Drill it backwards from the Theories and Effects sweeps: read a concept, name the person, then check it here. All four sweeps together cover the "named X / who gave it" question type end to end. Sihan MET 2026 + NIMHANS prep · /notes/theorists/ · built 2026-05-24

chunks.heading: Therapy Components — what belongs to what
chunks.text: Therapy Components — what belongs to what Recognition drill for "which of these is a component of ___" items · Built 2026-05-21 Why this page exists. Sihan flagged that the real MET paper asks "which one of these is a component of DBT?" style questions across many therapies. Those are recognition items: they give you 4 things and you pick the one that genuinely belongs. The trap is always a real concept from a different therapy. So for each school below you get two lists: the components that belong and the distractors that don't (and where they actually come from) . Learn both sides and the question becomes free. This is the companion to the full psychotherapy cheatsheet , which covers founders + mechanism. This page is purely "what are the named parts."

chunks.heading: DBT — Dialectical Behaviour Therapy (Linehan)
chunks.text: DBT — Dialectical Behaviour Therapy (Linehan) 4 skill modules: Mindfulness · Distress Tolerance · Emotion Regulation · Interpersonal Effectiveness. Mnemonic: "My Dog Eats Iguanas" (Mindfulness, Distress tolerance, Emotion reg, Interpersonal). 4 modes of treatment: individual therapy · group skills training · phone/between-session coaching · therapist consultation team. NOT a DBT module: "cognitive restructuring" / "cognitive triad" (that's Beck) · "free association" (Freud) · "hexaflex" or "cognitive defusion" (ACT) · "unconditional positive regard" (Rogers). DBT uses acceptance + change ("dialectics") and is built for BPD with chronic suicidality .

chunks.heading: ACT — Acceptance & Commitment Therapy (Hayes)
chunks.text: ACT — Acceptance & Commitment Therapy (Hayes) Hexaflex, 6 processes: Acceptance · Cognitive Defusion · Self-as-Context · Present-Moment Contact · Values · Committed Action. Goal = psychological flexibility (not symptom reduction). NOT ACT: the 4 DBT modules · "ABC model" (Ellis) · "miracle question" (SFBT). If you see "hexaflex," "defusion," "values," or "I'm having the thought that…" it is ACT.

chunks.heading: CBT — Beck's Cognitive Therapy
chunks.text: CBT — Beck's Cognitive Therapy Components: cognitive triad (negative view of self / world / future) · schemas → automatic thoughts · cognitive distortions (all-or-nothing, overgeneralisation, catastrophising, etc.). Techniques: Socratic questioning (guided discovery) · thought records · downward arrow · behavioural experiments · activity scheduling. NOT Beck: "ABC model / irrational beliefs / dispute" → that's Ellis (REBT) . "Reciprocal inhibition" → Wolpe. The cognitive triad is Beck; the ABC is Ellis. Examiners swap these constantly.

chunks.heading: REBT — Rational Emotive Behaviour Therapy (Ellis)
chunks.text: REBT — Rational Emotive Behaviour Therapy (Ellis) ABCDE model: A ctivating event → B elief (rational/irrational) → C onsequence → D ispute → E ffect (new). Core: three irrational demands ("I must do well; others must treat me well; the world must be fair"), aka "musturbation." NOT REBT: "cognitive triad," "automatic thoughts," "Socratic questioning" → Beck. Ellis is more directly confrontational ; Beck uses gentle guided discovery.

chunks.heading: Person-Centred Therapy (Rogers)
chunks.text: Person-Centred Therapy (Rogers) 3 core conditions (necessary & sufficient): Empathy · Unconditional Positive Regard (UPR) · Congruence (genuineness). Mnemonic: "EUC" / "the 3 C's if you count empathic-understanding, unconditional-regard, congruence." NOT Rogers: "interpretation," "transference" (Freud) · "empty chair" (Gestalt) · "directive advice" (Rogers is non-directive ). Driver = the client's actualising tendency.

chunks.heading: Motivational Interviewing (Miller & Rollnick)
chunks.text: Motivational Interviewing (Miller & Rollnick) Spirit — PACE: P artnership · A cceptance · C ompassion · E vocation. 4 processes: Engaging → Focusing → Evoking → Planning. Core skills — OARS: O pen questions · A ffirmations · R eflections · S ummaries. Change talk — DARN-CAT: Desire, Ability, Reason, Need → Commitment, Activation, Taking steps. NOT MI: "confrontation / arguing the client out of it" (the opposite of MI) · "OARS" is MI, not a family-therapy term. Used most for ambivalence in substance use.

chunks.heading: IPT — Interpersonal Therapy (Klerman & Weissman)
chunks.text: IPT — Interpersonal Therapy (Klerman & Weissman) 4 problem areas (pick one focus): Grief · Role disputes · Role transitions · Interpersonal deficits. Time-limited (12–16 sessions), originally for depression. NOT IPT: "transference" (it deliberately stays in the here-and-now of relationships, not the past) · "cognitive distortions" (Beck). If you see "role dispute / role transition" it's IPT.

chunks.heading: Group Therapy — Yalom's 11 therapeutic factors
chunks.text: Group Therapy — Yalom's 11 therapeutic factors The 11: Instillation of hope · Universality · Imparting information · Altruism · Corrective recapitulation of the primary family group · Development of socialising techniques · Imitative behaviour · Interpersonal learning (the engine) · Group cohesiveness (group analogue of the alliance) · Catharsis · Existential factors. NOT a Yalom factor: "transference interpretation," "free association," "the miracle question." Tag words: social microcosm + here-and-now + interpersonal learning → Yalom.

chunks.heading: Gestalt Therapy (Perls)
chunks.text: Gestalt Therapy (Perls) Components/techniques: empty chair · top-dog / underdog dialogue · here-and-now awareness · figure-ground · exaggeration · "I" statements · integration of polarities. NOT Gestalt: "free association / dream interpretation" (Freud) · "core conditions" (Rogers). Goal = integrate disowned parts into wholeness.

chunks.heading: Psychoanalysis / Psychodynamic (Freud)
chunks.text: Psychoanalysis / Psychodynamic (Freud) Components/techniques: free association (the fundamental rule) · interpretation of resistance and transference · dream analysis (manifest vs latent) · working through. NOT psychoanalysis: "behavioural experiment," "thought record" (CBT) · "miracle question" (SFBT). Working through = repeated re-encounter with a conflict until integrated, NOT a single interpretation or free association — classic NIMHANS trap.

chunks.heading: Reality / Choice Therapy (Glasser)
chunks.text: Reality / Choice Therapy (Glasser) WDEP framework: W ants · D oing · E valuation · P lanning. Present-focused, responsibility, "total behaviour." NOT Glasser: "WDEP" is uniquely his — don't confuse with MI's "PACE/OARS" or DBT's modules.

chunks.heading: Mindfulness-based programmes
chunks.text: Mindfulness-based programmes MBCT (Segal, Williams, Teasdale): 8-week group, MBSR + cognitive therapy. Indication = relapse prevention in recurrent depression (≥3 episodes). MBSR (Kabat-Zinn): 8-week group, body scan + sitting meditation + mindful movement. Stress, chronic pain. Trap: MBCT is for preventing relapse , not treating an acute episode. MBSR came first (1979); MBCT added the cognitive layer.

chunks.heading: EMDR (Shapiro)
chunks.text: EMDR (Shapiro) 8-phase protocol pairing brief recall of the traumatic memory with bilateral stimulation (eye movements). Indication = PTSD / trauma. NOT EMDR: "exposure + response prevention" (that's ERP for OCD). EMDR = trauma + bilateral stimulation + 8 phases.

chunks.heading: Family / Systemic therapies — match the tool
chunks.text: Family / Systemic therapies — match the tool School Signature components Structural (Minuchin) Family map · boundaries (clear / rigid-disengaged / diffuse-enmeshed) · joining · enactment · restructuring Strategic (Haley, Watzlawick) Directives · paradoxical intervention · ordeal therapy · "symptom serves a function" Bowenian Differentiation of self · triangles · genogram · emotional cutoff Satir / experiential Communication stances (placater, blamer, computer, distractor, leveller) · family sculpting Milan Circular questioning · hypothesising · neutrality · reflecting team Narrative (White, Epston) Externalising the problem · re-authoring · unique outcomes SFBT (de Shazer, Berg) Miracle question · scaling questions · exception-seeking

chunks.heading: Logotherapy (Frankl)
chunks.text: Logotherapy (Frankl) Techniques: paradoxical intention · dereflection. 3 sources of meaning: creative (work), experiential (love/beauty), attitudinal (stance toward unavoidable suffering). Note: "paradoxical intention" appears in BOTH Frankl (logotherapy) and strategic family therapy. Context decides.

chunks.heading: Master "match the component to the therapy" table
chunks.text: Master "match the component to the therapy" table Cover the right column, name the therapy from the cue. If you see this component / cue word… …the therapy is Mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation, interpersonal effectiveness DBT Hexaflex · cognitive defusion · self-as-context · values ACT Cognitive triad · automatic thoughts · Socratic questioning CBT (Beck) ABC model · irrational belief · dispute · musturbation REBT (Ellis) Empathy · unconditional positive regard · congruence Person-centred (Rogers) PACE · OARS · change talk · DARN-CAT Motivational Interviewing Grief · role dispute · role transition · interpersonal deficit IPT Universality · cohesiveness · interpersonal learning · catharsis Group therapy (Yalom) Empty chair · top-dog/underdog · figure-ground Gestalt (Perls) Free association · transference · working through · dream analysis Psychoanalysis (Freud) WDEP (wants, doing, evaluation, planning) Reality therapy (Glasser) 8-week group · relapse prevention in recurrent depression MBCT 8-phase protocol · bilateral eye movements · trauma EMDR (Shapiro) Miracle question · scaling · exceptions SFBT Externalising the problem · re-authoring Narrative therapy Differentiation of self · triangles · genogram Bowenian family Family map · enmeshment · joining · enactment Structural family (Minuchin) Reciprocal inhibition · fear hierarchy · relaxation pairing Systemati

chunks.heading: The 6 traps that catch everyone
chunks.text: The 6 traps that catch everyone Triad vs ABC. Cognitive triad = Beck. ABC = Ellis. Both are CBT-family, easy to swap. DBT modules vs ACT hexaflex. 4 modules (mindfulness/distress tolerance/emotion reg/interpersonal) = DBT. 6 hexaflex processes = ACT. Both use "mindfulness," so don't decide on that word alone. Working through. It is the repeated re-examination of a conflict until integrated, NOT free association and NOT one interpretation. Empty chair = Gestalt, not psychoanalysis. People assume "chair → couch → Freud." Wrong. ERP vs EMDR. ERP (exposure + response prevention) = OCD. EMDR (8 phases + eye movements) = trauma. Different conditions. Paradoxical intention shows up in BOTH Frankl and strategic family therapy. Read the stem for context.
